# Welcome: the map and the toolkit

This course teaches you to build GraphRAG yourself: turning documents into a knowledge graph, summarizing it, searching it and grounding an LLM's answers in it. This first chapter gives you the whole picture, the running example you will use in every chapter, and a working copy of the reference code on your machine.

## GraphRAG in one picture

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers a question by first retrieving relevant material from your own data and then asking a large language model (LLM) to answer from that material, with citations. Classic RAG retrieves text chunks whose embeddings are similar to the question. That works well for lookups (“Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?”) and poorly for questions whose evidence is scattered (“Why did Kestrel start Project Tern?”) or spread across the whole collection (“What are the main themes here?”).

GraphRAG is the family of methods that put a graph between the documents and the model. At indexing time, an LLM reads the documents and extracts entities (people, organizations, projects) and the relationships between them. Duplicate names are merged, the graph is partitioned into communities of closely connected entities, and each community gets a written summary. At query time, a retriever uses that structure: it starts from the entities a question names and follows edges, or it reads community summaries to answer questions about the whole corpus. The LLM then writes an answer from the retrieved entities, relationships, summaries and source text.

[Diagram]

The whole course in one figure. Parts 1 and 2 build the top row; Part 3 builds the retrieval box in many variations; Part 4 is about the context and answer boxes; Parts 5 and 6 are about making all of it measurable, affordable and current.

Applied to Kestrel Labs, the graph lets retrieval answer “Why did Kestrel start Project Tern?” by starting at Project Tern, stepping to Deepcast (whose sonar Tern replaces) and on to Marlow Dynamics (which acquired Deepcast), collecting the three facts that explain the decision. Plain vector search, as you will measure in Chapter 3, ranks the article about the acquisition 21st of 24 chunks for that question.

**GraphRAG is a family of methods

“GraphRAG” is also the name of Microsoft Research's paper and open-source project, which popularized the approach in 2024. This course uses the word for the whole family: Microsoft-style community summaries, LightRAG's keyword-level retrieval, HippoRAG's Personalized PageRank, path- and subgraph-based retrieval, Text2Cypher over existing knowledge graphs and agentic graph search. You will build a small version of each.

## A short history

You do not need the history to build anything, but it explains why the field looks the way it does and why so many methods have similar names.

When | Milestone | Why it matters here

2020 | Lewis et al. name retrieval-augmented generation: a dense retriever plus a generator. REALM and Dense Passage Retrieval appear the same year. | The retrieve-then-generate loop every chapter uses (Chapter 1).

2022–2023 | Chat models make RAG the default way to answer from private data: chunk, embed, vector search, prompt. Iterative methods such as IRCoT and ReAct interleave retrieval with reasoning. Think-on-Graph (2023) has an LLM explore a knowledge graph step by step. | The vector baseline (Chapter 2) and its multi-hop limits (Chapter 3).

Early 2024 | RAPTOR builds a tree of recursive summaries over chunks. G-Retriever retrieves subgraphs for graph question answering. Microsoft Research describes GraphRAG and publishes From Local to Global: LLM-extracted entity graphs, community reports and map-reduce global search. | Community detection and reports (Chapters 11, 12, 15), subgraph retrieval (19).

Mid–late 2024 | Microsoft open-sources GraphRAG. HippoRAG ranks passages with Personalized PageRank over an entity graph. LightRAG proposes dual-level keyword retrieval with incremental updates. The first GraphRAG surveys appear. Microsoft Research announces LazyGraphRAG to cut indexing cost. | PPR (17), LightRAG (16), cost (26).

2025 | A second survey organizes the field into knowledge organization, retrieval and integration. HippoRAG 2 and PathRAG refine graph retrieval. Graph-R1 trains agentic graph retrievers with reinforcement learning, and GraphSearch proposes an agentic deep-search workflow over graphs. Temporal graph memory for agents (Zep, Graphiti) goes into production use. | Paths and agents (18, 30), training with graphs (24), temporal graphs (27).

2026 | Microsoft GraphRAG is in maintenance mode while the ideas spread into many frameworks. Research focuses on cost (for example LiteRAG), bi-temporal graph engines on ordinary databases (post-graph-rag), and careful comparisons of when hybrid GraphRAG beats classic RAG on real domains. | Frameworks, production and the research map (28, 29, 33).

Two threads run through that history. One builds a better index (graphs, trees, communities) so that retrieval has more to work with. The other builds a better retriever (PageRank, paths, agents) that uses structure at query time. Most current systems combine both, plus plain vector and keyword search.

## The taxonomy this course follows

With dozens of GraphRAG papers a month, you need a map. This course uses the three-stage structure from the survey by Zhang et al., A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models, and the curated DEEP-PolyU/Awesome-GraphRAG list organized by it. Every method answers three questions: how is knowledge organized into a graph, how is it retrieved, and how is it integrated into the model's generation?

[Diagram]

The survey's three stages, with its main sub-areas, mapped to the parts of this course. Part 1 builds the foundations for all three; Parts 5 and 6 cover evaluation, operations and frontier topics that cut across them.

When you read a new paper, place it on this map first. LightRAG, for example, is mostly an organization choice (entities and relations with keyword descriptions) plus a similarity-based dual-level retriever. Think-on-Graph is an LLM-based, multi-round retriever over an existing knowledge graph. Chapter 33 returns to this map with the papers you have met along the way.

## How chapters are built

Every chapter follows the same structure, so you always know where to find what you need.

Element | What it is for | How to use it

Objectives and lede | What you will be able to do afterwards | Read first; check yourself against them at the end

Explanations | Motivation, intuition, mechanism, code and trade-offs, in that order | Read with the reference code open next to you

Interactive visualizations | Step through algorithms on the Kestrel graph: BFS, PageRank, Louvain, map-reduce | Press Next slowly and predict the next step before you see it

Diagrams | Static pictures of structures and data flow | Redraw the important ones from memory

Code | Real minigraphrag code, labeled with its file path | Run it, change it, break it

Exercises | Warm-up (by hand), core (coding and analysis), stretch (open-ended) | Attempt before opening the hint; every exercise has a full worked answer

Quiz | Five or more questions that check understanding, not recall | Wrong answers explain themselves; the score is only for you

Questions learners often ask | The follow-up questions that come up when people learn this | Skim; open what you were wondering about

Project | A small build with a checklist and a “done when” line | Do at least the projects on your learning path

Capstones | Four end-to-end builds (MiniGraphRAG, code graph, temporal memory, enterprise KG QA) | Milestones with starter code, checkpoints and reference solutions

## Meet Kestrel Labs

Every example, exercise and project in the course uses one fictional world, so you can watch the same graph grow from raw text to communities to answers. Because it is fictional, no language model knows anything about it: when a model answers a Kestrel question correctly, your retrieval did the work.

Kestrel Labs is an ocean-technology startup in the coastal city of Port Avalon, founded in 2021 by Dr. Mira Okafor (CEO, formerly a researcher at Tidewater Institute) and Jonas Vehl (CTO until March 2026, then Chief Scientist). It builds autonomous underwater drones. Its reef-monitoring program, Project Sentinel, runs with Tidewater Institute as research partner, and in August 2024 its drones detected a mass bleaching event at Halden Reef before divers saw it. Kestrel bought all its sonar from Deepcast until competitor Marlow Dynamics acquired Deepcast in April 2025 and ended outside supply. Kestrel responded with Project Tern, an in-house sonar module co-led by Vehl and Priya Nair, a former Marlow engineer who became CTO in March 2026. Brightwater Capital led Kestrel's Series A ($12M, 2022) and Series B ($40M, 2025); its partner Lena Park sits on Kestrel's board. The regional Ocean Health Act (2025) requires quarterly reef monitoring, which led the Port Avalon City Council to contract Kestrel in November 2025.

### The twelve documents

File | Kind | Date | Main facts

01_herald_kestrel_founding | Newspaper article | Oct 2021 | Founding by Okafor and Vehl; Okafor's Tidewater past

02_brightwater_series_a | Press release | Mar 2022 | $12M Series A; Lena Park joins the board

03_deepcast_supply_agreement | Trade press | Aug 2022 | Deepcast to supply sonar; single-supplier risk

04_twi_sentinel_launch | Institute blog | Feb 2023 | Project Sentinel launched; Ana Ruiz leads the science

05_kestrel_blog_priya_nair | Company blog | Sep 2023 | Priya Nair joins from Marlow Dynamics

06_twi_bleaching_research_note | Research note | Sep 2024 | Sentinel drones detect the 2024 bleaching

07_marlow_acquires_deepcast | Trade press | Apr 2025 | Marlow buys Deepcast; outside contracts end

08_kestrel_board_memo_supply | Confidential memo | May 2025 | Supply disruption; proposal to build in-house sonar

09_kestrel_eng_blog_project_tern | Engineering blog | Jun 2025 | Project Tern kicks off to replace Deepcast sonar

10_brightwater_series_b | Press release | Sep 2025 | $40M Series B; Ocean Health Act creates demand

11_city_council_minutes | Meeting minutes | Nov 2025 | Council contracts Kestrel for Act compliance

12_interview_leadership_change_2026 | Podcast transcript | Mar 2026 | Priya Nair becomes CTO; risks the company faces

The corpus is small (5,427 words) on purpose: you can read all of it in twenty minutes, check every answer by hand, and run the whole pipeline offline in well under a second. It is also written so that facts are spread realistically: the board memo never names Marlow Dynamics, the bleaching note never names Kestrel Labs, and names appear under aliases such as “TWI”, “Okafor” and “Tern”.

### The canonical questions

Seven questions recur throughout the course. data/questions.jsonl contains them and sixteen more, each with a reference answer and supporting documents.

- Multi-hop: (1) Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern? (2) Which investor's board member oversees the company whose drones detected the Halden Reef bleaching? (3) What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?

- Global: (4) What are the main themes in this corpus? (5) What risks does Kestrel Labs face?

- Temporal: (6) Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs? (7) Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?

Step through the graph below to see the path each question needs. This is the hand-drawn “ideal” graph from the running-example specification; the graph your code extracts will be close to it but not identical, and comparing the two is part of the fun.

## Set up the reference code

minigraphrag is a small, readable GraphRAG written for this course: chunking, extraction with gleaning, entity resolution, communities, community reports, eight retrieval methods, Text2Cypher, a bi-temporal graph and evaluation. Chapters show its real code. It depends only on networkx and numpy by default and runs fully offline.

### Install

You need Python 3.10 or newer. From the repository root:

```python  # terminal
cd code
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest -q
```

-e installs the package in editable mode, so changes you make to minigraphrag/ take effect without reinstalling; several exercises have you edit it. [dev] adds pytest. The test suite should pass in well under a second.

### Build an index offline

```python  # terminal
# mock LLM + hashing embedder: no network, no API key, about a second
python -m minigraphrag index --input data/corpus --output .index

# ask questions with different retrieval methods
python -m minigraphrag query --method basic  "Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?"
python -m minigraphrag query --method local  "Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?"
python -m minigraphrag query --method global "What are the main themes in this corpus?"
python -m minigraphrag query --method hybrid --show-context "Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?"
```

Indexing prints one line per stage. On the Kestrel corpus with the defaults you should see:

```python  # output
chunked 12 documents into 24 text units
extracted 194 entity mentions, 154 relationship mentions
graph: 17 entities, 54 relationships
4 communities, 4 reports
saved index to .index
```

[Interactive figure: What python -m minigraphrag index just did (flow)]

The index folder contains plain artifacts you can open in an editor: text_units.json, entities.json, relationships.json, graph.graphml (opens in Gephi or yEd), communities.json, community_reports.json, claims.json, the *_embeddings.npz/.json pairs and config.json.

**The mock is a teaching device

MockLLM recognizes each course prompt by a marker phrase and answers with deterministic heuristics: a small gazetteer of Kestrel names for extraction, co-occurrence for relationships, and extractive answers that return context sentences with [Data: ...] citations. It shows you what each retriever put into the context, reproducibly and for free. To judge how well a method actually answers, switch to a real LLM.

### Switch to a real LLM

The --llm flag picks a provider; environment variables configure it.

--llm | Install | Environment variables | Default model

mock | nothing | none | none

openai | pip install -e ".[openai]" | OPENAI_API_KEY; optional OPENAI_MODEL, OPENAI_BASE_URL | gpt-4o-mini

anthropic | pip install -e ".[anthropic]" | ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; optional ANTHROPIC_MODEL | claude-sonnet-5

ollama | pip install -e ".[openai]" (Ollama speaks the OpenAI API) | optional OLLAMA_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:11434/v1), OLLAMA_MODEL | llama3.1

```python  # terminal
pip install -e ".[anthropic]"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
python -m minigraphrag index --llm anthropic --cache-dir .cache/llm --output .index-claude
python -m minigraphrag query --llm anthropic --index .index-claude --method local "Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?"
```

--cache-dir wraps the LLM in CachedLLM, a disk cache keyed by a hash of the model, system prompt, prompt and JSON flag, so rerunning indexing after a code change does not pay for identical calls again. vLLM, LM Studio and other OpenAI-compatible servers work through OPENAI_BASE_URL. For neural embeddings, pass --embedder openai or --embedder st:all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (after installing the st extra); the embedder name is saved in config.json and reused at query time.

### The same thing from Python

Most exercises use the Python API directly:

```python  # examples/ch00_first_index.py
from minigraphrag import HashingEmbedder, IndexConfig, build_index, load_index
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.search.basic import basic_search
from minigraphrag.search.local import local_search

llm = get_llm("mock")                        # "openai", "anthropic" or "ollama", configured by env vars
build_index("data/corpus", ".index", llm, HashingEmbedder(), IndexConfig(max_gleanings=1), log=print)

index = load_index(".index")
print(index.graph.number_of_nodes(), "entities,", index.graph.number_of_edges(), "relationships")

for search in (basic_search, local_search):
    result = search(index, "Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?", llm)
    print(result.method, result.llm_calls, result.sources)
    print(result.answer[:300], "\n")
```

Every search method returns a SearchResult with the answer, the method name, the context_text the model saw, structured context_data, the sources (document ids that reached the context) and the number of llm_calls. Comparing sources across methods is the quickest way to see what a retriever found.

## Suggested learning paths

The course map on the home page shows chapter prerequisites. Three paths through it:

Path | For | Chapters | Rough time

Full path | Engineers new to RAG or graphs who want to understand everything from first principles | All chapters in order, every core exercise, all projects, then Capstone 1 and one more capstone | Around 30 hours of reading plus projects and capstones

“I already know RAG” | You have built vector RAG and want the graph part fast | 3 (skim), 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 21, 22, 25, then Capstone 1 | About half of the full path

“I need production” | You will ship or run a GraphRAG system and need to decide what to build | 3, 6, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21, 25–29, then Capstone 4 | Similar to the fast path, weighted toward Part 5

Whatever path you choose, do not skip Chapter 3. Once you know which failures your questions hit, you can choose techniques instead of collecting them.

#### Exercise 0.2 Warm-up

Without looking at the visualization, read documents 02, 04 and 06 and sketch by hand the smallest graph that answers canonical question 2: “Which investor's board member oversees the company whose drones detected the Halden Reef bleaching?” List nodes with types, edges with labels and the document each edge comes from, then write the path.

▸ Show answer

Edge | Source document | Supporting text

Project Sentinel (PROJECT) —detected→ 2024 Halden Reef bleaching event (EVENT) | 06 research note | “autonomous drones operating under the Sentinel program recorded the onset of a mass coral bleaching event at Halden Reef”

2024 Halden Reef bleaching event —occurred at→ Halden Reef (LOCATION) | 06 | same sentence

Kestrel Labs (ORGANIZATION) —runs→ Project Sentinel | 04 Sentinel launch | “Kestrel Labs runs Project Sentinel”

Lena Park (PERSON) —board member of→ Kestrel Labs | 02 Series A | “Lena Park, a partner at Brightwater Capital, will join the Kestrel Labs board of directors”

Lena Park —partner at→ Brightwater Capital (ORGANIZATION) | 02 | same sentence

Path: 2024 bleaching event ← detected ← Project Sentinel ← runs ← Kestrel Labs ← board member of ← Lena Park → partner at → Brightwater Capital. Answer: Brightwater Capital, through Lena Park.

Two things to notice. First, you had to decide that “the Sentinel program” in document 06 is the same entity as “Project Sentinel” in document 04; that is entity resolution, Chapter 9. Second, Halden Reef is not needed for the answer but is a natural node to extract; real graphs always contain more than any one question needs.

#### Exercise 0.3 Core

Classify each question as local (answerable from a few connected facts), global (needs a summary across much of the corpus) or temporal (the answer depends on time), and say whether it is also multi-hop. Then check your labels against the type field in data/questions.jsonl and explain any disagreement.

- How much did Kestrel Labs raise in its Series A and who led it?

- Who was the CTO of Kestrel Labs when the Halden Reef bleaching event was detected?

- How has Kestrel Labs' leadership evolved since its founding?

- Where did the CEO of Kestrel Labs work before founding the company, and how is that organization involved with Project Sentinel?

- What role does regulation play in Kestrel Labs' business?

- When did Marlow Dynamics acquire Deepcast?

▸ Show answer

```python
import json
for q in map(json.loads, open("data/questions.jsonl")):
    print(q["id"], q["type"], q["question"])
```

# | Your label | Multi-hop? | Dataset type (id) | Comment

1 | Local | No | single-hop (q09) | One press release states both facts.

2 | Temporal | Yes | temporal (q15) | Find the detection date (Aug 2024), then the CTO valid at that date (Jonas Vehl). Both labels are defensible; the dataset files it under its harder aspect.

3 | Global (and temporal) | Yes | global (q21) | A narrative across four documents and five years. “Evolved” signals change over time, but the task is summarization.

4 | Local | Yes, two hops | multi-hop (q16) | Okafor → formerly at → Tidewater Institute → partners on → Project Sentinel.

5 | Global | Partly | global (q22) | Evidence spans the Series B release, council minutes and interview. Could be answered locally from the Ocean Health Act's neighborhood, which is why local search does reasonably on some “global” questions.

6 | Local | No | temporal (q13) | The dataset calls it temporal because the answer is a date. Retrieval-wise it is a simple lookup. Question type labels describe the answer, not necessarily the retrieval difficulty.

The disagreements are the lesson: real questions mix types, and a system that routes each question to exactly one retrieval method will sometimes route wrongly. Chapter 21 discusses routers and hybrids for this reason.

#### Exercise 0.4 Core

Open the index you built. Using load_index, print each community's members, find the relationship between MARLOW DYNAMICS and DEEPCAST with its description and weight, and list the neighbors of PROJECT TERN. Compare the communities with the “expected communities” in the running example. Where do they differ, and why might a mock extractor produce that?

▸ Show answer

```python
from minigraphrag import load_index

index = load_index(".index")
G = index.graph
for c in index.communities:
    print(c.id, c.level, sorted(c.nodes))

edge = G.edges["MARLOW DYNAMICS", "DEEPCAST"]
print(edge.get("weight"), edge.get("description", "")[:200])
print(sorted(G.neighbors("PROJECT TERN")))
```

With the mock and default settings, the four level-0 communities are:

- 2024 bleaching event, Ana Ruiz, Halden Reef, Port Avalon, Project Sentinel, Project Tern, Tidewater Institute

- Mira Okafor, Jonas Vehl, Kestrel Labs, Port Avalon City Council, Priya Nair

- Brightwater Capital, Lena Park, Ocean Health Act

- Deepcast, Marlow Dynamics

The running example expects five: a Kestrel core that includes Project Tern; reef science around Sentinel; Marlow and Deepcast; Brightwater and Lena Park; and regulation (Ocean Health Act, City Council, Port Avalon). Differences: Project Tern lands with the reef-science group, because the mock links entities that co-occur in a sentence and Tern is mentioned alongside Sentinel and Halden Reef in the engineering blog; the regulation community dissolves, with the Ocean Health Act joining Brightwater (the Series B release discusses both) and the City Council joining the Kestrel core. Marlow–Deepcast comes out as expected because those two co-occur heavily in one article.

Community detection reflects the graph it is given, and a co-occurrence extractor produces co-occurrence graphs. A real LLM extractor writes more specific relationships and usually gets closer to the expected grouping. You will measure that difference yourself in Chapters 8 and 11. Exact community membership can also change if the reference code's extraction or clustering is updated, so rely on your own output.

#### Exercise 0.5 Stretch

Build a second index with a real LLM (OpenAI, Anthropic or a local Ollama model) using a cache directory. Compare the two indexes: number of entities and relationships, the entity names that appear in only one of them, and the local answer to “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?”. Estimate how many LLM calls indexing made.

▸ Show answer

```python
pip install -e ".[openai]"          # or [anthropic]; Ollama also uses the openai extra
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...
python -m minigraphrag index --llm openai --cache-dir .cache/llm --output .index-real
python -m minigraphrag query --llm openai --index .index-real --method local "Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?"
```

```python
from minigraphrag import load_index

mock, real = load_index(".index"), load_index(".index-real")
for name, idx in (("mock", mock), ("real", real)):
    print(name, idx.graph.number_of_nodes(), idx.graph.number_of_edges(), len(idx.communities))
only_mock = set(mock.graph) - set(real.graph)
only_real = set(real.graph) - set(mock.graph)
print("only in mock:", sorted(only_mock))
print("only in real:", sorted(only_real))
```

Counting calls: the pipeline calls the LLM once per text unit for extraction, plus one “continue extracting” call per unit and gleaning round (with max_gleanings=1 there is no follow-up “anything left?” check, since nothing would be done with the answer), once per unit for claims, once per merged description that needs summarizing, and once per community report. With 24 units that is at least 24 × 3 = 72 calls before summaries and reports. The offline mock run made 122 calls in total. The files in .cache/llm give you the exact number of distinct calls for the real run: one file per call.

What to expect: a real model typically extracts more entities than the mock's gazetteer allows, including things such as the Series A and Series B rounds, the Sentinel sonar array, or the harbour survey firms quoted in articles, and it writes relationship descriptions in its own words rather than copying sentences. Some names will differ in form (“MIRA OKAFOR” vs. “DR. MIRA OKAFOR”), which is why resolution matters. The local answer from a real model should mention the Marlow acquisition if local search pulled in Deepcast's relationships. Rerunning the same command is nearly free thanks to the cache, which is worth verifying: the second run should be fast and make no API calls.

## Check your understanding

What distinguishes GraphRAG from classic vector RAG?

- GraphRAG does not use an LLM at query time

- ✓ (correct) GraphRAG builds an index of entities, relationships and often community summaries, and retrieval uses that structure

- GraphRAG only works with graph databases such as Neo4j

- GraphRAG replaces embeddings entirely
Answer: The loop is still retrieve-then-generate. What changes is what is indexed and how retrieval navigates it. Most GraphRAG systems still use embeddings, for example to find seed entities.

In the survey taxonomy, where does Personalized PageRank retrieval over an entity graph (HippoRAG) belong?

- Knowledge organization

- Knowledge integration

- ✓ (correct) Knowledge retrieval

- Evaluation
Answer: PPR is a way of finding evidence in a graph that already exists. How the graph was built is organization; how the evidence reaches the model's answer is integration.

Why is the Kestrel Labs corpus fictional?

- Real documents would be too long to index

- Licensing prevents using real news articles

- Graph algorithms only work on synthetic data

- ✓ (correct) No model has parametric knowledge of it, so correct answers must come from retrieval
Answer: With a real company, a model might answer from memory and hide retrieval failures. The fictional world makes every success and failure attributable.

Canonical question 6, “Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?”, is filed as temporal. What makes it hard even with a perfect graph?

- The CTO is never named in the corpus

- ✓ (correct) Two people held the role at different times, so the graph needs validity periods to return the current one

- CTO is an alias that cannot be resolved

- It requires a global summary of the corpus
Answer: Jonas Vehl was CTO until March 2026 and Priya Nair since then. Without time on edges, both are “the CTO”.

You run python -m minigraphrag index with no --llm flag and no API keys. What happens?

- It fails asking for OPENAI_API_KEY

- It downloads a small local model

- ✓ (correct) It runs offline with MockLLM and HashingEmbedder, producing a deterministic index in about a second

- It skips extraction and builds only a vector index
Answer: The mock is the default so the whole course runs offline and in CI. Use --llm openai|anthropic|ollama for real answers.

What does --cache-dir .cache/llm do?

- Stores the index artifacts

- Caches embeddings for faster search

- Saves query answers for the evaluation harness

- ✓ (correct) Wraps the LLM in CachedLLM, so identical calls (same model, system, prompt, JSON flag) are read from disk instead of paid for again
Answer: Indexing makes many calls. Deterministic prompts plus a hash-keyed cache make reruns after code changes cheap.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Do I need to know graph theory or machine learning before starting?

No. You need to be comfortable with Python and with reading short formulas. Chapter 4 teaches the graph ideas you need (adjacency, traversal, shortest paths, PageRank, modularity) from scratch, and Chapter 2 covers embeddings. Chapter 24, on training models with graphs, is the only one that assumes some familiarity with model training, and it is optional on every path except the full one.

▸ Why build from scratch instead of using Microsoft GraphRAG, LightRAG or LlamaIndex?

Because configuration without understanding fails in production: you cannot tune extraction prompts, pick a community level, or explain a bad answer if the pipeline is a black box. The frameworks are good, and Chapter 28 teaches them. After building minigraphrag, you will read their configuration files and source code as variations on things you have already written.

▸ How much will a real LLM cost for the exercises?

For the Kestrel corpus, very little: indexing makes about 120 LLM calls over roughly 5,400 words of source text (122 with the mock and default settings), and a query makes between one and a few dozen calls depending on the method. With a small hosted model this is typically cents to low dollars across the whole course, and --cache-dir means you pay for each distinct call once. A local model through Ollama costs nothing but time. Chapter 26 does the cost math for large corpora, where it matters.

▸ The mock's answers look like copied sentences. Is something broken?

No. The mock answers extractively on purpose: it returns the context sentences that best match the question, each with a [Data: ...] citation. That makes it a window into what the retriever found. If the right sentences appear, retrieval worked; turning them into a well-written answer is the real model's job.

▸ Can I use my own documents instead of Kestrel?

Yes: --input takes any folder of .md files. Do the chapters on Kestrel first, because the exercises and answers refer to it, then rerun your favorite exercises on your own data. You will need a real LLM for that, since the mock's gazetteer only knows Kestrel names.

### Project: your workbench and learning journal

Set up the environment you will use for the rest of the course and start a record of the questions you want it to answer.

- A working code/.venv with pytest -q passing and a mock index in .index/

- A real-LLM configuration that works (hosted or Ollama), tested with one query --llm ... command and a cache directory

- A journal.md with the seven canonical questions and at least five questions of your own about Kestrel, each labeled local, global or temporal and multi-hop or not

- For each journal question, your prediction of whether plain vector RAG will answer it, to check after Chapter 3

- If you have a real use case, five questions from it with the same labels, and one sentence on why the answers matter

Done when you can build and query an index with both the mock and a real LLM, and your journal has at least twelve labeled questions with predictions.

## Key takeaways

- GraphRAG keeps retrieve-then-generate and adds a graph of entities, relationships and community summaries between documents and the model.

- The field grew from RAG (2020) through Microsoft's GraphRAG, HippoRAG and LightRAG (2024) to agentic and temporal graph retrieval (2025–2026).

- Place every method on the map: knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, knowledge integration.

- Kestrel Labs is fictional so that every correct answer is earned by retrieval; its seven canonical questions cover multi-hop, global and temporal needs.

- minigraphrag runs offline with a mock LLM and switches to OpenAI, Anthropic or Ollama with one flag.

- Choose a learning path, but do not skip Chapter 3.

# Part: Foundations

## Why LLMs need retrieval

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/01-llms-and-context.html
Summary: Parametric vs. non-parametric knowledge, context windows, hallucination and grounding.

# Why LLMs need retrieval

A language model answers from what it absorbed during training, and it will answer confidently even when that is not enough. This chapter explains what a model can and cannot know, what it costs to paste your documents into its context, and why “retrieve, then generate” became the default way to ground answers in your own data.

## You will be able to

- Explain next-token prediction and why it produces fluent answers whether or not the model knows the facts

- Distinguish parametric knowledge (in the weights) from non-parametric knowledge (in documents you supply)

- Estimate the token count, cost and fit of a prompt, and decide when “stuff the whole corpus” stops working

- Describe the lost-in-the-middle effect and what it implies for how you order context

- Call an LLM through the minigraphrag interface and build a stuffed-context baseline with citations

- Argue the trade-off between long-context prompting and retrieval-augmented generation for a given workload

## What a language model does

Every chat model you will use in this course is, at its core, a function that takes a sequence of tokens and returns a probability distribution over the next token. A token is a chunk of text from a fixed vocabulary: often a whole common word, sometimes a word piece, a space plus a word, or punctuation. Generation is a loop: pick a token from the distribution, append it, run the function again.

Formally, a model with parameters θ defines

P(xt | x1, …, xt−1; θ)

and the probability of a whole answer is the product of those per-step probabilities. Training adjusts θ so that real text from the training corpus gets high probability. Nothing in that objective says “only emit true statements”. It says “emit what text like this usually continues with”. Instruction tuning and preference training make the model more helpful and more willing to say “I don't know”, but they sit on top of the same next-token machinery.

[Interactive figure: Next-token prediction, one step at a time — Illustrative probabilities, not measured from a real model (ch01-next-token)]

The walk-through above is illustrative, but the shape is real: the tokens that carry facts are often the ones with the flattest distributions, and the output text does not show you that. The correct answer, from the corpus, is Priya Nair (since March 2026), with Jonas Vehl before her. No amount of sampling tricks can recover a fact the model never saw.

### Parametric and non-parametric knowledge

Researchers call what a model absorbed during training its parametric knowledge: facts stored implicitly in the weights. Petroni et al. showed in 2019 that pretrained language models can answer many fill-in-the-blank factual queries without any retrieval, which is why chat models seem to “know” things. The same line of work also showed the limits: recall is uneven, rare facts are unreliable, and you cannot tell which facts the model has from the outside.

Non-parametric knowledge is knowledge you supply at inference time: documents, database rows, graph facts, pasted into the prompt. It can be updated by editing a file, it can be private, and it can be cited.

[Diagram]

Two sources of knowledge meet in the prompt. Retrieval-augmented generation deliberately leans on the lower path for facts, and uses the upper path for language, reasoning and general background.

### Three things the weights cannot give you

- Anything after the knowledge cutoff. Training data stops at some date. The Kestrel leadership change happened in March 2026; a model trained before that would, at best, name Jonas Vehl.

- Private data. Kestrel's confidential board memo about the sonar supply disruption was never on the public web. No model has it in its weights, however large.

- Provenance. Even when the weights hold a fact, the model cannot point to the document it came from. In most business settings an answer without a source is not usable.
**The Kestrel test

The running example is fictional so that parametric knowledge cannot help. When a model answers a Kestrel question correctly in this course, it is because your retrieval put the evidence in front of it. When it answers incorrectly, you can trace the failure to what was or was not retrieved.

## Hallucination and grounding

A hallucination is generated content that is fluent but not supported by the source or by reality. The survey by Ji et al. distinguishes intrinsic hallucinations, which contradict the provided source, from extrinsic ones, which add claims the source cannot verify. Both matter for RAG:

- Extrinsic: the context mentions that Kestrel lost its sonar supplier, and the model adds “because Deepcast went bankrupt”. Nothing in the context says that. The real reason, Marlow Dynamics' acquisition of Deepcast, is in a different document.

- Intrinsic: the context says Brightwater Capital led a $12 million Series A, and the answer says $40 million, mixing it up with the Series B figure from another sentence.

Grounding means constraining the answer to evidence that is present in the prompt and making that link checkable. In practice it has three parts, and you will build all three:

- Put the relevant evidence in the context (retrieval; most of this course).

- Instruct the model to answer only from that evidence and to say when it does not know.

- Require citations to evidence ids, so a person or a program can check each claim.

Grounding reduces hallucination; it does not eliminate it. Models still misread context, merge two facts into one, or cite the wrong id. That is why evaluation (Chapter 25) checks faithfulness as well as correctness.

**Missing evidence is the most common cause

When a RAG answer is wrong, the first question to ask is “was the evidence in the context?” If it was not, no prompt wording will fix it. Most of the failures in Chapter 3 are of this kind, and they are what graph-based retrieval is designed to address.

## Context windows, tokens and cost

If the model needs evidence in its prompt, the obvious move is to paste in everything. Whether that works depends on three budgets: the context window (the maximum number of tokens a model can take as input plus output), money (providers bill per input and output token), and latency (the model must process every input token before producing the first output token).

### Token math you can do in your head

For English prose with common tokenizers, a useful rule of thumb is that one token is about four characters, or about three quarters of a word. minigraphrag uses the same idea when tiktoken is not installed: it estimates 4 tokens for every 3 words.

Item | Words | Approximate tokens

A canonical question (“Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?”) | 6 | 8

One Kestrel document (the Series B press release) | 453 | ≈ 600

The whole Kestrel corpus (12 documents) | 5,427 | ≈ 7,200

A 50,000-document company wiki at 600 tokens per page | ≈ 22.5 million | ≈ 30 million

The Kestrel corpus fits comfortably in any modern context window. A company wiki does not fit in any of them: current long-context models accept inputs on the order of hundreds of thousands to about a million tokens, which is still 30 times too small for 30 million tokens.

### What a prompt costs

Cost per question is roughly

cost = Tin × pin + Tout × pout

where T are token counts and p are per-token prices. Output tokens are usually priced several times higher than input tokens, but in RAG the input dominates because the context is long and the answer is short. Prices change constantly, so this course uses an illustrative input price of $3 per million tokens. Plug in your provider's current numbers.

Stuffing the Kestrel corpus: 7,236 corpus tokens plus about 150 tokens of instructions and question gives about 7,390 input tokens per question. At 1,000 questions a day that is 7.39 million input tokens, about $22 a day. Retrieving five chunks of about 400 tokens each instead gives about 2,150 input tokens per question and about $6.45 a day. For a 12-document corpus both numbers are small. The gap is what grows: the stuffed prompt scales with the corpus, the retrieved prompt scales with k.

[Interactive figure: Stuff everything or retrieve? — Drag the sliders; prices are illustrative (ch01-cost)]

Two more costs do not show up on the invoice. Latency: the model processes the whole prompt before the first answer token, so time-to-first-token grows with prompt length. In a standard transformer, self-attention compares every token with every other token, so that prefill compute grows faster than linearly with length. Prompt caching, which most providers now offer, cuts the price and latency of a repeated prompt prefix. It helps when the same long corpus prefix is reused across many questions, and it does nothing when every question needs different documents.

### Budgeting the window

Even when you retrieve, the context window is a shared budget. Instructions, conversation history, retrieved evidence, the question and room for the answer all compete for it. Every GraphRAG method in this course ends with a budgeting step that decides how many tokens each kind of evidence gets. Local search, for example, splits its budget between text chunks, community reports and entity and relationship tables.

[Interactive figure: An 8,000-token RAG prompt (token-budget)]

## More context is not always better: lost in the middle

Suppose money were no object and your corpus fit in the window. Pasting everything in would still not reliably give the best answers. Liu et al. (“Lost in the Middle”, 2023) placed the one document that contained the answer at different positions among many distractor documents. Models did best when the relevant document was at the beginning or the end of the context, and noticeably worse when it sat in the middle, producing a U-shaped curve. Adding more distractor documents also tended to hurt.

[Diagram]

The shape reported by Liu et al.: evidence at the edges of a long context is used more reliably than evidence in the middle. How deep the dip is varies by model and has not been measured for every model you might use, so treat it as a risk to test for: fewer, better-ordered documents are the safer default.

Three practical consequences follow, and they recur throughout the course:

- Rank, then order. Put the strongest evidence first (or first and last), not in retrieval-index order.

- Precision matters. A retriever that returns the answer plus forty distractors can do worse than one that returns the answer plus four.

- Structure helps. Tables with ids, short summaries and explicit relationships, which GraphRAG produces, are easier for a model to use than a wall of raw chunks.
**Liu et al., Lost in the Middle (2023)

Using multi-document question answering and a synthetic key-value retrieval task, the authors found that performance was highest when relevant information appeared at the start or end of the input and degraded when it appeared in the middle, including for models built for long contexts. The effect motivates careful ordering and aggressive filtering of retrieved context.

## Retrieve, then generate

The pattern that fixes the knowledge problem without paying for the whole corpus on every question is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Lewis et al. introduced the name in 2020: a neural retriever (Dense Passage Retrieval over Wikipedia) selects passages for a question, and a sequence-to-sequence generator (BART) conditions on them to write the answer. They trained the retriever's query encoder and the generator together, and showed strong results on open-domain question answering and more specific, more factual generations than a comparable model without retrieval. The same year, REALM (Guu et al.) built retrieval into language model pre-training.

Modern RAG systems rarely train anything end to end. They keep the idea and swap the parts: an off-the-shelf embedding model, a vector index, and a general-purpose LLM steered by a prompt. The loop is retrieve, augment, generate, with an optional check at the end.

[Interactive figure: Retrieve, augment, generate (flow)]

What goes in the “Retrieve” box is the subject of the rest of this course. Chapter 2 builds the classic version: chunks, embeddings, nearest-neighbor search. Chapter 3 shows the questions it cannot answer. Parts 2 and 3 replace the box with a knowledge graph, community summaries and graph traversal.

### Calling an LLM through minigraphrag

Everything in minigraphrag talks to language models through one method. That is the whole interface:

```python  # minigraphrag/llm.py
from typing import Protocol

class LLM(Protocol):
    def complete(self, prompt: str, system: str | None = None, json: bool = False) -> str: ...
```

Any object with that method works: OpenAICompatibleLLM (OpenAI, Ollama, vLLM and other OpenAI-compatible servers), AnthropicLLM, MockLLM for offline runs, and CachedLLM, which wraps any of them with a disk cache. get_llm builds one from a short name and environment variables.

```python  # examples/ch01_call_llm.py
import os
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm

# "mock" runs offline. Set OPENAI_API_KEY and use "openai", ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and
# "anthropic", or run Ollama locally and use "ollama" (OLLAMA_MODEL picks the model).
llm = get_llm(os.getenv("LLM", "mock"), cache_dir=".cache/llm")

closed_book = llm.complete(
    "Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?",
    system="Answer in one sentence. If you do not know, say so.",
)
print(closed_book)
```

With a real model, the closed-book answer should be some form of “I don't know”, or a made-up name. With MockLLM you will see OK: the mock recognizes each of the course's prompt templates by a marker sentence and returns a deterministic answer for it, and a free-form prompt matches none of them. That is intentional. The mock has no world knowledge to fall back on, so everything it says in later chapters comes from context you retrieved.

### Counting tokens

```python  # examples/ch01_tokens.py
from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

docs = load_documents("data/corpus")                 # {doc_id: text}, 12 documents
per_doc = {doc_id: count_tokens(text) for doc_id, text in docs.items()}
total = sum(per_doc.values())

for doc_id, n in sorted(per_doc.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:3]:
    print(f"{doc_id:40s} {n:5d}")
print("corpus total:", total)                         # about 7,200 with the 4/3 estimate
```

count_tokens uses tiktoken's cl100k_base encoding when it is installed (pip install -e ".[tokens]") and falls back to the 4-tokens-per-3-words estimate otherwise. Expect the two to differ by a few percent; the estimate exists for budgeting, and no budget in this course is tight enough for that to matter. Different providers use different tokenizers, so treat any count as an estimate and leave headroom.

### A “stuff the whole corpus” baseline

Before building retrieval, build the thing retrieval must beat. The baseline below puts every document into the same grounded prompt that later search methods use, as a table of sources with ids, and refuses to run when the prompt would not fit.

```python  # examples/ch01_stuffed_baseline.py
from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents
from minigraphrag.context import format_table
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.search.common import generate_answer
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

class ContextTooLarge(Exception):
    pass

def stuffed_answer(llm, docs: dict[str, str], question: str,
                   max_context_tokens: int = 100_000, price_per_million: float = 3.0):
    rows = [[doc_id, text] for doc_id, text in docs.items()]
    context = format_table("Sources", ["id", "text"], rows)   # -----Sources----- / id|text / ...
    n = count_tokens(context)
    if n > max_context_tokens:
        raise ContextTooLarge(f"{n} tokens > budget {max_context_tokens}; you need retrieval")
    answer = generate_answer(llm, question, context)          # context goes in the system prompt
    cost = n / 1_000_000 * price_per_million                  # input side only, illustrative price
    return answer, n, cost

docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
llm = get_llm("mock")
answer, n, cost = stuffed_answer(llm, docs, "Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?")
print(f"{n} context tokens, about ${cost:.4f} per question")
print(answer)
```

generate_answer formats LOCAL_SEARCH_SYSTEM_PROMPT from minigraphrag/prompts.py. It tells the model to answer from the data tables, say when it does not know, and cite records as [Data: Sources (id)]. The mock answers by picking sentences that overlap the question and citing their rows, so the output is extractive but has the same citation format a real model will use.

**Keep the baseline around

For a corpus this small, a strong model with the whole corpus in context is a hard baseline to beat on many questions. That is useful information, not an embarrassment. Every later chapter compares against it, and Capstone 1 asks you to show where GraphRAG wins and at what cost.

## Long context or retrieval?

Context windows grew dramatically between 2023 and 2026, and every increase prompted the question “is RAG dead?” The answer so far has been that the two are complementary. Xu et al. (2023) compared the approaches directly and found that a model with a 4K window plus simple retrieval could perform comparably to a version fine-tuned for a 16K window, and that retrieval also improved the long-context model. The trade-offs are practical:

Concern | Stuff everything into a long context | Retrieve, then generate

Corpus size | Must fit in the window; hard ceiling | Unbounded; the index grows, the prompt does not

Cost per question | Grows with the corpus (prompt caching helps for a fixed corpus) | Grows with k and chunk size

Latency | Long prefill on every uncached call | Retrieval step plus a short prompt

Recall | Everything is present, though the model may not use it (lost in the middle) | Only what the retriever finds; misses are silent

Cross-document reasoning | Possible in principle, since all documents are visible | Only across what was retrieved together

Freshness and access control | Rebuild the prompt; hard to filter per user | Update the index; filter results per user

Citations | Possible, with ids on every document | Natural: every retrieved piece has an id

Engineering effort | Minimal | Chunking, embeddings, index, tuning, evaluation

A reasonable rule in 2026: if your corpus fits well within the window, changes rarely, serves few questions and does not need per-user filtering, try long context first and measure. Otherwise retrieve. Most real systems do both: retrieve to narrow down, then use a generous context for the survivors.

**Where graphs come in

Retrieval's weakness sits in the row labeled “cross-document reasoning”. A retriever that scores chunks one at a time cannot see that the chunk about Deepcast's acquisition explains the chunk about Project Tern. GraphRAG keeps the retrieve-then-generate loop and changes what is indexed and retrieved: entities, relationships, paths and community summaries instead of isolated chunks.

## Exercises

#### Exercise 1.1 Warm-up

By hand, using 4 tokens per 3 words and an input price of $3 per million tokens: (a) estimate the input tokens and daily input cost of answering 1,000 questions a day by stuffing the 5,427-word Kestrel corpus plus 150 tokens of instructions and question; (b) do the same for retrieving five chunks of 300 words each plus the same 150 tokens; (c) repeat (a) for a 50,000-document wiki with 600 tokens per document, and say whether it fits in a 1,000,000-token window.

▸ Show answer

(a) 5,427 × 4/3 = 7,236 tokens. Plus 150 gives 7,386 tokens per question. Per day: 7,386 × 1,000 = 7.386 million tokens, times $3 = $22.16 a day.

(b) Five chunks of 300 words = 1,500 words = 2,000 tokens. Plus 150 gives 2,150 tokens per question, 2.15 million a day, $6.45 a day. That is about 3.4 times cheaper.

(c) 50,000 × 600 = 30,000,000 tokens per question. It does not fit in a 1,000,000-token window: it is 30 times too large. Even if it did, one question would cost 30 × $3 = $90 in input alone, and 1,000 a day would cost $90,000. Retrieval (b) stays at $6.45 a day regardless of corpus size, as long as k and chunk size stay fixed.

#### Exercise 1.2 Core

Answers that cite sources are only checkable if the citations are real. Write check_citations(answer: str, context: str) -> dict that extracts every id cited as [Data: Sources (a, b)] in the answer, compares them to the ids present in the Sources table of the context, and returns the cited ids, the ids that do not exist in the context, and whether the answer cites anything at all. Test it on the output of the stuffed baseline.

▸ Hint

minigraphrag.context.parse_tables turns the context back into {"Sources": [{"id": ..., "text": ...}]}. A single [Data: ...] block can cite several datasets separated by semicolons.

▸ Show answer

```python
import re
from minigraphrag.context import parse_tables

CITE = re.compile(r"\[Data:([^\]]*)\]")
DATASET = re.compile(r"(\w+)\s*\(([^)]*)\)")

def check_citations(answer: str, context: str) -> dict:
    known = {row["id"] for row in parse_tables(context).get("Sources", [])}
    cited = []
    for block in CITE.findall(answer):
        for dataset, ids in DATASET.findall(block):
            if dataset != "Sources":
                continue
            cited += [i.strip() for i in ids.split(",") if i.strip() and i.strip() != "+more"]
    return {
        "cited": sorted(set(cited)),
        "unknown": sorted(set(cited) - known),
        "has_citations": bool(cited),
    }

# Tests
ctx = "-----Sources-----\nid|text\n03_deepcast_supply_agreement|Deepcast signs...\n08_kestrel_board_memo_supply|Memo..."
ok = "Deepcast supplied Kestrel. [Data: Sources (03_deepcast_supply_agreement, 08_kestrel_board_memo_supply)]"
bad = "Deepcast supplied Kestrel. [Data: Sources (99_made_up)]"
assert check_citations(ok, ctx)["unknown"] == []
assert check_citations(bad, ctx)["unknown"] == ["99_made_up"]
assert check_citations("No citations here.", ctx)["has_citations"] is False
```

Microsoft GraphRAG's prompts let the model write +more when a claim has more sources than it lists; minigraphrag's prompt does not ask for it, but the parser skips it so the checker works on either output. A check like this catches invented ids cheaply. It cannot tell whether a real cited source actually supports the claim; that needs an entailment check or an LLM judge (Chapter 25).

#### Exercise 1.3 Core

For each of the seven canonical questions in the running example, answer: (a) could a general-purpose model answer it closed-book? (b) would the stuffed baseline give it everything it needs? (c) what is the main risk even when the evidence is in the context?

▸ Show answer

Question | (a) Closed-book | (b) Stuffed has the evidence | (c) Main risk with evidence present

1. Why did Kestrel start Project Tern? | No, fictional and private | Yes (docs 07, 08, 09) | Stopping at “to reduce supplier dependence” without linking Marlow's acquisition, because the memo never names Marlow

2. Which investor's board member oversees the company whose drones detected the bleaching? | No | Yes (docs 06, 04, 02) | Three hops across documents; the research note says “Sentinel program”, not “Kestrel Labs”

3. What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast? | No | Yes (docs 05, 07, 09, 12) | Listing facts without the connecting chain; confusing “Priya worked at Marlow” with “Priya worked at Deepcast”

4. Main themes | No | Yes, all documents | Over-weighting whatever is first or last in the context; missing a theme buried in the middle

5. Risks Kestrel faces | No | Yes (docs 03, 07, 08, 12) | Echoing only the risks listed explicitly in the 2026 interview and missing the single-supplier analysis from 2022

6. Who is the CTO? | No | Yes (docs 01, 12) | Stale answer: “Jonas Vehl” appears as CTO in several older documents, “Priya Nair” in one newer one

7. Sonar supplier in 2024? | No | Yes (docs 03, 08) | Low: the answer is stated directly. The risk is date reasoning if the model latches onto “no longer available” from 2025

The pattern: for a small corpus, stuffing solves the presence problem for every question, but not the use problem. Questions 1–3 need chains across documents, 4–5 need synthesis across all of them, and 6–7 need time awareness. Later chapters address those three problems with graphs, community summaries and temporal facts.

#### Exercise 1.4 Stretch

Reproduce a small lost-in-the-middle experiment on Kestrel with a real model. Ask “Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs as of April 2026?” with all 12 documents in context, moving document 12 (the only one with the answer) to each position 0–11 while keeping the others in a fixed order. Run each position several times and record accuracy. Then repeat with only three distractors. What do you expect, and what might make your results differ from the paper's?

▸ Show answer

```python
import os
from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents
from minigraphrag.context import format_table
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.search.common import generate_answer

docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
target_id = "12_interview_leadership_change_2026"
others = [(d, t) for d, t in docs.items() if d != target_id]
question = "Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs as of April 2026? Answer with a name."
llm = get_llm(os.getenv("LLM", "openai"))   # a real model; the mock cannot show position effects

def run(distractors, trials=5):
    results = {}
    for pos in range(len(distractors) + 1):
        ordered = distractors[:pos] + [(target_id, docs[target_id])] + distractors[pos:]
        context = format_table("Sources", ["id", "text"], [list(p) for p in ordered])
        hits = sum("priya" in generate_answer(llm, question, context).lower() for _ in range(trials))
        results[pos] = hits / trials
    return results

print("11 distractors:", run(others))
print(" 3 distractors:", run(others[:3]))
```

CachedLLM would return the same answer for every trial, so do not pass cache_dir here, and use a provider setting that allows some sampling variation, or vary the distractor order across trials instead.

What to expect: with only about 7,000 tokens of context, many 2026 models will answer correctly at every position, so you may see no dip at all. That is a legitimate finding: the effect in the paper appeared with longer contexts and more distractors, and newer models have been trained to reduce it. A more telling failure here is the stale answer “Jonas Vehl”, because documents 01, 03 and 08 call him CTO. If you see errors, check whether they cluster in middle positions (position effect) or are spread evenly (distractor effect). To make a dip more likely, pad the context with longer distractors, such as the corpus repeated with Kestrel names swapped out, until it reaches tens of thousands of tokens.

#### Exercise 1.5 Core

A team runs an internal assistant over 4,000 policy documents averaging 1,500 tokens each. Documents change weekly, answers must respect each employee's access rights, and about 20,000 questions arrive per day. A colleague proposes a 1-million-token-context model with the whole corpus in the prompt. Write a short recommendation with numbers.

▸ Show answer

Corpus size: 4,000 × 1,500 = 6,000,000 tokens. It does not fit in a 1M-token window: it is six times too large, so the proposal fails before cost is even considered. Suppose you split it into six 1M-token shards and queried each: that is 6M input tokens per question, 120 billion tokens a day at 20,000 questions, $360,000 a day at $3 per million before any caching discount. Access control is the second blocker: one shared prompt cannot hide documents from users who are not allowed to see them, so you would need a different prompt per permission group, which breaks prompt caching.

Recommendation: retrieval with per-user filtering at query time. With, say, eight 500-token chunks plus 500 tokens of overhead, that is 4,500 tokens per question, 90 million tokens a day, about $270 a day at the same price. Weekly updates become index upserts. Keep a long-context model for the final generation step so you can afford generous k for hard questions.

## Check your understanding

A model trained before March 2026 is asked “Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?” with no context. What is the best description of the problem?

- The context window is too small

- The model is lost in the middle

- ✓ (correct) The fact is non-parametric for this model: it is private, fictional and after its cutoff, so only supplied context can provide it

- The tokenizer cannot represent the name “Priya Nair”
Answer: No weights contain this fact. The only fix is to supply the evidence in the prompt, which is what retrieval does.

Why does next-token prediction produce confident-sounding hallucinations?

- ✓ (correct) The objective rewards plausible continuations; a flat distribution at a fact-bearing token still yields a fluent sentence once a token is sampled

- Models are trained to avoid saying “I don't know”

- Sampling temperature is always too high

- Hallucinations only happen when the context is too long
Answer: Uncertainty lives in individual token distributions, which the final text hides. Temperature 0 makes the choice deterministic, not correct.

With a price of $3 per million input tokens, a prompt of 2,150 tokens and 1,000 questions a day, what is the daily input cost?

- $0.65

- $2.15

- $21.50

- ✓ (correct) $6.45
Answer: 2,150 × 1,000 = 2.15 million tokens; 2.15 × $3 = $6.45.

What did Liu et al. find about where relevant information sits in a long context?

- Position does not matter for modern models

- Models use information best when it is in the middle

- ✓ (correct) Models tended to use it best at the beginning or end, and worse in the middle

- Only the last document in the context is ever used
Answer: The U-shaped curve motivates putting the best evidence first and keeping retrieved context short and precise.

In Lewis et al.'s original RAG, what were the two main components?

- A BM25 index and GPT-3

- ✓ (correct) A dense passage retriever over Wikipedia and a BART sequence-to-sequence generator

- A knowledge graph and a graph neural network

- A long-context transformer and a reranker
Answer: RAG combined DPR-style retrieval with BART generation and fine-tuned the query encoder and generator together.

Which workload most favors pasting the whole corpus into a long context over building retrieval?

- Millions of documents, updated hourly, with per-user permissions

- A support bot answering 100,000 questions a day over a product wiki

- A multi-tenant SaaS search over each customer's files

- ✓ (correct) A one-off analysis of a 40-page contract that fits easily in the window, asked a handful of questions
Answer: Small, static, few questions, no access control: the engineering cost of retrieval is not worth it. Measure quality anyway.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ If context windows keep growing, will RAG become unnecessary?

For small, static corpora it already is sometimes unnecessary. For large, changing or access-controlled data it is not, for three reasons that bigger windows do not remove: cost and latency grow with prompt length, models do not use every part of a long context equally well, and access control and freshness are easier to enforce in an index than in a giant prompt. What is changing is the balance: retrieval can afford to be less precise because the generator can read more.

▸ Why not fine-tune the model on our documents instead?

Fine-tuning changes parametric knowledge, which brings back the problems retrieval avoids: you cannot cite where an answer came from, updating a fact means training again, deleting a document's influence is hard, and small fine-tunes are an unreliable way to inject new facts. Fine-tuning is better for style, format and task behavior, such as teaching a small model to follow your extraction format. Chapter 24 covers training with graphs.

▸ Does temperature 0 stop hallucinations?

No. Temperature 0 makes the model pick the most likely token at each step, which makes outputs more reproducible. If the most likely name is wrong because the evidence is missing, you get the same wrong name every time. Use low temperature for reproducibility and caching, and grounding for correctness. The reference code's AnthropicLLM sends no temperature at all, because the Claude models it was written against reject sampling parameters; providers change these rules, so check the current API documentation rather than assuming the knob exists.

▸ Why does the course put the context in the system prompt and the question in the user message?

It mirrors Microsoft GraphRAG's search prompts, which minigraphrag follows: the system prompt carries the role, rules and data tables, and the user turn carries only the question. That keeps the question easy to find for logging and caching. Putting everything in one user message also works. What matters is that instructions, evidence with ids, and the question are clearly separated.

▸ Why does the mock LLM answer “OK” to my own prompt?

MockLLM is not a language model. It recognizes the course's prompt templates by a marker sentence in each (listed in prompts.MARKERS) and runs a deterministic heuristic for that task, such as extracting entities with a gazetteer or picking overlapping sentences to answer from data tables. A free-form prompt matches no marker, so it returns OK. Use it to run pipelines offline and in tests; use a real model to judge answer quality.

### Project: a closed-book versus stuffed-context baseline report

Measure the starting point every later chapter will be compared against, with a real model if you have access to one and the mock otherwise.

- A script that answers all questions in data/questions.jsonl twice: closed-book, and with the whole corpus stuffed into the grounded prompt

- For each run, the input tokens per question, total LLM calls and an estimated cost at a price you state

- The citation checker from Exercise 1.2 applied to every stuffed answer, with the count of answers that have no citations or invalid ids

- A hand-graded accuracy column (correct, partial, wrong) against the reference answers, broken down by question type

- A short paragraph naming the question types where the stuffed baseline struggles most, and your guess at why

Done when you have a table of accuracy and cost by question type that you would be willing to show a colleague as “the number to beat”.

## Key takeaways

- A language model predicts plausible next tokens. Fluency does not signal that a fact is known.

- Parametric knowledge is frozen, public and uncitable. Private, recent and checkable facts must be supplied in the prompt.

- Grounding means evidence in context, instructions to use only that evidence, and citations you can verify.

- Stuffing the corpus works for small, static data; cost, latency and window limits grow with the corpus, while retrieval grows with k.

- More context is not automatically better: models use evidence in the middle of long contexts less reliably, so rank, filter and order.

- Retrieve-then-generate is the backbone of the course; GraphRAG changes what is retrieved, not the loop.

## Build vector RAG from scratch
