# Build vector RAG from scratch

Before you can see why GraphRAG exists, you need the thing it improves on, built well and understood down to the dot product. In this chapter you chunk the Kestrel corpus, embed it, search it and assemble a cited prompt, then measure where the result is good enough.

## You will be able to

- Split documents into overlapping text units and predict how many units a corpus produces

- Explain what an embedding vector represents and compute cosine similarity by hand

- Implement exact top-k search over a matrix of unit vectors and wrap it in a small vector store

- Assemble a grounded prompt with numbered sources and verifiable citations using basic_search

- Describe how approximate nearest-neighbor indexes such as HNSW trade recall for speed

- Run a retrieval smoke test that measures supporting-document recall by question type

## The shape of a vector RAG system

Vector RAG has two phases that run at different times. Indexing happens once per corpus change: split documents into pieces, turn each piece into a vector, store the vectors. Querying happens per question: turn the question into a vector with the same model, find the nearest stored vectors, paste their text into a prompt, and generate.

[Diagram]

Everything in this chapter fits in these two rows. The dashed lines are the two things both phases share: the embedding model and the stored vectors.

The minigraphrag package already has every piece: chunking.py, embeddings.py, vector_store.py and search/basic.py. You will read each one, understand why it is written that way, and then run the whole pipeline on Kestrel.

## Chunking: choosing the unit of retrieval

A retriever returns pieces of documents, not whole documents, for two reasons. Whole documents are too long to put several in a prompt, and one long document embedded as a single vector blurs many topics into one point. The pieces are called chunks in vector-RAG vocabulary and text units in GraphRAG's. This chapter and the next say chunk, because the thing being retrieved is a plain slice of text; from Chapter 7 on, where the slice also carries extracted entities and provenance, the course says text unit. Chunk size is the first and most consequential knob in any RAG system.

### Fixed windows with overlap

The simplest chunker slides a window of S words over the document and advances it by a stride of S − O words, where O is the overlap. Consecutive chunks share exactly O words, so a fact that straddles a boundary survives whole in at least one chunk as long as it is at most O words long. A document of N words yields

chunks = ⌈(N − O) / (S − O)⌉   (for N > S; otherwise 1)

The Kestrel founding article has 481 words. With S = 300 and O = 50: ⌈431 / 250⌉ = ⌈1.72⌉ = 2 chunks. Every Kestrel document has between 395 and 492 words, so each yields 2 chunks and the corpus yields 24 text units, which is exactly what minigraphrag reports.

[Interactive figure: Chunking the Marlow–Deepcast article (chunker)]

```python  # minigraphrag/chunking.py
@dataclass
class TextUnit:
    """A chunk of a source document; the unit of extraction and of citation."""
    id: str
    doc_id: str
    text: str
    n_tokens: int
    start: int  # character offset (inclusive) in the document
    end: int    # character offset (exclusive)

def chunk_fixed(text: str, size: int = 300, overlap: int = 50, doc_id: str = "doc") -> list[TextUnit]:
    """Sliding window of `size` words that advances by `size - overlap` words."""
    if overlap >= size:
        raise ValueError("overlap must be smaller than size")
    spans = [(m.start(), m.end()) for m in re.finditer(r"\S+", text)]
    if not spans:
        return []
    stride = size - overlap
    units: list[TextUnit] = []
    for i, first in enumerate(range(0, len(spans), stride)):
        window = spans[first : first + size]
        start, end = window[0][0], window[-1][1]
        piece = text[start:end]
        units.append(TextUnit(f"{doc_id}-{i:03d}", doc_id, piece, count_tokens(piece), start, end))
        if first + size >= len(spans):  # this window reached the end of the document
            break
    return units
```

Three details are worth copying into any chunker you write. Word boundaries come from a regex over the original string, so start and end are exact character offsets, which lets you highlight a cited chunk in the source document. The id 07_marlow_acquires_deepcast-000 encodes the document and position, so a citation is human-readable. And the loop stops as soon as a window reaches the end, so the last chunk is never a tiny tail that is entirely overlap.

### Sentence packing and size trade-offs

chunk_by_sentences packs whole sentences until a token budget is reached and repeats the last sentence at the start of the next chunk. Chunks never end mid-sentence, at the cost of uneven sizes. chunk_documents(docs, size, overlap, method="fixed" | "sentences") applies either strategy to a whole corpus. Chapter 7 goes deeper into structure-aware splitting; for now the trade-off is the one that matters:

Chunk size | Kestrel units (overlap) | Good for | Costs

Small (≈ 60–120 words) | 111 (10), 58 (20) | Precise matches for single facts; many distinct hits fit in a prompt | Facts get separated from their subject; “it” and “the company” lose their referent

Medium (≈ 200–300 words) | 36 (30), 24 (50) | A paragraph or two of context around each fact | Each vector averages several topics, so similarity scores get fuzzier

Large (a whole document) | 12 (none) | Keeps every relationship within a document intact | Few results fit in the prompt; one vector per document is a blurry summary

## Embeddings: meaning as geometry

An embedding is a function that maps a piece of text to a fixed-length vector of numbers, chosen so that texts that should match end up close together. Close is measured by angle. The vector itself has no human-readable coordinates in a neural model; what matters is the geometry: which vectors point in similar directions.

### Cosine similarity

For vectors a and b, cosine similarity is

cos(a, b) = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖) = Σi aibi / (√Σai² · √Σbi²)

It ranges from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated, orthogonal) to 1 (same direction). Length does not matter, only direction, so a long chunk that mentions “sonar” ten times does not automatically beat a short one that mentions it twice. If every vector is first scaled to length 1 (L2-normalized), the denominator is 1 and cosine similarity is just the dot product. That is why stores normalize once at insert time and then search with a single matrix multiplication.

### A worked example in three dimensions

Imagine a toy embedding whose three coordinates count the words sonar, supply and reef. The query “sonar supplier” becomes q = (1, 1, 0). Three simplified Kestrel chunks:

Chunk | Vector (sonar, supply, reef) | q · c | ‖c‖ | cos(q, c)

03 Deepcast supply deal | (3, 2, 0) | 3 + 2 + 0 = 5 | √13 = 3.606 | 5 / (1.414 × 3.606) = 0.981

09 Project Tern blog | (3, 0, 1) | 3 | √10 = 3.162 | 3 / (1.414 × 3.162) = 0.671

06 Bleaching research note | (1, 0, 4) | 1 | √17 = 4.123 | 1 / (1.414 × 4.123) = 0.171

‖q‖ = √2 = 1.414. Ranking by cosine gives the supply deal, then the Tern blog, then the bleaching note. Converting to angles with arccos makes the geometry visible.

[Diagram]

The toy vectors from the table, drawn by their angle from the query. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, but ranking still means “which arrows point most nearly the same way”.

### Real embedders and the hashing stand-in

Neural embedding models (sentence-transformers models such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2, OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small, and many others) are trained on huge sets of text pairs that should match, such as questions and their answers, so that “CTO” lands near “chief technology officer” and “supplier” near “vendor”. Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) and Dense Passage Retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020) are the classic papers behind this style of retriever.

minigraphrag ships three embedders behind one protocol, embed(texts) -> (n, d) array of unit vectors, plus a factory:

```python  # minigraphrag/embeddings.py
class HashingEmbedder:
    """Deterministic bag-of-words hashing embedder (offline)."""

    def __init__(self, dim: int = 512):
        self.dim = dim
        self.name = f"hashing:{dim}"

    def _bucket(self, token: str) -> tuple[int, float]:
        # Python's hash() is randomised per process, so use a stable digest.
        h = int.from_bytes(hashlib.blake2b(token.encode(), digest_size=8).digest(), "little")
        return h % self.dim, 1.0 if (h >> 63) & 1 else -1.0  # sign reduces collision bias

    def embed(self, texts: Sequence[str]) -> np.ndarray:
        mat = np.zeros((len(texts), self.dim), dtype=np.float32)
        for row, text in enumerate(texts):
            for tok in simple_tokenize(text):          # lowercase, drop stopwords, strip plural "s"
                idx, sign = self._bucket(tok)
                mat[row, idx] += sign
        norms = np.linalg.norm(mat, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        return mat / np.where(norms == 0, 1.0, norms)

# OpenAIEmbedder("text-embedding-3-small") and SentenceTransformerEmbedder("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
# implement the same embed() method. get_embedder("hashing" | "hashing:256" | "openai" | "st:<model>")
```

HashingEmbedder is the “hashing trick”: each word is hashed to one of 512 buckets, with a sign taken from one bit of the hash, and the vector counts signed bucket hits. It is exactly the toy example above, with 512 hashed dimensions instead of three hand-picked words. It needs no download, is identical on every machine, and makes retrieval behavior observable in tests. What it cannot do is meaning. “CTO” and “chief technology officer” share no words, so their hashing vectors are orthogonal. Keep that in mind when you read retrieval numbers in this chapter and the next: they are lexical-overlap numbers. Swapping in a neural embedder changes the scores. As Chapter 3 shows, it does not change the structural problems.

[Interactive figure: Kestrel documents in a 2-D sketch of embedding space (embedding-space)]

## Searching: exact top-k and a vector store

With all stored vectors as the rows of a matrix M (shape N × d) and a normalized query q, every cosine score comes out of one matrix-vector product: s = Mq. Then take the k largest entries.

```python  # minigraphrag/embeddings.py
def cosine_top_k(query_vec: np.ndarray, matrix: np.ndarray, k: int = 5) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    """Indices and cosine scores of the k rows of `matrix` most similar to `query_vec`.

    Vectors are assumed L2-normalised, so cosine similarity is a dot product.
    """
    if matrix.size == 0:
        return []
    scores = matrix @ query_vec.reshape(-1)
    k = min(k, len(scores))
    top = np.argpartition(-scores, k - 1)[:k]            # O(N): the k best, unordered
    top = top[np.argsort(-scores[top], kind="stable")]   # O(k log k): order just those
    return [(int(i), float(scores[i])) for i in top]
```

Cost: the product is O(N·d) floating-point work, and argpartition avoids a full O(N log N) sort. For Kestrel that is 24 × 512 ≈ 12,000 multiplications, which is nothing. For 1 million chunks with 1,536-dimensional vectors it is about 1.5 billion multiplications per query and a 6 GB float32 matrix, which is where approximate indexes start to pay off (see below).

A vector store adds the bookkeeping around that function: ids, metadata and persistence.

```python  # minigraphrag/vector_store.py
class VectorStore:
    def __init__(self, dim: int | None = None):
        self.ids: list[str] = []
        self.metadata: list[dict] = []
        self.matrix = np.zeros((0, dim or 0), dtype=np.float32)

    def add(self, ids: list[str], vectors: np.ndarray, metadata: list[dict] | None = None) -> None:
        vectors = np.asarray(vectors, dtype=np.float32)
        if len(ids) != len(vectors):
            raise ValueError("ids and vectors must have the same length")
        self.matrix = vectors if len(self.ids) == 0 else np.vstack([self.matrix, vectors])
        self.ids.extend(ids)
        self.metadata.extend(metadata or [{} for _ in ids])

    def search(self, query_vec: np.ndarray, k: int = 5) -> list[tuple[str, float, dict]]:
        """Return up to k (id, score, metadata) tuples, best first."""
        return [(self.ids[i], s, self.metadata[i]) for i, s in cosine_top_k(query_vec, self.matrix, k)]

    # save(path) writes path.npz (vectors) and path.json (ids + metadata); VectorStore.load(path) reads them.
```

**Why the store trusts you to normalize

VectorStore assumes rows are unit vectors, because every minigraphrag embedder returns unit vectors. If you add vectors from somewhere else, normalize them first, or longer vectors will score higher for reasons that have nothing to do with relevance. Production stores such as FAISS, pgvector and LanceDB make you choose the metric (inner product, cosine or L2) explicitly for the same reason.

## From hits to a grounded, cited prompt

Retrieval gives you ids and scores. The generator needs text, in a format that makes it easy to cite. minigraphrag follows Microsoft GraphRAG's convention: evidence goes into pipe-delimited tables with an id column, and the model cites rows as [Data: Sources (id)]. Here is the real basic_search:

```python  # minigraphrag/search/basic.py
def basic_search(index, query: str, llm: LLM, top_k: int = 5, max_context_tokens: int = 4000,
                 response_type: str = DEFAULT_RESPONSE_TYPE) -> SearchResult:
    hits = index.text_unit_store.search(index.embedder.embed([query])[0], k=top_k)
    rows, used = [], 0
    for unit_id, score, _ in hits:
        text = index.text_units[unit_id].text
        if used + count_tokens(text) > max_context_tokens:
            break
        rows.append([unit_id, text])
        used += count_tokens(text)
    context = format_table("Sources", ["id", "text"], rows)
    answer = generate_answer(llm, query, context, response_type)
    return SearchResult(answer, "basic", context, {"sources": [{"id": r[0], "text": r[1]} for r in rows]},
                        doc_ids_for_units(index, [r[0] for r in rows]), llm_calls=1)
```

And the pieces it uses from search/common.py and prompts.py:

```python  # minigraphrag/search/common.py
@dataclass
class SearchResult:
    answer: str
    method: str
    context_text: str = ""
    context_data: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    sources: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)  # document ids that reached the context
    llm_calls: int = 0

def generate_answer(llm: LLM, query: str, context_text: str, response_type: str = DEFAULT_RESPONSE_TYPE) -> str:
    """Final generation step: the context goes into the system prompt, the question is the user turn."""
    system = P.LOCAL_SEARCH_SYSTEM_PROMPT.format(context_data=context_text, response_type=response_type)
    return llm.complete(query, system=system)

# prompts.LOCAL_SEARCH_SYSTEM_PROMPT (abridged):
# ---Role---
# You are a helpful assistant responding to questions about data in the tables provided.
# ---Goal---
# ... If you don't know the answer, just say so. Do not make anything up.
# Points supported by data should list their data references as [Data: <dataset name> (record ids)] ...
# ---Target response length and format---
# {response_type}
# ---Data tables---
# {context_data}
```

Four design decisions are packed into those few lines:

- Ids are the chunk ids, not positions like 1, 2, 3. A position changes when the ranking changes; 08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-000 means the same thing in every run, in logs and in evaluation.

- The budget is enforced greedily in rank order. If the fourth chunk would exceed max_context_tokens, the loop stops there, even if a shorter fifth chunk would still fit. The context is always an unbroken prefix of the ranking.

- Best evidence first. Rows appear in similarity order, which puts the most likely evidence at the start of the context, where models use it most reliably (Chapter 1).

- The result records what reached the model. SearchResult.sources lists the documents in the context, which is what evaluation needs to separate retrieval failures from generation failures.

[Interactive figure: basic_search on “Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?” (flow)]

## Running it end to end on Kestrel

basic_search needs an object with three attributes: text_units, text_unit_store and embedder. The full GraphRAG Index built by minigraphrag.indexer.build_index has them, but building it also runs entity extraction and community detection, which you have not learned yet. A small dataclass with the same three attributes is enough for vector RAG:

```python  # examples/ch02_vector_rag.py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from minigraphrag.chunking import TextUnit, chunk_documents, load_documents
from minigraphrag.embeddings import Embedder, get_embedder
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.search.basic import basic_search
from minigraphrag.vector_store import VectorStore

@dataclass
class VectorIndex:
    """The three attributes basic_search reads; a full GraphRAG Index has them too."""
    text_units: dict[str, TextUnit]
    text_unit_store: VectorStore
    embedder: Embedder

def build_vector_index(docs_dir: str, embedder: Embedder, size: int = 300, overlap: int = 50) -> VectorIndex:
    units = chunk_documents(load_documents(docs_dir), size=size, overlap=overlap)
    store = VectorStore()
    store.add([u.id for u in units],
              embedder.embed([u.text for u in units]),
              [{"doc_id": u.doc_id} for u in units])
    return VectorIndex({u.id: u for u in units}, store, embedder)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    index = build_vector_index("data/corpus", get_embedder("hashing"))   # or "openai", "st:all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
    llm = get_llm("mock")                                                 # or "openai", "anthropic", "ollama"
    result = basic_search(index, "Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?", llm, top_k=5)
    for row in result.context_data["sources"]:
        print(row["id"])
    print("documents in context:", result.sources)
    print(result.answer)
```

With the hashing embedder the retrieved chunks and scores are fully deterministic:

Rank | Chunk | Cosine | Contains the answer?

1 | 08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-000 | 0.269 | Yes: “Deepcast has supplied every sonar module in our fleet since 2022.”

2 | 10_brightwater_series_b-001 | 0.260 | No: mentions “the loss of its sonar supplier” without naming it

3 | 10_brightwater_series_b-000 | 0.245 | No: overlaps with rank 2

4 | 03_deepcast_supply_agreement-000 | 0.202 | Yes: the 2022 multi-year supply agreement

5 | 03_deepcast_supply_agreement-001 | 0.171 | Partly: shipments and the first drones carrying Deepcast sonar

This is vector RAG working as intended. The answer, Deepcast, is stated in a single place in plain words that overlap the question. A capable model will answer correctly and cite chunk 08 or 03. With MockLLM, the answer is a set of extracted sentences with [Data: Sources (...)] citations, enough to confirm the plumbing without an API key.

**Notice the weak spot already

Ranks 2 and 3 are near-duplicates from the Series B press release, which talks about losing a sonar supplier in 2025. Overlapping chunks from the same document often crowd the top-k with repeated evidence. Exercise 2.5 fixes that with maximal marginal relevance. The press release also scores high for a reason that will matter in Chapter 3: it mentions the supply problem without naming either company involved.

## Scaling up: approximate nearest-neighbor indexes

Exact search is O(N·d) per query. With numpy on one machine that is fast enough well into hundreds of thousands of vectors for many applications, so start there. Beyond that, or under tight latency budgets, you trade a little recall for a lot of speed with an approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index.

### HNSW intuition

Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs (Malkov and Yashunin) are the most widely used ANN structure, available in FAISS, hnswlib, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate and others. The idea is a skip list made of proximity graphs:

- Every vector is a node in the bottom layer, linked to up to M near neighbors.

- Each node also appears in higher layers with exponentially decreasing probability, so the top layer has a handful of nodes with long-range links.

- Search is greedy descent. Start at the entry point in the top layer, repeatedly move to whichever neighbor is closer to the query until no neighbor improves, then drop a layer and continue from there. In the bottom layer, keep a candidate list of size efsearch to avoid stopping at a local optimum.

[Diagram]

A one-dimensional cartoon of HNSW. Real indexes link each node to several neighbors in many dimensions; the search idea is the same: greedy moves on sparse upper layers find the right region fast, and the dense bottom layer refines.

Index | Query cost | Recall | Memory and build | Use when

Brute force (this chapter) | O(N·d) | Exact | Just the matrix; no build | Up to hundreds of thousands of vectors, or when you need exact results for evaluation

HNSW | Empirically close to logarithmic in N | High, tunable with efsearch | Extra memory for links; slower inserts | Low-latency search over millions of vectors

IVF (inverted file with clustering) | Scan only the nprobe nearest clusters | Tunable with nprobe | Needs a training pass (k-means) | Very large collections, often combined with quantization

Product quantization | Fast approximate distances on compressed codes | Lower; often reranked exactly | Much smaller vectors | When memory is the binding constraint

None of these change what is retrieved in principle; they only approximate the exact top-k faster. If exact top-k does not contain the evidence, a faster index will not either. That is the subject of the next chapter.

## A retrieval smoke test

Before tuning anything, measure. data/questions.jsonl lists 23 Kestrel questions with a type (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, global), a reference answer and the supporting_docs that contain the evidence. That is enough for a retrieval-only metric that needs no LLM: supporting-document recall@k, the fraction of a question's supporting documents that appear among the documents of the top-k chunks.

```python  # examples/ch02_smoke_test.py
import collections
import json

from ch02_vector_rag import build_vector_index
from minigraphrag.embeddings import get_embedder

def doc_recall_at_k(index, questions: list[dict], k: int) -> dict[str, float]:
    by_type = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for q in questions:
        hits = index.text_unit_store.search(index.embedder.embed([q["question"]])[0], k=k)
        got = {index.text_units[uid].doc_id for uid, _, _ in hits}
        need = set(q["supporting_docs"])
        by_type[q["type"]].append(len(got & need) / len(need))
    return {t: round(sum(v) / len(v), 2) for t, v in by_type.items()}

questions = [json.loads(line) for line in open("data/questions.jsonl")]
index = build_vector_index("data/corpus", get_embedder("hashing"))
for k in (1, 3, 5, 10):
    print(k, doc_recall_at_k(index, questions, k))
```

Results with the hashing embedder, 300-word chunks and 50-word overlap:

k | Single-hop (5) | Temporal (5) | Multi-hop (8) | Global (5)

1 | 0.40 | 0.37 | 0.17 | 0.09

3 | 0.80 | 0.37 | 0.56 | 0.19

5 | 0.80 | 0.77 | 0.60 | 0.37

10 | 1.00 | 0.93 | 0.88 | 0.66

Read the table by row, then by column. Single-hop questions reach 0.80 by k = 3. Global questions lag at every k, and multi-hop questions trail single-hop ones at every k (at k = 3, temporal questions do worse still). Multi-hop recall reaches 0.88 only at k = 10, which is 10 of 24 chunks, over 40% of the corpus; global recall never passes 0.66. At that point you are not retrieving so much as stuffing with extra steps, and on a real corpus k = 10 would be a tiny fraction and recall would not climb like this. Recall also measures only whether a supporting document is present, not whether the model can connect the pieces. Chapter 3 looks at why the bottom-right of this table is low and why raising k is not the fix.

**Separate retrieval from generation

Always log recall-style retrieval metrics next to answer quality. If recall is low, change chunking, embeddings or retrieval. If recall is high but answers are wrong, change the prompt, the ordering or the model. Mixing the two is the most common way RAG tuning goes in circles.

## Exercises

#### Exercise 2.1 Warm-up

Using the toy (sonar, supply, reef) embedding, compute the cosine similarity between the query “reef sonar” = (1, 0, 1) and each of the three chunks in the worked example: (3, 2, 0), (3, 0, 1) and (1, 0, 4). Which ranks first? Then normalize (3, 0, 1) to unit length and confirm the dot product with the normalized query gives the same number.

▸ Show answer

‖q‖ = √2 = 1.414.

- Supply deal (3, 2, 0): q · c = 3, ‖c‖ = √13 = 3.606, cos = 3 / (1.414 × 3.606) = 3 / 5.099 = 0.588.

- Tern blog (3, 0, 1): q · c = 3 + 1 = 4, ‖c‖ = √10 = 3.162, cos = 4 / (1.414 × 3.162) = 4 / 4.472 = 0.894.

- Bleaching note (1, 0, 4): q · c = 1 + 4 = 5, ‖c‖ = √17 = 4.123, cos = 5 / (1.414 × 4.123) = 5 / 5.831 = 0.857.

The Tern blog ranks first, just ahead of the bleaching note. The ranking flipped completely from the “sonar supplier” query because the direction of the query changed.

Normalization: q̂ = (1, 0, 1) / 1.414 = (0.707, 0, 0.707). ĉ = (3, 0, 1) / 3.162 = (0.949, 0, 0.316). q̂ · ĉ = 0.707 × 0.949 + 0.707 × 0.316 = 0.671 + 0.224 = 0.894. Same as before, which is why normalized stores can use a plain dot product.

#### Exercise 2.2 Warm-up

Using the chunk-count formula, predict how many text units chunk_fixed produces for (a) the 492-word leadership interview with size 120 and overlap 20, (b) the 395-word Series A press release with the same settings, and (c) a 300-word document with size 300 and overlap 50. Then check (a) and (b) in code.

▸ Show answer

Stride = 120 − 20 = 100.

(a) ⌈(492 − 20) / 100⌉ = ⌈4.72⌉ = 5. Windows start at words 0, 100, 200, 300, 400; the last covers words 400–491 and reaches the end.

(b) ⌈(395 − 20) / 100⌉ = ⌈3.75⌉ = 4. Starts at 0, 100, 200, 300; the last covers 300–394.

(c) N = S, so the first window covers the whole document and the loop stops: 1 chunk.

```python
from minigraphrag.chunking import chunk_fixed, load_documents
docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
for doc_id in ("12_interview_leadership_change_2026", "02_brightwater_series_a"):
    units = chunk_fixed(docs[doc_id], size=120, overlap=20, doc_id=doc_id)
    print(doc_id, len(docs[doc_id].split()), "words", len(units), "units")
```

The formula is also a quick sanity check on a whole corpus: at size 120 and overlap 20 the Kestrel corpus yields 58 units, and at size 60 and overlap 10 it yields 111.

#### Exercise 2.3 Core

Extend the smoke test into a small grid: chunk sizes 120 (overlap 20) and 300 (overlap 50), k in {3, 5, 10}. Report supporting-document recall by question type and also the fraction of questions where all supporting documents were retrieved. Which question type benefits least from smaller chunks, and why might that be?

▸ Show answer

```python
def full_coverage(index, questions, k):
    by_type = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for q in questions:
        hits = index.text_unit_store.search(index.embedder.embed([q["question"]])[0], k=k)
        got = {index.text_units[uid].doc_id for uid, _, _ in hits}
        by_type[q["type"]].append(set(q["supporting_docs"]) <= got)
    return {t: f"{sum(v)}/{len(v)}" for t, v in by_type.items()}

emb = get_embedder("hashing")
for size, overlap in ((300, 50), (120, 20)):
    index = build_vector_index("data/corpus", emb, size, overlap)
    for k in (3, 5, 10):
        print(size, k, doc_recall_at_k(index, questions, k), full_coverage(index, questions, k))
```

Size | k | Single-hop | Temporal | Multi-hop | Global

300 | 3 | 0.80 (4/5) | 0.37 (1/5) | 0.56 (2/8) | 0.19 (0/5)

300 | 5 | 0.80 (4/5) | 0.77 (3/5) | 0.60 (2/8) | 0.37 (0/5)

300 | 10 | 1.00 (5/5) | 0.93 (4/5) | 0.88 (6/8) | 0.66 (0/5)

120 | 3 | 0.80 (4/5) | 0.57 (2/5) | 0.46 (1/8) | 0.19 (0/5)

120 | 5 | 0.80 (4/5) | 0.67 (2/5) | 0.58 (1/8) | 0.24 (0/5)

120 | 10 | 1.00 (5/5) | 0.87 (4/5) | 0.73 (3/8) | 0.63 (1/5)

Multi-hop questions lose the most from smaller chunks: full coverage drops from 2/8 to 1/8 at k = 5 and from 6/8 to 3/8 at k = 10. A multi-hop question needs several documents, and with smaller chunks each document is split into more pieces that compete for the same k slots. The chunk that matches the question's words best tends to be one piece of one document, and the pieces that carry the other hops do not share the question's words. Global questions almost never reach full coverage: 0 of 5 at every setting with 300-word chunks, and 1 of 5 with 120-word chunks at k = 10, because their supporting documents span up to eight of the twelve documents.

Caveat: 23 questions is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Differences of one question are noise. The direction of the effect is what to take away.

#### Exercise 2.4 Core

Show the lexical limit of HashingEmbedder. Compute the cosine between “Who is the CTO?” and “chief technology officer”, and between “Who supplied the sonar?” and “Deepcast is the sonar vendor”. If you can install the st extra, repeat with get_embedder("st:all-MiniLM-L6-v2"). Then run “Who is the chief technology officer of Kestrel Labs?” through the hashing index and explain the top-3.

▸ Show answer

```python
import numpy as np
from minigraphrag.embeddings import get_embedder

pairs = [("Who is the CTO?", "chief technology officer"),
         ("Who supplied the sonar?", "Deepcast is the sonar vendor")]
for name in ("hashing", "st:all-MiniLM-L6-v2"):
    emb = get_embedder(name)
    for a, b in pairs:
        va, vb = emb.embed([a, b])
        print(name, f"{float(va @ vb):.3f}", a, "|", b)
```

Hashing: the first pair scores exactly 0.000 because after stopword removal the tokens are cto versus chief, technology, officer, with no overlap. The second pair shares only sonar and scores about 0.41. A sentence-transformer model gives both pairs clearly positive similarity because it was trained on paraphrases; the exact numbers depend on the model version, so measure rather than assume.

On the hashing index, “Who is the chief technology officer of Kestrel Labs?” returns 10_brightwater_series_b-001 (0.405), 05_kestrel_blog_priya_nair-000 (0.345) and 03_deepcast_supply_agreement-000 (0.314). The first two win mostly on repeated “Kestrel Labs”. The third contains “Kestrel Labs chief technology officer Jonas Vehl”, a 2022 statement. The 2026 interview that names Priya Nair as CTO is not in the top 3. A neural embedder fixes the synonym problem but not the freshness problem: both the 2022 and 2026 chunks are about the CTO, and nothing in cosine similarity prefers the newer one. That is a Chapter 3 failure and a Chapter 10 fix.

A side note on the tokenizer: simple_tokenize turns “Kestrel's” into kestrel and s, and strips the final s from “corpus”. Crude tokenization is fine for a teaching embedder, but it is a real source of mismatches in lexical retrieval such as BM25 (Chapter 21).

#### Exercise 2.5 Stretch

Overlapping chunks from the same document crowd the top-k. Implement maximal marginal relevance (MMR): fetch the top 20 candidates, then repeatedly pick the candidate maximizing λ · sim(q, c) − (1 − λ) · maxs ∈ selected sim(c, s). Run it for “Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?” with λ = 0.85 and λ = 0.7 and compare with plain top-5.

▸ Show answer

```python
from minigraphrag.embeddings import cosine_top_k

def mmr(query_vec, matrix, k=5, lam=0.7, fetch=20):
    candidates = [i for i, _ in cosine_top_k(query_vec, matrix, fetch)]
    relevance = {i: float(matrix[i] @ query_vec) for i in candidates}
    chosen = []
    while candidates and len(chosen) < k:
        def score(i):
            redundancy = max((float(matrix[i] @ matrix[j]) for j in chosen), default=0.0)
            return lam * relevance[i] - (1 - lam) * redundancy
        best = max(candidates, key=score)
        chosen.append(best)
        candidates.remove(best)
    return chosen

store = index.text_unit_store
q = index.embedder.embed(["Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?"])[0]
for lam in (1.0, 0.85, 0.7):
    print(lam, [store.ids[i] for i in mmr(q, store.matrix, lam=lam)])
```

λ = 1.0 is plain top-5: memo 08-000, Series B 10-001 and 10-000, supply deal 03-000 and 03-001. With λ = 0.85 the last pick changes: the second supply-deal chunk (03-001), which overlaps 03-000, gives way to the city council minutes (11-001). With λ = 0.7 the list becomes 08-000, 11-001, 10-000, 07-000 (Marlow acquires Deepcast), 03-001: only one chunk per document, and the Marlow article appears.

MMR trades a little relevance for coverage. Here it happens to pull in the acquisition article, useful for “why” questions and irrelevant for this “who” question. It is a cheap improvement, but it only reshuffles chunks that already look similar to the query. It cannot find evidence that shares no words or meaning with the question.

## Check your understanding

A 700-word document is chunked with size 300 and overlap 50. How many chunks result?

- 2

- ✓ (correct) 3

- 4

- 5
Answer: Stride 250. ⌈(700 − 50) / 250⌉ = ⌈2.6⌉ = 3. Windows start at words 0, 250 and 500; the third reaches the end.

Why does VectorStore compute scores with a plain matrix-vector product?

- Dot products are more accurate than cosine similarity

- The store uses Euclidean distance internally

- ✓ (correct) All vectors are L2-normalized, so the dot product equals cosine similarity

- numpy cannot compute vector norms efficiently
Answer: With unit vectors the cosine denominator is 1. Normalizing once at insert time makes every query a single matrix multiplication.

HashingEmbedder gives “CTO” and “chief technology officer” a similarity of 0. Why?

- The hash function has too few buckets

- The vectors were not normalized

- Stopword removal deleted both phrases

- ✓ (correct) It only captures shared words, and the two phrases share none
Answer: The hashing trick is a bag of words in disguise. Synonyms and paraphrases need a model trained on meaning, such as a sentence-transformer.

In basic_search, why are rows identified by chunk id such as 08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-000 rather than by 1, 2, 3?

- ✓ (correct) A chunk id is stable across runs and rankings, so citations can be checked, logged and evaluated

- LLMs cannot read numbers

- Numbered sources exceed the token budget

- Microsoft GraphRAG requires string ids
Answer: Positions change whenever the ranking changes. Stable ids make a citation mean the same thing in every run.

What does an HNSW index change compared with brute-force search?

- It retrieves evidence that shares no meaning with the query

- It guarantees the exact top-k with fewer computations

- ✓ (correct) It approximates the exact top-k with far fewer distance computations, at some cost in recall and memory

- It removes the need for an embedding model
Answer: ANN indexes speed up nearest-neighbor search without changing which neighbors are nearest. If the exact top-k misses the evidence, HNSW will too.

Supporting-document recall at k = 10 looks good for multi-hop questions on Kestrel. What is the main caveat?

- Recall cannot be computed without an LLM

- ✓ (correct) Ten of 24 chunks is over 40% of the corpus, so this is closer to stuffing than retrieval, and presence does not mean the model connects the pieces

- Recall is always 1.0 at k = 10

- Multi-hop questions have only one supporting document
Answer: On a realistic corpus, k = 10 is a tiny fraction and recall would not climb like this. And recall measures retrieval only, not reasoning across what was retrieved.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Which embedding model should I use?

For learning and tests, the hashing embedder: it is deterministic and free. For real work, start with a well-known general model from a provider you already use, or a sentence-transformers model if you need to run locally, then measure on your own questions with the smoke test from this chapter. Public leaderboards are a starting point, not a decision. Domain vocabulary, document length and question style matter more than a point or two on a benchmark. Whatever you choose, record the model name with the index (minigraphrag writes it to config.json) so queries use the same one.

▸ Should I embed the question as-is, or rewrite it first?

Start as-is. Rewriting helps when questions are short, conversational or phrased very differently from documents. Common techniques are query rewriting with an LLM (Ma et al., 2023) and HyDE, which embeds a hypothetical answer instead of the question (Gao et al., 2022). Both cost an LLM call per query. Neither helps when the evidence shares nothing with the question or its likely answer, which is the multi-hop case in Chapter 3.

▸ Do I need a vector database?

Not to start. A numpy matrix handles the Kestrel corpus and far larger ones. Reach for a database when you need persistence with concurrent writers, metadata filtering at scale, access control, or ANN search over millions of vectors. If you already run Postgres, pgvector is a low-friction first step. Chapter 13 compares storage options for graphs and embeddings together.

▸ What about keyword search? Is vector search always better?

No. Keyword methods such as BM25 are strong on exact names, ids, error codes and rare terms, where embeddings can blur things. Embeddings are strong on paraphrase. Most production systems run both and fuse the rankings. You will build BM25 and reciprocal rank fusion in Chapter 21.

▸ How big should k be?

Big enough that recall on your smoke test flattens, small enough that the context stays focused and cheap. For chunks of a few hundred tokens, 3 to 10 is a common range. If you find yourself needing a very large k for a class of questions, that is a signal that similarity search is the wrong retrieval method for those questions, not that k is too small.

### Project: a vector RAG baseline with an evaluation harness

Build the baseline that every GraphRAG method in this course must beat, and make its behavior measurable.

- A vector_rag.py command that indexes a folder with a chosen chunk size, overlap and embedder, saves the VectorStore to disk and reloads it for queries

- A query command that prints the retrieved chunk ids with scores, the context token count and the cited answer from basic_search

- The smoke test from this chapter, run for at least two chunk sizes and two embedders (hashing plus one neural model if available), saved as a table

- The citation checker from Chapter 1 applied to every answer on questions.jsonl

- A one-page note choosing default settings for Kestrel and listing the three questions your baseline handles worst

Done when one command rebuilds the index and prints recall by question type, and you can name the settings you will use as the baseline for Chapter 3.

## Key takeaways

- Vector RAG is two pipelines sharing an embedder and a store: chunk and embed offline, embed and search online.

- Chunk size decides what a single retrieved piece can contain; overlap protects facts that straddle boundaries.

- Cosine similarity compares directions. Normalize once and search with one matrix product and a partial sort.

- Ground the prompt with stable ids, best evidence first and a token budget, and record which sources reached the model.

- ANN indexes such as HNSW approximate the exact top-k with less work; they cannot find evidence that exact search misses.

- Measure retrieval separately from generation. On Kestrel, single-hop questions reach 0.80 recall at k = 3; global questions stay below 0.40 until k = 10.

## Where vector RAG breaks

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/03-where-rag-breaks.html
Summary: Multi-hop questions, global sensemaking questions, and lost relationships between chunks.

# Where vector RAG breaks

The baseline from Chapter 2 answers “who supplied the sonar?” well. This chapter runs the harder canonical questions through the same pipeline, shows chunk by chunk what retrieval returns and what it misses, and names each failure precisely enough that the rest of the course can fix it.

## You will be able to

- Trace a multi-hop question through vector retrieval and identify the missing bridge evidence

- Explain why global “sensemaking” questions have no good nearest neighbor, using the query-focused summarization framing

- Recognize alias, split-fact, staleness and dilution failures in retrieved context

- Implement iterative retrieval with follow-up queries and explain why it is only a partial fix

- Map each failure type to the GraphRAG technique and chapter that addresses it

## The setup: same index, harder questions

Every number in this chapter comes from the Chapter 2 baseline, unchanged: the 12 Kestrel documents cut into 24 text units of 300 words with 50 words of overlap, embedded with HashingEmbedder, searched with exact cosine top-k, k = 5 unless stated. You can reproduce all of them with build_vector_index from Chapter 2 and store.search.

Because the hashing embedder only sees shared words, you might suspect the failures are just a weak embedder. Some are. The important ones are not, and for each failure this chapter separates the part a better embedding model would fix from the part it structurally cannot. The test is simple: does any single chunk contain what the question needs, in words or meaning close to the question? If not, no similarity function over single chunks can rank the right evidence first.

Here is the retrieval footprint of the seven canonical questions at a glance. Each row is a question; each column is a document. The supporting documents come from data/questions.jsonl.

[Diagram]

Question 7, a direct lookup, is fully covered. The multi-hop and global rows are where red appears, and question 4's row is mostly red because its evidence spans eight documents. Question 3 shows two misses, yet its top-ranked chunk, from the 2026 interview (not in the reference list), restates most of the connection; more on that below.

## Multi-hop questions: the evidence does not look like the question

### Question 1: “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?”

The answer is a chain of three facts from three documents:

- Marlow Dynamics acquired Deepcast in April 2025 and ended outside supply contracts (document 07, a trade-press article).

- Deepcast stopped supplying Kestrel Labs: “Deepcast will not renew our supply agreement” (document 08, the board memo).

- Kestrel built its own sonar: “Project Tern will replace the Deepcast sonar in Project Sentinel” (document 09, the engineering blog).

Top-5 retrieval for the question:

Rank | Chunk | Cosine | What it contributes

1 | 10_brightwater_series_b-001 | 0.434 | “We cannot depend on a single outside supplier … Project Tern, our in-house sonar program, is the answer to that.” No supplier named.

2 | 09_kestrel_eng_blog_project_tern-000 | 0.326 | Fact 3: Tern replaces Deepcast sonar; “Deepcast units will no longer be available to us.” No reason given.

3 | 05_kestrel_blog_priya_nair-000 | 0.321 | Priya Nair's 2023 profile. Mentions Marlow Dynamics, as her former employer only.

4 | 02_brightwater_series_a-001 | 0.278 | Series A boilerplate; matches “Kestrel Labs”.

5 | 02_brightwater_series_a-000 | 0.240 | Series A announcement; matches “Kestrel Labs”.

The board memo's first chunk ranks 11th of 24. The Marlow acquisition article's best chunk ranks 21st of 24. A capable model given this context will write something like “Kestrel started Project Tern to stop depending on an outside sonar supplier after Deepcast units became unavailable.” That is fluent, cited and missing the actual cause. It is the worst kind of wrong answer: a plausible partial one.

[Interactive figure: Question 1 lands next to the effect, far from the cause (embedding-space)]

### Why the missing chunks score so low

After stopword removal the question is five words: kestrel, labs, start, project, tern. The Marlow article shares exactly one of them, labs, and only by accident: it never mentions Kestrel Labs or Project Tern at all. It is a story about a defense contractor buying a sonar maker. The board memo does share kestrel, labs, start, project, but its first chunk is 300 words of supply-chain detail, so those four words are a small part of its vector. It also never names the buyer: it says “Deepcast's change of ownership” and “the new owner”.

A neural embedder would rank the memo higher, since “sonar supply disruption and proposed response” is semantically close to “why start an in-house sonar project”. It would not rescue the Marlow article, because that article is not about Kestrel, Tern or why anyone started anything. The evidence for hop 1 resembles the evidence for hop 2, not the question. The link between them is a shared entity, Deepcast, and cosine similarity between the question and each chunk has no way to follow a shared entity.

[Diagram]

The dots are connected by an entity the question never names. Vector search scores each box against the question independently, so only the box on the right lights up. A graph stores the dashed links explicitly.

**Larson and Truitt, the GraphRAG announcement (2024)

The blog post that introduced GraphRAG named this failure directly: baseline RAG struggles to connect the dots when answering requires traversing disparate pieces of information through their shared attributes to produce new synthesized insights. The chain Marlow → Deepcast → Kestrel → Tern is that kind of traversal.

### Question 2: a fragile success

“Which investor's board member oversees the company whose drones detected the Halden Reef bleaching?” needs three hops: the bleaching was detected by Sentinel drones (document 06), Kestrel Labs runs Sentinel (document 04), and Lena Park of Brightwater Capital sits on Kestrel's board (document 02). Top-5 retrieval covers all three facts anyway: the research note ranks 1st, the Sentinel launch post 2nd, and at rank 4 the Series B press release contributes “Lena Park, partner at Brightwater Capital and a member of the Kestrel Labs board”, a sentence that sits in the same chunk as a mention of the 2024 bleaching event.

That is luck, not capability. Remove the Series B press release from the corpus and rerun the query: the top 5 become the research note, the launch post, Priya Nair's profile, the founding article and the research note again. The Series A release, the only other source of the board fact, ranks 11th. Nothing about the question changed; a redundant document disappeared. Vector RAG answers multi-hop questions reliably only when some document already states the connection in one place.

### Question 3: someone already connected the dots

“What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?” is answered almost entirely by the top-ranked chunk, the first part of the 2026 leadership interview. In it the host says Priya “joined in 2023 from Marlow Dynamics”, and Mira Okafor says “Marlow Dynamics bought Deepcast last year”. The Marlow article ranks 3rd. The retrieved context supports the chain Priya → Marlow → Deepcast. What is missing is the second path, Priya co-leads Project Tern, which replaces Deepcast sonar: the Tern blog ranks 7th.

The lesson generalizes. On real corpora, multi-hop questions often seem to work in demos because someone wrote a summary, an FAQ or an interview that connects the facts. The questions your users care about most are frequently the ones nobody has written up yet.

[Interactive figure: What vector search sees versus the paths the questions need (graph-steps)]

## Global questions: no chunk is about the whole corpus

### Question 4: “What are the main themes in this corpus?”

This question has no nearest neighbor. Its content words after tokenization are main, theme, corpu (the crude plural stripper eats the s of “corpus”). The best chunk scores 0.078; from rank 6 on, every chunk scores zero or slightly below. The “top 5” is noise: the Series A release twice, Priya Nair's profile, the Deepcast supply deal and the bleaching note, chosen because a word like “main” happens to appear.

A better embedder produces nonzero scores and a different noisy top 5, but it cannot fix the underlying problem. The reference answer names four themes: reef science and monitoring; supply-chain risk and vertical integration; funding and growth; regulation creating demand. Evidence for them is spread over eight documents. No single chunk is about “themes”, and five chunks cannot cover eight documents. Even with perfect ranking, the model would see a sample and summarize the sample.

**Edge et al., From Local to Global (2024)

The GraphRAG paper frames questions like “What are the main themes in the dataset?” as query-focused summarization (QFS) over an entire corpus, a sensemaking task rather than a lookup. It argues that RAG fails on such global questions because they are not answered by retrieving a few relevant records, and proposes community summaries built at indexing time and combined with map-reduce at query time. You will build that pipeline in Chapters 11, 12 and 15.

### Question 5: “What risks does Kestrel Labs face?”

This one sits between local and global. There is a chunk about risk, and retrieval finds it: the 2022 Deepcast supply deal (rank 4) quotes an analyst on single-source components. But the full answer is spread across four documents written over four years: that 2022 analysis, the Marlow acquisition in 2025 (rank 19), the board memo calling supply “the most serious operational risk” (rank 9), and the 2026 interview in which the CEO lists execution risk on Tern, competition from Marlow, dependence on the Ocean Health Act and concentration on one reef and one partner (rank 10). Top-5 context yields a one-risk answer. The chunks that list the most risks rank 9th and 10th because the question's other words, “Kestrel Labs”, are everywhere in the corpus and dominate the similarity.

Question type | What “relevant” means | Why top-k struggles

Local lookup (Q7) | One or two chunks that state the fact | It usually does not

Multi-hop (Q1–Q3) | A set of chunks linked by shared entities | Later hops do not resemble the question

Aggregative (Q5) | Every chunk that contributes one item to a list | Items are scattered; k caps how many can appear

Global sensemaking (Q4) | The corpus as a whole, summarized | No chunk is about the whole; no ranking helps

## Lost relationships: aliases, split facts, stale facts and dilution

### Aliases and indirect references

The same entity appears under different surface forms, and some references never use a name at all:

- The bleaching research note says “the Sentinel program” and “Sentinel drones”, never “Project Sentinel” and never “Kestrel Labs”.

- The council minutes call Tidewater Institute “TWI” and Kestrel's CEO “the vendor's CEO”.

- The board memo calls Marlow Dynamics “the new owner”. No embedding model can resolve that without reading another document.

- The 2026 interview says “Tern”, “Okafor”, “Vehl” and “Nair”.

Neural embedders handle easy aliases (“TWI” near “Tidewater” may or may not work, depending on the model). Coreference across documents, such as “the new owner” meaning Marlow Dynamics, needs the fact to be resolved once, at indexing time, and stored. That is what entity extraction and resolution do in Chapters 8 and 9.

### Facts split across chunk boundaries

With 120-word chunks, the Series B press release is cut in the middle of Okafor's quote. Chunk 10_brightwater_series_b-002 ends mid-sentence: “Project Tern, our in-house sonar program, is the”. Chunk -003 starts 20 words earlier, at “outside supplier for the most important part of our drones,” and carries the quote through “is the answer to that”, but it has lost the opening “Spring 2025 taught us that we cannot depend on a single”. One vector holds the cause without the conclusion; the other holds the conclusion without its time anchor. And neither names the supplier, which appears only in other documents. Overlap protects short facts; it cannot protect relationships that span more than the overlap.

The effect on question 1 is stark. Count a fact as present when any retrieved chunk states it, whichever document it comes from:

Chunk size (overlap) | Units | k = 3 | k = 5 | k = 10

300 words (50) | 24 | 2 of 3 facts | 2 of 3 | 3 of 3

120 words (20) | 58 | 0 of 3 | 0 of 3 | 0 of 3

60 words (10) | 111 | 0 of 3 | 0 of 3 | 0 of 3

At 300 words, k = 3 already gives two facts, both from the Tern blog's first chunk: Tern replaces the Deepcast sonar, and Deepcast units are no longer available. The third arrives at k = 10, and not from the acquisition article, which is still 21st. It comes from the 2026 interview at rank 6, where Okafor mentions in passing that “Marlow Dynamics bought Deepcast last year”. At 120 words, even ten chunks contain none of the three: the top ranks go to fragments of the Series B and Series A releases, the Sentinel launch post and Priya Nair's profile, which repeat “Kestrel Labs” and “Project”, plus the Tern blog's first fragment, which announces the project and stops before the sentence about Deepcast (that sentence is in the blog's third fragment, at rank 18). Smaller chunks sharpen single-fact matching and shred multi-fact reasoning.

### Stale facts

Question 6, “Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?”, retrieves the 2026 interview chunk at rank 5, which says Priya Nair has been CTO since March 2026. At rank 6 comes the 2022 supply deal article, which calls Jonas Vehl the chief technology officer, and the 2021 founding article and the 2025 board memo say the same. Cosine similarity has no notion of time: an old statement of a fact scores as high as a new one, and more old statements mean more chances to outrank the new one. With k = 5 a careful model reads the datelines carried by each document's first chunk and answers correctly. With a slightly different embedder, or k = 6 and a less careful model, it answers “Jonas Vehl”. Question 15 in questions.jsonl, “Who was the CTO when the bleaching event was detected?”, needs time-aware reasoning on purpose. Temporal facts are the subject of Chapter 10 and Chapter 27.

### Top-k dilution

Two kinds of noise crowd the top-k. Redundancy: overlapping chunks of the same document, like the two Series B chunks at ranks 2 and 3 for question 7, spend two slots on one piece of evidence. Hub words: “Kestrel Labs” appears in almost every document, so any question that names Kestrel rewards chunks that repeat the name, which is why the Series A boilerplate keeps appearing in the top 5 for questions 1, 5 and 6.

The instinctive fix is a bigger k. Chapter 2's smoke test showed multi-hop recall rising from 0.60 at k = 5 to 0.88 at k = 10. But on this corpus k = 10 means reading 42% of all chunks, precision drops, the evidence that matters lands in the middle of a long context, and on a corpus of 100,000 chunks the same k would still be a tiny sample. Raising k converts a retrieval problem into a long-context problem; it does not solve it.

## Partial fixes: rewriting, decomposition and iterative retrieval

Before graphs, the RAG community attacked multi-hop failures by making retrieval a loop. Self-Ask (Press et al., 2022) prompts the model to ask itself follow-up questions. IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2022) interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought, using each reasoning step as the next query. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) generalizes this to tool use. The shared idea: read what you retrieved, notice the bridge entity, and search for it.

[Interactive figure: Iterative retrieval on question 1 (flow)]

The numbers in that animation are real hashing-embedder results. Iterative retrieval works here. A reference implementation looks like this:

```python  # examples/ch03_iterative.py
from minigraphrag.context import format_table
from minigraphrag.search.common import generate_answer

FOLLOW_UP_PROMPT = """You are answering a question by searching a document collection one query at a time.

Question: {question}

Evidence so far:
{evidence}

If the evidence fully answers the question, reply with exactly DONE.
Otherwise reply with ONE short search query for the most important missing fact.
Use specific names that appear in the evidence."""

def iterative_search(index, question: str, llm, max_hops: int = 3, k: int = 3):
    seen: list[str] = []
    query, calls = question, 0
    for hop in range(max_hops):
        qvec = index.embedder.embed([query])[0]
        for unit_id, _, _ in index.text_unit_store.search(qvec, k=k):
            if unit_id not in seen:
                seen.append(unit_id)
        if hop == max_hops - 1:
            break
        evidence = "\n---\n".join(index.text_units[u].text[:800] for u in seen)
        reply = llm.complete(FOLLOW_UP_PROMPT.format(question=question, evidence=evidence)).strip()
        calls += 1
        if not reply or reply.upper().startswith("DONE"):
            break
        query = reply.splitlines()[0]
    context = format_table("Sources", ["id", "text"], [[u, index.text_units[u].text] for u in seen])
    return generate_answer(llm, question, context), seen, calls + 1
```

This needs a real model: MockLLM does not recognize the follow-up prompt and replies OK, which becomes a useless query. Exercise 3.3 shows how to test the loop offline with scripted follow-ups.

### Why iterative retrieval is only a partial fix

Limitation | What happens on Kestrel

The model must spot the bridge entity in raw text | Hop 1 must surface a chunk that names Deepcast. If the Series B chunk alone had been retrieved (“a single outside supplier”), there would be no name to follow.

Errors compound | A bad follow-up (“Kestrel Labs sonar history”) retrieves the 2022 supply deal and another Series B chunk, and the loop drifts. Each hop multiplies the chance of going off track.

Cost and latency scale with hops | Each hop adds an embedding call, a search and an LLM call that reads the growing evidence. Latency grows roughly with the number of hops, and each LLM call reads a longer context than the last.

Aliases still break queries | A follow-up for “who owns Deepcast now?” works; a follow-up built from the memo's “the new owner” does not.

Global questions do not decompose | “Main themes” has no natural follow-up query. Covering eight documents by hopping means reading most of the corpus, one slow step at a time.

Nothing is learned | The link Marlow → Deepcast → Kestrel is rediscovered, at full cost, for every user who asks a related question.

GraphRAG moves that work from query time to indexing time. Entities and relationships are extracted once, aliases are resolved once, communities are summarized once. At query time, following a bridge entity is a dictionary lookup instead of an LLM call. Iterative, agentic retrieval does not disappear; in Chapter 18 and Chapter 30 the agent walks a graph instead of guessing search strings.

## A failure taxonomy and the GraphRAG toolbox

Here is every failure from this chapter, what causes it, and where in the course it gets fixed.

Failure | Kestrel symptom | Root cause | GraphRAG technique | Chapters

Missing bridge evidence (multi-hop) | Q1 retrieves Tern's effect, not Marlow's acquisition (rank 21) | Chunks scored independently against the question | Entity-relationship graph; neighborhood expansion from query entities; Personalized PageRank; path retrieval | 8, 14, 17, 18

Global sensemaking | Q4 top 5 is noise; evidence spans 8 documents | No chunk is about the whole corpus | Community detection, community reports, map-reduce global search, hierarchical summaries | 11, 12, 15

Aggregation | Q5 gets one risk out of five | k caps how many list items can appear | Entity-centric context tables; claims; community-level answers | 10, 14, 15

Aliases and coreference | “Sentinel program”, “TWI”, “the new owner” | Different surface forms for one entity | Extraction with descriptions; entity resolution and merging | 8, 9

Split relationships | “Spring 2025” and “Project Tern” in different 120-word chunks | Chunk boundaries cut sentences and paragraphs | Relationships as first-class records with provenance; text units sized for extraction | 7, 8

Stale facts | Q6: 2022 “CTO Jonas Vehl” competes with 2026 “Priya is our CTO” | Similarity ignores time | Claims with dates; bi-temporal edges; as-of queries | 10, 27

Top-k dilution | Duplicate Series B chunks; Series A boilerplate on “Kestrel Labs” | Similarity rewards repetition and hub words | Token-budgeted context across entities, relations and sources; reranking; hybrid fusion | 14, 21, 22

Vocabulary mismatch | “CTO” vs. “chief technology officer” scores 0 with hashing | Lexical embedder; or exact names blurred by neural ones | Neural embeddings plus BM25 with rank fusion; entity-name matching | 2, 21

Unexplainable answers | A correct answer to Q1 cannot show the chain it used | Context is a bag of chunks, not a path | Path-based context and provenance for every hop | 18, 21, 23

**GraphRAG is not free, and not always better

Every fix in the right-hand columns costs indexing time and LLM calls, adds components that can fail, and can lose to vector RAG on simple lookups like question 7. The goal for the rest of the course is to know which failures your questions hit and to pay only for the techniques that fix them. Chapter 25 and Chapter 26 make that trade-off measurable.

#### Exercise 3.1 Warm-up

For question 1, by hand: (a) list the bridge entity between each consecutive pair of the three evidence documents (07, 08, 09); (b) using the tokenized question kestrel, labs, start, project, tern, state which of those words each of the three documents contains, and explain why the memo still ranks only 11th.

▸ Show answer

(a) 07 → 08: Deepcast (acquired in 07; will not renew in 08). 08 → 09: Deepcast again (its sonar is what Tern replaces), plus the in-house sonar module the memo proposes, which becomes Project Tern. Document 08 never names the project; it only proposes “a dedicated internal engineering project”. Linking the proposal to Tern relies on the blog's dates and its statement that Deepcast units are no longer available. The 07 → 08 link also requires resolving “the new owner” to Marlow Dynamics.

(b) Document 07 contains only labs, and that only by coincidence (“university labs”). Document 08 contains kestrel, labs, start, project. Document 09 contains kestrel, labs, project, tern.

The memo shares four of five words yet ranks 11th because cosine similarity normalizes by vector length. The memo's first chunk has 300 words of supply-chain detail, so the four shared words are a small fraction of its vector. Short, name-dense chunks such as the Series A boilerplate, which repeats “Kestrel Labs” many times, point more directly at a question that says “Kestrel Labs”. #### Exercise 3.2 Core

Test how fragile question 2's success is. Build the Chapter 2 index twice: once on the full corpus and once without 10_brightwater_series_b. For each, print the top 5 for question 2 and check whether any retrieved chunk says Lena Park sits on Kestrel's board. Then find the rank of the best chunk from 02_brightwater_series_a in the reduced index.

▸ Show answer

```python
import re
from ch02_vector_rag import VectorIndex
from minigraphrag.chunking import chunk_documents, load_documents
from minigraphrag.embeddings import HashingEmbedder
from minigraphrag.vector_store import VectorStore

Q2 = "Which investor's board member oversees the company whose drones detected the Halden Reef bleaching?"
BOARD = re.compile(r"Lena Park[^.]*board")

def index_from(docs, emb):
    units = chunk_documents(docs, 300, 50)
    store = VectorStore()
    store.add([u.id for u in units], emb.embed([u.text for u in units]), [{"doc_id": u.doc_id} for u in units])
    return VectorIndex({u.id: u for u in units}, store, emb)

emb = HashingEmbedder()
docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
for name, subset in [("full", docs), ("without doc 10", {k: v for k, v in docs.items() if k != "10_brightwater_series_b"})]:
    idx = index_from(subset, emb)
    ranked = idx.text_unit_store.search(emb.embed([Q2])[0], k=len(idx.text_units))
    top5 = [uid for uid, _, _ in ranked[:5]]
    has_board = any(BOARD.search(" ".join(idx.text_units[u].text.split())) for u in top5)
    series_a = next(r + 1 for r, (uid, _, _) in enumerate(ranked) if uid.startswith("02_"))
    print(name, top5, "board fact:", has_board, "best Series A rank:", series_a)
```

Full corpus: top 5 are 06-000, 04-000, 05-001, 10-000, 01-000; the board fact is present (from 10-000). Without document 10: 06-000, 04-000, 05-001, 01-000, 06-001; no board fact. The best Series A chunk ranks 11th of 22.

Interpretation: the “investor” hop is only reachable when some chunk happens to mention the board next to words from the question (drones, bleaching, Halden Reef). The Series A release is about funding in 2022, before Sentinel existed, so it shares almost nothing with the question even though it holds the needed fact. A graph answers the question with the same three hops either way, because the edge Lena Park → board member of → Kestrel Labs exists regardless of which document stated it.

#### Exercise 3.3 Core

Run iterative_search on question 1 offline by writing a ScriptedLLM that returns a fixed list of follow-up queries and then DONE, and delegates the final answer to MockLLM. Try two scripts: a good follow-up (“Why are Deepcast sonar units no longer available?”) and a vague one (“Kestrel Labs sonar history”). For each, report the retrieved chunk ids and which of the three facts they contain.

▸ Hint

Distinguish the follow-up prompt from the answer prompt by a phrase only the follow-up prompt contains, such as “one query at a time”.

▸ Show answer

```python
from ch02_vector_rag import build_vector_index
from ch03_iterative import iterative_search
from minigraphrag.embeddings import HashingEmbedder
from minigraphrag.llm import MockLLM

class ScriptedLLM:
    def __init__(self, follow_ups):
        self.follow_ups, self.mock = list(follow_ups), MockLLM()
    def complete(self, prompt, system=None, json=False):
        if "one query at a time" in prompt:
            return self.follow_ups.pop(0) if self.follow_ups else "DONE"
        return self.mock.complete(prompt, system=system, json=json)

FACTS = {"Marlow acquired Deepcast": "07_marlow_acquires_deepcast",
         "Deepcast ends supply": "08_kestrel_board_memo_supply",
         "Tern replaces Deepcast sonar": "09_kestrel_eng_blog_project_tern"}
index = build_vector_index("data/corpus", HashingEmbedder())
q1 = "Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?"
for script in (["Why are Deepcast sonar units no longer available?"], ["Kestrel Labs sonar history"]):
    answer, seen, calls = iterative_search(index, q1, ScriptedLLM(script), max_hops=3, k=3)
    found = [f for f, doc in FACTS.items() if any(u.startswith(doc) for u in seen)]
    print(script[0], seen, found, calls)
```

Good follow-up. Hop 1 retrieves 10_brightwater_series_b-001, 09_kestrel_eng_blog_project_tern-000, 05_kestrel_blog_priya_nair-000. Hop 2 adds 08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-000 and 07_marlow_acquires_deepcast-000 (the Tern chunk is already seen). The script then returns DONE. All three facts are present, from five chunks and three LLM calls in total (two follow-up decisions and the answer). Coverage is document-level here: check that 07-000 actually contains the acquisition sentence, which it does.

Vague follow-up. Hop 2 adds 03_deepcast_supply_agreement-000 and 10_brightwater_series_b-000: the 2022 supply deal and more of the Series B release. Only the Tern fact is present; the memo and the Marlow article stay out of reach, at the same cost of three LLM calls. A query made of hub words (“Kestrel Labs”, “sonar”) is pulled toward the same chunks as the original question. The quality of iterative retrieval is the quality of its follow-up queries, and a vague follow-up is no better than raising k.

#### Exercise 3.4 Core

Classify these questions from questions.jsonl using the failure taxonomy: which failures would vector RAG hit, and which GraphRAG technique would you reach for first? (q15) “Who was the CTO of Kestrel Labs when the Halden Reef bleaching event was detected?” (q17) “Why did the Port Avalon City Council contract Kestrel Labs?” (q19) “Which investor led Kestrel's funding both before and after the Deepcast supply disruption, and how much did those rounds total?” (q23) “Summarize the relationship between Kestrel Labs and Tidewater Institute.”

▸ Show answer

Question | Failures | First technique

q15 CTO at bleaching time | Multi-hop (event date, then role at that date) and stale facts: the 2026 “Priya is CTO” chunk looks most similar to “CTO” but is the wrong time | Temporal claims with validity intervals, then an as-of lookup at August 2024 (Chapter 10)

q17 Why the council contract | Multi-hop across the council minutes and the Series B release (Ocean Health Act passed July 2025, requires quarterly monitoring); “Why” questions match the effect document better than the cause | Local search from the entities Port Avalon City Council and Kestrel Labs, expanding to the Ocean Health Act (Chapter 14)

Notice that almost no real question hits exactly one failure. That is why GraphRAG systems combine techniques, and why Chapter 21 exists.

#### Exercise 3.5 Stretch

Build a poor man's graph without an LLM: for each chunk, find entity mentions with minigraphrag.llm.find_mentions (the mock's gazetteer). Retrieve the top 3 chunks, collect the entities they mention (excluding entities named in the question), and add the 4 other chunks that share the most of those entities. Compare supporting-document recall with plain top-7 at the same budget of 7 chunks. Then weight shared entities by inverse document frequency, log(N / df), and compare again. Does question 1 now retrieve the Marlow article?

▸ Show answer

```python
import collections, json, math
from ch02_vector_rag import build_vector_index
from minigraphrag.embeddings import HashingEmbedder
from minigraphrag.llm import find_mentions

index = build_vector_index("data/corpus", HashingEmbedder())
store, units = index.text_unit_store, index.text_units
mentions = {uid: {m[2].upper() for m in find_mentions(u.text)} for uid, u in units.items()}
df = collections.Counter(e for ents in mentions.values() for e in ents)
N = len(units)

def expand(question, k=3, extra=4, idf=False):
    qvec = index.embedder.embed([question])[0]
    seeds = [uid for uid, _, _ in store.search(qvec, k)]
    q_ents = {m[2].upper() for m in find_mentions(question)}
    bridge = set().union(*(mentions[s] for s in seeds)) - q_ents
    weight = (lambda e: math.log(N / df[e])) if idf else (lambda e: 1.0)
    score = {uid: sum(weight(e) for e in mentions[uid] & bridge) for uid in units if uid not in seeds}
    extra_ids = sorted((u for u in score if score[u] > 0), key=lambda u: -score[u])[:extra]
    return seeds + extra_ids

def recall(fn):
    by_type = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for q in map(json.loads, open("data/questions.jsonl")):
        got = {units[u].doc_id for u in fn(q["question"])}
        need = set(q["supporting_docs"])
        by_type[q["type"]].append(len(got & need) / len(need))
    return {t: round(sum(v) / len(v), 2) for t, v in by_type.items()}

print("top-7 ", recall(lambda q: [u for u, _, _ in store.search(index.embedder.embed([q])[0], 7)]))
print("expand", recall(expand))
print("idf   ", recall(lambda q: expand(q, idf=True)))
print(expand("Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?", idf=True))
```

Method (7 chunks) | Single-hop | Temporal | Multi-hop | Global

Plain top-7 | 0.80 | 0.77 | 0.69 | 0.39

Top-3 + co-mention expansion | 0.80 | 0.67 | 0.73 | 0.41

Top-3 + IDF-weighted expansion | 0.80 | 0.67 | 0.77 | 0.46

Multi-hop recall improves from 0.69 to 0.77 at the same chunk budget, and global recall rises a little. Temporal recall drops, because expansion displaces lower-ranked but directly relevant chunks.

Question 1 still does not retrieve the Marlow article. The expanded set is 10-001, 09-000, 05-000 plus 12-001, 12-000, 10-000, 08-000: the memo arrives, the acquisition article does not. The seeds mention seventeen bridge entities, most of them common (Port Avalon, Sentinel, Jonas Vehl and Halden Reef each appear in 13 or 14 of the 24 chunks), and chunks that mention many of them outrank the Marlow article, which shares only Deepcast, Marlow and Marlow Dynamics with the seeds, the last two being one company the gazetteer has not merged. With IDF weights it scores 4.3; the weakest chunk that made the cut scores 5.2. IDF helps but cannot overcome a pile of moderately common entities.

What this tells you about the design of real GraphRAG: linking chunks by co-mention is too coarse. You want entities as nodes with typed, described relationships (Marlow Dynamics —acquired→ Deepcast), retrieval that starts from the entities the question names, and scoring that spreads relevance along edges while discounting hubs. That is local search (Chapter 14) and Personalized PageRank (Chapter 17).

Why does the Marlow acquisition article rank 21st of 24 for “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?”

- The article is too long to embed

- The hashing embedder has too few dimensions

Vector RAG answered question 2 at k = 5. What made that possible?
