## Text units and document structure

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/07-chunking-text-units.html
Summary: Chunk size trade-offs for extraction, overlap, structure-aware splitting and provenance ids.

# Text units and document structure

Every entity, relationship and citation in a GraphRAG index points back to a text unit, so the way you cut documents decides what the extractor can see, what the index costs, and whether re-indexing is repeatable. This chapter builds the chunking layer of minigraphrag and the provenance and metadata that ride along with it.

## You will be able to

- Explain why chunking for LLM extraction has different goals from chunking for vector search

- Compute the number of chunks, duplicated tokens and extraction calls for a given size, overlap and gleaning setting

- Use chunk_fixed, chunk_by_sentences and chunk_documents, and add structure-aware splitting on markdown headings

- Design provenance ids that stay stable across re-indexing, and reason about what breaks them

- Carry document metadata such as title, date and section into every unit's extraction prompt

## Why chunking for extraction is different

You chunked documents in Chapter 2 for vector search. There, a chunk is a retrieval target: it gets one embedding, and the goal is that a question's embedding lands near the chunk that answers it. Chunks that mix topics blur their embeddings, so vector RAG prefers small, focused chunks.

In GraphRAG the chunk has a second, more expensive job: it is the input to an extraction call (Chapter 8). The LLM reads the text unit once and writes down every entity and relationship it can find. That changes what “good” means:

Concern | Chunking for vector search | Chunking for graph extraction

Unit's role | A retrieval target with one embedding | An LLM input that produces many records, and later a citation

Main failure | Diluted embedding: the chunk is about several things | Missed entities in long inputs; relationships split across a boundary; pronouns without antecedents

Size pressure | Small enough to be topically focused | Small enough for high recall, large enough to keep both ends of a relationship together

Cost per unit | One embedding, cheap | One or more LLM calls with long structured output

Context outside the chunk | Rarely needed at indexing time | Needed for title, date and section references such as “the company” and “last month”

Identity | Nice to have | Required: every entity and edge stores the ids of units it came from

Here is the tension in one sentence from the Kestrel board memo (document 08): “The notice follows Deepcast's change of ownership last month; the new owner intends to reserve its production for internal programs.” The relationship “Deepcast stopped supplying Kestrel because of its new owner” needs the previous sentence (which says Deepcast will not renew our supply agreement), the memo's author (Kestrel's CEO) and its date (14 May 2025, so “last month” is April 2025). A chunk boundary in the wrong place, or a chunk stripped of its document header, loses the edge.

### The chunk size and recall trade-off

Two forces pull in opposite directions.

- Smaller units raise recall. LLMs asked to list everything in a long passage tend to stop early and skip facts, especially toward the end. Each extra unit is another fresh look at the text.

- Larger units keep relationships together and cost less. A relationship can only be extracted if both entities and the sentence connecting them are in the same unit. Fewer units also means fewer calls and fewer repeated prompt tokens.
**Edge et al., From Local to Global (2024)

The GraphRAG paper examined this trade-off directly. On HotPotQA, GPT-4 extracted almost twice as many entity references from 600-token chunks as from 2400-token chunks in a single pass (Appendix A.2 of the paper), and the extra self-reflection passes the paper calls gleaning let the larger chunks catch up. Smaller chunks and gleaning are two ways to buy the same recall, and both cost LLM calls. The paper does not give a universal best size; you measure it on your corpus (Exercise 8.3 does exactly that).

Recall is not the only quality signal. Very small units produce many duplicate mentions that entity resolution must merge (Chapter 9), and they give each extraction so little context that descriptions become thin. In practice, a few hundred to about a thousand tokens is the common range for extraction, and minigraphrag's default, 300 words with 50 words of overlap (roughly 400 tokens), sits at the small end because the Kestrel documents are short and fact-dense.

## Fixed-size chunking with overlap

The simplest chunker slides a window of S units over the text and advances by the stride S − O, where O is the overlap. Consecutive windows share exactly O units, so a fact that straddles one boundary is fully contained in at least one window, as long as it is no longer than O.

minigraphrag measures windows in whitespace-delimited words, not tokenizer tokens. Words keep the code dependency-free and make start and end exact character offsets into the original document. Each unit still records its token count via count_tokens, which uses tiktoken when installed and otherwise estimates 4 tokens per 3 words. Microsoft GraphRAG counts in tokenizer tokens; the math is identical.

[Diagram]

chunk_fixed(text, size=300, overlap=50) on a 455-word article. The second window reaches the end of the document, so the loop stops there. Word ranges are drawn to scale.

### How many chunks?

For a document of N words, window size S and overlap O (with O < S), windows start at 0, S − O, 2(S − O), and so on, and the chunker stops at the first window that reaches the end. That window starts at k(S − O) with k(S − O) + S ≥ N, so:

chunks(N) = max(1, ⌈(N − O) / (S − O)⌉) for N > 0

For doc 07 with S = 300, O = 50: ⌈405 / 250⌉ = ⌈1.62⌉ = 2. With S = 100, O = 20: ⌈435 / 80⌉ = ⌈5.44⌉ = 6.

Two consequences are easy to miss:

- Chunking is per document. The Kestrel corpus has 5,427 words. Treated as one long text, it would give ⌈5377 / 250⌉ = 22 chunks. Chunked per document, as chunk_documents does, every one of the 12 documents (all between 395 and 492 words) yields 2 chunks, so 24. Never let a window cross a document boundary: a unit that mixes the end of a press release with the start of council minutes invents co-occurrences.

- Overlap multiplies tokens. Roughly O / S of every full window is repeated text, so you pay for it twice in extraction. On Kestrel at 300/50, the 24 units total 8,039 estimated tokens against 7,241 for the documents themselves, 11% more. At 100/20 it is 8,824, or 22% more. Overlap also means the same relationship is extracted twice, which resolution must merge.

Try it on a passage from the board memo. Watch where boundaries fall relative to “the new owner” and the bullet list, and how much text overlap duplicates.

[Interactive figure: Fixed windows over the board memo — Document 08, sections 1 and 2 (192 words) (chunker)]

### The implementation

```python  # minigraphrag/chunking.py
@dataclass
class TextUnit:
    """A chunk of a source document; the unit of extraction and of citation."""

    id: str
    doc_id: str
    text: str
    n_tokens: int
    start: int  # character offset (inclusive) in the document
    end: int  # character offset (exclusive)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return asdict(self)


def chunk_fixed(text: str, size: int = 300, overlap: int = 50, doc_id: str = "doc") -> list[TextUnit]:
    """Sliding window of `size` words that advances by `size - overlap` words.

    With stride = size - overlap, consecutive chunks share exactly `overlap`
    words, and a document of N words yields ceil((N - overlap) / stride) chunks.
    """
    if overlap >= size:
        raise ValueError("overlap must be smaller than size")
    spans = [(m.start(), m.end()) for m in re.finditer(r"\S+", text)]
    if not spans:
        return []
    stride = size - overlap
    units: list[TextUnit] = []
    for i, first in enumerate(range(0, len(spans), stride)):
        window = spans[first : first + size]
        start, end = window[0][0], window[-1][1]
        piece = text[start:end]
        units.append(TextUnit(f"{doc_id}-{i:03d}", doc_id, piece, count_tokens(piece), start, end))
        if first + size >= len(spans):  # this window reached the end of the document
            break
    return units
```

Three details are worth copying into any chunker you write:

- Offsets as well as text. re.finditer(r"\S+") records where each word starts and ends, so text[unit.start:unit.end] == unit.text always holds. Citations can highlight the exact span in the source, and ids can be derived from positions.

- The early break. Without if first + size >= len(spans): break, the loop would emit extra trailing windows that are strict subsets of the last full one: pure duplicate cost.

- The guard. overlap >= size would make the stride zero or negative, an infinite loop or a crash.

Running it on doc 07 shows the weakness of fixed windows: unit 07_marlow_acquires_deepcast-000 ends with “…defense contractors, which have been snapping”, cut mid-sentence. The overlap rescues that sentence in unit 001, but the extractor reading unit 000 sees a fragment and may invent something to complete it.

## Respecting sentences and structure

### Sentence-aware packing

The fix for mid-sentence cuts is to split the text into sentences first, then pack whole sentences into units up to a token budget. Overlap is measured in sentences instead of words.

```python  # minigraphrag/chunking.py
_ABBREVIATIONS = ("Dr.", "Mr.", "Mrs.", "Ms.", "Prof.", "St.", "vs.", "e.g.", "i.e.", "Inc.")


def split_sentences(text: str) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Return (start, end) character spans of sentences, also breaking at newlines.

    Deliberately simple: split after . ! ? followed by whitespace, except after
    common abbreviations, so "Dr. Mira Okafor" stays in one sentence.
    """
    spans, start = [], 0
    for m in re.finditer(r"[.!?]+(?=\s)|\n", text):
        end = m.end()
        if m.group() != "\n" and text[:end].endswith(_ABBREVIATIONS):
            continue
        if text[start:end].strip():
            spans.append((start, end))
        start = end
    if text[start:].strip():
        spans.append((start, len(text)))
    return spans


def chunk_by_sentences(
    text: str, max_tokens: int = 300, overlap_sentences: int = 1, doc_id: str = "doc"
) -> list[TextUnit]:
    """Pack whole sentences into chunks of at most `max_tokens`."""
    sents = split_sentences(text)
    units: list[TextUnit] = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(sents):
        j, tokens = i, 0
        while j < len(sents):
            t = count_tokens(text[sents[j][0] : sents[j][1]])
            if j > i and tokens + t > max_tokens:
                break
            tokens += t
            j += 1
        start, end = sents[i][0], sents[j - 1][1]
        piece = text[start:end].strip()
        units.append(TextUnit(f"{doc_id}-{len(units):03d}", doc_id, piece, count_tokens(piece), start, end))
        if j >= len(sents):
            break
        i = max(i + 1, j - overlap_sentences)
    return units
```

Read the packing loop carefully, because each line encodes a decision:

- if j > i and tokens + t > max_tokens: a unit always takes at least one sentence, even if that sentence alone exceeds the budget. Otherwise a single 400-token sentence would loop forever. The budget is therefore a soft limit.

- i = max(i + 1, j - overlap_sentences): the next unit starts overlap_sentences back from where this one ended, but always makes progress by at least one sentence.

- The text is stripped, but start and end keep the sentence spans' exact boundaries, which may include a leading space or newline. Use the offsets for highlighting and the text for prompts.

On doc 07 with max_tokens=150, this produces 5 units of 110 to 147 tokens, each ending at a sentence boundary. Across the corpus, chunk_documents(docs, 150, method="sentences") gives 65 units ranging from 31 to 148 tokens: the uneven sizes are the price of clean boundaries. For this method, chunk_documents passes size as max_tokens, so the same number means words for fixed chunking and tokens for sentence chunking.

**Sentence splitting is harder than it looks

The simple splitter handles “Dr. Mira Okafor” through its abbreviation list, but it still splits the doc 07 dateline “Maritime Industry Journal, Deals. 17 April 2025.” into two pieces, and it would split “U.S. Navy” or “Kestrel Labs Inc. and Marlow” wherever the abbreviation is not listed. For extraction this is usually harmless, because packing puts the pieces back in the same unit. For languages other than English or for legal and scientific text, use a trained splitter such as spaCy's or NLTK's Punkt, and keep the same packing loop.

### Structure-aware splitting

Documents are not flat streams of sentences. The Kestrel corpus is markdown: the board memo has numbered sections (“1. What happened”, “3. Options considered”), the Project Tern blog post has a bullet list of technical goals and a numbered timeline, and the Series A press release has a key-value list (“Amount: $12 million”, “Lead investor: Brightwater Capital”). Authors put boundaries there on purpose. A structure-aware chunker uses them:

- Never cross a section boundary. Split on headings first, so a unit never mixes “Options considered” with “Recommendation”.

- Keep small sections whole. If a section fits the budget, it is one unit, however short.

- Pack long sections by sentence. Within a long section, fall back to sentence packing.

- Keep blocks intact. A list item or table row is a line; the sentence splitter breaks at newlines, so packing keeps items whole. Tables need more: when a table is split, repeat its header row in every unit, or the extractor sees rows of numbers without column names.

- Remember the heading path. Store “Memo to the Board > 3. Options considered” as metadata for the unit; it is often the only place the topic is named.

[Diagram]

Fixed windows ignore the memo's structure; unit 000 stops mid-sentence in option B (“…signal-processing boards. Jonas”) and unit 001 starts inside option A. The structure-aware chunker below aligns units with sections and splits only section 2, which is over budget, repeating one sentence of overlap between its two parts. Token counts are the package's word-based estimates.

minigraphrag does not ship a markdown chunker, so here is one built on its pieces. It returns ordinary TextUnits with document-level offsets, plus the heading path for each.

```python  # examples/ch07_structure.py
import re
from dataclasses import replace

from minigraphrag.chunking import TextUnit, chunk_by_sentences
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

HEADING_RE = re.compile(r"^(#{1,6})\s+(.+?)\s*$", re.M)


def split_markdown_sections(text: str) -> list[tuple[list[str], int, int]]:
    """Return (heading_path, start, end) for each section of a markdown document."""
    marks = [(m.start(), len(m.group(1)), m.group(2)) for m in HEADING_RE.finditer(text)]
    if not marks or marks[0][0] > 0:
        marks.insert(0, (0, 0, ""))                      # text before the first heading
    sections, path = [], []
    for i, (start, level, title) in enumerate(marks):
        end = marks[i + 1][0] if i + 1 < len(marks) else len(text)
        if level:
            path = path[: level - 1] + [title]           # a level-2 heading replaces the old level-2 title
        if text[start:end].strip():
            sections.append((list(path), start, end))
    return sections


def chunk_markdown(text: str, doc_id: str, max_tokens: int = 300) -> list[tuple[TextUnit, list[str]]]:
    """Never cross a section boundary; pack sentences within long sections."""
    out = []
    for path, s_start, s_end in split_markdown_sections(text):
        section = text[s_start:s_end]
        if count_tokens(section) <= max_tokens:
            pieces = [TextUnit("", doc_id, section.strip(), count_tokens(section.strip()), s_start, s_end)]
        else:
            pieces = [replace(u, start=u.start + s_start, end=u.end + s_start)   # section offsets -> document offsets
                      for u in chunk_by_sentences(section, max_tokens, overlap_sentences=1, doc_id=doc_id)]
        for u in pieces:
            out.append((replace(u, id=f"{doc_id}-{len(out):03d}"), path))
    return out
```

On the memo with max_tokens=150 it yields the seven units in the diagram. Over the whole corpus at 300 tokens it yields 54 units, compared with 24 fixed windows: many Kestrel sections are short, and keeping them separate multiplies calls. A common refinement is to merge adjacent small sections under the same parent until the budget is reached. Exercise 7.3 puts a price on the difference.

### Semantic chunking

Semantic chunking puts boundaries where the topic changes, detected from embeddings rather than markup. The usual recipe: embed each sentence, compute the cosine similarity between each sentence and the next (or between sliding groups of sentences), and cut where similarity drops sharply, for example below a low percentile of all adjacent similarities. Then pack the resulting segments to the size budget.

It helps with long unstructured text, such as interview transcripts like the Kestrel podcast in doc 12, where one speaker moves from the Deepcast shock to the new CTO without a heading. The costs: an embedding per sentence, a threshold to tune per corpus and embedder, and boundaries that change whenever you change embedding models, which also changes every unit id downstream. For well-structured documents, headings are a better and free signal. Exercise 7.4 builds a semantic chunker.

Strategy | Boundaries | Unit sizes | Extra cost | Best for

Fixed windows with overlap | Arbitrary, may cut sentences | Uniform | None | Baselines, uniform prose, strict cost planning

Sentence packing | Sentence ends | Uneven, under a soft budget | Sentence splitting | Most prose; the usual default for extraction

Structure-aware | Headings, list and table blocks | Very uneven unless small sections are merged | Format-specific parsing | Markdown, HTML, reports, filings, manuals

Semantic | Topic shifts in embeddings | Uneven | Embedding every sentence | Long unstructured text: transcripts, chats

## Provenance: ids that survive re-indexing

Every entity and relationship in the graph carries source_ids pointing to text units. Community reports cite them, local search pulls their text into prompts, and an evaluation run is only reproducible if they mean the same thing tomorrow. The id scheme therefore has a hard requirement: indexing the same input twice must produce the same ids. That property, idempotence, is what makes caching, incremental updates and diffing two index runs possible.

### Three id schemes

- Random ids (uuid4()): unique, and useless for this purpose. Every run produces new ids, so an LLM cache keyed on unit id never hits and yesterday's citations dangle.

- Positional ids: minigraphrag uses f"{doc_id}-{i:03d}", the document id plus the unit's index. Deterministic, readable (“07_marlow_acquires_deepcast-001” tells you where to look), and stable as long as the document and chunking settings do not change.

- Hashed ids: a digest of the document id, the unit's offsets and its text. Deterministic, fixed-length, safe in any storage system, and they change if and only if one of those inputs changes.

```python  # examples/ch07_ids.py
import hashlib
from dataclasses import replace

from minigraphrag.chunking import TextUnit


def stable_unit_id(doc_id: str, start: int, end: int, text: str) -> str:
    """Same document, same span, same text -> same id, on every machine and every run."""
    text_digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    key = f"{doc_id}\x1f{start}\x1f{end}\x1f{text_digest}"   # unit separator avoids "a-1"+"2" == "a"+"-12"
    return hashlib.sha256(key.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]


def with_stable_ids(units: list[TextUnit]) -> list[TextUnit]:
    return [replace(u, id=stable_unit_id(u.doc_id, u.start, u.end, u.text)) for u in units]
```

Details that matter:

- Use a cryptographic or otherwise stable hash, never Python's built-in hash(). String hashing is randomized per process, so hash("x") differs between runs. HashingEmbedder in minigraphrag uses blake2b for the same reason.

- Separate the fields unambiguously. Concatenating "doc-1" + "2" and "doc-" + "12" gives the same string. A separator character that cannot appear in the fields prevents collisions.

- Include the doc id. Boilerplate paragraphs (“About Kestrel Labs”, which appears in both funding press releases) have identical text in different documents. A pure content hash would give them the same id and merge their provenance.

- Sixteen hex characters are 64 bits: for a million units the chance of any collision is roughly one in 37 million. Use the full digest if that is not enough for you.

### What still changes the ids

No scheme is stable under every edit. Suppose someone fixes a typo in the last paragraph of doc 07 and re-indexes.

Change | Positional doc-NNN | Hash of doc id, offsets and text

Re-run with no changes | Stable | Stable

Same-length typo fix in the last unit | Ids stable, but unit 001 now has different text under the same id, so caches return stale extractions | Only unit 001's id changes; the stale cache entry is simply never hit

A sentence inserted at the top | Ids may be unchanged while every unit's text shifts | All units after the insertion change id

Chunk size or chunker changed | Everything changes meaning silently | Everything changes id

The pattern: positional ids fail silently by keeping an id while its text changes; hashed ids fail loudly by changing the id. Loud failure is what you want: a changed id triggers re-extraction of exactly that unit, and an unchanged id is proof the cached extraction is still valid. Exercise 7.2 walks through the cases by hand, and Chapter 27 builds incremental updates on top of hashed ids.

**Also version the chunking config

Store the chunker name, size, overlap and tokenizer with the index (IndexConfig already records chunk_size and chunk_overlap). When they change, you know every unit id is invalid without comparing texts. Some systems fold a config hash into each unit id for the same reason.

## Carrying document metadata into every unit

A text unit cut from the middle of a document has lost its title, its author, its date and its section. For vector search this is a minor issue. For extraction it is a correctness issue, because so much of what text means is relative:

- Relative time. “Last month” in the board memo means April 2025 only if the model knows the memo is dated 14 May 2025. Temporal facts in Chapter 10 depend on this.

- Implicit subjects. “We will receive the units already on order” is Kestrel Labs speaking, which only the memo header says.

- Source reliability and recency. A 2021 newspaper profile and a 2026 interview can disagree about who is CTO; both are right for their date. Keeping each unit's publication date lets later stages prefer the newer claim.

- Topic. A section heading like “What Tern replaces” is often the clearest statement of what a unit is about.

[Interactive figure: From document to text units with metadata (flow)]

minigraphrag's TextUnit deliberately has no metadata field: it stays a plain record of where the text came from, and anything else lives in a side table keyed by doc_id or unit id. This keeps units serializable and lets you add metadata without re-chunking.

```python  # examples/ch07_metadata.py
import re

from minigraphrag.chunking import TextUnit

MONTHS = "January|February|March|April|May|June|July|August|September|October|November|December"
DATE_RE = re.compile(rf"\b(\d{{1,2}}) ({MONTHS}) (\d{{4}})\b")


def document_metadata(doc_id: str, text: str) -> dict:
    """Title from the first '# ' heading; date from the first 'D Month YYYY' in the first 400 characters."""
    title = next((line[2:].strip() for line in text.splitlines() if line.startswith("# ")), doc_id)
    m = DATE_RE.search(text[:400])
    date = None
    if m:
        month = MONTHS.split("|").index(m.group(2)) + 1
        date = f"{m.group(3)}-{month:02d}-{int(m.group(1)):02d}"
    return {"doc_id": doc_id, "title": title, "date": date}


def unit_header(unit: TextUnit, doc_meta: dict, section: list[str] | None = None) -> str:
    """A short header prepended to the unit text in extraction prompts (not stored in unit.text)."""
    lines = [f"Document: {doc_meta['title']}"]
    if doc_meta.get("date"):
        lines.append(f"Published: {doc_meta['date']}")
    if section:
        lines.append("Section: " + " > ".join(section))
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n\n" + unit.text
```

On the corpus this recovers a title and date for all 12 documents, from datelines such as “Published 4 October 2021”, “Posted 30 June 2025”, the memo's “Date: 14 May 2025” and the podcast's “Recorded 26 March 2026”. The header for unit 002 of the memo looks like this:

```python
Document: CONFIDENTIAL: Memo to the Board of Directors
Published: 2025-05-14
Section: CONFIDENTIAL: Memo to the Board of Directors > 2. Why it matters

## 2. Why it matters

Every Sentinel drone depends on these modules. Our current inventory covers ...
```

How to use it with the existing extractor: extract_from_unit formats unit.text into the prompt, so pass it a copy whose text includes the header, and keep the original unit for storage and citations.

```python  # examples/ch07_extract_with_context.py
from dataclasses import replace

from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents
from minigraphrag.extraction import extract_from_unit
from minigraphrag.llm import MockLLM

from ch07_ids import with_stable_ids
from ch07_metadata import document_metadata, unit_header
from ch07_structure import chunk_markdown

llm = MockLLM()
docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
meta = {doc_id: document_metadata(doc_id, text) for doc_id, text in docs.items()}

units, sections = [], {}
for doc_id, text in docs.items():
    pairs = chunk_markdown(text, doc_id, max_tokens=300)
    stable = with_stable_ids([u for u, _ in pairs])
    for u, (_, path) in zip(stable, pairs):
        units.append(u)
        sections[u.id] = path

results = []
for u in units:
    prompt_view = replace(u, text=unit_header(u, meta[u.doc_id], sections[u.id]))
    results.append(extract_from_unit(llm, prompt_view, max_gleanings=1))   # ExtractionResult.unit_id == u.id
```

Because replace keeps the id, every extracted record's source_id still points to the stored unit, whose text and offsets are the clean source span.

**Headers can leak into the graph

A header that says “Document: Kestrel Labs Raises $40 Million Series B” invites the extractor to emit Series B relationships from every unit of that document, including units that never mention the round. Keep headers short and factual, tell the extraction prompt that the header is context and that only the text below it should be extracted from, and spot-check provenance on a few units.

## What chunking costs

Chunking is free; what it causes is not. Every design decision above changes the number of units, and every unit is at least one extraction call. Put the pieces together.

### Calls

For U units and max_gleanings = g, extract_from_unit makes one extraction call, up to g “continue” calls, and a yes/no loop check between gleaning rounds but not after the last, so at most:

calls per unit = 1 + g + max(0, g − 1) (1 for g = 0, 2 for g = 1, 4 for g = 2)

The indexer adds one claim-extraction call per unit when extract_claims is on (the default), then description summaries and community reports, which depend on the graph rather than directly on U. So the chunking-driven part is roughly U × (calls per unit + 1).

### Tokens

Let P be the extraction prompt template's tokens, T the unit's tokens, R the tokens of each response and C the continue prompt. Because gleaning replays the whole transcript in each call, input tokens grow with every round:

- Extraction call: input P + T, output R.

- Gleaning round r (1-based): input P + T + r·R + r·C, output about R (often less). Loop checks send the same transcript plus a short question, but extract_from_unit does not append them to the transcript, so they do not grow later calls.

Worked example on Kestrel with minigraphrag defaults: U = 24 fixed units averaging 335 tokens (8,039 / 24), g = 1. By the package's word-based estimate the extraction template is about 330 tokens and the continue prompt about 40. Assume responses of R = 300 tokens.

- Extraction call: input 330 + 335 = 665; output 300.

- Gleaning call: input 665 + 300 + 40 = 1,005; output up to 300.

- Per unit: 2 calls, 1,670 input tokens, up to 600 output tokens.

- Corpus: 48 calls, about 40,000 input and 14,400 output tokens for entity extraction, plus 24 claim calls.

Now switch to structure-aware units at 300 tokens: U = 54, averaging far fewer tokens each. Calls rise to 108 plus 54 claim calls. Input tokens rise less than calls, because the template P is paid per call while the text is split among more units, and outputs rise because each call writes its own records, including duplicate mentions of Kestrel Labs from every unit. Whether that buys enough recall to be worth it is an empirical question: that is exactly the measurement in Exercise 8.3.

**Three levers, in the order to try them

First, remove waste that buys nothing: cross-document windows, trailing duplicate windows, boilerplate sections such as the “About Kestrel Labs” paragraph that both funding press releases carry (deduplicate them by content hash). Second, choose size and gleaning together on a sample, measuring entities found per call. Third, put the fixed part of the prompt first so provider-side prompt caching can discount the template P on every call; Chapter 26 covers the rest.

## Exercises

#### Exercise 7.1 Warm-up

The Project Tern blog post (doc 09) has 460 words. By hand, for chunk_fixed with (a) size 300, overlap 50; (b) size 100, overlap 20; (c) size 100, overlap 0: give the number of units, the word range of the last unit, and how many words are processed more than once. Then check with code.

▸ Hint

Windows start at multiples of the stride. The last window is the first one whose start plus size reaches 460.

▸ Show answer

(a) Stride 250. ⌈(460 − 50)/250⌉ = ⌈1.64⌉ = 2 units: words 0–299 and 250–459. The last unit has 210 words. Words in both: 250–299, so 50 duplicated words.

(b) Stride 80. ⌈(460 − 20)/80⌉ = ⌈5.5⌉ = 6 units starting at 0, 80, 160, 240, 320, 400. Checks: 320 + 100 = 420 < 460, so continue; 400 + 100 = 500 ≥ 460, stop. The last unit is words 400–459 (60 words). Overlaps: each of the 5 boundaries between consecutive units shares 20 words, so 100 duplicated words (22% of the document).

(c) Stride 100. ⌈460/100⌉ = 5 units: 0–99, …, 400–459. 0 duplicated words, but any relationship stated across words 99/100, 199/200, 299/300 or 399/400 can be split.

```python
from minigraphrag.chunking import chunk_fixed, load_documents

text = load_documents("data/corpus")["09_kestrel_eng_blog_project_tern"]
for size, overlap in [(300, 50), (100, 20), (100, 0)]:
    units = chunk_fixed(text, size, overlap, "09")
    last = units[-1]
    print(size, overlap, len(units), len(last.text.split()))
# 300 50 2 210
# 100 20 6 60
# 100 0 5 60
```

#### Exercise 7.2 Core

Doc 07 is chunked at 300/50 into units 000 (words 0–299) and 001 (words 250–454), and extractions are cached by unit id. For each change below, say which unit ids change and whether the cache would serve a stale extraction, under (i) positional ids doc-NNN and (ii) stable_unit_id: (a) re-run unchanged; (b) “harbour” is corrected to “harbor” in the paragraph about Marlow's headquarters, near the end of the article; (c) a one-sentence editor's note is inserted before the first paragraph; (d) the file is renamed from 07_marlow_acquires_deepcast.md to 07_marlow_deepcast.md.

▸ Show answer

- (a) Unchanged: both schemes produce identical ids, and cached extractions are valid.

- (b) “harbour” to “harbor” shortens the text by one character at word 403, in unit 001's exclusive part (after word 299). Unit 000's text and offsets are unchanged. (The article's other “harbour”, at word 254, sits inside the overlap; fixing that one would change both units.) Unit 001's end offset and text change. (i) Positional: both ids unchanged, so the cache serves unit 001's stale extraction for new text. Here it is harmless, but the same silent reuse happens for a meaningful edit, such as a corrected acquisition price. (ii) Hashed: unit 000 keeps its id and cache entry; unit 001 gets a new id and is re-extracted. Correct.

- (c) Inserting a sentence shifts every word index, so both windows now cover different text. (i) Positional: ids -000 and -001 are unchanged, so both cached extractions are stale. The document might now even need a third unit, the only change you would notice. (ii) Hashed: both ids change, both units are re-extracted. Correct, at the cost of re-extracting text that only moved. (A content-anchored scheme that hashes only text, plus doc id, would still change here, because window boundaries moved by one sentence's worth of words.)

- (d) The doc id is the file stem, so it changes. (i) and (ii) both change every id. The cache misses and everything in the document is re-extracted, and old source_ids in the graph dangle. The fix is not in the chunker: give documents ids that do not depend on file names, for example a registry mapping paths to permanent ids, or a hash of the canonical source URL.

#### Exercise 7.3 Core

Using the cost formulas in this chapter, compare two configurations for indexing a corpus of 10,000 documents of 2,000 words each with gleaning g = 2: (A) fixed 600/100 words; (B) fixed 300/50 words. Assume 4 tokens per 3 words, a template of P = 1,500 tokens, responses of R = 500 tokens for A and 300 for B, and a continue prompt and loop check of 50 tokens each. Give chunks, calls, and input and output tokens for entity extraction only, assuming the model always answers yes to the loop check.

▸ Show answer

Chunks. A: ⌈(2000 − 100)/500⌉ = ⌈3.8⌉ = 4 per document, 40,000 total. B: ⌈(2000 − 50)/250⌉ = ⌈7.8⌉ = 8 per document, 80,000 total.

Calls. 1 + g + (g − 1) = 4 per unit. A: 160,000. B: 320,000.

Unit tokens. Full A windows are 600 words = 800 tokens; B windows 300 words = 400 tokens. (The last window of each document is shorter; use full windows for an upper bound.)

Input per unit, with transcript replay. Let B0 = P + T.

- A: extraction 1,500 + 800 = 2,300. Glean 1: 2,300 + 500 + 50 = 2,850. Loop check: 2,850 + 500 + 50 = 3,400 (transcript after round 1 plus the answer to it, plus the check question). Glean 2: the transcript holds both earlier answers and two continue prompts, but not the loop check, which extract_from_unit does not append: 2,300 + 500 + 50 + 500 + 50 = 3,400. Total ≈ 11,950.

- B: extraction 1,500 + 400 = 1,900. Glean 1: 1,900 + 300 + 50 = 2,250. Loop check: 2,250 + 300 + 50 = 2,600. Glean 2: 1,900 + 300 + 50 + 300 + 50 = 2,600. Total ≈ 9,350.

Output per unit: three responses (extraction and two gleanings) plus a one-token check. A: about 1,500. B: about 900.

Units | Calls | Input tokens | Output tokens

A: 600/100 | 40,000 | 160,000 | ≈ 478 million | ≈ 60 million

B: 300/50 | 80,000 | 320,000 | ≈ 748 million | ≈ 72 million

Halving the chunk size doubles calls but raises input tokens by only about 56%, because the template dominates each call's input, and raises output by 20% under these assumptions. Two insights: prompt caching of P matters more for small chunks, and g = 2 is expensive in both, since three of four calls replay a growing transcript. Before choosing B for recall, check whether A with g = 1 (half the calls) reaches similar recall on a sample.

#### Exercise 7.4 Core

Implement chunk_semantic(text, doc_id, max_tokens=300, percentile=20, embedder=None) that returns TextUnits with correct document offsets: split with split_sentences, embed sentences with HashingEmbedder, cut between adjacent sentences whose cosine similarity is at or below the given percentile of all adjacent similarities, and never exceed max_tokens (cut early if needed). Test it on doc 12, the leadership interview.

▸ Show answer

```python
import numpy as np

from minigraphrag.chunking import TextUnit, split_sentences
from minigraphrag.embeddings import HashingEmbedder
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

def chunk_semantic(text, doc_id, max_tokens=300, percentile=20, embedder=None):
    spans = split_sentences(text)
    if not spans:
        return []
    embedder = embedder or HashingEmbedder()
    vecs = embedder.embed([text[a:b] for a, b in spans])        # rows are L2-normalized
    sims = np.sum(vecs[:-1] * vecs[1:], axis=1)                 # cosine of sentence i and i+1
    threshold = np.percentile(sims, percentile) if len(sims) else 0.0

    units, first, tokens = [], 0, 0
    def emit(last):
        start, end = spans[first][0], spans[last][1]
        piece = text[start:end].strip()
        units.append(TextUnit(f"{doc_id}-{len(units):03d}", doc_id, piece, count_tokens(piece), start, end))

    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(spans):
        t = count_tokens(text[a:b])
        if i > first and tokens + t > max_tokens:              # budget cut
            emit(i - 1)
            first, tokens = i, 0
        tokens += t
        if i < len(sims) and sims[i] <= threshold:             # topic cut after sentence i
            emit(i)
            first, tokens = i + 1, 0
    if first < len(spans):
        emit(len(spans) - 1)
    return units

from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents
text = load_documents("data/corpus")["12_interview_leadership_change_2026"]
units = chunk_semantic(text, "12_interview_leadership_change_2026", max_tokens=150)
assert all(text[u.start:u.end].strip() == u.text for u in units)
print(len(units), [u.n_tokens for u in units])
```

Things to check in your output. Offsets must round-trip, which the assert verifies. Newlines count as sentence breaks, so speaker labels and blank lines become short “sentences” whose word-hash vectors share little with their neighbors; with a hashing embedder those produce many low similarities and therefore many small units. That is a real lesson: semantic chunking is only as good as the embedder, and lexical hashing mistakes “different words” for “different topic”. Swap in SentenceTransformerEmbedder and the cuts should move toward genuine topic shifts, such as from the Deepcast supply shock to the leadership change. A practical fix for both is to merge units under a minimum size, for example 40 tokens, into their neighbor.

#### Exercise 7.5 Stretch

Chunking decides which relationships an extractor can possibly see: both entities must appear in the same unit. Build a cheap, LLM-free proxy. For the 22 entity pairs of the running example's key relationships (with a small alias list), count pair-mentions: the number of (unit, pair) combinations where both entities appear in the unit. Compare fixed 300/50, 100/20, 100/0 and 40/0, sentence packing at 150 tokens, chunk_markdown at 300, and whole documents. Also count units that contain the full Q1 chain: Marlow Dynamics, Deepcast, Kestrel Labs and Project Tern. Interpret the results.

▸ Show answer

```python
from minigraphrag.chunking import chunk_documents, load_documents
from ch07_structure import chunk_markdown

ALIASES = {
    "Kestrel Labs": ["Kestrel"], "Mira Okafor": ["Okafor"], "Jonas Vehl": ["Vehl"], "Priya Nair": ["Priya", "Nair"],
    "Tidewater Institute": ["Tidewater", "TWI"], "Ana Ruiz": ["Ruiz"], "Project Sentinel": ["Sentinel"],
    "Project Tern": ["Tern"], "Halden Reef": ["Halden"], "Brightwater Capital": ["Brightwater"],
    "Lena Park": ["Lena Park"], "Marlow Dynamics": ["Marlow"], "Deepcast": ["Deepcast"],
    "Ocean Health Act": ["Ocean Health Act"], "Port Avalon City Council": ["City Council", "council"],
    "Port Avalon": ["Port Avalon"],
}
PAIRS = [
    ("Mira Okafor", "Kestrel Labs"), ("Jonas Vehl", "Kestrel Labs"), ("Priya Nair", "Kestrel Labs"),
    ("Mira Okafor", "Tidewater Institute"), ("Priya Nair", "Marlow Dynamics"), ("Ana Ruiz", "Tidewater Institute"),
    ("Kestrel Labs", "Project Sentinel"), ("Tidewater Institute", "Project Sentinel"), ("Priya Nair", "Project Sentinel"),
    ("Project Sentinel", "Halden Reef"), ("Ana Ruiz", "Halden Reef"), ("Brightwater Capital", "Kestrel Labs"),
    ("Lena Park", "Brightwater Capital"), ("Lena Park", "Kestrel Labs"), ("Deepcast", "Kestrel Labs"),
    ("Marlow Dynamics", "Deepcast"), ("Marlow Dynamics", "Kestrel Labs"), ("Kestrel Labs", "Project Tern"),
    ("Jonas Vehl", "Project Tern"), ("Priya Nair", "Project Tern"), ("Project Tern", "Deepcast"),
    ("Port Avalon City Council", "Kestrel Labs"),
]
CHAIN = ("Marlow Dynamics", "Deepcast", "Kestrel Labs", "Project Tern")

def mentions(text, name):
    return any(a in text for a in [name] + ALIASES.get(name, []))

docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
configs = {
    "fixed 300/50": [u.text for u in chunk_documents(docs, 300, 50)],
    "fixed 100/20": [u.text for u in chunk_documents(docs, 100, 20)],
    "fixed 100/0": [u.text for u in chunk_documents(docs, 100, 0)],
    "fixed 40/0": [u.text for u in chunk_documents(docs, 40, 0)],
    "sentences 150": [u.text for u in chunk_documents(docs, 150, method="sentences")],
    "markdown 300": [u.text for d, t in docs.items() for u, _ in chunk_markdown(t, d, 300)],
    "whole documents": list(docs.values()),
}
for name, texts in configs.items():
    per_pair = [sum(mentions(t, a) and mentions(t, b) for t in texts) for a, b in PAIRS]
    chain = sum(all(mentions(t, x) for x in CHAIN) for t in texts)
    print(f"{name:16s} units={len(texts):3d} pair-mentions={sum(per_pair):4d} "
          f"pairs-in-one-unit-only={sum(p == 1 for p in per_pair)} chain-units={chain}")
```

```python
fixed 300/50     units= 24 pair-mentions= 142 pairs-in-one-unit-only=0 chain-units=2
fixed 100/20     units= 70 pair-mentions= 159 pairs-in-one-unit-only=0 chain-units=1
fixed 100/0      units= 59 pair-mentions= 140 pairs-in-one-unit-only=0 chain-units=1
fixed 40/0       units=141 pair-mentions= 104 pairs-in-one-unit-only=4 chain-units=0
sentences 150    units= 65 pair-mentions= 153 pairs-in-one-unit-only=0 chain-units=0
markdown 300     units= 54 pair-mentions= 147 pairs-in-one-unit-only=0 chain-units=2
whole documents  units= 12 pair-mentions=  95 pairs-in-one-unit-only=0 chain-units=1
```

Interpretation:

- Every configuration covers all 22 pairs somewhere, because the Kestrel corpus restates its central facts across documents. Real corpora are less forgiving, so look at the next columns.

- Tiny windows destroy co-occurrence. At 40 words, pair-mentions drop to 104 and four relationships survive in only a single unit: one missed extraction and the edge is gone.

- Overlap adds chances. 100/20 has 159 pair-mentions against 140 for 100/0, the highest of all, at the cost of 11 more units.

- Whole documents score lowest on pair-mentions (95) only because each document counts once. They maximize co-occurrence per unit but are exactly the long inputs where extraction recall drops, which this proxy cannot see.

- The full causal chain rarely sits in one unit (at most 2), and never in 150-token sentence units. That is expected and fine: Q1 is answered by joining edges from different units through shared entities, which is the whole point of building a graph.

Caveats: substring alias matching is crude (“Tern” also matches “Western”, “council” matches any council), and co-occurrence is necessary, not sufficient, for an extractable relationship. Use this proxy to rule out bad settings cheaply, then measure real extraction recall on the survivors.

## Check your understanding

A 1,000-word document is chunked with chunk_fixed(text, size=200, overlap=40). How many units result?

- 5

- ✓ (correct) 6

- 7

- 8
Answer: Stride is 160. ⌈(1000 − 40)/160⌉ = ⌈6.0⌉ = 6. Windows start at 0, 160, 320, 480, 640 and 800; the last covers words 800–999 and reaches the end.

Why does GraphRAG extraction benefit from smaller text units than a single long document, even with a large context window?

- Smaller units are cheaper per token

- Large context windows cannot hold markdown

- ✓ (correct) Models asked to list every entity in a long input tend to miss many; each smaller unit gets a fresh, focused pass

- Entity resolution only works on short texts
Answer: On HotPotQA the GraphRAG paper observed almost twice as many entity references from 600-token chunks as from 2400-token chunks with one pass. Fitting in the window is not the same as being read thoroughly.

Which id scheme lets an extraction cache detect that a unit's text changed while its position in the document did not?

- Positional ids like doc-001

- Random UUIDs generated at chunking time

- Python's built-in hash() of the text

- ✓ (correct) A SHA-256 digest of doc id, offsets and text
Answer: Positional ids stay the same while text changes, so stale cache entries are served. UUIDs never match across runs. Built-in hash() is randomized per process. A stable digest that includes the text changes exactly when the text does.

The board memo says “the new owner intends to reserve its production”. What most directly helps the extractor connect this to the right date?

- ✓ (correct) Prepending the document's title and date (14 May 2025) to the unit in the extraction prompt

- Increasing the overlap to 100 words

- Switching to semantic chunking

- Using hashed ids
Answer: “Last month” is relative to the memo's date, which only the document header states. Overlap and boundary strategies cannot recover information that lives outside the body text.

In chunk_by_sentences, what does the condition if j > i and tokens + t > max_tokens guarantee?

- No unit ever exceeds max_tokens

- Units never overlap

- Every unit ends with a period

- ✓ (correct) Each unit takes at least one sentence, so a sentence longer than the budget still makes progress
Answer: Without j > i, a single over-budget sentence would never be added and the loop would not advance. The budget is therefore soft.

Going from structure-aware units that keep every short section separate to merged sections nearer the token budget will usually…

- Increase calls and decrease input tokens

- ✓ (correct) Decrease calls and template tokens, at some risk to recall in the longer merged units

- Change nothing, because tokens are the same

- Break provenance, because merged units cannot have offsets
Answer: Fewer units means fewer calls, and the prompt template is paid once per call. Merged units are longer, which can reduce recall. Merged units still have a start and end offset.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ What chunk size should I start with?

For extraction, start in the range of a few hundred tokens to about a thousand, with 10–15% overlap, and sentence or structure-aware boundaries. Then run the extraction on a sample at two sizes and compare entities per call and a hand-checked recall on a few units. Microsoft GraphRAG's default has long been 1,200 tokens with 100 of overlap, at the large end of that range; check the configuration docs for your version rather than copying a number.

▸ Should chunks for extraction and chunks for vector search be the same?

They do not have to be. Some systems extract from larger units and embed smaller ones, linking them with PART_OF edges (the parent-child pattern from Chapter 6). Using one set is simpler, and minigraphrag does that: the same text units feed extraction, the text-unit vector store and citations.

▸ Why count words instead of tokens?

It keeps chunking independent of any tokenizer, deterministic across machines, and exactly aligned with character offsets. The cost is that 300 words is only roughly 400 tokens, and much more for code, numbers or non-English text. If you budget tightly against a model's limit, chunk with the model's tokenizer and map token spans back to character offsets.

▸ How should I handle PDFs, HTML and tables?

Convert to a structured intermediate first, such as markdown with headings, lists and tables preserved, then apply structure-aware chunking. Keep a mapping from intermediate offsets back to the original page or element for citations. For tables, either keep a whole table in one unit or repeat the header row in each unit; a table row without its header is a list of numbers the extractor cannot interpret.

▸ Does overlap create duplicate entities in the graph?

It creates duplicate mentions, not duplicate nodes: the same name extracted from two units merges into one entity with two source ids, and relationship weights add up. That summing slightly inflates weights for facts that happen to fall in overlaps. It is usually negligible, but it is one more reason not to use very large overlaps.

### Project: a chunking lab for the Kestrel corpus

Build a small command-line tool that makes chunking decisions visible and comparable before you pay for extraction.

- chunklab --method fixed|sentences|markdown --size N --overlap M prints units per document, token distribution (min, median, max) and duplicated-token percentage

- Every unit gets a stable_unit_id; a test proves two runs produce identical ids and that editing one paragraph changes only the affected units' ids

- A metadata table (units.jsonl) with unit id, doc id, offsets, title, date and heading path, and a test that text[start:end] matches every unit

- A cost estimate per configuration: calls and input and output tokens for a chosen gleaning setting, using the formulas in this chapter

- The pair-mention proxy from Exercise 7.5 reported for each configuration

- A one-paragraph recommendation for which configuration to use in Chapter 8, with the numbers that justify it

Done when you can rerun the lab after changing one setting and explain every number that moved.

## Key takeaways

- In GraphRAG a text unit is an extraction input, citation unit and retrieval target; size it for recall, relationship co-occurrence and cost.

- Fixed windows give max(1, ⌈(N − O)/(S − O)⌉) units per document; chunk per document, and remember overlap duplicates roughly O/S of the tokens.

- Sentence packing avoids mid-sentence cuts; structure-aware splitting respects headings, lists and tables and records the heading path.

- Provenance ids must be deterministic; hashes of doc id, offsets and text fail loudly when text changes, which keeps caches and incremental updates correct.

- Carry title, date and section into the extraction prompt, but keep the stored unit text and offsets clean.

- Units × calls per unit (with gleaning) × replayed transcript tokens is the cost you choose when you choose a chunker.

## Extracting entities and relationships with LLMs

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/08-entity-relation-extraction.html

# Extracting entities and relationships with LLMs

The graph in GraphRAG is only as good as the extractor that builds it. In this chapter you write the prompt, the parser and the gleaning loop that turn a text unit into nodes and edges.

## You will be able to

- Explain what an extraction step must produce for later stages: names, types, descriptions, relationships and strengths

- Write an extraction prompt with entity types, a strict output format and a worked example

- Parse delimited LLM output without trusting it, and say when JSON output is the better choice

- Implement gleaning and measure how much recall it buys per extra LLM call

- Recognize the common failure modes: missed entities, invented relations, type drift and name variants

## What the extractor has to produce

In the previous chapter you split the Kestrel Labs corpus into text units, each with a stable id. Extraction reads one text unit at a time and returns two lists:

- Entities: a name, a type from a fixed list, and a short description written from this chunk's point of view.

- Relationships: a source entity, a target entity, a description of how they relate, and a strength score.

Two design choices matter more than they look. First, descriptions are free text, not a single label. When the same entity shows up in twelve chunks you get twelve descriptions, and Chapter 9 merges and summarizes them into one profile. Second, every record keeps the id of the text unit it came from. That provenance is what lets local search cite sources and lets you debug a bad edge back to the sentence that produced it.

[Interactive figure: One text unit becomes a subgraph — Step through the extractor's output (text-to-graph)]

Notice what the extractor did not do. It did not write an edge from Marlow Dynamics to Project Tern, even though one caused the other. That causal chain spans two hops, and keeping it implicit is correct: the graph stores what the text states, and retrieval (Chapter 18) follows the path later.

## Anatomy of an extraction prompt

The prompt Microsoft GraphRAG popularized has four parts. Each exists because of a specific failure seen without it.

[Diagram]

Each block of the prompt guards against a specific failure. Keeping the variable text at the end also makes the long fixed prefix cacheable, which matters when you run it on thousands of chunks.

Here is the prompt as shipped in minigraphrag/prompts.py. It is a shortened descendant of Microsoft GraphRAG's, with one worked example instead of several. The delimiters are the module constants TUPLE_DELIMITER (<|>), RECORD_DELIMITER (##) and COMPLETION_DELIMITER (<|COMPLETE|>). The worked example is about a company that is not in the corpus. Keep it that way when you tune the prompt: an example drawn from your own documents teaches the model those particular names as much as it teaches the format, and they start turning up in chunks that never mention them.

```python  # minigraphrag/prompts.py
ENTITY_EXTRACTION_PROMPT = """-Goal-
Given a text document and a list of entity types, identify all entities of those types from the text and all relationships among the identified entities.

-Steps-
1. Identify all entities. For each identified entity, extract:
- entity_name: Name of the entity, capitalized
- entity_type: One of the following types: [{entity_types}]
- entity_description: Comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities
Format each entity as ("entity"{tuple_delimiter}<entity_name>{tuple_delimiter}<entity_type>{tuple_delimiter}<entity_description>)

2. From the entities identified in step 1, identify all pairs of (source_entity, target_entity) that are *clearly related* to each other. For each pair, extract:
- source_entity: name of the source entity, as identified in step 1
- target_entity: name of the target entity, as identified in step 1
- relationship_description: explanation of why the source and target are related, including dates when stated
- relationship_strength: a numeric score from 1 to 10 indicating the strength of the relationship
Format each relationship as ("relationship"{tuple_delimiter}<source_entity>{tuple_delimiter}<target_entity>{tuple_delimiter}<relationship_description>{tuple_delimiter}<relationship_strength>)

3. Return output in English as a single list of all the entities and relationships identified in steps 1 and 2. Use **{record_delimiter}** as the list delimiter.

4. When finished, output {completion_delimiter}

######################
-Example-
######################
Entity_types: ORGANIZATION,PERSON
Text:
Harbor Robotics hired Dana Lee as head of research in 2019.
######################
Output:
("entity"{tuple_delimiter}HARBOR ROBOTICS{tuple_delimiter}ORGANIZATION{tuple_delimiter}Harbor Robotics is a company that hired Dana Lee in 2019)
{record_delimiter}
("entity"{tuple_delimiter}DANA LEE{tuple_delimiter}PERSON{tuple_delimiter}Dana Lee is head of research at Harbor Robotics)
{record_delimiter}
("relationship"{tuple_delimiter}DANA LEE{tuple_delimiter}HARBOR ROBOTICS{tuple_delimiter}Dana Lee became head of research at Harbor Robotics in 2019{tuple_delimiter}9)
{completion_delimiter}

######################
-Real Data-
######################
Entity_types: {entity_types}
Text:
{input_text}
######################
Output:
"""
```

**Why names are uppercased

Asking for capitalized names is a cheap first pass at entity resolution: “Kestrel labs” and “Kestrel Labs” collapse to the same key before any fuzzy matching runs. It does nothing for “Kestrel” vs. “Kestrel Labs”; that is Chapter 9's job.

### Choosing entity types

Types are a schema in disguise. Too few (just “THING”) and you cannot filter or reason by type. Too many and the model spends its attention choosing between near-synonyms, and you get the same company typed as ORGANIZATION in one chunk and COMPANY in the next. Start with five to eight types that match the questions your users ask. For Kestrel Labs that is ORGANIZATION, PERSON, PROJECT, LOCATION, EVENT and LAW. Microsoft GraphRAG's auto prompt tuning can propose domain-specific types by sampling your corpus; you will try it in Chapter 28.

## Delimited tuples or JSON?

You have two broad ways to ask for structured output, and both are in production use.

Concern | Delimited tuples | JSON (with schema or structured outputs)

Partial output | Every complete record before a truncation is still usable | A truncated JSON document fails to parse unless you repair it

Token cost | Lower: no quotes, keys or braces per field | Higher: quotes, keys and braces are repeated on every record

Validity guarantees | None: you must write a tolerant parser | Strong when the provider enforces a schema

Streaming | Easy: split on the record delimiter as text arrives | Needs an incremental JSON parser

Small local models | Often follow the pattern well from one example | Can struggle without constrained decoding

A reasonable default in 2026: use schema-enforced JSON when your provider supports it and your chunks are small enough that truncation is rare; use tuples with a tolerant parser for local models or very long outputs. The rest of this chapter uses tuples because the parser teaches you what can go wrong.

## Parsing without trusting the model

LLM output is almost-structured. Over thousands of chunks you will see stray whitespace, missing parentheses, a strength of “high” instead of 8, relationships to entities never declared, and the occasional chatty sentence before the first record. The parser's job is to keep every record it can and drop, not crash on, the rest.

```python  # minigraphrag/extraction.py
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict

from . import prompts as P
from .chunking import TextUnit
from .llm import LLM


@dataclass
class Entity:
    name: str
    type: str
    description: str
    source_id: str = ""  # TextUnit id the mention came from

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return asdict(self)


@dataclass
class Relationship:
    source: str
    target: str
    description: str
    strength: float = 1.0
    source_id: str = ""

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return asdict(self)


@dataclass
class ExtractionResult:
    """Everything extracted from one TextUnit."""

    unit_id: str
    entities: list[Entity] = field(default_factory=list)
    relationships: list[Relationship] = field(default_factory=list)
    llm_calls: int = 0


def _clean_field(value: str) -> str:
    return value.strip().strip('"').strip("'").strip()


def _split_records(text: str, record_delimiter: str, completion_delimiter: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split raw output into candidate records.

    Models sometimes forget the record delimiter and use newlines, or glue
    records together as `(...)(...)`, so we split on all three.
    """
    text = text.replace(completion_delimiter, "")
    records = []
    for chunk in re.split(re.escape(record_delimiter) + r"|\n", text):
        for piece in re.split(r"(?<=\))\s*(?=\()", chunk):
            piece = piece.strip()
            if "(" in piece and ")" in piece:  # drop chatter around the parentheses
                piece = piece[piece.index("(") : piece.rindex(")") + 1]
            if piece:
                records.append(piece)
    return records


def parse_extraction_output(
    text: str,
    source_id: str = "",
    tuple_delimiter: str = P.TUPLE_DELIMITER,
    record_delimiter: str = P.RECORD_DELIMITER,
    completion_delimiter: str = P.COMPLETION_DELIMITER,
) -> tuple[list[Entity], list[Relationship]]:
    """Parse `("entity"<|>...)##("relationship"<|>...)` output. Bad records are skipped, not fatal."""
    entities, relationships = [], []
    for record in _split_records(text, record_delimiter, completion_delimiter):
        record = record.strip()
        if record.startswith("(") and record.endswith(")"):
            record = record[1:-1]
        fields = [_clean_field(f) for f in record.split(tuple_delimiter)]
        kind = fields[0].lower()
        if kind == "entity" and len(fields) >= 4 and fields[1]:
            entities.append(Entity(fields[1].upper(), fields[2].upper().replace(" ", "_"),
                                   tuple_delimiter.join(fields[3:]), source_id))
        elif kind == "relationship" and len(fields) >= 4 and fields[1] and fields[2]:
            strength = 1.0
            desc_fields = fields[3:]
            if len(fields) >= 5:
                try:
                    strength = float(re.sub(r"[^\d.]", "", fields[-1]) or "1")
                    desc_fields = fields[3:-1]
                except ValueError:
                    pass
            relationships.append(Relationship(fields[1].upper(), fields[2].upper(),
                                              tuple_delimiter.join(desc_fields), strength, source_id))
    return entities, relationships
```

**What about relationships to undeclared entities?

This parser, like Microsoft GraphRAG, keeps a relationship even when one of its endpoints was never declared as an entity; the graph builder then creates the missing node with an empty description. That preserves recall but lets misspelled names become nodes. A stricter policy drops those relationships. There is no universally right answer, so count them and decide with data. Exercise 8.2 asks you to write the strict variant.

## Gleaning: asking “did you miss anything?”

A single pass over a dense chunk misses entities, especially late in long chunks. Gleaning is a simple loop: after the first extraction, append the model's answer to the conversation and say that many entities were missed, then ask it to add them in the same format. After each round, ask a yes/no question about whether anything is still missing, and stop when the answer is no or you hit a round limit.

[Interactive figure: The gleaning loop (flow)]

```python  # minigraphrag/extraction.py
def extract_from_unit(
    llm: LLM, unit: TextUnit, entity_types: list[str] | None = None, max_gleanings: int = 1
) -> ExtractionResult:
    """Extract entities/relationships from one chunk, with up to `max_gleanings` extra passes.

    Our LLM interface is single-turn, so the "conversation" is replayed by
    concatenating: original prompt + previous answers + follow-up instruction.
    """
    types = ",".join(entity_types or P.DEFAULT_ENTITY_TYPES)
    prompt = P.ENTITY_EXTRACTION_PROMPT.format(
        entity_types=types, input_text=unit.text, tuple_delimiter=P.TUPLE_DELIMITER,
        record_delimiter=P.RECORD_DELIMITER, completion_delimiter=P.COMPLETION_DELIMITER,
    )
    response = llm.complete(prompt)
    calls, transcript, outputs = 1, prompt + response, [response]
    for i in range(max_gleanings):
        more = llm.complete(transcript + P.GLEANING_CONTINUE_PROMPT)
        calls += 1
        outputs.append(more)
        transcript += P.GLEANING_CONTINUE_PROMPT + more
        if i >= max_gleanings - 1:
            break  # no point asking "anything left?" if we won't act on it
        answer = llm.complete(transcript + P.GLEANING_LOOP_CHECK_PROMPT)
        calls += 1
        if answer.strip().upper()[:1] != "Y":
            break

    result = ExtractionResult(unit.id, llm_calls=calls)
    for out in outputs:
        ents, rels = parse_extraction_output(out, source_id=unit.id)
        result.entities.extend(ents)
        result.relationships.extend(rels)
    return result
```

**Edge et al., From Local to Global (2024)

In the paper's appendix on self-reflection, on a sample of HotPotQA, GPT-4 extracted almost twice as many entity references with 600-token chunks as with 2400-token chunks in a single pass. Their Figure 3 then shows gleaning rounds lifting the larger chunks back up. Chunk size and gleaning are two knobs on the same recall budget: smaller chunks cost more calls per document, gleaning costs more calls per chunk.

Every gleaning round re-sends the whole transcript, so the cost grows faster than linearly with rounds. The pattern people report after measuring it is that the first round adds a handful of real entities per dense chunk and the second adds mostly aliases and noise. That is other people's corpora; Exercise 8.3 has you measure it on yours.

## Failure modes to watch for

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix

“Sentinel” and “Project Sentinel” are separate nodes | Aliases in different chunks | Entity resolution (Chapter 9); add alias guidance to the prompt

Types like COMPANY or STARTUP appear | Type drift | Map unknown types to the nearest allowed type or to OTHER after parsing

Edges no sentence supports | Model inferring from world knowledge | Add “only relationships stated in the text”; spot-check with provenance ids

Pronouns become entities (“THE COMPANY”) | No coreference guidance | Instruct to resolve pronouns to named entities; drop generic nouns

Very few records from long chunks | Attention thins over long inputs | Smaller chunks or one gleaning round

Parser drops many records | Delimiter mismatch or chatty output | Log raw outputs; tighten the example; switch to schema-enforced JSON

Making the event a node lets you attach a date and connect it to both the reef and the detector, which a single edge cannot do.

#### Exercise 8.2 Core

Write three unit tests for parse_extraction_output that cover: (a) a record wrapped in leading prose, (b) a relationship strength written as "high (8)", and (c) a relationship to an undeclared entity. For (c), also write a strict drop_dangling helper and test both policies.

▸ Hint

Build the strings with the delimiter constants from minigraphrag.prompts so a delimiter change does not silently break your tests.

▸ Show answer

```python
from minigraphrag.extraction import parse_extraction_output
from minigraphrag.prompts import TUPLE_DELIMITER as T, RECORD_DELIMITER as R, COMPLETION_DELIMITER as DONE

def test_prose_before_record():
    out = f'Sure! Here you go: ("entity"{T}DEEPCAST{T}ORGANIZATION{T}Sonar maker){R}{DONE}'
    ents, rels = parse_extraction_output(out, source_id="u1")
    assert [e.name for e in ents] == ["DEEPCAST"] and ents[0].source_id == "u1"

def test_strength_with_words():
    out = (f'("entity"{T}A{T}ORGANIZATION{T}x){R}("entity"{T}B{T}ORGANIZATION{T}y){R}'
           f'("relationship"{T}A{T}B{T}a buys b{T}high (8))')
    _, rels = parse_extraction_output(out)
    assert rels[0].strength == 8.0 and rels[0].description == "a buys b"

def drop_dangling(entities, relationships):
    known = {e.name for e in entities}
    return [r for r in relationships if r.source in known and r.target in known]

def test_dangling_relationship():
    out = f'("entity"{T}A{T}ORGANIZATION{T}x){R}("relationship"{T}A{T}GHOST{T}?{T}5)'
    ents, rels = parse_extraction_output(out)
    assert len(rels) == 1                      # the parser keeps it (recall-first policy)
    assert drop_dangling(ents, rels) == []     # the strict policy removes it
```

The re.sub(r"[^\d.]", "", ...) in the parser is what rescues “high (8)”: it strips everything except digits and dots. It has a weakness: “8 of 10” becomes “810”. A stricter version would take the first number with re.search, which is a good follow-up change to make and test.

#### Exercise 8.3 Core

Run extraction over the whole Kestrel corpus with max_gleanings set to 0, 1 and 2. For each setting record: total LLM calls, total input and output tokens, unique entity names, and how many of the 17 canonical entities in the running example were found (after uppercasing). Where does the curve flatten?

▸ Show answer

A good test runner keeps everything else fixed (chunk size, model, temperature 0) and wraps the LLM to count calls and tokens:

```python
from minigraphrag.chunking import chunk_documents, load_documents
from minigraphrag.extraction import extract_from_unit
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.prompts import DEFAULT_ENTITY_TYPES as TYPES

docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
real_llm = get_llm("openai")    # or "anthropic" / "ollama"; the mock is gazetteer-based and not a fair test

CANON = {"KESTREL LABS", "DR. MIRA OKAFOR", "JONAS VEHL", "PRIYA NAIR", "TIDEWATER INSTITUTE",
         "DR. ANA RUIZ", "PROJECT SENTINEL", "PROJECT TERN", "HALDEN REEF", "PORT AVALON",
         "2024 HALDEN REEF BLEACHING EVENT", "BRIGHTWATER CAPITAL", "LENA PARK",
         "MARLOW DYNAMICS", "DEEPCAST", "OCEAN HEALTH ACT", "PORT AVALON CITY COUNCIL"}

class Counting:
    def __init__(self, llm): self.llm, self.calls, self.chars = llm, 0, 0
    def complete(self, prompt, **kw):
        self.calls += 1; out = self.llm.complete(prompt, **kw)
        self.chars += len(prompt) + len(out); return out

for g in (0, 1, 2):
    llm = Counting(real_llm)
    names = set()
    for unit in chunk_documents(docs, size=600, overlap=50):
        result = extract_from_unit(llm, unit, TYPES, max_gleanings=g)
        names |= {e.name for e in result.entities}
    print(g, llm.calls, llm.chars // 4, len(names), len(CANON & names))
```

What you should observe: going from 0 to 1 round roughly doubles calls and adds a noticeable number of names, including some canonical ones that appear late in long chunks. Going from 1 to 2 adds far fewer names, many of them aliases or noise, at a higher cost per round because the transcript is longer. Exact numbers depend on the model. Strict matching against canonical names undercounts, because “MIRA OKAFOR” will not match “DR. MIRA OKAFOR”; that gap is the motivation for Chapter 9.

#### Exercise 8.4 Stretch

Implement a JSON-mode extractor using a Pydantic schema, then compare it with the tuple extractor on the same chunks: parse failure rate, output tokens and entity recall. Under what conditions did JSON win?

▸ Show answer

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError
import json

class EntityOut(BaseModel):
    name: str
    type: str
    description: str

class RelOut(BaseModel):
    source: str
    target: str
    description: str
    strength: int = Field(ge=1, le=10)

class ExtractionOut(BaseModel):
    entities: list[EntityOut]
    relationships: list[RelOut]

def extract_json(llm, unit, types):
    prompt = (f"Extract entities of types {types} and relationships among them from the text. "
              f"Return JSON matching this schema:\n{json.dumps(ExtractionOut.model_json_schema())}\n\n"
              f"Text:\n{unit.text}")
    raw = llm.complete(prompt, json=True)
    try:
        return ExtractionOut.model_validate_json(raw), None
    except ValidationError as err:
        return None, err
```

Typical findings: with a provider that enforces the schema, JSON's parse failure rate drops to near zero, while tuple parsing loses a small percentage of records to formatting slips. JSON uses more output tokens per record. Tuples degrade more gracefully when output hits the max-token limit, because every record before the cut survives. JSON tends to win for hosted models with structured outputs and small chunks; tuples tend to win for small local models and dense chunks.

## Check your understanding

Why does the extractor store a free-text description for each entity instead of just a type?

- Descriptions are required by the graph database

- ✓ (correct) Descriptions from many chunks are later summarized into a profile that search and reports can use

- Types are unreliable, so descriptions replace them

- Descriptions make the extraction prompt shorter
Answer: Each chunk contributes its own view of the entity. Resolution merges these, and an LLM summarizes them into one description that gets embedded for local search and quoted in community reports.

An extraction output is cut off by the max-token limit halfway through the 14th record. Which format loses less?

- JSON, because it has a schema

- ✓ (correct) Delimited tuples, because the first 13 complete records still parse

- Both lose everything

- Neither loses anything if temperature is 0
Answer: Tuple records are independent, so a tolerant parser keeps all complete ones. A truncated JSON document is invalid as a whole unless you add repair logic.

What does the gleaning loop-check prompt decide?

- Whether the extracted relationships are correct

- Which entity types to use

- ✓ (correct) Whether to run another round of “add what you missed”

- Whether to split the chunk into smaller pieces
Answer: It is a one-token Y/N question asked after a gleaning round. N (or the round limit) ends the loop.

The text says Marlow acquired Deepcast, and separately that Kestrel started Project Tern after losing its supplier. Should the extractor emit MARLOW DYNAMICS → PROJECT TERN?

- Yes, because it is true and saves a hop later

- ✓ (correct) No, not unless a sentence states it; multi-hop connections are for retrieval to discover

- Yes, but only with strength 10

- No, because organizations cannot relate to projects
Answer: Inferred edges are unverifiable and compound errors. Keep the graph faithful to the text and let path retrieval connect the dots, with each hop citable.

You see entity types COMPANY, FIRM and ORGANIZATION in your graph. What is the cheapest reliable fix?

- Increase temperature

- Add more gleaning rounds

- ✓ (correct) Normalize types after parsing, mapping unknown types to allowed ones or OTHER, and tighten the prompt

- Remove types entirely
Answer: Post-parse normalization is deterministic and free. Pair it with a prompt that lists allowed types explicitly and an example that uses them.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Can I use a classical NER model instead of an LLM?

Yes, for entities. spaCy or GLiNER-style models are fast and cheap and work well for standard types. They are weaker at relationship extraction with free-text descriptions, which is what GraphRAG's summaries rely on. A common hybrid: classical NER proposes entity spans, and a smaller LLM writes relationships and descriptions only for chunks with two or more entities. LightRAG's and LazyGraphRAG's cost ideas (Chapter 26) push this further.

▸ Should I extract per chunk or per document?

Per chunk. Long inputs reduce recall, and chunk ids give you precise provenance. Pass document-level context (title, date, section heading) into each chunk's prompt so the model can resolve “the company” and date relative references.

▸ How do I pick relationship strength?

The model's 1–10 score is a rough signal of how central and explicit the relation is. Its main use is as an edge weight: summed across chunks it tells you which relations are repeated, which helps community detection and ranking. Don't treat a single score as calibrated.

▸ Is a fixed relation vocabulary (CEO_OF, ACQUIRED) better than free-text descriptions?

It depends on your queries. Fixed relation types enable precise graph queries such as Text2Cypher and metapaths (Chapters 20 and 21). Free-text descriptions capture nuance that summarization and embedding search can use. Many systems do both: a typed label plus a description. minigraphrag stores only the description. If you want a label as well, add a label field drawn from a fixed list to the JSON schema in Exercise 8.4.

▸ What temperature should extraction use?

0, or as low as your provider allows. You want reproducible graphs so that re-indexing a document does not churn nodes, and so caching (keyed on prompt hash) actually hits.

### Project: an extraction workbench

Build a small command-line tool that makes extraction quality visible, so you can tune prompts with evidence instead of vibes.

- extract --unit <id> prints the raw LLM output, the parsed records and any dropped records with the reason

- A run over the full corpus writes entities.jsonl and relationships.jsonl with each record's source_id

- A report: records per chunk, type distribution, dropped-record rate, gleaning yield per round

- A gold file of hand-labeled entities for three chunks, and precision and recall against it

- One prompt change you made because of the report, with before and after numbers

Done when you can point at a number that got better and the prompt diff that caused it.

## Key takeaways

- Every extracted entity and relationship carries a free-text description and the id of the text unit it came from.

- A good prompt names allowed types, fixes the output format, shows a worked example, and puts variable input last.

- Parse defensively: keep complete records, normalize names and types, log what you drop.

- Gleaning trades extra calls for recall with quickly diminishing returns. Measure it on your data.

- Keep the graph faithful to the text; let retrieval discover multi-hop connections.
