## Storing and indexing the graph

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/13-storage-indexing.html
Summary: Parquet/JSON artifacts, NetworkX, Neo4j, Postgres, and embedding entities, edges and reports.

# Storing and indexing the graph

Everything you built in Part 2 is expensive to compute and cheap to read. This chapter turns it into a durable index: a small set of tables with stable ids, the right things embedded, a storage backend that fits your queries, and a pipeline you can re-run without paying for it twice.

## You will be able to

- Describe the eight artifacts a GraphRAG index produces, their columns and how they join

- Decide what text to embed for entities, relationships, text units and reports, and justify each choice

- Compare files plus NetworkX, Neo4j, Postgres with pgvector or Apache AGE, and a split vector and graph store

- Structure indexing as a cached DAG with idempotent ids so re-runs only redo what changed

- Load the Kestrel index into Neo4j with constraints, MERGE and a vector index, and run a two-hop query in Postgres

## Why the index is a set of tables

By the end of Chapter 12 the Kestrel Labs pipeline has made hundreds of LLM calls: extraction and gleaning per text unit, claim extraction, description summaries per merged entity and relationship, and one report per community. On a real corpus that is hours of work and a noticeable bill. Query time is the opposite: local search makes one generation call, and even global search only reads reports that already exist.

That asymmetry drives the design. Indexing is a batch job that writes artifacts: plain, inspectable tables. Query engines load those tables and never re-derive them. Separating the two gives you three things you will want in production:

- Debuggability. When local search cites a wrong relationship, you open relationships.json, find id 16 and follow its source_ids back to the sentence that produced it.

- Swappable serving. The same artifacts can be served from memory with NetworkX, loaded into Neo4j, or copied into Postgres. The retrieval algorithm does not change, only the queries that fetch neighbors and vectors.

- Incremental work. If each step's output is keyed by its inputs, a re-run after a prompt tweak only redoes the steps downstream of that prompt.

### The eight artifacts

Microsoft GraphRAG writes its index as parquet files, one per table. minigraphrag writes the same information as JSON (so you can read it in an editor), GraphML for the graph, and a .npz/.json pair per vector store. The names differ slightly; the shapes are the same.

Artifact | One row per | Microsoft GraphRAG output | minigraphrag file | Joins to

documents | input file | documents.parquet | (implicit: doc_id is the file stem) | text units by document id

text_units | chunk | text_units.parquet | text_units.json | documents; entities and relationships through their source ids

entities | resolved entity | entities.parquet | entities.json | text units, communities

relationships | merged edge | relationships.parquet | relationships.json | entities by name; text units

claims | dated claim | covariates.parquet (optional) | claims.json | entities by subject and object; one text unit

communities | community at a level | communities.parquet | communities.json | entities, relationships, parent and children

community_reports | report | community_reports.parquet | community_reports.json | communities by community id

embeddings | embedded text | a vector store (LanceDB by default), not a parquet table | entity_embeddings, relationship_embeddings, text_unit_embeddings, report_embeddings (.npz + .json) | the row whose id it stores

Two more files round out a minigraphrag index: config.json, which records the IndexConfig and the embedder name so load_index can rebuild the same embedder, and graph.graphml, an export you can open in Gephi or yEd.

### Schemas, column by column

The tables below list the columns that matter for retrieval. GraphRAG names come from its output documentation; the right-hand column shows where the same fact lives in minigraphrag.

text_units

GraphRAG column | Meaning | minigraphrag field

id | Stable id (a content hash in GraphRAG) | id, for example 07_marlow_acquires_deepcast-000

human_readable_id | Short integer used in citations | (the id is already readable)

text, n_tokens | Chunk content and its token count | text, n_tokens

document_id | Parent document | doc_id, plus start/end character offsets

entity_ids, relationship_ids, covariate_ids | What was extracted from this chunk | stored the other way round, as source_ids on entities and relationships

entities

GraphRAG column | Meaning | minigraphrag field

id, human_readable_id | Global id and short citation id | name is the key; human_id is the citation id

title | Entity name | name (uppercase, resolved)

type | Entity type | type (majority vote across mentions)

description | Summarized description | description, plus the raw descriptions list and aliases

text_unit_ids | Chunks that mention it | source_ids

frequency, degree | Mention count and number of graph neighbors | frequency, degree, and rank (= degree)

relationships

GraphRAG column | Meaning | minigraphrag field

id, human_readable_id | Global id and short citation id | human_id

source, target | Entity names | source, target (undirected in minigraphrag)

description | Summarized description | description and raw descriptions

weight | Summed extraction strength | weight

combined_degree | Degree of source plus degree of target | combined_degree and rank

text_unit_ids | Supporting chunks | source_ids

claims, communities and community_reports

GraphRAG column | Meaning | minigraphrag field

subject_id, object_id, type, status | Claim about an entity; status TRUE, FALSE or SUSPECTED | subject, object, type, status

start_date, end_date, source_text, text_unit_id | When it held, the quoted evidence and its chunk | start_date, end_date, source_text, source_id

community, level, parent, children | Position in the hierarchy | id, level, parent, children

entity_ids, relationship_ids, size | Membership | nodes, edges

title, summary, full_content | Generated report text | title, summary, full_content (rendered from findings)

rank, rating_explanation, findings | Importance rating, its reason, 5 to 10 insights | rating, rating_explanation, findings

**Two ids per row, on purpose

GraphRAG keeps a long globally unique id for joins and a small human_readable_id for prompts. The model cites [Data: Relationships (16)], which costs a few tokens and is easy to verify, rather than a 128-character hash it might mangle. Keep both kinds of id in your own schema: one for machines, one for the LLM.

### The schema as a graph

The artifacts form three layers stacked on each other. The lexical layer is documents and chunks. The entity layer is what extraction found. The community layer is what clustering and summarization added. Provenance edges tie the layers together, and they are what make citations possible. Step through one slice of the Kestrel index.

[Interactive figure: Lexical, entity and community layers — One slice of the Kestrel Labs index (graph-steps)]

## What gets embedded, and why

Vectors are how a query enters the graph. A query has no node id; it has words. Every retrieval method in Part 3 starts by embedding something about the query and comparing it with something stored. So the indexing question is: which text, for which row, will a future query need to be close to?

Store | Text embedded in minigraphrag | Why this text | Used by

Entities | "{name}: {description}" | Queries often describe things by role (“the sonar supplier”) rather than by name. The description carries those words. | Local search seeds (Ch. 14), LightRAG low-level keywords (Ch. 16), HippoRAG seeds (Ch. 17)

Relationships | "{source} {target}: {description}" | Themes such as “supply-chain risk” live on edges, not nodes. Including endpoint names keeps the vector anchored. | LightRAG high-level keywords (Ch. 16)

Text units | The chunk text | The baseline and fallback: exact wording, numbers and quotes. | Basic search, hybrid retrieval (Ch. 21)

Reports | full_content (title, summary and findings) | Lets a query find the right region of the corpus without reading every report. | DRIFT primer (Ch. 15)

Microsoft GraphRAG's current defaults embed three of these: entity title:description, community report full_content, and text unit text. It does not embed relationship descriptions by default, because none of its built-in search methods query them. LightRAG does, because its global mode is relationship-first. Embed what your retrieval methods read, and nothing else: every extra store costs embedding calls on every re-index and has to stay in sync with the rows it points at.

Here is the relevant part of build_index. The metadata stored next to each vector is exactly what the caller needs to jump back into the graph: a human_id for entities, endpoints for relationships, a doc_id for chunks, a level for reports.

```python  # minigraphrag/indexer.py
def entity_embedding_text(name: str, data: dict) -> str:
    return f"{name}: {data.get('description', '')}"


def relationship_embedding_text(u: str, v: str, data: dict) -> str:
    return f"{u} {v}: {data.get('description', '')}"


# inside build_index(...), after reports are generated
entity_store = _embed_store(
    embedder, list(G.nodes()), [entity_embedding_text(n, d) for n, d in G.nodes(data=True)],
    [{"human_id": d["human_id"]} for _, d in G.nodes(data=True)])
relationship_store = _embed_store(
    embedder, [str(d["human_id"]) for _, _, d in G.edges(data=True)],
    [relationship_embedding_text(u, v, d) for u, v, d in G.edges(data=True)],
    [{"source": u, "target": v} for u, v in G.edges()])
text_unit_store = _embed_store(embedder, [u.id for u in units], [u.text for u in units],
                               [{"doc_id": u.doc_id} for u in units])
report_store = _embed_store(embedder, [str(r.community_id) for r in reports],
                            [r.full_content for r in reports], [{"level": r.level} for r in reports])
```

### Why the description matters

Try it on Kestrel. The query “Who designed the sonar array on the drones?” shares no words with the string JONAS VEHL. It shares several with his summarized description, “Co-founder of Kestrel Labs and its CTO from 2021 to March 2026; designed the Sentinel sonar array; co-leads Project Tern.” Embedding name: description lets the name match name-style queries and the description match role-style ones. The cost is that a wrong or bloated description drags the vector away from the entity. That is one more reason the summarization step in Chapter 9 caps description length.

### What the vectors cost

Embedding tokens are cheap next to extraction tokens, so cost is rarely the constraint. Memory and index build time are. A vector of d float32 dimensions takes 4d bytes before any index overhead. A mid-size corpus with 40,000 entities, 90,000 relationships, 60,000 chunks and 3,000 reports has 193,000 vectors; at 1,536 dimensions that is 193,000 × 6,144 bytes ≈ 1.19 GB of raw floats, and an HNSW graph adds more on top. Halving dimensions or using half-precision storage halves that. minigraphrag's default HashingEmbedder uses 512 dimensions, which is why its stores are tiny.

**The embedding model is part of the index

Vectors from two different models are not comparable, even at the same dimension. save_index writes the embedder name into config.json, and load_index rebuilds the same embedder from it. If you change models, re-embed every store. A query embedded with model B against vectors from model A returns confident nonsense, not an error.

## Choosing a storage backend

Retrieval needs a handful of primitive operations, whatever the algorithm on top:

- Vector top-k: nearest entities, relationships, chunks or reports to a query vector.

- Neighbor expansion: the edges of a set of nodes, sometimes to two or three hops.

- Lookup by id: the text units, claims and reports for a set of ids.

- Upsert: add or replace rows when documents change (Chapter 27).

The backends below differ in how well they do each, and in how many systems you have to run to get all four.

Option | Vector top-k | Multi-hop traversal | Updates and concurrency | Operations | Good fit

Files (JSON or parquet) + NetworkX in memory | Brute force with numpy; exact and fast to roughly 105 rows; add FAISS or LanceDB beyond | Python loops over adjacency dicts; fine for small hops | Rewrite files; one writer; reload to see changes | None: a folder | Learning, research, CI, corpora that fit in RAM, read-only serving

Neo4j with vector indexes | Native HNSW indexes on node and relationship properties | Excellent: variable-length patterns and graph algorithms | ACID transactions, MERGE for idempotent upserts | One more database to run; Cypher skills | Graph-heavy retrieval, Text2Cypher (Ch. 20), path queries, many concurrent users

Postgres + pgvector + recursive CTEs | HNSW or IVFFlat indexes; filters in the same SQL | Recursive CTEs: fine for 2 to 3 hops with indexed edge columns, clumsy beyond | ACID; joins with your existing app tables and permissions | Usually already running | Teams already on Postgres, access control joined to data (Ch. 29)

Postgres + Apache AGE (+ pgvector) | pgvector alongside | openCypher inside SQL via cypher() | ACID | Extension to install and upgrade; smaller community | Cypher on Postgres without a second database

Dedicated vector DB + graph DB | Best-in-class ANN, filtering, sharding | Best-in-class in the graph DB | Two systems to keep consistent; no cross-store transaction | Highest | Very large corpora, separate teams owning search and graph

A useful rule: stay with files and NetworkX until one of three things happens: the graph no longer fits comfortably in memory, several processes need to write, or you need queries that are painful to hand-code (variable-length paths, graph algorithms at query time). LightRAG's documentation makes the same point about its own defaults: its file-backed stores are meant for testing, and it recommends PostgreSQL for production.

### Loading the Kestrel index into Neo4j

A good loader has three properties. It declares uniqueness constraints first, so duplicates are impossible and MERGE lookups hit an index. It uses MERGE on the key and SET for everything else, so running it twice changes nothing. And it sends rows in batches through UNWIND $rows with parameters, never by pasting values into query strings.

```python  # neo4j/schema.cypher
// Uniqueness constraints also create the lookup indexes MERGE needs.
CREATE CONSTRAINT document_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (d:Document) REQUIRE d.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT chunk_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (c:Chunk) REQUIRE c.id IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT entity_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Entity) REQUIRE e.name IS UNIQUE;
CREATE CONSTRAINT community_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (c:Community) REQUIRE c.id IS UNIQUE;

// Vector indexes: dimensions must match the embedder (512 for HashingEmbedder).
CREATE VECTOR INDEX entity_embedding IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (e:Entity) ON e.embedding
OPTIONS { indexConfig: {
  `vector.dimensions`: 512,
  `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'
}};

CREATE VECTOR INDEX related_embedding IF NOT EXISTS
FOR ()-[r:RELATED]-() ON (r.embedding)
OPTIONS { indexConfig: {
  `vector.dimensions`: 512,
  `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'
}};
```

minigraphrag already ships a minimal exporter, graph_to_cypher_statements(G) in search/text2cypher.py, which emits one MERGE statement per node and edge as text. That is handy for pasting into Neo4j Browser. For a real load you want parameters and batches, plus the lexical and community layers. The script below does that using the official neo4j Python driver (pip install minigraphrag[neo4j]).

```python  # examples/load_neo4j.py
from neo4j import GraphDatabase
from minigraphrag.indexer import load_index

CHUNKS = """
UNWIND $rows AS row
MERGE (d:Document {id: row.doc_id})
MERGE (c:Chunk {id: row.id})
SET c.text = row.text, c.n_tokens = row.n_tokens, c.embedding = row.embedding
MERGE (d)-[:HAS_CHUNK]->(c)
"""

ENTITIES = """
UNWIND $rows AS row
MERGE (e:Entity {name: row.name})
SET e.human_id = row.human_id, e.type = row.type, e.description = row.description,
    e.degree = row.degree, e.embedding = row.embedding
WITH e, row
UNWIND row.source_ids AS uid
MATCH (c:Chunk {id: uid})
MERGE (c)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
"""

RELATIONSHIPS = """
UNWIND $rows AS row
MATCH (a:Entity {name: row.source}), (b:Entity {name: row.target})
MERGE (a)-[r:RELATED]-(b)
SET r.human_id = row.human_id, r.description = row.description,
    r.weight = row.weight, r.source_ids = row.source_ids, r.embedding = row.embedding
"""

COMMUNITIES = """
UNWIND $rows AS row
MERGE (c:Community {id: row.id})
SET c.level = row.level, c.title = row.title, c.summary = row.summary,
    c.full_content = row.full_content, c.rating = row.rating
WITH c, row
UNWIND row.nodes AS name
MATCH (e:Entity {name: name})
MERGE (e)-[:IN_COMMUNITY]->(c)
"""

PARENTS = """
UNWIND $rows AS row
MATCH (child:Community {id: row.id}), (parent:Community {id: row.parent})
MERGE (child)-[:PARENT]->(parent)
"""


def batched(rows, size=500):
    for i in range(0, len(rows), size):
        yield rows[i:i + size]


def export_to_neo4j(index_dir, uri="bolt://localhost:7687", auth=("neo4j", "password")):
    index = load_index(index_dir)
    G = index.graph
    ent_vec = dict(zip(index.entity_store.ids, index.entity_store.matrix.tolist()))
    rel_vec = dict(zip(index.relationship_store.ids, index.relationship_store.matrix.tolist()))
    unit_vec = dict(zip(index.text_unit_store.ids, index.text_unit_store.matrix.tolist()))
    reports = {r.community_id: r for r in index.reports}

    chunks = [{**u.to_dict(), "embedding": unit_vec.get(u.id)} for u in index.text_units.values()]
    entities = [{"name": n, "human_id": d["human_id"], "type": d.get("type", ""),
                 "description": d.get("description", ""), "degree": d.get("degree", 0),
                 "source_ids": d.get("source_ids", []), "embedding": ent_vec.get(n)}
                for n, d in G.nodes(data=True)]
    relationships = [{"source": u, "target": v, "human_id": d["human_id"],
                      "description": d.get("description", ""), "weight": d.get("weight", 1.0),
                      "source_ids": d.get("source_ids", []), "embedding": rel_vec.get(str(d["human_id"]))}
                     for u, v, d in G.edges(data=True)]
    communities = []
    for c in index.communities:
        r = reports.get(c.id)
        communities.append({"id": c.id, "level": c.level, "parent": c.parent, "nodes": c.nodes,
                            "title": r.title if r else "", "summary": r.summary if r else "",
                            "full_content": r.full_content if r else "", "rating": r.rating if r else 0.0})

    with GraphDatabase.driver(uri, auth=auth) as driver:
        # Order matters: chunks before MENTIONS, entities before RELATED and IN_COMMUNITY.
        for query, rows in [(CHUNKS, chunks), (ENTITIES, entities), (RELATIONSHIPS, relationships),
                            (COMMUNITIES, communities),
                            (PARENTS, [c for c in communities if c["parent"] is not None])]:
            for batch in batched(rows):
                driver.execute_query(query, rows=batch)
```

Setting a property to a list of floats is enough for the vector index to pick it up. Neo4j also has the procedure db.create.setNodeVectorProperty, which checks that the value is a valid vector before storing it, and Neo4j 2025.10 added a native VECTOR property type under Cypher 25; any of these works with the index above.

Now local search's first two steps are one query. Find the five entities nearest the query vector, then fetch their relationships and the chunks that mention them:

```python  # neo4j/local_seed.cypher
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes('entity_embedding', 5, $query_vector)
YIELD node AS e, score
OPTIONAL MATCH (e)-[r:RELATED]-(nbr:Entity)
WITH e, score, r, nbr ORDER BY r.weight DESC
WITH e, score, collect({id: r.human_id, other: nbr.name, description: r.description})[..10] AS rels
OPTIONAL MATCH (c:Chunk)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
RETURN e.human_id AS id, e.name AS entity, score, rels, collect(c.id) AS chunk_ids
ORDER BY score DESC
```

**The SEARCH subclause in newer Neo4j

Neo4j 2026.01 introduced a Cypher 25 SEARCH subclause for MATCH, and the documentation marks db.index.vector.queryNodes as deprecated from 2026.04, though it still runs. The equivalent seed step is MATCH (e:Entity) SEARCH e IN (VECTOR INDEX entity_embedding FOR $query_vector LIMIT 5) SCORE AS score. Check which Cypher version your server defaults to before choosing.

### Two hops in Postgres

If you already run Postgres, the same index fits in three tables. pgvector adds a vector(n) column type, a cosine distance operator <=> and HNSW indexes. Traversal is a recursive common table expression.

```python  # postgres/schema.sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE text_units (
  id        text PRIMARY KEY,
  doc_id    text NOT NULL,
  text      text NOT NULL,
  n_tokens  int,
  embedding vector(512)
);

CREATE TABLE entities (
  name        text PRIMARY KEY,
  human_id    int UNIQUE,
  type        text,
  description text,
  degree      int,
  source_ids  text[],
  embedding   vector(512)
);

CREATE TABLE relationships (
  human_id    int PRIMARY KEY,
  source      text NOT NULL REFERENCES entities(name),
  target      text NOT NULL REFERENCES entities(name),
  description text,
  weight      real,
  source_ids  text[],
  embedding   vector(512)
);
CREATE INDEX ON relationships (source);
CREATE INDEX ON relationships (target);
CREATE INDEX ON entities USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- The graph is undirected: expose each edge in both directions once.
CREATE VIEW edges AS
  SELECT source AS a, target AS b, human_id, weight FROM relationships
  UNION ALL
  SELECT target AS a, source AS b, human_id, weight FROM relationships;
```

```python  # postgres/two_hops.sql
-- Every entity within two hops of PROJECT TERN, with its distance.
WITH RECURSIVE hops(name, depth, path) AS (
    SELECT 'PROJECT TERN'::text, 0, ARRAY['PROJECT TERN']::text[]
  UNION ALL
    SELECT e.b, h.depth + 1, h.path || e.b
    FROM hops h
    JOIN edges e ON e.a = h.name
    WHERE h.depth < 2
      AND NOT e.b = ANY(h.path)          -- no cycles
)
SELECT name, min(depth) AS distance
FROM hops
GROUP BY name
ORDER BY distance, name;
```

On the Kestrel graph (17 entities, 31 relationships) this returns 16 rows: Project Tern itself, five neighbors at distance 1 (Deepcast, Jonas Vehl, Kestrel Labs, Priya Nair, Project Sentinel) and ten entities at distance 2. Only Dr. Ana Ruiz is missing. Two hops from one project touched almost the whole graph, because one of its neighbors is the hub Kestrel Labs with 11 edges. Keep that in mind for local search: raw hop count is a poor relevance signal once a hub is involved.

The recursive CTE enumerates paths, not nodes, so its intermediate result grows roughly as the product of degrees along the way. That is fine at two hops with indexed a columns and a LIMIT; at four hops on a real graph it can explode. Vector search and traversal can share one statement, which is the main ergonomic win of keeping both in Postgres:

```python  # postgres/seed_and_expand.sql
WITH seeds AS (
  SELECT name, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity
  FROM entities
  ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
  LIMIT 5
)
SELECT s.name AS seed, s.similarity, r.human_id, r.source, r.target, r.description, r.weight
FROM seeds s
JOIN relationships r ON r.source = s.name OR r.target = s.name
ORDER BY s.similarity DESC, r.weight DESC;
```

Apache AGE takes the other route: it adds a graph catalog to Postgres and lets you run openCypher inside SQL. After CREATE EXTENSION age; and SELECT create_graph('kestrel');, each session runs LOAD 'age'; and puts ag_catalog on the search path, and a two-hop query looks like this:

```python  # postgres/age_two_hops.sql
LOAD 'age';
SET search_path = ag_catalog, "$user", public;

SELECT * FROM cypher('kestrel', $$
  MATCH (t:Entity {name: 'PROJECT TERN'})-[:RELATED*1..2]-(other:Entity)
  RETURN DISTINCT other.name
$$) AS (name agtype);
```

## The indexing pipeline as a cached DAG

Indexing is a directed acyclic graph of steps: each step reads some artifacts and writes one. Seeing it as a DAG answers two practical questions: what can run in parallel, and what must re-run when something changes.

[Interactive figure: The full indexing pipeline — What build_index does, in order (flow)]

[Diagram]

The indexing DAG. Claims and entity extraction both read text units and can run side by side; chunk embeddings need nothing but chunks. The dashed arrow is a light dependency: claims only need the alias map to rename their subjects. A change invalidates exactly the steps reachable from it.

### Two layers of caching

The first layer caches LLM responses. CachedLLM wraps any client and keys each response by a SHA-256 hash of the model name, system prompt, prompt and JSON flag. Because extraction runs at temperature 0 and the prompt contains the chunk text, re-running the pipeline after an unrelated code change makes zero paid calls. You get it from the CLI with --cache-dir:

```python  # terminal
python -m minigraphrag index --input data/corpus --output .index --llm openai --cache-dir .cache/llm
# edit the community report prompt, then re-run: extraction and summaries are cache hits,
# only the report calls go to the API
python -m minigraphrag index --input data/corpus --output .index --llm openai --cache-dir .cache/llm
```

The second layer caches step outputs. A response cache still re-runs the Python around every call: parsing, resolution, graph building. For large corpora you also want to skip a whole step when its inputs have not changed. The recipe is the same one build systems use: hash the inputs, look for an artifact stored under that hash, and only compute on a miss. Exercise 13.5 builds this for minigraphrag.

Step | Inputs that belong in its cache key | LLM or embedding calls

Chunk | document text hashes, chunk_size, chunk_overlap, tokenizer | none

Extract entities | text unit hash, entity types, max_gleanings, prompt version, model | units × (1 + rounds) + loop checks

Extract claims | text unit hash, claim description, prompt version, model | one per unit

Resolve | hash of all raw entity names and types, alias_threshold | none (or embeddings if enabled)

Build graph | resolved mentions, summarize_max_tokens, summary prompt version | one per node or edge with several descriptions

Communities | graph structure and weights, max_cluster_size, seed | none

Reports | community membership plus member descriptions, report_max_tokens, prompt version | one per community

Embed | the exact embedded strings, embedder name | one batch per store

### Idempotent ids

Caching only works if the same input produces the same ids. Otherwise every re-run looks like new data, and loaders that MERGE on id create duplicates. There are three kinds of id in play, and they behave differently:

- Content-derived ids are stable by construction. GraphRAG derives document and text unit ids from a SHA-512 hash of their content. Change one character and you get a new id, which is exactly what a cache wants.

- Position-derived ids are stable until something shifts. minigraphrag names chunks {doc_id}-{i:03d}. Readable, and stable if a document is unchanged, but inserting a paragraph near the top renumbers every later chunk of that document.

- Run-derived ids are not stable at all. GraphRAG assigns entities, relationships and communities fresh UUIDs on each run, and minigraphrag's human_id is an entity's position in sorted order, so adding one entity named “AARDVARK” renumbers every other entity.

For entities, the natural stable key is the canonical name after resolution (that is what minigraphrag uses as the node key and what the Neo4j loader merges on). For relationships, use the sorted pair of endpoint names. Keep human_id for prompts only, and regenerate it at load time rather than storing it as a foreign key anywhere.

**Resolution decisions change ids

If a new document makes resolution merge “SENTINEL” into “PROJECT SENTINEL”, the key for that entity changes. A name-keyed store needs an explicit merge operation: re-point edges and MENTIONS from the old node to the survivor, then delete the old node. Chapter 27 builds this. Log every merge so you can undo a bad one.

### Reading the index back

load_index is the other half of the contract. It rebuilds the NetworkX graph from the entity and relationship tables, the dataclasses from their JSON, and the four vector stores from disk, and it makes no model calls except to construct the embedder named in config.json:

```python  # minigraphrag/indexer.py
def load_index(out_dir: str | Path, embedder: Embedder | None = None) -> Index:
    """Load artifacts written by `build_index`. The embedder is rebuilt from config unless given."""
    out = Path(out_dir)
    load = lambda name: json.loads((out / name).read_text())  # noqa: E731
    cfg = load("config.json")
    embedder_name = cfg.pop("embedder", "hashing")
    config = IndexConfig(**{k: v for k, v in cfg.items() if k in IndexConfig.__dataclass_fields__})
    embedder = embedder or get_embedder(embedder_name)

    G = nx.Graph()
    for e in load("entities.json"):
        G.add_node(e.pop("name"), **e)
    for r in load("relationships.json"):
        G.add_edge(r.pop("source"), r.pop("target"), **r)

    communities = [Community(**{**c, "edges": [tuple(e) for e in c["edges"]]}) for c in load("communities.json")]
    reports = [CommunityReport(**{k: v for k, v in r.items() if k != "full_content"})
               for r in load("community_reports.json")]
    claims = [Claim(**c) for c in load("claims.json")]
    units = {u["id"]: TextUnit(**u) for u in load("text_units.json")}
    stores = {name: VectorStore.load(out / f"{name}_embeddings")
              for name in ("entity", "relationship", "text_unit", "report")}
    return Index(G, units, communities, reports, claims, stores["entity"], stores["relationship"],
                 stores["text_unit"], stores["report"], embedder, config)
```

The returned Index is what every search function in Part 3 takes as its first argument. It also has three helpers you will use constantly: index.report(community_id), index.community(community_id) and index.communities_of(entity).

```python  # terminal
from minigraphrag.indexer import build_index, load_index
from minigraphrag.llm import MockLLM

index = build_index("data/corpus", ".index", MockLLM(), log=print)
# chunked 12 documents into 24 text units
# ... graph, communities and reports lines ...
again = load_index(".index")
assert set(again.graph.nodes) == set(index.graph.nodes)
print(again.communities_of("PROJECT TERN"))
```

## Trade-offs and failure modes

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix

Duplicate nodes after a second load into Neo4j | CREATE instead of MERGE, or merging on a run-derived id | Constraint on the natural key; MERGE on that key only; SET the rest

MERGE gets slower as the graph grows | No index behind the merge key | Create uniqueness constraints before loading

Local search returns unrelated entities after an upgrade | Query and stored vectors from different embedding models | Record the embedder in the index; refuse to load on mismatch; re-embed

Citations point at the wrong row after re-indexing | Position-based human_id shifted | Store answers with stable ids; map human ids only inside one prompt

Re-index costs as much as the first run | No response cache, or prompts contain run-specific text such as timestamps | CachedLLM; keep prompts deterministic

Recursive CTE times out | Path explosion through hubs; missing edge index | Index edge columns; cap depth; exclude hub nodes or filter by weight inside the recursion

Vector store and graph disagree | Two systems updated separately, one write failed | Write graph first, vectors second, with a reconciliation job keyed on ids

## Exercises

#### Exercise 13.1 Warm-up

Your company corpus indexes to 25,000 entities, 60,000 relationships, 80,000 text units and 2,000 community reports. You plan to embed entities, text units and reports (GraphRAG's defaults) with a 1,536-dimension model, stored as float32. (a) How much raw vector memory is that? (b) How much does adding relationship embeddings cost? (c) What if you store everything as half-precision (float16) instead?

▸ Show answer

Each float32 vector takes 1,536 × 4 = 6,144 bytes.

(a) 25,000 + 80,000 + 2,000 = 107,000 vectors. 107,000 × 6,144 = 657,408,000 bytes ≈ 627 MiB (about 0.66 GB).

(b) Relationships add 60,000 × 6,144 = 368,640,000 bytes ≈ 352 MiB, a 56% increase, bringing the total to 167,000 vectors ≈ 979 MiB. Worth it only if a retrieval method (LightRAG's global mode, Chapter 16) actually queries them.

(c) Half precision halves each vector to 3,072 bytes: 167,000 × 3,072 ≈ 489 MiB for all four stores. The HNSW graph structure is extra in every case and depends on the m parameter, so budget headroom beyond these raw numbers.

#### Exercise 13.2 Core

Canonical question 3 asks “What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?” Write a Postgres recursive CTE over the edges view that returns every simple path of at most three hops from PRIYA NAIR to DEEPCAST, shortest first. Then, by hand on the Kestrel graph, list the two-hop paths it returns. Which one actually answers the question?

▸ Hint

Carry the path array in the recursion, stop expanding once you reach the target or depth 3, and filter the final rows on the last element.

▸ Show answer

```python
WITH RECURSIVE walk(name, depth, path) AS (
    SELECT 'PRIYA NAIR'::text, 0, ARRAY['PRIYA NAIR']::text[]
  UNION ALL
    SELECT e.b, w.depth + 1, w.path || e.b
    FROM walk w
    JOIN edges e ON e.a = w.name
    WHERE w.depth < 3
      AND w.name <> 'DEEPCAST'           -- do not walk past the target
      AND NOT e.b = ANY(w.path)
)
SELECT depth AS hops, array_to_string(path, ' -> ') AS path
FROM walk
WHERE name = 'DEEPCAST'
ORDER BY hops, path;
```

The Kestrel graph has three two-hop paths:

- PRIYA NAIR → KESTREL LABS → DEEPCAST (she works at Kestrel, which Deepcast supplied)

- PRIYA NAIR → MARLOW DYNAMICS → DEEPCAST (she formerly worked at Marlow, which acquired Deepcast)

- PRIYA NAIR → PROJECT TERN → DEEPCAST (she co-leads Tern, which replaces Deepcast sonar)

and six three-hop paths (for example PRIYA NAIR → PROJECT SENTINEL → PROJECT TERN → DEEPCAST). The canonical answer uses the Marlow and Tern paths together; the Kestrel path is true but generic, because it goes through the hub. A database gives you all paths; deciding which ones matter is a ranking problem, which is what Chapter 18 on path retrieval tackles.

#### Exercise 13.3 Core

Make text unit and relationship ids idempotent. Write stable_unit_id(doc_text, start, end) and stable_relationship_id(source, target) so that (a) re-chunking an unchanged document gives identical ids, (b) inserting a paragraph at the top of a document changes the ids only of chunks whose text changed, and (c) the relationship id is the same whichever endpoint is listed first. Explain why (b) is only partly achievable with a fixed-size sliding window.

▸ Show answer

```python
import hashlib

def _h(s: str, n: int = 16) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(s.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:n]

def stable_unit_id(doc_text: str, start: int, end: int) -> str:
    # Hash only the chunk's own text, not its position or document offset.
    return "tu-" + _h(doc_text[start:end])

def stable_relationship_id(source: str, target: str) -> str:
    a, b = sorted((source, target))
    return "rel-" + _h(a + "␟" + b)   # a separator that never occurs in names

assert stable_relationship_id("DEEPCAST", "MARLOW DYNAMICS") == stable_relationship_id("MARLOW DYNAMICS", "DEEPCAST")
```

(a) holds because the same text gives the same hash. (c) holds because the pair is sorted before hashing, and the separator prevents ("AB", "C") colliding with ("A", "BC").

(b) is only partly achievable because a fixed word window is anchored to the start of the document. Inserting 40 words at the top shifts every window boundary by 40 words, so every chunk's text changes and every hash changes, even though most of the content is the same. Two remedies: chunk on structure (headings and paragraphs, Chapter 7), so an insertion only changes the section it lands in; or use content-defined chunking, where boundaries are chosen where a rolling hash of the text hits a pattern, so boundaries move with the content instead of with the offset. Either way, identical text keeps its id, which is what makes the extraction cache hit.

#### Exercise 13.4 Core

Load the Kestrel index into a local Neo4j with the loader from this chapter. Write the Cypher that checks (a) node counts per label, (b) that no two RELATED relationships connect the same pair of entities, and (c) that every entity is MENTIONS-linked to at least one chunk. Then run the loader a second time and explain why all counts stay the same.

▸ Show answer

```python
// (a) counts per label
MATCH (n) UNWIND labels(n) AS label
RETURN label, count(*) AS nodes ORDER BY label;

// (b) duplicate edges between the same pair (either direction)
MATCH (a:Entity)-[r:RELATED]-(b:Entity)
WHERE elementId(a) < elementId(b)
WITH a, b, count(r) AS n WHERE n > 1
RETURN a.name, b.name, n;

// (c) entities without provenance
MATCH (e:Entity) WHERE NOT (:Chunk)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
RETURN e.name;
```

For a clean index, (a) shows one Document per file, one Chunk per text unit, one Entity per node and one Community per community; (b) returns no rows; (c) returns no rows, unless extraction created entities only from relationship mentions, which build_graph allows and which leave source_ids empty. That is a real finding worth inspecting.

A second run is a no-op on counts because every write is a MERGE on a key protected by a uniqueness constraint (Document.id, Chunk.id, Entity.name, Community.id) and every relationship MERGE matches the existing pattern between the same two already-matched nodes. The undirected MERGE (a)-[r:RELATED]-(b) matches an existing edge in either direction, so it never adds a reverse copy. Properties are overwritten with SET, which is idempotent for identical values.

#### Exercise 13.5 Stretch

Add a step-level cache to indexing. Write cached_step(cache_dir, name, version, key_parts, compute) that returns a stored JSON result when the hash of (name, version, key_parts) has been seen and otherwise calls compute() and stores the result. Wrap chunking, resolution and community detection with it. Then predict which of the three recompute when you change (i) alias_threshold, (ii) chunk_overlap, (iii) seed.

▸ Show answer

```python
import hashlib, json
from pathlib import Path

def _digest(obj) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, default=str).encode()).hexdigest()

def cached_step(cache_dir, name, version, key_parts, compute):
    path = Path(cache_dir) / name / f"{_digest([name, version, key_parts])}.json"
    if path.exists():
        return json.loads(path.read_text())
    result = compute()
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(result))
    return result

# usage inside a custom build function
from minigraphrag.chunking import chunk_documents, TextUnit
from minigraphrag.resolution import resolve_entities
from minigraphrag.communities import hierarchical_communities, Community

docs_key = {d: _digest(t) for d, t in docs.items()}
units = [TextUnit(**u) for u in cached_step(
    ".cache/steps", "chunk", 1, [docs_key, config.chunk_size, config.chunk_overlap],
    lambda: [u.to_dict() for u in chunk_documents(docs, config.chunk_size, config.chunk_overlap)])]

mentions_key = sorted((e.name, e.type) for e in raw_entities)
name_map = cached_step(".cache/steps", "resolve", 1, [mentions_key, config.alias_threshold],
                       lambda: resolve_entities(raw_entities, alias_threshold=config.alias_threshold))

graph_key = sorted((u, v, d["weight"]) for u, v, d in G.edges(data=True))
communities = [Community(**{**c, "edges": [tuple(e) for e in c["edges"]]}) for c in cached_step(
    ".cache/steps", "communities", 1, [graph_key, config.max_cluster_size, config.seed],
    lambda: [c.to_dict() for c in hierarchical_communities(G, config.max_cluster_size, config.seed)])]
```

Predictions:

- (i) alias_threshold: chunking is a hit. Resolution misses. Communities recompute only if the new name map actually changes the graph; if no additional merges happen, the graph key is identical and it is a hit. That is the benefit of keying on the output of the previous step, not on the config of every earlier step.

- (ii) chunk_overlap: chunking misses, units change, so extraction (through CachedLLM) misses for every changed chunk, raw mentions change, and resolution and communities almost certainly miss too.

- (iii) seed: chunking and resolution hit; communities miss. Reports downstream then miss only for communities whose membership changed.

Bump version whenever you change a step's code in a way that changes its output; the inputs alone cannot tell the cache that the function changed.

## Check your understanding

Why do GraphRAG tables carry both a long id and a short human_readable_id?

- Parquet requires two key columns

- The short id is a checksum of the long id

- ✓ (correct) The long id is for joins and uniqueness; the short one is cheap for the LLM to cite and for people to check

- The short id is used for vector search
Answer: Prompts show [Data: Relationships (16)]-style ids. A small integer costs few tokens and is hard to mistype, while the long id keeps rows unique across runs and systems.

Which text does minigraphrag embed for an entity, and what is the main reason?

- ✓ (correct) name: description, so queries that describe an entity's role can match it even when they do not name it

- Only the name, because descriptions change

- The concatenated text of every chunk that mentions it

- The community report of its community
Answer: “Who designed the sonar array?” shares no words with JONAS VEHL but several with his description. Local search seeds rely on that.

You change only the community report prompt and re-run indexing with a response cache. Which steps make new paid LLM calls?

- All of them, because the pipeline re-runs top to bottom

- Extraction and reports

- Description summarization and reports

- ✓ (correct) Only report generation (and then report embeddings, which are embedding calls)
Answer: Every other prompt is byte-identical, so its cache key is unchanged. Reports have new prompts and miss; their new text then changes what gets embedded for the report store.

A loader runs MERGE (e:Entity {name: row.name, description: row.description}). After the description summary changes, what happens on the next load?

- The existing node's description is updated

- ✓ (correct) A second node with the same name is created, because MERGE matches on the whole pattern including description

- Neo4j raises a syntax error

- Nothing, because MERGE ignores properties
Answer: MERGE matches the entire pattern. Put only the key in the pattern and set other properties with SET. A uniqueness constraint on name would turn this silent duplicate into a loud error, which is another reason to create constraints first.

A two-hop recursive CTE from PROJECT TERN returns 16 of the 17 Kestrel entities. What is the most useful conclusion?

- The CTE has a bug in its cycle check

- Two hops is always the right radius for local search

- Postgres cannot handle graphs

- ✓ (correct) A hub (Kestrel Labs, degree 11) makes hop distance a weak relevance signal, so retrieval needs ranking as well as expansion
Answer: Through the hub, two hops reaches almost everything. Local search ranks relationships and text units instead of taking whole neighborhoods, and HippoRAG uses PageRank-style scores for the same reason.

When is files plus NetworkX in memory a reasonable production choice?

- Never; production requires a graph database

- ✓ (correct) When the index fits in memory, is rebuilt in batch, and is served read-only

- Only when you have no embeddings

- When many users update the graph concurrently
Answer: A read-only index reloaded after each batch build needs no transactions. Concurrent writers, graphs larger than memory, or complex query-time traversals are the signals to move to a database.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Why parquet in GraphRAG but JSON in minigraphrag?

Parquet is columnar, typed and compressed, and pandas reads it quickly, which matters when an entity table has hundreds of thousands of rows with list columns. JSON is slower and larger but readable in any editor, which matters more when you are learning what each step produced. Converting is a few lines with pandas, so choose by audience: JSON for inspection, parquet for scale.

▸ Should entity descriptions live in the graph database or only in the vector store?

In the graph, with the vector next to them if your database supports it. The description is what the LLM reads in the context tables, so you need it at query time anyway. Many vector databases can store it as metadata too, but then you have two copies to keep in sync. Store text once, where you read it from.

▸ Do I need a graph database to use Cypher-style queries during development?

No. For the Kestrel-sized graph, NetworkX functions such as single_source_shortest_path_length or all_simple_paths cover the same questions in a few lines. Load into Neo4j when you want to explore interactively in Neo4j Browser, practice Text2Cypher (Chapter 20), or test query plans before production.

▸ Should relationships be directed?

Extraction produces a source and a target, but many relations are symmetric or were extracted in an arbitrary order (“Kestrel competes with Marlow”). minigraphrag and GraphRAG's community detection treat the graph as undirected, which makes neighbor expansion simpler. If you add typed relations such as ACQUIRED or CTO_OF, store direction, because “Marlow acquired Deepcast” is not symmetric; traversals can still ignore it with undirected patterns like -[:RELATED]-.

▸ How big does a graph have to be before HNSW beats brute force?

Brute-force cosine is one matrix multiplication; with numpy it stays fast into the tens or low hundreds of thousands of vectors per query on a laptop, and it is exact. Approximate indexes win when you have millions of vectors, many queries per second, or you need filtering and persistence from a database. Measure latency at your size before adding an index you have to tune.

### Project: one index, two backends

Prove that storage is swappable by serving the same Kestrel index from memory and from a database, with a parity test between them.

- A small interface with three methods: nearest_entities(vector, k), neighbors(names, hops) and text_units(ids)

- An in-memory implementation over load_index and a Neo4j or Postgres implementation over the loaders from this chapter

- A parity test that runs all seven canonical questions' seed entities through both implementations and asserts identical neighbor sets

- An idempotency test: load twice, assert identical counts

- A timing table for each method on the Kestrel index and on a synthetic graph 100 times larger

Done when the parity and idempotency tests pass and you can say, with numbers, at what graph size the database implementation becomes faster than the in-memory one for two-hop expansion, or that it never does for your data.

## Key takeaways

- An index is a set of tables: documents, text units, entities, relationships, claims, communities, reports and embeddings, joined by ids and provenance lists.

- Embed the text each retrieval method will compare against: entity name plus description, relationship descriptions if you search edges, chunk text, and report content.

- Files plus NetworkX are enough until size, concurrent writes or query-time traversal push you to Neo4j or Postgres; pick the backend by the four primitives you need.

- Treat indexing as a DAG. Cache LLM responses by prompt hash and step outputs by input hash so a change only re-runs what depends on it.

- Stable, content-derived ids and MERGE on natural keys make re-runs and reloads idempotent; keep short ids for prompts only.

# Part: Retrieval

## Local search: entity-anchored retrieval

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/14-local-search.html
Summary: Seed entities from embeddings, expand neighborhoods, budget tokens across tables, cite sources.

# Local search: entity-anchored retrieval

Local search answers questions about specific things by starting from the entities a query is about and collecting the evidence around them. You will implement GraphRAG's version step by step and trace it by hand on “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?”

## You will be able to

- Map a query to seed entities with description embeddings, and explain why names alone are not enough

- Rank candidate relationships (in-network, then out-of-network by shared links and rank), text units and community reports around the seeds

- Split a context window into proportional token budgets and fill each slice best-first

- Render context as id-bearing tables and verify the model's [Data: …] citations

- Diagnose the main failure modes, wrong seeds and hub flooding, and apply fixes

## Why anchor retrieval on entities

Ask plain vector RAG (Chapter 2) “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?” and it retrieves the chunks that look most like the question: the engineering blog post announcing Tern, and perhaps the Series B press release that mentions it. The blog post says Deepcast units “will no longer be available to us” but not why. The explanation is in a trade press article about Marlow Dynamics buying Deepcast, which never mentions Kestrel Labs or Tern. By similarity to the question it ranks low. That is the multi-hop failure from Chapter 3.

The graph already contains the missing link. The Tern chunk produced the edge PROJECT TERN – DEEPCAST, and the trade article produced MARLOW DYNAMICS – DEEPCAST. Local search exploits this in three moves:

- Anchor. Find the entities the question is about by comparing the query with entity descriptions.

- Expand. Collect what is attached to those entities: relationships, including ones that lead one step outside the anchor set, the chunks they were extracted from, their communities' reports and their claims.

- Budget. Rank each pool, give each pool a share of the context window, and fill it best-first.

The result is a context that follows the structure of the corpus rather than the wording of the question. GraphRAG's documentation describes the method as suited to questions “that require an understanding of specific entities mentioned in the input documents”. For themes across the whole corpus you want global search instead.

[Diagram]

The shape of local search. Every pool is ranked independently and then cut to its share of the window. The percentages are GraphRAG's configuration defaults (community 0.15, text units 0.5, the remainder for entities, relationships and claims); minigraphrag uses the same split.

## The algorithm, step by step

This section follows Microsoft GraphRAG's LocalSearchMixedContext.build_context and minigraphrag.search.local.build_local_context side by side. They agree on the structure; where the details differ, both are shown.

### Step 1: map the query to seed entities

Embed the query q and score every entity e by the cosine similarity between the query vector and the vector of the entity's embedding text, name: description (Chapter 13):

sim(q, e) = (vq · ve) / (‖vq‖ ‖ve‖)

Take the top k as seeds, in similarity order. That order matters later: it decides whose text units go first. GraphRAG's details:

- It asks the vector store for k × 2 results (an “oversample scaler” of 2), so that excluded entities can be dropped and k still remain. The configured default is top_k_entities = 10.

- exclude_entity_names removes entities you never want as seeds; include_entity_names forces entities in, placed before the similarity matches.

- If the query is empty, it falls back to the highest-rank entities.

minigraphrag adds one cheap boost GraphRAG does not have: any entity whose name or alias appears literally in the query goes first, and among those the entity with the fewest source text units leads, because a rare name says more about the question than a hub does. Embeddings are good at meaning and surprisingly bad at rare proper nouns, especially the offline HashingEmbedder, so this rescues questions that name their subject outright.

```python  # minigraphrag/search/local.py
def map_query_to_entities(index, query: str, top_k: int = 10, include_name_matches: bool = True) -> list[str]:
    """Entities most relevant to the query, by description embedding.

    GraphRAG uses embeddings only; `include_name_matches` additionally puts
    entities whose name or alias literally occurs in the query first, a cheap
    and very effective boost.
    """
    G = index.graph
    hits = [name for name, _, _ in index.entity_store.search(index.embedder.embed([query])[0], k=top_k * 2)]
    mentioned = []
    if include_name_matches:
        q = query.upper()
        for n, d in G.nodes(data=True):
            if any(re.search(rf"(?<!\w){re.escape(s)}(?!\w)", q) for s in [n, *d.get("aliases", [])]):
                mentioned.append(n)
    # Rarer entities first: "PROJECT TERN" says more about the question than the hub "KESTREL LABS".
    mentioned.sort(key=lambda n: len(G.nodes[n].get("source_ids", [])))
    return list(dict.fromkeys(mentioned + hits))[:top_k]
```

### Step 2: rank candidate relationships

Let S be the set of seeds. Every relationship touching S is a candidate, and they fall into two groups:

- In-network: both endpoints are in S. These describe how the seeds relate to each other, which is usually what the question is about. They all go first, sorted by rank (GraphRAG's relationship rank is combined_degree, the sum of the endpoint degrees).

- Out-of-network: one endpoint is outside S. These are how local search reaches one hop beyond its seeds. For each outside entity x, count its links: the number of distinct seeds it is connected to. Sort out-of-network relationships by (links of the outside endpoint, rank), both descending.

The links count is the heart of the method. An outside entity connected to several seeds is a bridge: it probably sits on the path the question is asking about. Out-of-network relationships are then cut to a budget of top_k_relationships × |S|; in-network ones are never cut at this stage. The configured default for top_k_relationships is 10.

```python  # graphrag/query/context_builder/local_context.py (abridged)
# First priority: relationships between selected entities
in_network = get_in_network_relationships(selected_entities, relationships, ranking_attribute)
# Second priority: relationships from a selected entity to an outside entity
out_network = get_out_network_relationships(selected_entities, relationships, ranking_attribute)

# links = number of selected entities each outside entity is connected to
for rel in out_network:
    rel.attributes["links"] = out_network_entity_links[outside_endpoint(rel)]
out_network.sort(key=lambda r: (r.attributes["links"], r.rank), reverse=True)

relationship_budget = top_k_relationships * len(selected_entities)
return in_network + out_network[:relationship_budget]
```

minigraphrag implements the same two groups but breaks ties among out-of-network edges by edge weight (summed extraction strength) instead of combined degree, and it applies only the token budget, not the count budget:

```python  # minigraphrag/search/local.py
in_network = [(u, v) for u, v in G.subgraph(entities).edges()]
out_network = [(e, n) for e in entities for n in G.neighbors(e) if n not in selected]
# External neighbours linked to several selected entities are the best bridges.
links = Counter(n for _, n in out_network)
out_network.sort(key=lambda e: (-links[e[1]], -G.edges[e].get("weight", 0)))
edges = list(dict.fromkeys(tuple(e) for e in in_network + out_network))
```

**Ranking by combined degree favors hubs

Combined degree is a cheap proxy for importance: an edge between two well-connected entities is probably central. It is also biased toward whatever is attached to the biggest hub. Keep that in mind; it is the root of the hub flooding failure later in this chapter.

### Step 3: rank candidate text units

Candidate text units are the source_ids of the seed entities. GraphRAG walks seeds in similarity order. For each seed it takes that seed's text units not already taken and scores each by how many of that seed's relationships list the unit as a source. The final order is by (seed position ascending, relationship count descending). The effect: all chunks of the best seed come first, and within a seed, chunks that support many of its edges beat chunks that merely mention it.

```python  # graphrag/query/structured_search/local_search/mixed_context.py (abridged)
for index, entity in enumerate(selected_entities):
    entity_relationships = [r for r in relationships if entity.title in (r.source, r.target)]
    for text_id in entity.text_unit_ids or []:
        if text_id not in seen and text_id in text_units:
            unit = text_units[text_id]
            num_relationships = count_relationships(entity_relationships, unit)
            seen.add(text_id)
            unit_info_list.append((unit, index, num_relationships))

# sort by entity order and the number of relationships desc
unit_info_list.sort(key=lambda x: (x[1], -x[2]))
```

minigraphrag's variant keeps the seed order but counts, for each unit, how many of all selected relationships (in-network and out-of-network) cite it. That lets a chunk supporting a bridge edge rise within its seed's group.

### Step 4: rank community reports and gather claims

For each seed, look up the communities it belongs to and count matches per community. Sort communities by (number of seeds in it, report rank) descending. A community that contains four of your seeds is almost certainly about your question; its report gives the model background that no single chunk states, such as “Kestrel's supply chain depended on one vendor”.

Claims (GraphRAG calls them covariates) are filtered to those whose subject is a seed. They add dated, status-tagged facts, which is especially useful for temporal questions such as “Who supplied Kestrel's sonar in 2024?”. minigraphrag's build_local_context does not include claims yet; the project at the end of this chapter adds them.

### Step 5: split the budget and fill each slice

Given a total T tokens for data (after any conversation history is subtracted), GraphRAG computes three slices:

Slice | Formula | GraphRAG defaults, T = 12,000 | minigraphrag defaults, T = 8,000

Community reports | ⌊T × community_prop⌋ | 0.15 → 1,800 | 0.15 → 1,200

Entities, relationships, claims | ⌊T × (1 − community_prop − text_unit_prop)⌋ | 0.35 → 4,200 | 0.35 → 2,800

Text units | ⌊T × text_unit_prop⌋ | 0.5 → 6,000 | 0.5 → 4,000

The two proportions must sum to at most 1, and GraphRAG raises an error otherwise. Each slice is filled greedily from its ranked list until the next row would overflow. Unused tokens in one slice are not handed to another. Inside the local slice, GraphRAG adds the entity table first, then grows the relationship and claim tables one seed at a time, and stops (reverting to the previous state) as soon as adding the next seed's rows would exceed the slice.

[Interactive figure: Local search context budget — Drag the sliders; shares are renormalized (token-budget)]

### Step 6: render tables and generate

Each slice becomes a pipe-delimited table headed by -----Name-----, with an id column the model can cite. The context goes into the system prompt; the question is the user turn. Here is minigraphrag's full context builder, then the generation call:

```python  # minigraphrag/search/local.py
def build_local_context(
    index,
    query: str,
    top_k_entities: int = 10,
    max_context_tokens: int = 8000,
    community_prop: float = 0.15,
    text_unit_prop: float = 0.5,
) -> tuple[str, dict]:
    """Return (context text, {table name: rows}) for local search."""
    G = index.graph
    entities = map_query_to_entities(index, query, top_k_entities)
    selected = set(entities)

    # --- community reports: communities containing the most selected entities first
    counts = Counter(c.id for e in entities for c in index.communities_of(e))
    community_rows = []
    for cid, _ in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda x: (-x[1], -(index.report(x[0]).rating if index.report(x[0]) else 0))):
        report = index.report(cid)
        if report:
            community_rows.append([cid, report.title, report.full_content])
    community_rows = _fill(community_rows, int(max_context_tokens * community_prop))

    # --- entities and relationships share the "local" slice
    local_budget = int(max_context_tokens * (1 - community_prop - text_unit_prop))
    entity_rows = _fill([[G.nodes[e]["human_id"], e, G.nodes[e].get("description", ""), G.degree(e)]
                         for e in entities], local_budget // 2)
    in_network = [(u, v) for u, v in G.subgraph(entities).edges()]
    out_network = [(e, n) for e in entities for n in G.neighbors(e) if n not in selected]
    links = Counter(n for _, n in out_network)
    out_network.sort(key=lambda e: (-links[e[1]], -G.edges[e].get("weight", 0)))
    edges = list(dict.fromkeys(tuple(e) for e in in_network + out_network))
    rel_rows = _fill([[G.edges[e]["human_id"], e[0], e[1], G.edges[e].get("description", ""),
                       G.edges[e].get("weight", 0)] for e in edges],
                     local_budget - sum(count_tokens("|".join(map(str, r))) for r in entity_rows))

    # --- text units: from the best entities first, then by how many selected relationships cite them
    rel_sources = Counter(s for e in edges for s in G.edges[e].get("source_ids", []))
    unit_order: dict[str, tuple] = {}
    for rank, e in enumerate(entities):
        for uid in G.nodes[e].get("source_ids", []):
            unit_order.setdefault(uid, (rank, -rel_sources[uid]))
    unit_ids = sorted(unit_order, key=lambda u: unit_order[u])
    unit_rows = _fill([[u, index.text_units[u].text] for u in unit_ids if u in index.text_units],
                      int(max_context_tokens * text_unit_prop))

    parts = []
    if community_rows:
        parts.append(format_table("Reports", ["id", "title", "content"], community_rows))
    parts.append(format_table("Entities", ["id", "entity", "description", "number of relationships"], entity_rows))
    parts.append(format_table("Relationships", ["id", "source", "target", "description", "weight"], rel_rows))
    parts.append(format_table("Sources", ["id", "text"], unit_rows))
    data = {
        "reports": [dict(zip(["id", "title", "content"], r)) for r in community_rows],
        "entities": [dict(zip(["id", "entity", "description", "degree"], r)) for r in entity_rows],
        "relationships": [dict(zip(["id", "source", "target", "description", "weight"], r)) for r in rel_rows],
        "sources": [dict(zip(["id", "text"], r)) for r in unit_rows],
    }
    return "\n\n".join(parts), data
```

```python  # minigraphrag/search/local.py
def local_search(index, query: str, llm: LLM, top_k_entities: int = 10, max_context_tokens: int = 8000,
                 community_prop: float = 0.15, text_unit_prop: float = 0.5,
                 response_type: str = DEFAULT_RESPONSE_TYPE) -> SearchResult:
    context, data = build_local_context(index, query, top_k_entities, max_context_tokens, community_prop, text_unit_prop)
    answer = generate_answer(llm, query, context, response_type)
    sources = doc_ids_for_units(index, [s["id"] for s in data["sources"]])
    return SearchResult(answer, "local", context, data, sources, llm_calls=1)
```

The system prompt, LOCAL_SEARCH_SYSTEM_PROMPT in prompts.py, tells the model to answer from the tables, say so if it does not know, and cite in a fixed format: [Data: <dataset name> (record ids)]. GraphRAG's own prompt gives the example [Data: Sources (15, 16), Reports (1), Entities (5, 7); Relationships (23); Claims (2, 7, 34, 46, 64, +more)] and asks for at most five ids per reference, with +more for the rest.

[Interactive figure: One local search call (flow)]

## Worked example: why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?

This trace uses the clean Kestrel graph from the running example: 17 entities and 31 relationships, with human_ids assigned in sorted name order as add_rank_attributes does, and the two-level community hierarchy hierarchical_communities(G, max_cluster_size=4) produces for it. To keep the tables readable we use k = 4 seeds and top_k_relationships = 2. Similarity scores are illustrative values of the kind a sentence embedding model produces; the ranking steps after them are computed exactly.

3 | 7 | KESTREL LABS | 0.55 | 11 | Named in the query; long, general description dilutes the score

### Community reports

In the max_cluster_size = 4 hierarchy this trace uses (Chapter 15 draws it; Chapter 12 clustered the same graph with max_cluster_size = 5, so its community ids differ), TERN and JONAS VEHL are in community 2 (the Tern team), DEEPCAST in community 3 (Marlow and Deepcast), KESTREL LABS in community 1 (founders and board), and all four are in their level-0 parent, community 0. Match counts: community 0 has 4, community 2 has 2, communities 1 and 3 have 1 each. Community 0's report (“Kestrel Labs: leadership, funding and supply”) goes first, then community 2's; whichever of 1 and 3 has the higher rating comes next if the 1,800-token slice still has room.

Every factual sentence carries ids that exist in the tables above, so a reviewer, or a script, can check them.

### Checking citations

Models occasionally cite ids that were never in context, or cite a real id for a claim it does not support. You cannot cheaply detect the second, but the first is a regex away, and it is a strong hallucination signal:

```python  # examples/check_citations.py
import re

REF = re.compile(r"\[Data:\s*(.*?)\]", re.S)
PART = re.compile(r"(\w+)\s*\(([^)]*)\)")

def cited_ids(answer: str) -> dict[str, set[str]]:
    """{'relationships': {'4', '5'}, 'sources': {...}} from [Data: ...] references."""
    out: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
    for ref in REF.findall(answer):
        for table, ids in PART.findall(ref):
            vals = {i.strip() for i in ids.split(",") if i.strip() and i.strip() != "+more"}
            out.setdefault(table.lower(), set()).update(vals)
    return out

def unknown_citations(answer: str, context_data: dict) -> dict[str, set[str]]:
    """Ids the answer cites that were not in the context tables it was given."""
    known = {t: {str(row["id"]) for row in rows} for t, rows in context_data.items()}
    return {t: ids - known.get(t, set()) for t, ids in cited_ids(answer).items()
            if ids - known.get(t, set())}

# result = local_search(index, "Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?", llm)
# print(unknown_citations(result.answer, result.context_data))   # {} when every id is real
```

## Conversation history

In a chat, the follow-up “And who leads it?” has no entity in it. GraphRAG handles this in two places:

- Entity mapping. Before embedding, it appends the previous user questions (up to conversation_history_max_turns, default 5) to the current query. “And who leads it?” plus “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?” maps to PROJECT TERN again.

- Context. It renders the recent turns as a conversation table at the top of the context (user turns only by default) and subtracts its tokens from the total before the proportional split.

Both are blunt. Appending old questions keeps pulling old entities after the user changes topic: if the next question is “What does Brightwater Capital invest in?”, the Tern question still in the window drags Tern-related seeds along and wastes budget. Two common improvements: rewrite the follow-up into a standalone question with a small LLM call before retrieval, or weight recent turns more heavily when you embed them. The rewrite costs one call but produces a query you can log, cache and evaluate like any other.

```python  # examples/standalone_question.py
REWRITE_PROMPT = """Rewrite the last user question so it can be understood without the conversation.
Keep names exactly as written earlier. Return only the rewritten question.

Conversation:
{history}

Last question: {question}
Standalone question:"""

def standalone_question(llm, history: list[tuple[str, str]], question: str, max_turns: int = 5) -> str:
    turns = "\n".join(f"{role}: {text}" for role, text in history[-2 * max_turns:])
    return llm.complete(REWRITE_PROMPT.format(history=turns, question=question)).strip() or question

# q = standalone_question(llm, [("user", "Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?"),
#                               ("assistant", "Because Deepcast ...")], "And who leads it?")
# -> "Who leads Project Tern?"; then local_search(index, q, llm)
```

## Failure modes and fixes

### Wrong seed entities

Everything downstream depends on step 1. If the seeds are wrong, the relationships, chunks and reports are all about the wrong thing, and the model answers confidently from irrelevant evidence. Typical causes on Kestrel-like corpora:

- Name-only queries and weak embedders. “What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?” is mostly names. A sentence embedding of that query may be closer to a generic “connections” description than to either entity. The literal name-match boost fixes most of these cases.

- Unresolved aliases. If resolution left “TWI” and “TIDEWATER INSTITUTE” as separate nodes, half the evidence hangs off a seed you did not pick. Fix resolution (Chapter 9); name matching on aliases helps.

- Bloated descriptions. Hubs accumulate long descriptions that mention everything, so they match many queries weakly and crowd out specific entities. Cap summary length and consider embedding a short profile rather than the full summary.

- Abstract questions. “What risks does Kestrel face?” has one entity and one theme. Local search will anchor on Kestrel Labs and dump its neighborhood. That question belongs to global search or DRIFT (Chapter 15).

### Hubs flooding the context

A hub is an entity with far more edges than typical. In the Kestrel graph, KESTREL LABS has degree 11 while the median is 3. When a hub is a seed, three things go wrong at once: its edges dominate the out-of-network pool, its combined degree inflates the rank of each of those edges, and its many chunks fill the text slice if it is an early seed. The worked example shows the milder version: five of eight out-of-network edges were Kestrel's.

Mitigations, from cheapest to most involved:

Fix | How | Trade-off

Cap per-seed relationships | At most m out-of-network edges per seed before merging lists | Can drop a relevant hub edge

Degree-damped bridge score | Rank outside entities by links / log2(1 + degree) instead of raw links, and ties by weight instead of combined degree | Slightly penalizes genuinely central entities

Exclude known hubs as seeds | exclude_entity_names for the corpus's “about” entity | Manual; wrong for questions about the hub itself

Query-aware reranking | Embed relationship descriptions and sort candidates by similarity to the query within each group | Needs a relationship vector store; more compute per query

Personalized PageRank from the seeds | Score candidates by random-walk mass, which naturally discounts hubs' spread-out mass | A different method: see Chapter 17

### Other symptoms

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix

Correct entities, answer still misses the cause | Bridge chunk ranked below the text budget | Raise text_unit_prop, rank chunks by support for selected relationships, or shorten chunks

Answer quotes community report generalities, not facts | community_prop too high for a fact question | Lower it, or set it to 0 for single-hop lookups

Citations to ids not in context | Model pattern-matching the citation format | Verify citations; strip or flag unknown ids; lower temperature

Two different CTOs in the answer | Both edges in context without dates | Include claims with dates, or a temporal graph (Chapter 27)

Latency spikes on some queries | Hub seeds produce huge candidate pools before trimming | Cap candidates per seed before sorting; precompute per-entity top edges at index time

**Edge et al., From Local to Global (2024)

The GraphRAG paper focuses its evaluation on global, sensemaking questions and positions entity-based retrieval as the complement for questions about specific entities. The local search algorithm in this chapter is documented and implemented in the microsoft/graphrag repository rather than specified in the paper, so treat the defaults (0.15, 0.5, top 10) as engineering choices to tune, not results.

## Exercises

#### Exercise 14.1 Warm-up

A chat session has 900 tokens of conversation history. With GraphRAG's defaults (max_context_tokens = 12,000, community_prop = 0.15, text_unit_prop = 0.5), how many tokens does each slice get? How many 400-token chunks fit in the text slice?

▸ Show answer

History is subtracted first: 12,000 − 900 = 11,100 tokens remain.

- Community reports: ⌊11,100 × 0.15⌋ = 1,665.

- Entities, relationships and claims: ⌊11,100 × (1 − 0.15 − 0.5)⌋. In floating point, 1 − 0.15 − 0.5 is a hair below 0.35, so 11,100 × it is 3,884.999… and the floor is 3,884, not 3,885. Harmless, but it is why you should never assert exact slice sizes in tests.

- Text units: ⌊11,100 × 0.5⌋ = 5,550.

5,550 / 400 = 13.9, so 13 full 400-token chunks fit (5,200 tokens). The table header and row formatting also cost tokens, so in practice it may be 12.
