# Part: Generation

## Turning graphs into prompts

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/22-context-construction.html
Summary: Triples, tables, adjacency text, JSON; ordering, token budgets and citations.

# Turning graphs into prompts

Retrieval hands you nodes, edges, paths and passages; the model can only read text. This chapter is about the last step before generation: choosing a serialization, ordering and deduplicating evidence, splitting a token budget across sections, and making the answer cite what it used, so that good retrieval is not wasted by a bad prompt.

## You will be able to

- Serialize the same subgraph as triples, GraphRAG-style tables, markdown, adjacency lists, JSON, sentences and paths, and compare their token cost

- Summarize what research on graph encodings for LLMs found, without overstating it

- Order and deduplicate evidence to work with, not against, position effects such as “lost in the middle”

- Allocate a token budget across evidence sections and redistribute unused space

- Write a grounded system prompt with citation ids and an explicit “I don't know” path

- Measure whether citations are valid and actually support the sentences that carry them

## The last mile of GraphRAG

Everything in Part 3 ended with a list of things: entity ids from local search, community reports from global search, scored paths from path retrieval, fused passages and panels from the hybrid layer. None of that reaches the model until it becomes a string. That conversion, called linearization or serialization, decides three things:

- Cost. The same five facts can take 60 tokens or 250 tokens depending on format, and you pay for them on every query.

- What the model can see. A flat list of triples hides that two facts share an entity; an adjacency list hides edge descriptions; JSON hides nothing and is hard to skim. What is easy for the model to notice changes what it concludes.

- What the answer can cite. If rows have no stable ids, the answer cannot point back at evidence, and you cannot check it.

One small subgraph will run through the chapter: the evidence for canonical questions 1 and 3, “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?” and “What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?”. It has five entities (Marlow Dynamics, Deepcast, Kestrel Labs, Project Tern, Priya Nair) and five relationships.

## Serialization formats

### Triples, one per line

The most compact option: (subject, predicate, object). minigraphrag uses the edge's description as the predicate, because extracted edges carry free-text descriptions rather than typed labels.

```python  # minigraphrag/context.py
def triples_to_text(G: nx.Graph, edges: list[tuple[str, str]] | None = None) -> str:
    """One `(SOURCE, description, TARGET)` line per edge: the most compact format."""
    edges = edges if edges is not None else list(G.edges())
    return "\n".join(f"({u}, {G.edges[u, v].get('description', 'related to')}, {v})" for u, v in edges)


def to_markdown_tables(G: nx.Graph, nodes: list[str] | None = None) -> str:
    """Markdown entity and relationship tables for the induced subgraph on `nodes`."""
    nodes = nodes if nodes is not None else list(G.nodes())
    sub = G.subgraph(nodes)
    out = ["| id | entity | type | description |", "|---|---|---|---|"]
    for n in nodes:
        d = G.nodes[n]
        out.append(f"| {d.get('human_id', '')} | {n} | {d.get('type', '')} | {_clean(d.get('description', ''))} |")
    out += ["", "| id | source | target | description | weight |", "|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for u, v, d in sub.edges(data=True):
        out.append(f"| {d.get('human_id', '')} | {u} | {v} | {_clean(d.get('description', ''))} | {d.get('weight', 1)} |")
    return "\n".join(out)


def to_adjacency_text(G: nx.Graph, nodes: list[str] | None = None) -> str:
    """`NODE: neighbour1, neighbour2` lines: shows neighbourhood structure at a glance."""
    nodes = nodes if nodes is not None else list(G.nodes())
    return "\n".join(f"{n}: {', '.join(sorted(G.neighbors(n)))}" for n in nodes)


def to_json(G: nx.Graph, nodes: list[str] | None = None) -> str:
    """Node-link JSON of the induced subgraph (lists and scalars only)."""
    sub = G.subgraph(nodes if nodes is not None else list(G.nodes()))
    keep = ("type", "description")
    data = {
        "nodes": [{"id": n, **{k: d[k] for k in keep if k in d}} for n, d in sub.nodes(data=True)],
        "edges": [{"source": u, "target": v, "description": d.get("description", ""), "weight": d.get("weight", 1)}
                  for u, v, d in sub.edges(data=True)],
    }
    return json.dumps(data, indent=1)
```

Output for three edges of our subgraph:

```python
(MARLOW DYNAMICS, Marlow Dynamics acquired Deepcast in April 2025, DEEPCAST)
(DEEPCAST, Deepcast supplied sonar modules to Kestrel Labs from 2022 until June 2025, KESTREL LABS)
(KESTREL LABS, Kestrel Labs started Project Tern in June 2025 to build its own sonar, PROJECT TERN)
```

Triples are cheap and familiar to models that have seen a lot of knowledge-graph text. They have no row ids, so citation must go through the passage the triple came from, and they repeat entity names on every line, which costs tokens on dense subgraphs. On an undirected graph the tuple order is arbitrary; direction survives only inside the description.

### GraphRAG-style tables

Microsoft GraphRAG's local search renders each evidence type as a delimited table with a title line and an id column: entities, relationships, claims, community reports, sources. The answer then cites rows as [Data: Relationships (3, 8)]. minigraphrag uses the same shape:

```python  # minigraphrag/context.py
def format_table(title: str, header: list[str], rows: list[list]) -> str:
    """GraphRAG-style pipe-delimited table: `-----Title-----` then `a|b|c` lines."""
    lines = [f"-----{title}-----", "|".join(header)]
    lines += ["|".join(_clean(c) for c in row) for row in rows]
    return "\n".join(lines)
```

```python
-----Relationships-----
id|source|target|description|weight
0|MARLOW DYNAMICS|DEEPCAST|Marlow Dynamics acquired Deepcast in April 2025|9
1|DEEPCAST|KESTREL LABS|Deepcast supplied sonar modules to Kestrel Labs from 2022 until June 2025|8
2|KESTREL LABS|PROJECT TERN|Kestrel Labs started Project Tern in June 2025 to build its own sonar|8
```

The header is paid once rather than on every row, columns such as weight or degree tell the model what the retriever thought was important, and ids make citation checkable. Markdown tables (to_markdown_tables) carry the same information with extra | padding; they cost more tokens but render nicely in logs and are very familiar to models.

### Adjacency lists

NODE: neighbor1, neighbor2. Very cheap, and the only format in which “Kestrel Labs sits between Deepcast and Project Tern” is visible on a single line. It drops edge descriptions and direction, so on its own it supports structural questions (“who is connected to Deepcast?”) but not causal ones (“why?”). A useful hybrid is labeled adjacency: DEEPCAST: SUPPLIED KESTREL LABS; ACQUIRED BY MARLOW DYNAMICS.

### JSON

Node-link JSON is lossless and easy to generate and parse, and it is the natural choice when the model must return structured output that refers to the input. It is also the most token-hungry format here: quotes, keys and indentation are repeated for every node and edge, which can easily cost one and a half to two times a pipe table with the same content, and more for small tables. Minified JSON (no indentation) recovers some of that.

### Natural-language verbalization

Turn each edge into a sentence. When descriptions were written by an extractor, verbalization is mostly a matter of stitching them together; with typed relations you need a template per relation type (“{s} acquired {o} in {date}”). Sentences read the way the model's pretraining text reads, and they are the easiest format for a human to audit. They cost about as much as triples and, like triples, lack ids unless you add them.

```python  # examples/context_tools.py
def verbalize_edges(G, edges) -> str:
    """One plain sentence per relationship, using the stored description when there is one."""
    lines = []
    for u, v in edges:
        d = G.edges[u, v]
        desc = d.get("description") or "is related to"
        lines.append(f"{u.title()} and {v.title()}: {desc.rstrip('.')}.")
    return "\n".join(lines)

def dedupe(items: list[str], key=lambda s: re.sub(r"\W+", " ", s.lower()).strip()) -> list[str]:
    """Drop exact and near-exact duplicates (same text after lowercasing and stripping punctuation)."""
    seen, out = set(), []
    for item in items:
        k = key(item)
        if k not in seen:
            seen.add(k)
            out.append(item)
    return out
```

### Paths

For multi-hop questions, serialize the chain itself, in hop order: PRIYA NAIR --[worked at before 2023]--> MARLOW DYNAMICS --[acquired in April 2025]--> DEEPCAST. paths_to_text in minigraphrag/search/paths.py renders PathRAG-style paths this way (Chapter 18). A path puts the reasoning order on the page, so the model does not have to reassemble it from shuffled rows. The cost is duplication: two paths through the same edge repeat it.

The visualization below renders one five-edge Kestrel subgraph in every format. Token counts are the rough estimate of characters divided by four, which is close to what BPE tokenizers give for English and code-like text. Toggle descriptions off to see how much of the cost is description text rather than structure.

[Interactive figure: One subgraph, seven serializations — Evidence for “What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?” and “Why did Kestrel start Tern?” (ch22-serialize)]

Format | Relative tokens | Citable ids | Shows structure | Good for

Triples | Low | No (add them) | Edge by edge | Many small facts, tight budgets

GraphRAG tables | Low to medium | Yes | Rows, with rank columns | Local search contexts with citations

Markdown tables | Medium | Yes | Rows | Human-readable logs, models that like markdown

Adjacency list | Very low | No | Neighborhoods at a glance | Structural questions, overviews

JSON | Highest | Yes | Everything, hard to skim | Structured output, tool results

Sentences | Low to medium | No (add them) | Implicit | Small models, auditability

Paths | Medium, with repeats | Per path | Reasoning order | Multi-hop “why” and “how connected” questions

**Which token counter are you using?

count_tokens uses tiktoken when it is installed and otherwise estimates 4 tokens per 3 whitespace-separated words. The word estimate is fine for prose and badly wrong for delimiter-heavy text: 0|MARLOW DYNAMICS|DEEPCAST|ACQUIRED has two whitespace-separated “words”, so the fallback counts it as 3 tokens, while a BPE tokenizer splits it into a dozen or so. If you budget pipe tables with the fallback estimator, you will overfill the context. Install tiktoken or the tokenizer of your actual model before trusting budgets on tables and JSON.

### What research on graph encodings found

**Fatemi, Halcrow and Perozzi, Talk like a Graph: Encoding Graphs for Large Language Models (2023)

The first systematic study of how to write a graph as text for an LLM. Using a benchmark of basic graph reasoning tasks (edge existence, node degree, connectivity, cycle detection and others), the authors varied how nodes are named (integers or familiar names), how edges are phrased (an adjacency style, “incident” lists of each node's neighbors, or social framings such as friendship), how the question is posed, and which random-graph generator produced the graph. Their headline is that these choices matter a lot: the abstract reports that the right encoder can improve performance by 4.8% to 61.8% depending on the task. No single encoding won everywhere, and the structure of the graph itself also affected accuracy.

Three practical lessons carry over to GraphRAG even though their tasks were synthetic rather than question answering over extracted knowledge:

- Test formats on your own questions. Format effects are task-dependent, so a format that wins on “who is connected to X” can lose on “why did X happen”. Exercise 22.5 builds that test.

- Group by node when the question is about a node. Listing each node's neighbors together keeps related facts adjacent, which is what incident-style encodings do. GraphRAG's entity table followed by that entity's relationships approximates it.

- Meaningful names beat opaque ids for reasoning. Keep human-readable names in the text and put ids in a separate column for citation, rather than replacing names with ids to save tokens.

## Ordering, position and duplicates

### Lost in the middle

Long-context models do not read every position equally well. The best-known measurement is below; its lesson for GraphRAG is that where you put the Deepcast acquisition row can matter as much as whether you retrieved it.

**Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (2023)

In multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval tasks, model accuracy was often highest when the relevant document was at the beginning or the end of the context and dropped noticeably when it was in the middle, producing a U-shaped curve. The authors also report that giving the reader more retrieved documents stopped helping well before retrieval recall stopped improving. Later long-context models appear to have narrowed the effect without removing it, so measure it on your model.

[Diagram]

Left: the qualitative U shape reported for long contexts. Right: sandwich ordering places the highest-ranked rows at the start and end of a section and the weakest in the middle, so a position penalty falls on the evidence you trust least.

Ordering rules that work well in practice:

- Rank first, then place. Sort by retrieval score, then apply a placement policy. Sandwich ordering is one; “best first” is another and is easier to debug.

- Put the question close to the end. generate_answer puts the context in the system prompt and the question in the user turn, so the question is the last thing read. Restating it just before the tables helps smaller models focus.

- Use natural orders when they exist. Paths go in hop order, timelines in date order. A chronologically shuffled timeline makes “who was CTO in 2025” harder than it needs to be.

- Keep related rows adjacent. An entity followed by its relationships beats all entities then all relationships when the question is about one entity.

- Keep section order fixed across queries. A stable prefix is also what makes prompt caching work.

```python  # examples/context_tools.py
def sandwich(items_best_first: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Place rank 1 first, rank 2 last, rank 3 second, rank 4 second-to-last, ...

    The weakest items end up in the middle, where long-context models attend least.
    """
    front, back = [], []
    for i, item in enumerate(items_best_first):
        (front if i % 2 == 0 else back).append(item)
    return front + back[::-1]
```

### Deduplication

Graph retrieval produces duplicates in three ways. The same fact appears as a relationship row and inside a source passage. Two paths share edges. And entity resolution misses leave near-identical descriptions under two names (“Deepcast” and “Deepcast Inc.”). Duplicates cost tokens and they also bias the model: a fact stated three times looks more important than one stated once. Deduplicate at three levels: exact or normalized text within a section (the dedupe helper above), shared edges across paths (render each edge once and refer to paths by edge ids), and facts across sections (drop a relationship row when a source passage already selected states it, or keep the row and drop the passage if you need the id for citation).

## Token budgets across sections

A context window is a budget. Local search in minigraphrag splits it by proportion: 15% community reports, 50% source text, and the remaining 35% shared by entities and relationships (see build_local_context in Chapter 14). Each section is filled greedily with its best items until its slice runs out:

```python  # minigraphrag/context.py
def fit_to_budget(items: list[str], max_tokens: int, header: str = "") -> list[str]:
    """Greedily keep items (already ranked best-first) until the budget is used up."""
    used = count_tokens(header)
    kept = []
    for item in items:
        t = count_tokens(item)
        if used + t > max_tokens:
            break
        kept.append(item)
        used += t
    return kept
```

[Interactive figure: Splitting an 8,000-token local search context — Drag the sliders; shares are renormalized to the total (token-budget)]

Fixed shares waste space whenever a section has less evidence than its slice. A question about Lena Park might retrieve two entity rows and fill 40 of its 1,400 entity tokens. The fix is a second pass that hands leftover tokens to sections that still have items, starting with the largest share:

```python  # examples/context_tools.py
from minigraphrag.context import fit_to_budget
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

def allocate_budget(sections: dict[str, list[str]], total: int, shares: dict[str, float],
                    headers: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    """Fill each section up to its share, then hand unused tokens to sections that still have items."""
    headers = headers or {}
    kept = {name: fit_to_budget(items, int(total * shares[name]), headers.get(name, ""))
            for name, items in sections.items()}
    used = sum(count_tokens(headers.get(n, "")) + sum(count_tokens(x) for x in kept[n]) for n in kept)
    for name in sorted(sections, key=lambda n: -shares[n]):          # biggest share gets first pick
        rest = sections[name][len(kept[name]):]
        extra = fit_to_budget(rest, total - used)
        kept[name] += extra
        used += sum(count_tokens(x) for x in extra)
    return kept
```

### A worked allocation

Take a 6,000-token budget with shares Reports 15%, Entities 20%, Relationships 15%, Sources 50%. Available items: 2 reports of 500 tokens, 30 entity rows of 60 tokens, 40 relationship rows of 44 tokens, 12 passages of 400 tokens.

Section | Slice | First pass | Used | Second pass | Final

Sources | 3,000 | 7 passages (an 8th would need 3,200) | 2,800 | +1 passage (400 of the 620 left) | 8

Entities | 1,200 | 20 rows | 1,200 | +3 rows (180 of the 220 left) | 23

Reports | 900 | 1 report (2 would need 1,000) | 500 | none (40 left, report needs 500) | 1

Relationships | 900 | 20 rows (21 would need 924) | 880 | none (40 left, row needs 44) | 20

First pass total: 2,800 + 1,200 + 500 + 880 = 5,380 tokens, leaving 620. The second pass visits sections by share (Sources, then Entities, then the two 15% sections in their original order) and ends at 5,960 tokens. Without redistribution, 10% of the budget would have gone unused.

**Budget for the answer too

A model with a 128k window does not mean a 128k context is a good idea. Longer contexts cost more, respond slower and, as above, can bury evidence. Most GraphRAG systems use contexts between a few thousand and a few tens of thousands of tokens. Set the context budget from answer quality measurements, and always reserve room for the system prompt, the question and the maximum answer length.

## Citations and answer formats

### Ids that survive the round trip

Citations need ids that are short, unique within the prompt, and mappable back to real records. GraphRAG uses per-table integer ids (human_id in minigraphrag) for entities and relationships and text unit ids for sources. Two rules keep them trustworthy. Never renumber rows per query in a way that collides across sections: “Relationships (3)” and “Entities (3)” are fine because the table name disambiguates, but a bare “[3]” is not. And log the id-to-record map for every query, so a citation in a stored answer can still be resolved after the index is rebuilt.

### A grounded system prompt

The prompt minigraphrag ships for local search (LOCAL_SEARCH_SYSTEM_PROMPT, adapted from GraphRAG) already contains the two sentences that matter most: “If you don't know the answer, just say so. Do not make anything up.” and the [Data: ...] citation format. For question answering where faithfulness matters more than breadth, a stricter version helps:

```python  # examples/prompts_grounded.py
GROUNDED_ANSWER_SYSTEM = """---Role---
You answer questions about Kestrel Labs using only the evidence tables below.

---Rules---
1. Use only facts stated in the tables. Do not add outside knowledge, even if you are confident it is true.
2. End every sentence that states a fact with the rows it relies on: [Data: <table> (<id>, <id>)].
   Cite at most 5 ids per reference. Never cite an id that is not in the tables.
3. If the tables do not contain enough information to answer, reply:
   "I don't know based on the provided data." Then say in one sentence what is missing.
4. If two rows disagree, say so and cite both.
5. When facts have dates, use the one that was true at the time the question asks about.

---Answer format---
{response_type}

---Evidence tables---
{context_data}
"""

# The question goes in the user turn, after the evidence, like generate_answer does:
# llm.complete(question, system=GROUNDED_ANSWER_SYSTEM.format(context_data=context, response_type="2-4 sentences"))
```

Each rule targets an observed failure. Rule 1 stops the model from “helpfully” adding world knowledge, which is how answers about fictional companies acquire invented founders. Rule 2's “never cite an id that is not in the tables” reduces fabricated citations. Rule 3 gives the model a sanctioned exit; without it, models tend to answer anyway. Rule 4 surfaces conflicts instead of hiding them, and rule 5 is the prompt-side half of the temporal windows from Chapter 21: “Who is the CTO?” with both Vehl and Nair rows in context should produce Priya Nair with the date.

**Abstention has to be measured

Include unanswerable questions in your evaluation set, for example “Who is Kestrel Labs' CFO?” (the corpus never says). Measure how often the system abstains on those and how often it wrongly abstains on answerable ones. A prompt change that raises one usually raises the other.

### Structured answers

Free text with inline [Data: ...] markers is readable and easy to stream. When a downstream program consumes the answer, or when you want claim-level checking, ask for JSON with one entry per atomic claim:

```python  # examples/json_answer.py
import json
from minigraphrag.llm import parse_json_response

JSON_ANSWER_INSTRUCTIONS = """Return JSON only:
{"answer": "<one or two sentences, or null if the tables are insufficient>",
 "claims": [{"text": "<one atomic claim>", "citations": ["Relationships:1", "Sources:08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-000"]}],
 "missing": "<what evidence would be needed, or null>"}"""

def answer_as_json(llm, question: str, system: str) -> dict:
    out = parse_json_response(llm.complete(question + "\n\n" + JSON_ANSWER_INSTRUCTIONS, system=system, json=True))
    out.setdefault("claims", [])
    for claim in out["claims"]:                       # normalize "Table:id" strings into pairs
        claim["citations"] = [tuple(c.split(":", 1)) for c in claim.get("citations", []) if ":" in c]
    return out
```

### Measuring citation faithfulness

A citation can fail in three increasingly subtle ways, and each needs its own metric:

- Validity: the cited id exists in the context. Checkable with a regex and a lookup; failures are fabricated citations.

- Support (precision): the cited rows actually entail the sentence. Needs a judge: an NLI model or an LLM asked a narrow yes/no question.

- Coverage (recall): sentences that state facts carry citations at all.

Citation recall and precision in this sense were popularized by the ALCE benchmark (Gao et al., 2023), which judges support with an NLI model. The code below implements all three with the minigraphrag LLM protocol as the judge.

```python  # examples/citations.py
import re
from minigraphrag.context import parse_tables

CITATION = re.compile(r"\[Data:\s*([^\]]+)\]")

def extract_citations(answer: str) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """'[Data: Entities (5, 7); Relationships (23)]' -> [('Entities','5'), ('Entities','7'), ('Relationships','23')]"""
    out = []
    for block in CITATION.findall(answer):
        for part in block.split(";"):
            m = re.match(r"\s*(\w+)\s*\(([^)]*)\)", part)
            if m:
                out += [(m.group(1), rid.strip()) for rid in m.group(2).split(",") if rid.strip() and rid.strip() != "+more"]
    return out

def citation_validity(answer: str, context: str) -> float:
    """Share of cited (table, id) pairs that actually exist in the context tables."""
    tables = parse_tables(context)
    present = {(t, row.get("id", "")) for t, rows in tables.items() for row in rows}
    cited = extract_citations(answer)
    return 1.0 if not cited else sum(c in present for c in cited) / len(cited)
```

```python  # examples/citation_support.py
import re
from minigraphrag.context import parse_tables
from examples.citations import extract_citations
SUPPORT_PROMPT = """Statement: {statement}

Evidence:
{evidence}

Does the evidence fully support the statement? Answer with one word: SUPPORTED, PARTIAL or UNSUPPORTED."""

def citation_support(llm, answer: str, context: str) -> dict:
    """Per cited sentence, ask a judge whether the cited rows support it."""
    tables = parse_tables(context)
    rows = {(t, r.get("id", "")): " | ".join(r.values()) for t, rs in tables.items() for r in rs}
    sentences = [s for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", answer) if s.strip()]
    results = {"SUPPORTED": 0, "PARTIAL": 0, "UNSUPPORTED": 0, "uncited": 0, "invalid_id": 0}
    for sentence in sentences:
        cited = extract_citations(sentence)
        if not cited:
            results["uncited"] += 1
            continue
        evidence = [rows[c] for c in cited if c in rows]
        results["invalid_id"] += len(cited) - len(evidence)
        if not evidence:
            results["UNSUPPORTED"] += 1
            continue
        statement = re.sub(r"\[Data:[^\]]*\]", "", sentence).strip()
        verdict = llm.complete(SUPPORT_PROMPT.format(statement=statement, evidence="\n".join(evidence)))
        label = next((v for v in ("UNSUPPORTED", "PARTIAL", "SUPPORTED") if v in verdict.upper()), "UNSUPPORTED")
        results[label] += 1
    cited_total = results["SUPPORTED"] + results["PARTIAL"] + results["UNSUPPORTED"]
    results["citation_recall"] = cited_total / max(1, len(sentences))       # share of sentences with a citation
    results["citation_precision"] = results["SUPPORTED"] / max(1, cited_total)
    return results
```

For the answer “Marlow Dynamics acquired Deepcast [Data: Relationships (0)]. Deepcast then stopped supplying Kestrel, so Kestrel built Tern [Data: Relationships (1)]. It was a hard year.”, validity is 1.0 (both ids exist). Support is mixed: row 0 fully supports the first sentence, but row 1 only says Deepcast supplied Kestrel until June 2025, not that this caused Tern, so a careful judge returns PARTIAL. The third sentence has no citation, so coverage is 2 of 3. The partial citation is the dangerous one: it looks grounded, and the causal claim it carries came from the model.

**Judges have biases too

LLM judges tend to be lenient with fluent sentences and can be swayed by the statement's confidence. Keep the judge prompt narrow (one statement, only the cited rows, a three-way label), use a different model from the generator when you can, and spot-check a sample of verdicts by hand. Chapter 25 treats judge reliability in depth.

Serialize the three edges Marlow Dynamics ACQUIRED Deepcast, Deepcast SUPPLIED Kestrel Labs, Kestrel Labs RUNS Project Tern in three ways, using relation labels instead of descriptions: (a) triples, (b) a GraphRAG-style Relationships table with ids, (c) a JSON list of objects with source, relation, target keys on one line. Estimate tokens as characters divided by four (round up). Which one can be cited, and what does each cost relative to triples?

```python
(DEEPCAST, SUPPLIED, KESTREL LABS)
(KESTREL LABS, RUNS, PROJECT TERN)
```

```python
-----Relationships-----
id|source|target|relation
0|MARLOW DYNAMICS|DEEPCAST|ACQUIRED
1|DEEPCAST|KESTREL LABS|SUPPLIED
```

```python
[{"source": "MARLOW DYNAMICS", "relation": "ACQUIRED", "target": "DEEPCAST"}, {"source": "DEEPCAST", "relation": "SUPPLIED", "target": "KESTREL LABS"}, {"source": "KESTREL LABS", "relation": "RUNS", "target": "PROJECT TERN"}]
```

Character counts (newlines included): triples 107, table 151, JSON 225. Estimated tokens: 27, 38 and 57. With only three rows, the table's title and header lines (48 characters) make it 40% larger than triples; the header is a fixed cost, so the gap shrinks as rows grow. JSON costs about twice the triples, and the gap grows with rows because every row repeats its keys. Only the table has ids a model can cite as [Data: Relationships (1)]. count_tokens's word-based fallback reports 18, 12 and 30 for the same strings, ranking the table cheapest because pipes remove the spaces it counts. That is why real tokenizers matter for tables.

#### Exercise 22.2 Warm-up

Seven source passages are ranked r1 (best) to r7. Write the order produced by sandwich. Which rank sits exactly in the middle, and which two ranks are adjacent to the end of the section? Then give one kind of section where you should not use sandwich ordering.

▸ Show answer

Even indices (r1, r3, r5, r7) go to the front in order; odd indices (r2, r4, r6) go to the back reversed. Result: r1, r3, r5, r7, r6, r4, r2. Position 4 of 7, the exact middle, holds r7, the weakest. The last two positions hold r4 and r2, so r2 is the very last row and r1 the very first.

Do not sandwich sections that have a meaningful natural order: a timeline (the model needs chronology to answer “who was CTO in 2025”), a path (hops must stay in order), or a conversation history. Rank-based placement would scramble the structure the model relies on.

#### Exercise 22.3 Core

Repeat the worked allocation with a 4,000-token budget and the same shares and items (reports 500, entity rows 60, relationship rows 44, passages 400). Compute the first pass, the second pass and the total by hand, then check with allocate_budget.

▸ Hint

Slices are Reports 600, Entities 800, Relationships 600, Sources 2,000. The second pass visits Sources, Entities, Reports, Relationships.

▸ Show answer

First pass. Sources 2,000: 5 passages = 2,000 exactly. Entities 800: 13 rows = 780 (14 would be 840). Reports 600: 1 report = 500. Relationships 600: 13 rows = 572 (14 would be 616). Used: 2,000 + 780 + 500 + 572 = 3,852. Left: 148.

Second pass. Sources: next passage needs 400, skip. Entities: 2 more rows (120) fit, a third would need 180; used 3,972, left 28. Reports: 500, skip. Relationships: 44, skip.

Final. Reports 1, Entities 15, Relationships 13, Sources 5; total 3,972 tokens.

```python
import math
from examples.context_tools import allocate_budget
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

def item(n_tokens):
    # With the word-based fallback, ceil(words * 4 / 3) tokens; find a word count that hits n_tokens exactly.
    words = next(w for w in range(1, 5000) if math.ceil(w * 4 / 3) == n_tokens)
    return " ".join(["x"] * words)

sections = {"Reports": [item(500)] * 2, "Entities": [item(60)] * 30,
            "Relationships": [item(44)] * 40, "Sources": [item(400)] * 12}
kept = allocate_budget(sections, 4000, {"Reports": 0.15, "Entities": 0.2, "Relationships": 0.15, "Sources": 0.5})
print({k: len(v) for k, v in kept.items()}, sum(count_tokens(x) for v in kept.values() for x in v))
# {'Reports': 1, 'Entities': 15, 'Relationships': 13, 'Sources': 5} 3972
```

The helper only produces these exact numbers with the word-based fallback counter. With tiktoken installed, strings of repeated “x” tokenize differently; the arithmetic is what matters.

#### Exercise 22.4 Core

Extend citation_support to also report fabricated citations (ids not in the context) per answer, and add a rule that a sentence with any fabricated citation counts as UNSUPPORTED even if its other citations support it. Test it on: “Priya Nair co-leads Project Tern [Data: Relationships (3, 99)].” with a context whose Relationships table has ids 0 to 4.

▸ Show answer

```python
import re
from minigraphrag.context import parse_tables
from examples.citations import extract_citations
from examples.citation_support import SUPPORT_PROMPT

def citation_support_strict(llm, answer: str, context: str) -> dict:
    tables = parse_tables(context)
    rows = {(t, r.get("id", "")): " | ".join(r.values()) for t, rs in tables.items() for r in rs}
    out = {"SUPPORTED": 0, "PARTIAL": 0, "UNSUPPORTED": 0, "uncited": 0, "fabricated": []}
    for sentence in [s for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", answer) if s.strip()]:
        cited = extract_citations(sentence)
        if not cited:
            out["uncited"] += 1
            continue
        fake = [c for c in cited if c not in rows]
        out["fabricated"] += fake
        if fake:                                   # one invented id taints the whole sentence
            out["UNSUPPORTED"] += 1
            continue
        statement = re.sub(r"\[Data:[^\]]*\]", "", sentence).strip()
        verdict = llm.complete(SUPPORT_PROMPT.format(statement=statement,
                                                     evidence="\n".join(rows[c] for c in cited))).upper()
        out[next((v for v in ("UNSUPPORTED", "PARTIAL", "SUPPORTED") if v in verdict), "UNSUPPORTED")] += 1
    return out
```

On the test sentence, extract_citations returns [("Relationships", "3"), ("Relationships", "99")]. Row 3 exists, row 99 does not, so the result is {"UNSUPPORTED": 1, "fabricated": [("Relationships", "99")], ...} and the judge is never called. Note the order of the label check: “UNSUPPORTED” contains “SUPPORTED”, so it must be tested first. The strict rule is deliberately harsh. A model that invents one id is not reliably tracking where its claims come from, and in a user interface a broken citation link destroys trust faster than a missing one.

#### Exercise 22.5 Stretch

Design and run an experiment that measures, on your model, (a) whether serialization format changes answer quality on the Kestrel questions and (b) whether the position of the supporting passages matters. Control for retrieval: only include questions where the supporting documents were retrieved. Report token F1 per (format, position) cell and say what result would make you change your production format.

▸ Show answer

```python  # examples/format_position_experiment.py
import json, random
from collections import defaultdict
from minigraphrag.context import format_table
from minigraphrag.evaluation import load_questions, token_f1
from minigraphrag.indexer import load_index
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.search.common import generate_answer
from minigraphrag.search.local import build_local_context

def place(rows: list[list], gold_rows: list[list], position: str, rng) -> list[list]:
    """Put the gold rows at the start, middle or end of the distractor rows."""
    rest = [r for r in rows if r not in gold_rows]
    rng.shuffle(rest)
    cut = {"start": 0, "middle": len(rest) // 2, "end": len(rest)}[position]
    return rest[:cut] + gold_rows + rest[cut:]

def render(rows: list[list], fmt: str) -> str:
    if fmt == "table":
        return format_table("Sources", ["id", "text"], rows)
    if fmt == "json":
        return json.dumps([{"id": r[0], "text": r[1]} for r in rows], indent=1)
    return "\n".join(f"[{r[0]}] {r[1]}" for r in rows)            # "lines"

index = load_index("out/kestrel")
llm = get_llm("openai", cache_dir=".cache/llm")                  # MockLLM only parses tables; use a real model
questions = load_questions("data/questions.jsonl")
rng = random.Random(0)
scores = defaultdict(list)
for q in questions:
    gold_docs = set(q.get("supporting_docs", []))
    if not gold_docs:
        continue
    _, data = build_local_context(index, q["question"], max_context_tokens=6000)
    rows = [[s["id"], s["text"]] for s in data["sources"]]
    rows += [[u.id, u.text] for u in rng.sample(list(index.text_units.values()), 8) if [u.id, u.text] not in rows]
    gold = [r for r in rows if index.text_units[r[0]].doc_id in gold_docs]
    if not gold:
        continue                                                   # retrieval failed; not a formatting question
    for fmt in ("table", "lines", "json"):
        for position in ("start", "middle", "end"):
            context = render(place(rows, gold, position, rng), fmt)
            answer = generate_answer(llm, q["question"], context)
            scores[(fmt, position)].append(token_f1(answer, q["answer"]))
for key, vals in sorted(scores.items()):
    print(key, f"F1={sum(vals) / len(vals):.3f} over {len(vals)} questions")
```

Design choices that make the result interpretable: the same rows appear in every cell, only their rendering and placement change; distractor passages are added so position has room to matter; questions whose gold documents were not retrieved are skipped, because they measure retrieval, not formatting; and a fixed seed makes the shuffle reproducible. Run it with a real model: MockLLM only knows how to read GraphRAG-style tables, so with the mock you will see the table format win for a trivial reason, a reminder to check what your evaluation script is really measuring.

How to read the grid: with 20-odd questions, differences of a few F1 points are noise; rerun with two or three seeds and look for effects that hold across them. Change the production format only if one format wins consistently across seeds and positions, or if two formats tie and one is much cheaper in tokens (then take the cheaper one). If the “middle” column is clearly worse than “start” and “end” on your model, adopt sandwich ordering or shorten contexts. Token F1 punishes correct but verbose answers, so confirm any decision with an LLM judge on a sample.

## Check your understanding

Why do GraphRAG local search contexts use titled tables with an id column rather than plain triples?

- Tables always use fewer tokens than triples

- ✓ (correct) Row ids let the answer cite specific evidence, and extra columns like rank tell the model what the retriever considered important

- LLMs cannot read parentheses reliably

- Tables preserve edge direction and triples cannot
Answer: For a few rows, tables can cost more than triples because of the header. Their advantage is citation ([Data: Relationships (3)]) and room for ranking signals.

What is the most defensible summary of “Talk like a Graph” for a GraphRAG engineer?

- Adjacency lists are always the best encoding

- Graph encoding choices have no measurable effect on large models

- JSON is the best encoding for reasoning tasks

- ✓ (correct) Encoding choices can change accuracy a lot, the best choice depends on the task and graph, so test formats on your own questions
Answer: The paper found large, task-dependent effects and no universal winner. Its tasks were synthetic graph problems, so the transferable lesson is to measure, not a specific format.

Your context has 40 relationship rows. Accuracy drops when the key Deepcast row lands around row 20. Which change targets that problem directly?

- ✓ (correct) Order rows so the highest-ranked evidence is at the start and end of the section, or shorten the section

- Switch from tables to JSON

- Increase the temperature

- Add more distractor rows so the key row is less prominent
Answer: That is the lost-in-the-middle pattern. Placement and shorter contexts address it; format changes and more rows do not.

A section's fixed share is 1,200 tokens, but only 3 entity rows (180 tokens) were retrieved. What does a two-pass allocator do with the remaining 1,020 tokens?

- Leaves them empty to keep the prompt short

- Repeats the 3 entity rows to fill the slice

- ✓ (correct) Offers them to other sections that still have unplaced items, largest share first

- Adds them to the answer's max_tokens
Answer: Redistribution keeps the total budget fixed while letting sections with more evidence use space others do not need.

An answer cites [Data: Relationships (1)] for “Deepcast stopped supplying Kestrel, so Kestrel built Tern.” Row 1 exists and says Deepcast supplied Kestrel until June 2025. Which metric catches the problem?

- Citation validity

- Citation coverage (recall)

- ✓ (correct) Citation support (precision), judged by entailment

- Token F1 against the gold answer
Answer: The id is valid and the sentence is cited, but the row does not entail the causal claim. Only a support check that reads the row and the sentence catches it.

Why does a grounded system prompt explicitly allow “I don't know based on the provided data”?

- It reduces output tokens on every query

- ✓ (correct) Without a sanctioned way to abstain, models tend to answer anyway, filling gaps from world knowledge or invention

- It is required by the citation format

- It makes retrieval faster
Answer: Abstention has to be allowed and then measured on unanswerable questions, because prompts that increase abstention can also increase wrong abstentions.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Should I include community reports and raw passages when I already have entities and relationships?

Usually yes, but for different reasons. Entities and relationships are compressed and easy to cite; passages carry nuance, dates and quotes that extraction dropped; reports give global framing. The budget split is the lever: shift share toward passages for “what exactly did the memo say” questions and toward reports for “what are the risks” questions. If you must drop one, drop reports for local questions and passages for global ones.

▸ Is markdown or XML-style tagging better for section boundaries?

Both work; consistency matters more than the choice. Titled sections like -----Relationships----- (GraphRAG), markdown headings, or tags such as <relationships>…</relationships> all give the model clear boundaries. Tags have one practical advantage: retrieved passages can contain markdown headings or pipes, which blur markdown boundaries, while a closing tag is unlikely to appear in source text. Some model providers also recommend tags in their prompting guides.

▸ Can I just give the model the whole graph if it fits in the context window?

For a graph as small as Kestrel's, you could, and it is a useful baseline. It stops working for three reasons as graphs grow: cost scales with graph size on every query, position effects make distant facts less reliable, and irrelevant but plausible facts distract the model. Retrieval plus a focused context usually beats “everything” on both quality and cost once the graph is more than a few thousand tokens.

▸ Does prompt caching change how I should build contexts?

It rewards a stable prefix. Put fixed instructions, schema descriptions and few-shot examples first, then per-query evidence, then the question. Keep section order and headers identical across queries. Retrieved evidence differs per query, so it will not be cached, but a long fixed system prompt will be. Do not reorder instructions per query for small gains.

▸ How do I cite a path, which spans several edges?

Give each path an id and list its edge ids: P1: Priya Nair -[r4]-> Marlow Dynamics -[r0]-> Deepcast. Then the answer can cite [Data: Paths (P1)] for the chain and [Data: Relationships (0)] for the single hop it relies on most, and the support checker can verify each hop against its row. Chapter 23 verifies paths hop by hop against source passages.

### Project: a context builder with a report card

Build a context construction module that you can switch between formats and policies, and that grades its own output on every query.

- build_context(evidence, format, ordering, budget, shares) supporting at least tables, triples, sentences and paths, with sandwich or natural ordering per section

- Cross-section deduplication and two-pass budget redistribution, with a log line of tokens per section

- The grounded system prompt, with five unanswerable Kestrel questions added to your test set

- A per-answer report: citation validity, support precision, coverage, and whether the system abstained

- Results of the format and position experiment from Exercise 22.5 on a real model, with your production choice and its justification

Done when every answer your system produces comes with a report card, and you changed at least one default because of a number on it.

## Key takeaways

- Serialization is a design decision with measurable effects on cost, on what the model notices, and on whether answers can cite evidence.

- Tables with ids are the workhorse for cited answers; triples and adjacency lists are cheap; JSON is precise but costly; paths carry reasoning order.

- Encoding effects are real and task-dependent, so test formats on your own questions rather than adopting a universal favorite.

- Place strong evidence where the model attends best, keep natural orders for timelines and paths, and deduplicate within and across sections.

- Split the token budget by section and redistribute what a section does not use; count tokens with the real tokenizer for tables and JSON.

- Allow “I don't know”, require citations, and measure citation validity, support and coverage separately.

## Graph-guided reasoning

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/23-graph-reasoning.html
Summary: Graph chain-of-thought, reasoning on graphs, faithful paths and post-retrieval pruning.

# Graph-guided reasoning

So far the graph has been a place to fetch context from, once, before the model writes. This chapter lets the graph shape the reasoning itself: the model plans relation paths, calls graph functions step by step, is constrained to paths that really exist, and has each hop of its argument checked against the source text.

## You will be able to

- Implement a Graph Chain-of-Thought loop that alternates LLM reasoning, graph function calls and execution, using the minigraphrag LLM protocol

- Explain Reasoning on Graphs (RoG): planning relation paths, grounding them with constrained search, and reasoning over the retrieved paths

- Describe how graph-constrained decoding with a KG-Trie (GCR) and Decoding on Graphs make generated paths faithful by construction

- Verify a reasoning path hop by hop against source passages and prune the hops that no source supports

- Use self-consistency across paths, and decide when graph reasoning helps and when a single retrieval pass is better

## From retrieving a graph to reasoning with it

Every search method in Part 3 follows one pattern: retrieve, build a context, generate once. That works when the retriever can guess all the evidence in advance. It struggles when the next thing to look up depends on what you just found. Consider canonical question 2:

>

“Which investor's board member oversees the company whose drones detected the Halden Reef bleaching?”

A person answering it does not retrieve everything about reefs, drones, boards and investors at once. They reason: which drones detected the bleaching? Sentinel. Who runs Sentinel? Kestrel Labs. Who is on Kestrel's board? Lena Park. Where is she a partner? Brightwater Capital. Each step picks one relation to follow from the entity the previous step produced. Local search can get lucky here, and Chapter 18 showed Think-on-Graph exploring with beam search. This chapter looks at the broader family of methods where reasoning and graph access are interleaved, and at how to keep the resulting reasoning honest.

The chapter covers four ideas, from least to most structural:

Idea | What the model does | What the graph does | Representative work

Tool-using reasoning | Decides which graph function to call next | Answers function calls | Graph Chain-of-Thought

Plan, then ground | Writes a relation-path plan up front | Retrieves the paths that match the plan | Reasoning on Graphs (RoG)

Constrained generation | Generates a path token by token | Masks every token that would leave the graph | Graph-constrained Reasoning, Decoding on Graphs

Verification | Proposes a reasoning chain | Supplies the sources used to accept or cut each hop | Chain-of-Knowledge, post-retrieval pruning

## Graph Chain-of-Thought: reason, interact, execute

### The loop

Graph Chain-of-Thought (Graph-CoT) treats the graph as an environment an LLM agent explores. Each iteration has three sub-steps:

- Reasoning. The LLM states what it knows and what information it still needs, or decides it can answer.

- Interaction. The LLM writes a call to one of a small set of predefined graph functions.

- Execution. The system runs the call on the graph and appends the result to the transcript.

The loop repeats until the model emits a Finish[answer] action. The paper defines four graph functions that cover both the text attached to nodes and the structure around them:

- RetrieveNode(Text): find the related node with semantic search.

- NodeFeature(NodeID, FeatureName): read a textual feature of a node, such as its name or description.

- NeighborCheck(NodeID, NeighborType): return the node's neighbors of one type.

- NodeDegree(NodeID, NeighborType): return how many neighbors of that type the node has.

[Interactive figure: One Graph-CoT episode for “What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?” (flow)]

**Jin et al., Graph Chain-of-Thought: Augmenting Large Language Models by Reasoning on Graphs (2024)

Published at ACL 2024. The authors built GRBench, 1,740 questions over ten domain graphs (academic, e-commerce, literature, healthcare and legal), where answers need both node text and graph structure. Graph-CoT lets the LLM interact with the graph through the four functions above, with the procedure taught by in-context demonstrations rather than fine-tuning. The paper frames Graph-CoT explicitly as an agent: the LLM is the agent, the graph is the environment, and the functions are its action space. With each of the three LLM backbones they tested, it beat the plain-prompting and retrieval-augmented baselines.

### Tools backed by the minigraphrag index

The minigraphrag graph is a NetworkX Graph whose nodes carry type, description, aliases and source_ids, and whose edges carry description, weight and source_ids. That maps neatly onto Graph-CoT's functions: NeighborType becomes our entity type. We add one function the paper does not define, EdgeFeature, because our edges carry the evidence text and source ids we need for citations. Tool results are strings, because the model reads them.

```python  # examples/graph_cot.py
import re
from collections import Counter

GRAPH_COT_SYSTEM = """You answer questions by exploring a knowledge graph step by step.
At each step write one line starting with "Thought:" and one line starting with "Action:".
Available actions:
  RetrieveNode[text]                    find the node whose name or description best matches text
  NodeFeature[node, feature]            read a node attribute: type, description, aliases
  NeighborCheck[node, neighbor_type]    list neighbors of node, optionally only of one type (or ALL)
  NodeDegree[node, neighbor_type]       count neighbors of node of one type (or ALL)
  EdgeFeature[node_a, node_b]           read the description and source ids of the edge
  Finish[answer]                        give the final answer, or Finish[I don't know]
Use exact node names returned by earlier observations. Never invent facts that no observation showed."""

class GraphTools:
    """Graph functions in the style of Graph-CoT, backed by a minigraphrag Index."""

    def __init__(self, index, max_list: int = 15):
        self.index, self.G, self.max_list = index, index.graph, max_list

    def _node(self, name: str) -> str | None:
        name = name.strip().strip('"').upper()
        return name if name in self.G else None

    def retrieve_node(self, text: str) -> str:
        exact = self._node(text)
        if exact:
            return f"The best matching node is {exact}."
        hits = self.index.entity_store.search(self.index.embedder.embed([text])[0], k=3)
        return "Candidate nodes: " + ", ".join(f"{name} ({score:.2f})" for name, score, _ in hits)

    def node_feature(self, node: str, feature: str) -> str:
        n = self._node(node)
        if n is None:
            return f"No node named {node}. Use RetrieveNode first."
        value = self.G.nodes[n].get(feature.strip().lower())
        return f"{feature.strip()} of {n}: {str(value)[:500]}" if value else f"{n} has no feature {feature}."

    def neighbor_check(self, node: str, neighbor_type: str = "ALL") -> str:
        n = self._node(node)
        if n is None:
            return f"No node named {node}. Use RetrieveNode first."
        t = neighbor_type.strip().upper()
        nbrs = [m for m in self.G.neighbors(n) if t == "ALL" or self.G.nodes[m].get("type") == t]
        nbrs.sort(key=lambda m: -self.G.edges[n, m].get("weight", 0))
        more = f" (+{len(nbrs) - self.max_list} more)" if len(nbrs) > self.max_list else ""
        return f"Neighbors of {n} [{t}]: " + (", ".join(nbrs[: self.max_list]) or "none") + more

    def node_degree(self, node: str, neighbor_type: str = "ALL") -> str:
        n = self._node(node)
        if n is None:
            return f"No node named {node}."
        t = neighbor_type.strip().upper()
        return f"{n} has {sum(1 for m in self.G.neighbors(n) if t == 'ALL' or self.G.nodes[m].get('type') == t)} {t} neighbors."

    def edge_feature(self, a: str, b: str) -> str:
        u, v = self._node(a), self._node(b)
        if not (u and v and self.G.has_edge(u, v)):
            return f"There is no edge between {a} and {b}."
        d = self.G.edges[u, v]
        return f"Edge {u} -- {v}: {d.get('description', '')[:500]} [sources: {', '.join(d.get('source_ids', []))}]"

ACTION = re.compile(r"Action:\s*(\w+)\[(.*)\]\s*$", re.M)

def graph_cot(llm, tools: GraphTools, question: str, max_steps: int = 8) -> dict:
    dispatch = {
        "RetrieveNode": lambda a: tools.retrieve_node(a[0]),
        "NodeFeature": lambda a: tools.node_feature(a[0], a[1] if len(a) > 1 else "description"),
        "NeighborCheck": lambda a: tools.neighbor_check(a[0], a[1] if len(a) > 1 else "ALL"),
        "NodeDegree": lambda a: tools.node_degree(a[0], a[1] if len(a) > 1 else "ALL"),
        "EdgeFeature": lambda a: tools.edge_feature(a[0], a[1]),
    }
    transcript = f"Question: {question}\n"
    trace = []
    for step in range(max_steps):
        reply = llm.complete(transcript, system=GRAPH_COT_SYSTEM)       # 1. reason
        m = ACTION.search(reply)
        if not m:                                                       # malformed: tell the model, retry
            transcript += reply + "\nObservation: No valid Action line. Use Name[args].\n"
            continue
        name, raw_args = m.group(1), m.group(2)
        thought = reply[: m.start()].strip()
        if name == "Finish":
            trace.append((thought, f"Finish[{raw_args}]", ""))
            return {"answer": raw_args.strip(), "steps": step + 1, "trace": trace}
        args = [a.strip() for a in raw_args.split(",")]                 # 2. interact
        try:
            observation = dispatch[name](args) if name in dispatch else f"Unknown action {name}."
        except (IndexError, KeyError) as err:                          # 3. execute (safely)
            observation = f"Action failed: {err!r}"
        trace.append((thought, f"{name}[{raw_args}]", observation))
        transcript += f"{thought}\nAction: {name}[{raw_args}]\nObservation: {observation}\n"
    return {"answer": "I don't know (step limit reached)", "steps": max_steps, "trace": trace}
```

Design choices worth copying:

- Errors become observations. An unknown node or a malformed action is reported back in words (“Use RetrieveNode first”), never raised. The model can recover from a message; it cannot recover from a crashed loop.

- Lists are capped and sorted. NeighborCheck[KESTREL LABS, ALL] would return 15 names on the Kestrel graph and hundreds on a real one. Sorting by edge weight and saying “+N more” keeps observations short and tells the model to filter by type.

- A hard step limit with an explicit abstention. Without it, a confused model loops until your budget runs out.

- The LLM protocol is the only dependency. graph_cot calls llm.complete(prompt, system=...), so it works with OpenAICompatibleLLM, AnthropicLLM, CachedLLM or a scripted test double. MockLLM does not know this prompt and simply returns “OK”, so use a real model or a scripted one.

### A trace on the Kestrel index

These observations come from running the tools on an index built with MockLLM; the thoughts and actions are what a capable model typically writes.

```python
Question: What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?
Thought: I need the Priya Nair node.
Action: RetrieveNode[Priya Nair]
Observation: The best matching node is PRIYA NAIR.
Thought: Which organizations is she connected to?
Action: NeighborCheck[PRIYA NAIR, ORGANIZATION]
Observation: Neighbors of PRIYA NAIR [ORGANIZATION]: KESTREL LABS, DEEPCAST
Thought: There is a direct edge to Deepcast. What does it say?
Action: EdgeFeature[PRIYA NAIR, DEEPCAST]
Observation: Edge PRIYA NAIR -- DEEPCAST: We propose to start a dedicated internal engineering
  project in June, co-led by Jonas Vehl (CTO) and Priya Nair (lead engineer, Project Sentinel),
  with a goal of replacing every Deepcast unit in the fleet by the end of 2026.
  [sources: 08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-001]
Thought: Is there also a Marlow Dynamics link?
Action: EdgeFeature[PRIYA NAIR, MARLOW DYNAMICS]
Observation: There is no edge between PRIYA NAIR and MARLOW DYNAMICS.
Action: Finish[Priya Nair co-leads the in-house sonar project meant to replace every Deepcast unit
  (08_kestrel_board_memo_supply-001).]
```

The trace is honest about something one-shot retrieval would hide: the offline extractor missed the Priya Nair to Marlow Dynamics relationship, so the loop found only half of the expected answer. A stronger extractor, or a follow-up RetrieveNode[Priya Nair Marlow Dynamics] over passages, would find the other half. Traces make gaps like this visible, which is one of the best reasons to use them.

### Cost and failure modes

Each iteration is an LLM call whose prompt contains the entire transcript so far, so input tokens grow roughly quadratically with the number of steps: step t resends the t − 1 earlier steps. A five-step episode with 300-token steps and a 600-token system prompt sends about 600 × 5 + 300 × (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 6,000 input tokens, against perhaps 3,000 for a single local search call with a larger context. Latency is sequential steps, not parallel ones. Typical failures:

Failure | Symptom | Mitigation

Wrong starting node | Every later step explores the wrong neighborhood | Return several candidates with scores from RetrieveNode; let the model choose

Invented node names | Calls on “DEEPCAST INC” that does not exist | “Use exact names from observations” in the prompt; helpful error text

Hub flooding | Long neighbor lists crowd the transcript | Type filters, caps, sorting by weight

Premature finish | Answers after one hop | Demonstrations that show multi-hop episodes; a verifier after Finish

Looping | Repeats the same call | Step limit; detect repeated actions and say so in the observation

## Reasoning on Graphs: plan relation paths, then ground them

Graph-CoT decides one step at a time. Reasoning on Graphs (RoG) separates deciding the shape of the reasoning from finding the facts. Its planning–retrieval–reasoning framework works in three steps:

- Planning. Given the question, the LLM generates relation paths that should lead to the answer, such as ACQUIRED → SUPPLIED. A plan mentions relation types only, no entities, which is why it can be checked against the schema and reused.

- Retrieval. For each plan, a constrained breadth-first search starts at the question entity and follows only edges whose relation matches the next element of the plan. The results are concrete reasoning paths, instances of the plan in the graph.

- Reasoning. The LLM reads the retrieved paths and answers, discarding paths that do not fit the question.

[Interactive figure: Grounding a relation-path plan on Kestrel — Plan: Organization -ACQUIRED-> Organization -SUPPLIED-> Organization (graph-steps)]

**Luo, Li, Haffari and Pan, Reasoning on Graphs: Faithful and Interpretable Large Language Model Reasoning (2024)

Published at ICLR 2024. RoG fine-tunes LLaMA2-Chat-7B on two instruction tasks. Planning optimization teaches the model to generate relation paths that are valid in the KG, using the shortest paths between question entities and answer entities in the training data as supervision. Retrieval-reasoning optimization teaches it to answer from retrieved reasoning paths. Retrieval itself is a constrained BFS that follows the planned relations. The paper also shows the planning module is plug-and-play: plans generated by RoG improved other LLMs, including ChatGPT, when their retrieved paths were given to those models without retraining them.

You do not need RoG's fine-tuning to use the pattern. A prompted planner plus the constrained search gives you most of the structure, and Chapter 24 covers training when prompting is not enough. The code works on the typed Kestrel view from Chapter 21, because plans need relation types:

```python  # examples/rog.py
import networkx as nx

def ground_relation_plan(G: nx.MultiDiGraph, start: str, plan: list[str], max_paths: int = 20) -> list[list[tuple]]:
    """RoG-style retrieval: constrained BFS that follows the planned relation sequence from `start`."""
    paths = [[(None, None, start)]]
    for relation in plan:
        nxt = []
        for path in paths:
            node = path[-1][2]
            for _, v, d in G.out_edges(node, data=True):
                if d["relation"] == relation and all(v != hop[2] for hop in path):
                    nxt.append(path + [(node, relation, v)])
        paths = nxt[:max_paths]
        if not paths:
            break                                  # the plan does not exist in this graph
    return [p[1:] for p in paths]
```

```python  # examples/rog.py
from minigraphrag.llm import parse_json_response

PLAN_PROMPT = """Relation types in the knowledge graph: {relations}

Question: {question}
Topic entity: {topic}

Write up to {n} relation paths that, followed from the topic entity, would reach the answer.
A relation path is a list of relation types, for example ["ACQUIRED", "SUPPLIED"].
Return JSON: {{"plans": [[...], [...]]}}"""

def plan_relation_paths(llm, G, question: str, topic: str, n: int = 3) -> list[list[str]]:
    """Step 1 of RoG, done by prompting: propose relation paths, keep only those made of real relation types."""
    relations = sorted({d["relation"] for _, _, d in G.edges(data=True)})
    out = parse_json_response(llm.complete(PLAN_PROMPT.format(
        relations=", ".join(relations), question=question, topic=topic, n=n), json=True))
    valid = set(relations)
    return [p for p in out.get("plans", []) if isinstance(p, list) and p and all(r in valid for r in p)]

def rog_answer_context(G, topic: str, plans: list[list[str]]) -> str:
    """Step 2: ground every plan with constrained BFS and render the reasoning paths for the answer prompt."""
    lines = []
    for plan in plans:
        for path in ground_relation_plan(G, topic, plan):
            lines.append(" -> ".join([path[0][0]] + [f"{rel} -> {v}" for _, rel, v in path]))
    return "\n".join(dict.fromkeys(lines)) or "No reasoning path in the graph matches the plans."
```

Given plans [["ACQUIRED", "SUPPLIED"], ["ACQUIRED", "SUPPLIES_TO"], ["COMPETES_WITH"]], the schema check drops the second (no SUPPLIES_TO relation exists) and grounding returns two lines: Marlow Dynamics -> ACQUIRED -> Deepcast -> SUPPLIED -> Kestrel Labs and Marlow Dynamics -> COMPETES_WITH -> Kestrel Labs. Both reach Kestrel Labs, but only the first explains why; the reasoning step must tell them apart, which is why RoG trains its model to reason over paths after generating them.

**Plans and metapaths

A RoG plan is a metapath without node types, generated per question. The curated metapaths of Chapter 21 are the same object written by a person and reused. A practical system can use curated metapaths when a question matches a known shape and fall back to generated plans otherwise.

## Faithful paths by construction: constrained decoding

Both Graph-CoT and RoG let the model write whatever it likes and then check it against the graph. A different idea is to make it impossible for the model to write a path that is not in the graph at all. At each decoding step, a language model produces a probability for every token in its vocabulary. Constrained decoding sets the probability of every token that would leave the set of valid outputs to zero before choosing. The model still decides which valid continuation is best; it just cannot pick an invalid one.

### Graph-constrained Reasoning and the KG-Trie

To constrain decoding to graph paths, you need a fast way to answer “given the path written so far, which tokens may come next?” A trie (prefix tree) answers exactly that. Graph-constrained Reasoning (GCR) builds a KG-Trie: it enumerates reasoning paths within a few hops of the question entities, tokenizes them, and inserts them into a trie. During decoding, the allowed next tokens are the children of the current trie node.

[Diagram]

A KG-Trie of paths up to two hops from Marlow Dynamics, at the level of whole relation and entity tokens (a real KG-Trie works on subword tokens). Even if the model prefers INVESTED_IN, it is masked because no such edge leaves Marlow Dynamics. The highlighted branch is the decoded path ACQUIRED, Deepcast, SUPPLIED, Kestrel Labs.

```python  # examples/kg_trie.py
from collections import defaultdict
import networkx as nx

def build_kg_trie(G: nx.MultiDiGraph, start: str, max_hops: int = 2) -> dict:
    """A trie over every relation path of 1 to max_hops hops that starts at `start`.

    Keys are path prefixes, tuples of tokens (relation, entity, relation, entity, ...).
    Values are the tokens allowed next. "<END>" is allowed only right after an entity.
    """
    trie = defaultdict(set)

    def walk(node: str, prefix: tuple, hops: int) -> None:
        if prefix:
            trie[prefix].add("<END>")            # a complete path may stop here
        if hops == max_hops:
            return
        for _, v, d in G.out_edges(node, data=True):
            trie[prefix].add(d["relation"])
            trie[prefix + (d["relation"],)].add(v)
            walk(v, prefix + (d["relation"], v), hops + 1)

    walk(start, (), 0)
    return trie

def constrained_decode(score_next, trie: dict, max_len: int = 4) -> tuple:
    """Greedy decoding: `score_next(prefix, token)` plays the model, the trie masks every invalid token."""
    prefix = ()
    while len(prefix) < max_len:
        allowed = sorted(trie[prefix])
        token = max(allowed, key=lambda t: score_next(prefix, t))
        if token == "<END>":
            break
        prefix += (token,)
    return prefix
```

Try it with a “model” whose preferences are wrong: it likes INVESTED_IN (0.9) more than ACQUIRED (0.6), and after ACQUIRED it would rather say Kestrel Labs (0.95) than Deepcast (0.7). Decoding from Marlow Dynamics still returns ("ACQUIRED", "Deepcast", "SUPPLIED", "Kestrel Labs"): INVESTED_IN is not a child of the root, and after ACQUIRED the only allowed entity is Deepcast. Whatever the scores, the output is a path that exists.

**Luo et al., Graph-constrained Reasoning: Faithful Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs with Large Language Models (2024)

Accepted at ICML 2025. GCR builds a KG-Trie over KG paths and uses it to constrain the decoding of a lightweight KG-specialized LLM, which generates reasoning paths and hypothesis answers. A larger general-purpose LLM then reasons inductively over several generated paths to produce the final answer. Because every generated path is decoded through the trie, the paths cannot be hallucinated relative to the graph; the authors describe this as eliminating reasoning hallucination about the graph structure.

**Li et al., Decoding on Graphs: Faithful and Sound Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs through Generation of Well-Formed Chains (2024)

DoG defines a well-formed chain as a sequence of interrelated fact triples that starts from the question entities and leads to the answer, and applies graph-aware constrained decoding so the LLM's generated chains follow the KG's topology. It is training-free, and the authors show it working with several off-the-shelf open-weight models.

### What constrained decoding does and does not guarantee

Constraints guarantee that the path exists in the graph. They do not guarantee that it is relevant (Marlow Dynamics COMPETES_WITH Kestrel Labs is a valid path that explains nothing), that the graph is correct (an extraction error is a valid path too), or that the final answer follows from the path. They also require control over decoding, meaning open-weight models or providers that support custom logit masks, and the trie grows quickly with hops: from Marlow Dynamics there are 6 complete paths of up to two hops on our small typed view, from Priya Nair 11, and from a real hub, thousands. That is why GCR limits hops and why the paths come from the neighborhood of the question entities only.

## Checking the reasoning after the fact

### Chain-of-Knowledge

Two different papers use the name Chain-of-Knowledge, and both are about grounding reasoning steps in knowledge:

**Wang et al., Boosting Language Models Reasoning with Chain-of-Knowledge Prompting (2024)

Published at ACL 2024. Instead of free-form chain-of-thought, CoK prompting asks the model to write explicit evidence as structured triples before answering, mimicking a knowledge map. An F²-Verification step then checks the chain for factuality and faithfulness, and when the chain looks unreliable the model is prompted to reconsider. For GraphRAG, the useful move is that the reasoning is written in the same triple form as the graph, which makes each step checkable.

**Li et al., Chain-of-Knowledge: Grounding Large Language Models via Dynamic Knowledge Adapting over Heterogeneous Sources (2024)

Published at ICLR 2024. This framework first drafts rationales and answers and identifies relevant knowledge domains. When the drafts do not agree, it corrects the rationales step by step with knowledge retrieved from structured and unstructured sources, using an adaptive query generator that can write SPARQL, SQL or natural-language queries. Corrections are progressive: each corrected rationale informs the next, which limits error propagation.

### Post-retrieval pruning: verify every hop

A reasoning path is a chain of claims, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest hop. The simplest reliable check uses the provenance you have kept since Chapter 8: for each hop, (1) the edge must exist, (2) at least one of its source passages must mention both entities, and (3) a judge must agree that the passage states the specific claim the reasoning makes about that hop. The first two are cheap string checks; the third is one short LLM call per hop, and only for hops that pass the first two. Cut the path at the first hop that fails.

```python  # examples/verify_paths.py
import re

def _mentions(text: str, name: str, aliases: list[str]) -> bool:
    return any(re.search(rf"(?<!\w){re.escape(s)}(?!\w)", text, re.I) for s in [name, *aliases])

def verify_path(index, path: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    """Check every hop: the edge exists, it has sources, and one source mentions both endpoints."""
    G, report = index.graph, []
    for u, v in zip(path, path[1:]):
        hop = {"hop": (u, v), "edge": G.has_edge(u, v), "sources": [], "supported": False}
        if hop["edge"]:
            for uid in G.edges[u, v].get("source_ids", []):
                unit = index.text_units.get(uid)
                if unit and _mentions(unit.text, u, G.nodes[u].get("aliases", [])) \
                        and _mentions(unit.text, v, G.nodes[v].get("aliases", [])):
                    hop["sources"].append(uid)
            hop["supported"] = bool(hop["sources"])
        report.append(hop)
    return report

HOP_CHECK_PROMPT = """Passage:
{passage}

Claim: {claim}

Does the passage state the claim, directly or by clear paraphrase? Answer YES or NO."""

def prune_path(llm, index, hops: list[tuple[str, str, str]]) -> dict:
    """Verify a reasoning path hop by hop and cut it at the first hop no source passage states.

    `hops` are (entity_a, claim_text, entity_b), e.g.
    ("MARLOW DYNAMICS", "Marlow Dynamics acquired Deepcast", "DEEPCAST").
    """
    verified = []
    for u, claim, v in hops:
        lexical = verify_path(index, [u, v])[0]              # cheap: edge exists and a source names both
        evidence = None
        for uid in lexical["sources"]:                        # expensive: does a source state *this* claim?
            answer = llm.complete(HOP_CHECK_PROMPT.format(passage=index.text_units[uid].text, claim=claim))
            if answer.strip().upper().startswith("YES"):
                evidence = uid
                break
        if evidence is None:
            return {"verified": verified, "failed_at": (u, claim, v), "complete": False}
        verified.append((u, claim, v, evidence))
    return {"verified": verified, "failed_at": None, "complete": True}
```

**Co-mention is not support

On the offline index, verify_path accepts the hop KESTREL LABS to MARLOW DYNAMICS because Priya Nair's profile mentions both. That passage says she came to Kestrel from Marlow; it does not say Kestrel and Marlow have any relationship of their own. If the reasoning claims “Kestrel Labs partnered with Marlow Dynamics”, only the claim-level check in prune_path catches it. The lexical stage filters; it does not verify.

### Self-consistency across paths

Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) samples several reasoning chains and returns the most common final answer. With graphs, you can make the samples meaningfully different by giving each one a different retrieved path. If three of five evidence paths lead to “Marlow Dynamics” and two to “Brightwater Capital”, the vote is 0.6 and you can report low confidence or abstain below a threshold.

```python  # examples/self_consistency.py
from collections import Counter

def self_consistent_answer(llm, question: str, path_texts: list[str], samples: int = 5) -> tuple[str, float]:
    """Ask for an answer from each evidence path separately and return the majority answer and its share."""
    votes = Counter()
    for i in range(samples):
        evidence = path_texts[i % len(path_texts)]
        reply = llm.complete(f"Evidence path:\n{evidence}\n\nQuestion: {question}\n"
                             "Answer in at most five words, or say I don't know.")
        votes[reply.strip().rstrip(".").lower()] += 1
    answer, count = votes.most_common(1)[0]
    return answer, count / samples
```

Voting helps when errors are independent. It fails when they are correlated: if an extraction error created a wrong edge that sits on most paths, most votes will repeat the error confidently. Pair voting with hop verification rather than using it as a substitute.

## When graph reasoning helps and when it hurts

Situation | Better choice | Why

Single-hop factual question (“Who is the CTO?”) | One retrieval pass | An agent loop adds calls and latency and can wander

Global sensemaking (“main themes?”) | Global search over community reports | No path answers a summary question

Multi-hop question with a clear chain (canonical 2) | RoG-style plan and ground, or Graph-CoT | The next lookup depends on the previous answer

Recurring question shapes over a typed graph | Curated metapaths or Text2Cypher | Deterministic, cheap, reviewable

High-stakes answers, LLM-built graph | Any method plus hop verification | Faithful to the graph is not the same as faithful to the sources

Sparse or noisy graph, detailed text | Hybrid text retrieval, with the graph as a hint | Structural reasoning over missing edges finds nothing or the wrong thing

You control decoding and need zero invalid paths | Constrained decoding (GCR, DoG) | Guarantees validity by construction

The pattern across the table: graph reasoning pays off when the structure of the answer is a chain through the graph and the graph is good enough to contain that chain. When either condition fails, reasoning over the graph mainly adds cost, and sometimes adds confidence to wrong answers. Chapter 25 shows how to measure which regime you are in, and Chapter 30 extends the tool loop into full agents with memory.

#### Exercise 23.3 Core

Write unit tests for graph_cot without calling a real model. Cover: (a) a reply with no Action line is reported back and the loop continues, (b) an unknown node name produces guidance rather than an exception, (c) the step limit forces an abstention.

```python  # tests/test_graph_cot.py
from examples.graph_cot import GraphTools, graph_cot

class ScriptedLLM:
    """Returns canned replies in order and records every prompt it saw."""
    def __init__(self, replies):
        self.replies, self.prompts = list(replies), []

    def complete(self, prompt, system=None, json=False):
        self.prompts.append(prompt)
        return self.replies.pop(0)

def test_malformed_action_is_reported_and_loop_continues(index):
    llm = ScriptedLLM(["I think it is Marlow.",                                   # no Action line
                       "Thought: finish properly\nAction: Finish[Marlow Dynamics]"])
    out = graph_cot(llm, GraphTools(index), "Who acquired Deepcast?")
    assert out["answer"] == "Marlow Dynamics" and out["steps"] == 2
    assert "No valid Action line" in llm.prompts[1]                               # the model was told

def test_unknown_node_returns_guidance_not_exception(index):
    llm = ScriptedLLM(["Thought: check\nAction: NeighborCheck[DEEPCAST CORP, ALL]",
                       "Thought: give up\nAction: Finish[I don't know]"])
    out = graph_cot(llm, GraphTools(index), "Who owns Deepcast Corp?")
    assert "Use RetrieveNode first" in out["trace"][0][2]
    assert out["answer"] == "I don't know"

def test_step_limit_forces_abstention(index):
    llm = ScriptedLLM(["Thought: look\nAction: NodeDegree[KESTREL LABS, ALL]"] * 3)
    out = graph_cot(llm, GraphTools(index), "Loop forever", max_steps=3)
    assert out["answer"].startswith("I don't know") and len(out["trace"]) == 3
```
