## Cost, latency and scale

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/26-cost-scaling.html
Summary: Where indexing cost goes, LazyGraphRAG, FastGraphRAG, caching, batching and small extractor models.

# Cost, latency and scale

GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time, and that work is paid in LLM calls. In this chapter you build a cost model you can run before you index anything, then learn the levers that cut indexing and query cost without quietly wrecking quality.

## You will be able to

- Break indexing cost into extraction, gleaning, claims, summarization, reports and embeddings, and estimate each from corpus size and settings

- Estimate calls, tokens and latency per query for basic, local, global and DRIFT search

- Explain how LazyGraphRAG, FastGraphRAG, fast-graphrag and LightRAG reduce or defer LLM use, and what each gives up

- Decide when a small or distilled extractor model is good enough, and how to prove it

- Apply response caching, prompt-prefix caching, concurrency and rate limiting to an indexing run

## Where indexing cost goes

Vector RAG has one indexing cost that grows with the corpus: embeddings. GraphRAG adds LLM calls at almost every stage you built in Part 2. Before you optimize anything, count them. The pipeline in minigraphrag/indexer.py makes these calls:

Stage | Chapter | LLM calls | What drives the count

Entity and relationship extraction | 8 | 1 per text unit | Corpus size divided by chunk stride

Gleaning | 8 | Up to 2g − 1 extra per text unit | max_gleanings g; transcript grows each round

Claim extraction | 10 | 1 per text unit (if enabled) | IndexConfig.extract_claims

Description summarization | 9 | 1 per entity or relationship with several descriptions | How often things are mentioned more than once

Community reports | 12 | 1 per community with 2 or more nodes, at every level | Graph size and max_cluster_size

Embeddings | 13 | Not LLM calls; batched embedding requests | Tokens in text units, descriptions and reports

You can see the real counts on the Kestrel corpus right now, for free, by wrapping MockLLM in a counter that routes each prompt by the same markers MockLLM uses. With the default IndexConfig (300-word chunks, 50-word overlap, one gleaning round, claims on), the 12 documents become 24 text units and the run makes 122 LLM calls: 24 extraction, 24 gleaning continuations, 24 claim extractions, 46 summaries and 4 community reports. Set max_gleanings=0 and it drops to 84. The summary count is specific to what MockLLM extracts, but the shape is general: the per-chunk stages dominate the count, and every setting that multiplies per-chunk work multiplies the bill. Exercise 26.3 walks through the measurement.

### A cost model you can run before indexing

Let T be corpus tokens, c the chunk size and o the overlap, all in tokens. The number of text units is

N = ⌈(T − o) / (c − o)⌉

Extraction with g gleaning rounds mirrors extract_from_unit: one extraction call, then for each round a continue call, and a yes/no loop check after every round except the last. The upper bound on calls per chunk is therefore 1 + g + max(g − 1, 0), which is 1 when g = 0 and 2g otherwise. It is an upper bound because the loop stops early when the model answers N.

Calls are not the whole story, because each gleaning call re-sends the whole transcript. With a fixed prompt template of P tokens and a first-pass output of r·c tokens, the input of the first continuation call is already P + c + r·c plus the continue instruction. Cost per stage s is then

costs = (Is · pin + Os · pout) / 106

where Is and Os are total input and output tokens for the stage and the prices are per million tokens. Total indexing cost is the sum over stages plus embedding tokens times the embedding price. Summaries and reports scale with how much content the corpus has, not with chunk size, so the model estimates them per thousand corpus tokens.

[Diagram]

One chunk, two gleaning rounds, four calls and 9,641 input tokens, against 2,100 with no gleaning. Bar widths are to scale under the assumptions in the worked estimate below. The template and chunk repeat in every call, which is why putting variable text last (Chapter 8) matters for prompt caching.

### A worked estimate for a 1M-token corpus

Take a corpus of one million tokens, roughly a few thousand pages of reports and articles, and these stated assumptions. Change any of them and the arithmetic below changes with it; that is the point of writing them down.

- Chunks of 600 tokens with 100 overlap, one gleaning round, claims off.

- Extraction template of 1,500 tokens. Production prompts with several worked examples are often in the 1,000 to 2,000 range; measure yours with count_tokens. The minigraphrag template has no worked examples and comes to about 330 tokens by the word-count estimate.

- First-pass output is 0.4 × chunk tokens (240), each gleaning round outputs half that (120), the continue instruction is 50 tokens.

- Two summarization calls per thousand corpus tokens, at 500 tokens in and 150 out (summarize_max_tokens = 150).

- 0.2 community reports per thousand corpus tokens, at 3,000 tokens in (under report_max_tokens = 4,000) and 800 out.

- Prices are parameters. For the arithmetic we use placeholder prices of 1.00 per million input tokens, 4.00 per million output tokens and 0.02 per million embedding tokens, in some currency unit. They are not any provider's real prices; substitute your own.

Chunks: ⌈(1,000,000 − 100) / 500⌉ = 2,000. Per chunk, the extraction call reads 1,500 + 600 = 2,100 tokens and writes 240; the continuation reads 2,100 + 240 + 50 = 2,390 and writes 120. That is 4,490 in and 360 out per chunk, so 8.98M in and 0.72M out across the corpus.

Stage | Calls | Input tokens | Output tokens | Cost (placeholder prices) | Share

Extraction + 1 gleaning | 4,000 | 8,980,000 | 720,000 | 8.98 + 2.88 = 11.86 | 77%

Summaries | 2,000 | 1,000,000 | 300,000 | 1.00 + 1.20 = 2.20 | 14%

Community reports | 200 | 600,000 | 160,000 | 0.60 + 0.64 = 1.24 | 8%

Embeddings | n/a | 1,660,000 | n/a | 0.03 | under 1%

Total | 6,200 | 10,580,000 | 1,180,000 | 15.33 |

The embedding tokens are the 2,000 chunks at 600 tokens each (1.2M) plus summarized descriptions (0.3M) and reports (0.16M). Three things stand out. Extraction is about three quarters of the bill. Output tokens are a small fraction of the volume but, at a typical output-to-input price ratio, a large fraction of the cost. And embeddings are a rounding error next to the LLM stages.

Now vary one knob at a time. Two gleaning rounds raise extraction to 8,000 calls and 19.28M input tokens, and the total to 26.60: gleaning is the most expensive single setting in the pipeline. Halving the chunk size to 300 tokens gives 5,000 chunks and a total of 25.93, while 1,200-token chunks give 909 chunks and 11.48. Turning claims on (1,000-token template, output 0.2 × chunk) adds 2,000 calls and 4.16. None of these numbers say which setting is right; smaller chunks and gleaning buy recall, and Chapter 25 is how you find out whether you needed it.

**Microsoft GraphRAG documentation, Indexing methods

The GraphRAG docs describe graph extraction as roughly 75% of indexing cost, which is why their cheaper FastGraphRAG method replaces exactly that stage with NLP. The worked estimate above lands in the same place from first principles: under our assumptions extraction is 77% of the bill.

### Play with the model

The calculator runs the same model. Drag corpus size and chunk size, add gleaning rounds, and set your own prices. The method switch shows a FastGraphRAG-style index, where extraction and summarization use no LLM and only community reports do. The cache slider models a re-run where a fraction of calls hit a response cache.

[Interactive figure: Indexing cost calculator — Prices are placeholders; set your own (ch26-cost)]

Things to try: set gleanings to 3 and watch extraction input tokens grow faster than calls; drop chunk size to 200 and see the call count jump; switch to NLP extraction and notice that the bill is now dominated by reports, which is where FastGraphRAG still spends its LLM budget.

### The estimator in code

Put the model in code so a cost estimate is one function call away whenever someone proposes indexing a new corpus. This teaching module is not part of the minigraphrag package as shipped; add it yourself.

```python  # minigraphrag/cost.py
"""Back-of-envelope cost model for a GraphRAG index. Every number is an assumption you can override."""
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Prices:
    """Per 1M tokens. PLACEHOLDERS, not real prices: copy yours from your provider's price sheet."""
    input_per_m: float = 1.00
    output_per_m: float = 4.00
    embed_per_m: float = 0.02


@dataclass
class Assumptions:
    extraction_prompt_tokens: int = 1500   # template + worked examples
    continue_prompt_tokens: int = 50       # GLEANING_CONTINUE_PROMPT
    loop_check_prompt_tokens: int = 40     # GLEANING_LOOP_CHECK_PROMPT
    output_ratio: float = 0.4              # first-pass output tokens / chunk tokens
    gleaning_output_ratio: float = 0.5     # each gleaning round / first-pass output
    claims_prompt_tokens: int = 1000
    claims_output_ratio: float = 0.2
    summaries_per_1k_tokens: float = 2.0   # entities + relationships needing a summary
    summary_input_tokens: int = 500
    summary_output_tokens: int = 150       # IndexConfig.summarize_max_tokens
    reports_per_1k_tokens: float = 0.2     # communities at all levels
    report_input_tokens: int = 3000        # capped by IndexConfig.report_max_tokens
    report_output_tokens: int = 800


@dataclass
class Stage:
    calls: float = 0
    input_tokens: float = 0
    output_tokens: float = 0

    def cost(self, p: Prices) -> float:
        return (self.input_tokens * p.input_per_m + self.output_tokens * p.output_per_m) / 1e6

    def times(self, n: float) -> "Stage":
        return Stage(self.calls * n, self.input_tokens * n, self.output_tokens * n)


def n_chunks(corpus_tokens: int, chunk_size: int, overlap: int) -> int:
    return max(1, math.ceil((corpus_tokens - overlap) / (chunk_size - overlap)))


def extraction_per_chunk(chunk_size: int, max_gleanings: int, a: Assumptions) -> Stage:
    """Mirror extract_from_unit. Upper bound: assumes the loop check always answers Y."""
    first = a.output_ratio * chunk_size
    transcript = a.extraction_prompt_tokens + chunk_size
    s = Stage(1, transcript, first)
    transcript += first
    for i in range(max_gleanings):
        transcript += a.continue_prompt_tokens
        more = a.gleaning_output_ratio * first
        s.calls += 1; s.input_tokens += transcript; s.output_tokens += more
        transcript += more
        if i == max_gleanings - 1:
            break                                  # no loop check after the last round
        s.calls += 1; s.input_tokens += transcript + a.loop_check_prompt_tokens; s.output_tokens += 1
        transcript += a.loop_check_prompt_tokens + 1
    return s


def estimate_index_cost(corpus_tokens: int, chunk_size: int = 600, overlap: int = 100,
                        max_gleanings: int = 1, extract_claims: bool = False,
                        prices: Prices | None = None, a: Assumptions | None = None) -> dict:
    prices, a = prices or Prices(), a or Assumptions()
    n = n_chunks(corpus_tokens, chunk_size, overlap)
    k = corpus_tokens / 1000
    stages = {"extraction": extraction_per_chunk(chunk_size, max_gleanings, a).times(n)}
    if extract_claims:
        per = Stage(1, a.claims_prompt_tokens + chunk_size, a.claims_output_ratio * chunk_size)
        stages["claims"] = per.times(n)
    stages["summaries"] = Stage(1, a.summary_input_tokens, a.summary_output_tokens).times(
        round(k * a.summaries_per_1k_tokens))
    stages["reports"] = Stage(1, a.report_input_tokens, a.report_output_tokens).times(
        round(k * a.reports_per_1k_tokens))
    embed_tokens = n * chunk_size + stages["summaries"].output_tokens + stages["reports"].output_tokens
    rows = {name: {"calls": round(s.calls), "input": round(s.input_tokens),
                   "output": round(s.output_tokens), "cost": round(s.cost(prices), 2)}
            for name, s in stages.items()}
    rows["embeddings"] = {"tokens": round(embed_tokens), "cost": round(embed_tokens * prices.embed_per_m / 1e6, 2)}
    return {"chunks": n, "stages": rows, "total": round(sum(r["cost"] for r in rows.values()), 2)}


# estimate_index_cost(1_000_000)["total"]  -> 15.33 with the placeholder prices
```

### What the model leaves out

A spreadsheet estimate is a floor, not a forecast. Real runs add:

- Failures and retries. Rate-limit errors, timeouts and unparseable outputs are re-sent. Budget a few percent, and log retries so you know the real figure.

- Prompt tuning and experiments. You will index a sample many times while tuning prompts and chunk sizes. Those runs often cost more than the final full index.

- Re-indexing. A full rebuild after every document change repeats the whole bill. Chapter 27 shows how to pay only for what changed.

- Reasoning tokens. Models that think before answering bill hidden output tokens, which can multiply the output column for extraction.
**Sanchez and Dehnad, The Commercial Tax (2026)

This audit of multi-hop retrieval benchmarks points out that published results rarely report what systems cost to build. The authors report that three of the five systems they audited did not disclose indexing cost, and that published GraphRAG indexing-cost estimates for the same corpus varied by about 11 times. They model embedding, graph construction and question answering separately, and find embedding far cheaper than the downstream stages. They also distinguish API embedders, which charge on every re-index, from self-hosted ones. Report your own index cost next to your quality numbers.

## Query cost and latency by mode

Indexing is paid once per corpus version. Queries are paid forever, and latency is felt by every user. The search modes from Part 3 differ by more than an order of magnitude.

### Calls per query

Using the minigraphrag defaults and the same placeholder prices, with a 400-token system prompt and 500-token answers:

Mode | LLM calls | Input tokens | Output tokens | Cost per query | Latency shape

Basic (basic_search, 4,000-token context) | 1 | 4,400 | 500 | 0.0064 | One generation

Local (local_search, 8,000-token context) | 1 | 8,400 | 500 | 0.0104 | One generation; retrieval is in-memory

LightRAG or HippoRAG style | 2 | about 6,700 | about 560 | about 0.009 | Keyword or entity call, then generation

DRIFT (3 follow-ups) | 5 | 31,900 | 2,700 | 0.043 | Primer, parallel local searches, reduce

Global, static map-reduce | 41 | 142,400 | 12,800 | 0.19 | Parallel map calls, then reduce

The global row assumes 150 reports at the chosen level, 800 tokens each, packed into 3,000-token batches (global_search's default max_context_tokens). The map stage needs ⌈150 × 800 / 3,000⌉ = 40 calls, each reading 3,400 tokens and writing about 300; the reduce call reads the surviving half of the points. Global search costs about 30 times a basic query and nearly 20 times a local one here, and its cost grows with the number of reports, which grows with the corpus. Local search cost does not.

### Latency budgets for global search

Map calls are independent, so you run them in parallel. With M map calls, concurrency C, a typical map call time tmap and a reduce time treduce, wall-clock time is roughly

L ≈ ⌈M / C⌉ · tmap + treduce

The slowest call in each wave sets the pace, so use a high percentile for tmap, not the mean.

[Diagram]

Global search latency with 40 map calls at 5 s each and a 12 s reduce (illustrative timings; the sequential bar is not to scale). Concurrency collapses the map stage, but the reduce call is a floor you can only lower with a faster model, shorter inputs or streaming.

If an interactive product needs answers in a few seconds, static global search over a large corpus will not fit, however parallel. The options, roughly in order of how much they change the system:

- Search a coarser level. Higher-level reports are fewer, so M shrinks. You lose detail on specific questions.

- Dynamic community selection. global_search(..., dynamic=True) rates reports top-down and skips subtrees of irrelevant ones (Chapter 15). Rating calls are cheap per call but add a sequential phase per level.

- Stream the reduce. The user sees text as soon as the reduce starts. Time to first token matters more than total time for perceived latency.

- Route queries. Most questions are not global. A cheap classifier that sends "Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?" to local search and only "What are the main themes?" to global search changes average cost far more than any micro-optimization.

- Precompute. For a known set of dashboard-style sensemaking questions, run global search at indexing time and cache the answer until the index changes.

- Defer differently. DRIFT and LazyGraphRAG spend a bounded budget per query instead of touching every report.

## Cheaper graphs: defer or replace the LLM

If extraction is three quarters of the cost, the big wins come from not running an LLM over every chunk. There are two broad strategies: replace LLM extraction with cheaper NLP, or defer LLM work until a query tells you which part of the corpus matters.

### LazyGraphRAG: defer everything to query time

Microsoft Research described LazyGraphRAG in a November 2024 blog post. Its index uses no LLM at all. It extracts noun phrases as concepts, links concepts that co-occur, and uses graph statistics to optimize the concept graph and find a hierarchical community structure. The blog puts indexing cost at the same level as vector RAG and 0.1% of full GraphRAG's. All LLM use happens at query time, and one parameter, the relevance test budget, controls how much.

[Interactive figure: LazyGraphRAG: indexing without an LLM, spending a budget at query time (flow)]

The blog reports that at 4% of the query cost of GraphRAG global search, LazyGraphRAG significantly outperformed the competing methods on its test of 100 synthetic queries (50 local, 50 global) over 5,590 AP news articles, and that comparable quality came at more than 700 times lower query cost than global search. Treat these as one team's evaluation on one dataset. The durable lesson is structural: when most of the corpus is never relevant to any question, paying an LLM to summarize all of it up front is waste.

The price is paid elsewhere. There are no entity descriptions or community reports to browse, and query latency now includes relevance testing. If you need a navigable, curated graph (for analysts, for Text2Cypher, for audit), a lazy index is not a substitute.

### FastGraphRAG: NLP extraction inside Microsoft GraphRAG

Microsoft GraphRAG ships two indexing methods, chosen with graphrag index --method standard (the default) or --method fast. In FastGraphRAG, entities are noun phrases extracted with NLP libraries such as NLTK or spaCy and have no descriptions; relationships are defined by two noun phrases co-occurring in a text unit. The LLM is used only for community reports, which are written from the text units that contain each community's noun phrases. The docs are candid about the trade-off: the graph is noisier and less directly relevant, so FastGraphRAG fits summary questions answered by global search, while the standard method fits when you need high-fidelity entities and graph exploration. They also recommend much smaller text units for the fast method, 50 to 100 tokens, so that co-occurrence within a unit means something; with 600-token units almost every noun phrase co-occurs with every other. You will run both in Chapter 28.

On Kestrel, a noun-phrase extractor would happily produce nodes like "sonar module", "outside contracts" and "quarterly reef monitoring". Some are useful concepts; many are noise. Co-occurrence edges between "Marlow Dynamics" and "Deepcast" would appear, but with no description saying acquired. Question 1 ("Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?") depends on exactly that relation label, which is why fast indexing hurts local, multi-hop questions more than global ones.

### fast-graphrag, LightRAG and schema-constrained graphs

fast-graphrag (circlemind-ai) is a separate open-source project, not the Microsoft method with a similar name. It still uses an LLM to extract a graph, steered by a domain description, example queries and entity types you supply, but it skips community reports and answers queries with PageRank-based graph exploration, the Personalized PageRank you built in Chapter 17. Its README claims a large cost saving over Microsoft GraphRAG on a sample book; that is a vendor benchmark, useful as a direction rather than a number to plan with.

LightRAG (Chapter 16) also drops community reports. Its dual-level retrieval matches keywords against entity and relationship descriptions, so there is no report stage to pay for, and new documents are merged in by taking the union of the new and existing node and edge sets instead of re-clustering. You give up the global sensemaking answers that reports make possible.

Two 2026 papers push on what goes into the graph rather than how it is built:

- HCG-RAG builds schema-constrained causal graphs instead of extracting every entity and relationship. The authors report 3 to 20 times fewer nodes and 8 to 135 times fewer build-time LLM calls than the most LLM-intensive baseline, while matching or beating entity-relation systems on medical and clinical benchmarks. Their summary: what is placed in the graph matters more than how many nodes it has.

- LiteRAG attacks query cost. It replaces LLM-controlled retrieval with query-conditioned algorithmic exploration and reasoning-chain context construction. The abstract reports over 100 times lower latency and over 99% lower cost than GraphRAG Global and DRIFT on one benchmark, with ablations crediting query-adaptive thresholding and community-aware hub penalization.

Approach | LLM at indexing | LLM at query | Community reports | What you give up

Standard GraphRAG | Extraction, gleaning, summaries, reports | 1 call (local) to many (global) | Yes | Money and indexing time

FastGraphRAG (Microsoft) | Reports only | Same as standard | Yes, from raw text units | Entity descriptions, typed relations; noisier graph

LazyGraphRAG | None | Query refinement, relevance tests, claim extraction | No | A browsable graph; per-query latency

LightRAG | Extraction and profiling | Keyword extraction, answer | No | Corpus-wide sensemaking via reports

fast-graphrag | Guided extraction | Answer; retrieval via PageRank | No | Reports; relies on good domain hints

Schema-constrained (HCG-RAG) | Fewer, targeted calls | Answer | Depends on design | Anything outside the schema

## Smaller extractor models and distillation

The other way to cut extraction cost is to keep the stage and use a cheaper model. Extraction is a narrow, repetitive task with a fixed format and a fixed type list, which is exactly the kind of task where a small model can approach a large one.

**Komarov et al., RAGU (2026)

RAGU separates extraction from consolidation: two-stage typed extraction, DBSCAN-backed deduplication, LLM summarization and Leiden communities. The authors argue that the skills an in-pipeline LLM needs are language skills that grow only weakly with model size, and train Meno-Lite-0.1, a 7-billion-parameter model that they report outperforms Qwen2.5-32B on knowledge-graph construction. The system runs on a single GPU.

### A distillation recipe

- Label with a teacher. Run your best model over a few thousand representative chunks with your production prompt. Keep the raw outputs; you are building a supervised dataset of chunk to records.

- Clean the labels. Parse with parse_extraction_output, drop malformed records, normalize types. The student learns your format exactly as the parser wants it.

- Fine-tune a student. A 1B to 8B open model with parameter-efficient fine-tuning is typical. Train on the prompt and the teacher's output.

- Evaluate against gold, not the teacher. Hand-label a small set of Kestrel-style chunks and measure entity and relationship precision and recall for teacher and student (Chapter 25). Then run end-to-end question answering on both indexes. A student that loses a few points of relationship recall may lose nothing on your questions, or may lose the one edge question 1 needs.

- Cascade. Use the student by default and escalate a chunk to the teacher when parsing fails, when it yields suspiciously few records for its length, or when it contains entity types the student handles poorly.

Self-hosting changes the cost shape rather than removing it. Instead of paying per token you pay for GPU hours, which rewards batching and high utilization, and makes a one-off 10M-token index cheap while a trickle of small updates may cost more per token than an API.

## Engineering levers: caching, batching, concurrency, rate limits

These levers do not change what the pipeline computes. They change how many times you pay for it and how long you wait.

### Response caching with CachedLLM

You will re-run indexing many times: after a parser fix, a resolution threshold change, a new community algorithm. None of those change the extraction prompts, so none should pay for extraction again. CachedLLM in minigraphrag/llm.py wraps any LLM and stores each response on disk under the SHA-256 hash of the model name, system prompt, prompt and JSON flag.

```python  # examples/cached_index.py
from minigraphrag.llm import CachedLLM, MockLLM, get_llm
from minigraphrag.indexer import IndexConfig, build_index

# Explicit wrapping: works with any object that has complete(prompt, system=None, json=False).
llm = CachedLLM(MockLLM(), cache_dir=".cache/llm")
build_index("data/corpus", "out/run1", llm, config=IndexConfig(max_gleanings=1))
print(llm.hits, llm.misses)        # 0 122 : a cold cache pays for every call

# Change something downstream of extraction and re-run with a fresh wrapper on the same cache.
llm = CachedLLM(MockLLM(), cache_dir=".cache/llm")
build_index("data/corpus", "out/run2", llm, config=IndexConfig(max_gleanings=1, max_cluster_size=6))
print(llm.hits, llm.misses)        # 122 2 : smaller clusters add 2 communities; only their reports miss

# The factory does the same wrapping from a short name.
llm = get_llm("openai", cache_dir=".cache/llm")
```

The first run's 0 hits and 122 misses are what you will see on the Kestrel corpus with MockLLM; an identical second run gives 122 hits and 0 misses. In the second run, smaller clusters split the graph into 6 communities instead of 4: every earlier call hits, and only the 2 new communities' reports are paid for. Three properties make the cache safe:

- The key is the full input. Edit a prompt template and every key changes, so stale outputs are never served. The flip side: a one-character prompt edit invalidates the whole cache for that stage.

- The key includes the model name. Switching models does not return another model's answers.

- Determinism. Use temperature 0 where your provider allows it. A cache over a sampled model is still correct, but it freezes one sample, which can hide how unstable an extraction is.

Microsoft GraphRAG has the same idea built in: an LLM cache configured in the settings file that graphrag init generates, and a --cache / --no-cache switch on graphrag index and graphrag update.

### Prompt-prefix caching

Response caching helps when the whole input repeats. Provider-side prompt caching helps when only the beginning repeats. Many hosted LLM APIs can store the processed state of a long, identical prefix and bill later requests that reuse it at a reduced input rate, often with lower latency; some do this automatically, others need an explicit cache marker. Extraction is a near-perfect fit: a 1,500-token template followed by a 600-token chunk. In the gleaning diagram above, the template is identical across every call for every chunk, and the template plus chunk is identical across the four calls for one chunk.

To benefit, keep the fixed part first and byte-identical: no timestamps, request ids or shuffled examples in the template, and the chunk text last. Check your provider's minimum cacheable length, cache lifetime and pricing, and model the discount as a lower effective pin for the cached share of input tokens.

### Batching and concurrency

Extraction calls for different chunks are independent, so indexing is embarrassingly parallel up to your rate limits. Three kinds of batching are worth separating:

- Embedding batches. Send many texts per embedding request. Embedder.embed already takes a list.

- Concurrent LLM calls. Run many independent requests at once. This cuts wall-clock time, not cost.

- Provider batch APIs. Several providers accept a file of requests, process it asynchronously within a time window, and bill at a discount. Indexing rarely needs answers in seconds, so this is often the cheapest way to build a large index. Gleaning complicates it, because round two depends on round one: submit one batch per round.

### Rate limits set your floor on indexing time

Providers limit requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM). Whichever binds first sets the minimum wall-clock time:

timemin ≈ max(total tokens / TPM, total calls / RPM)

For the 1M-token worked estimate: 10.58M input plus 1.18M output is 11.76M tokens over 6,200 calls. At a TPM limit of 200,000 that is at least 11,760,000 / 200,000 ≈ 59 minutes, whatever your concurrency; the RPM limit would bind only below about 105 requests per minute (6,200 calls in 59 minutes). Raising concurrency past the point where you hit TPM only produces 429 errors and retries.

```python  # examples/parallel_extract.py
import random
import threading
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from minigraphrag.extraction import extract_from_unit
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens


class TokenBucket:
    """Allow at most `per_minute` tokens per minute, refilled continuously."""

    def __init__(self, per_minute: int):
        self.capacity = self.level = per_minute
        self.rate = per_minute / 60.0
        self.updated = time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def take(self, n: int) -> None:
        n = min(n, self.capacity)
        while True:
            with self.lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self.level = min(self.capacity, self.level + (now - self.updated) * self.rate)
                self.updated = now
                if self.level >= n:
                    self.level -= n
                    return
                wait = (n - self.level) / self.rate
            time.sleep(wait)


class RateLimitedLLM:
    """Wrap an LLM: reserve estimated tokens before each call, retry with jittered backoff."""

    def __init__(self, llm, tpm: int, expected_output: int = 400, retries: int = 5):
        self.llm, self.bucket = llm, TokenBucket(tpm)
        self.expected_output, self.retries = expected_output, retries

    def complete(self, prompt, system=None, json=False):
        self.bucket.take(count_tokens((system or "") + prompt) + self.expected_output)
        for attempt in range(self.retries):
            try:
                return self.llm.complete(prompt, system=system, json=json)
            except Exception:                        # narrow this to your client's rate-limit error
                if attempt == self.retries - 1:
                    raise
                time.sleep(min(60, 2 ** attempt) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5))


def extract_all(llm, units, entity_types, max_gleanings=1, workers=16, tpm=200_000):
    limited = RateLimitedLLM(llm, tpm)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers) as pool:
        return list(pool.map(lambda u: extract_from_unit(limited, u, entity_types, max_gleanings), units))
```

Put the rate limiter inside the cache (CachedLLM(RateLimitedLLM(real_llm, tpm))) so cache hits do not consume token budget. Order the rest of build_index the same way: extraction for all chunks in parallel, then resolution and graph building (no LLM), then summaries in parallel, then reports level by level, since a parent report may use its children's reports.

### Embedding cost

In the worked estimate, embeddings are 0.03 of 15.33. That matches the finding in The Commercial Tax that embedding is far cheaper than graph construction and answering. Embedding decisions still matter for scale in two other ways: a self-hosted embedder costs nothing per re-index, which matters if you rebuild often; and vector dimensionality drives storage and search memory across entities, relationships, text units and reports (Chapter 13). Do not let embedding price drive the choice; let retrieval quality on your evaluation set drive it.

## Choosing levers without losing quality

Every lever in this chapter trades something. The table puts them side by side with the check that tells you whether the trade was acceptable.

Lever | Typical saving | Quality risk | How to check

Fewer gleaning rounds | Large on extraction input tokens | Lower entity recall, especially late in long chunks | Entity recall against a gold set (Chapter 25)

Larger chunks | Fewer extraction calls | Fewer entity references per token | Same, plus multi-hop answer accuracy

Claims off | One call per chunk | Weaker temporal and claim-based answers | Temporal question slice (questions 6 and 7)

NLP extraction (FastGraphRAG) | Most of extraction and summary cost | Noisy nodes, no relation descriptions | Local and multi-hop slices; global slice usually holds up better

Deferred LLM (LazyGraphRAG) | Nearly all indexing cost | Query latency, no browsable graph | Per-query cost and latency at your target budget

Small or distilled extractor | Per-token price or GPU hours | Missed or mistyped relations | Extraction precision and recall, then end-to-end QA

Response cache | All repeated calls | None if keys include the full input | Hit rate on re-runs

Prompt-prefix cache | Discount on repeated prefix tokens | None | Cached-token counts in provider usage data

Query routing | Avoids global search for most questions | Misrouted global questions get thin answers | Router accuracy per question type

**Always report cost next to quality

Put indexing cost, cost per query and p95 latency in the same table as your answer metrics. A method that wins by two points at ten times the cost is a different decision from one that wins at the same cost, and a comparison that hides cost is not a fair comparison.

## Exercises

#### Exercise 26.1 Warm-up

By hand, estimate extraction calls and tokens for a 250,000-token corpus with 1,200-token chunks, 200-token overlap and max_gleanings=2. Use the chapter's assumptions (1,500-token template, output 0.4 × chunk, gleaning output half of that, 50-token continue prompt, 40-token loop check with a 1-token answer). Express the extraction cost in terms of pin and pout, then evaluate it with the placeholder prices.

▸ Hint

Write out the four calls for one chunk and the transcript length before each, as in the gleaning diagram, then multiply by the number of chunks.

▸ Show answer

Chunks: ⌈(250,000 − 200) / 1,000⌉ = ⌈249.8⌉ = 250.

One chunk: first output 0.4 × 1,200 = 480; each gleaning output 240.

- Extract: input 1,500 + 1,200 = 2,700; output 480. Transcript is now 3,180.

- Continue 1: input 3,180 + 50 = 3,230; output 240. Transcript 3,470.

- Loop check: input 3,470 + 40 = 3,510; output 1. Transcript 3,511.

- Continue 2: input 3,511 + 50 = 3,561; output 240. No loop check after the last round.

Per chunk: 4 calls, 2,700 + 3,230 + 3,510 + 3,561 = 13,001 input tokens, 480 + 240 + 1 + 240 = 961 output tokens.

Corpus: 1,000 calls, 3,250,250 input tokens, 240,250 output tokens. Cost = 3.25025 · pin + 0.24025 · pout. With the placeholders (1.00 and 4.00): 3.25 + 0.96 = 4.21. estimate_index_cost(250_000, 1200, 200, 2) returns the same 4.21 for extraction. The calls are an upper bound: if the model answers N at the loop check, the fourth call never happens and per-chunk input drops to 2,700 + 3,230 + 3,510 = 9,440.

#### Exercise 26.2 Core

A product team wants global search answers within 15 seconds. The index has 300 reports at the chosen level averaging 600 tokens, map batches hold 4,000 tokens of reports, p95 map latency is 4 s and reduce latency is 10 s. Your provider allows 16 concurrent requests and a TPM of 150,000. (a) What is the latency at concurrency 16? (b) Is concurrency alone enough to meet the budget? (c) Propose two changes that would, and estimate their effect.

▸ Show answer

(a) Map calls: ⌈300 × 600 / 4,000⌉ = ⌈45⌉ = 45. Waves at concurrency 16: ⌈45/16⌉ = 3. Latency ≈ 3 × 4 + 10 = 22 s.

(b) To reach 15 s the map stage must fit in 5 s, which means one wave: concurrency 45. Each map call reads about 4,000 + 400 = 4,400 tokens, so one wave is about 198,000 input tokens in a few seconds. That exceeds the TPM limit of 150,000 before counting outputs, and the provider allows only 16 concurrent requests. Concurrency alone cannot do it.

(c) Options, with estimates:

- Search one level up. If the parent level has 60 reports of 800 tokens: ⌈48,000 / 4,000⌉ = 12 map calls, one wave at concurrency 16, about 12 × 4,400 = 52,800 tokens. Latency ≈ 4 + 10 = 14 s. Specific questions lose detail.

- Dynamic community selection. If rating prunes to 40 relevant reports, map calls drop to ⌈24,000 / 4,000⌉ = 6, but the rating phase adds sequential levels of rating calls; with a fast small rater and parallel rating within a level it can fit, but measure it.

- Stream the reduce. Does not change the 22 s total, but first tokens arrive after about 12 s, which may satisfy the real requirement if it is about perceived responsiveness.

- Route and precompute. Send non-global questions to local search (one call, a few seconds), and precompute answers to the handful of recurring global questions ("What are the main themes?") at indexing time.

#### Exercise 26.3 Core

Write a wrapper that counts LLM calls and input tokens per task (extraction, continue, loop check, claims, summarize, report) and run build_index on the Kestrel corpus with MockLLM for max_gleanings of 0, 1 and 2. Then run it twice through a CachedLLM sharing one cache directory. Explain every difference in the counts.

▸ Hint

minigraphrag.prompts.MARKERS maps each task name to a phrase found in its prompt, in an order that checks gleaning prompts before the extraction prompt they contain.

▸ Show answer

```python
import collections, tempfile
from minigraphrag import prompts as P
from minigraphrag.indexer import IndexConfig, build_index
from minigraphrag.llm import CachedLLM, MockLLM
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

class TaskCounter:
    def __init__(self, llm):
        self.llm = llm
        self.calls, self.tokens = collections.Counter(), collections.Counter()

    def complete(self, prompt, system=None, json=False):
        full = f"{system or ''}\n{prompt}"
        task = next((t for t, marker in P.MARKERS.items() if marker in full), "other")
        self.calls[task] += 1
        self.tokens[task] += count_tokens(full)
        return self.llm.complete(prompt, system=system, json=json)

for g in (0, 1, 2):
    llm = TaskCounter(MockLLM())
    index = build_index("data/corpus", tempfile.mkdtemp(), llm, config=IndexConfig(max_gleanings=g))
    print(g, dict(llm.calls), sum(llm.calls.values()),
          index.graph.number_of_nodes(), index.graph.number_of_edges())

cache = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for run in (1, 2):
    llm = CachedLLM(MockLLM(), cache)
    build_index("data/corpus", tempfile.mkdtemp(), llm)
    print("run", run, "hits", llm.hits, "misses", llm.misses)
```

Output on the current corpus and MockLLM:

max_gleanings | extraction | continue | loop_check | claims | summarize | report | total | nodes / edges

0 | 24 | 0 | 0 | 24 | 32 | 4 | 84 | 17 / 33

1 | 24 | 24 | 0 | 24 | 46 | 4 | 122 | 17 / 54

2 | 24 | 24 | 24 | 24 | 46 | 4 | 146 | 17 / 54

Explanations. There are 24 text units, so extraction and claims are 24 each at every setting. One gleaning round adds one continue call per chunk. MockLLM deliberately omits weak relationships on the first pass and adds them when asked to continue, so edges rise from 33 to 54, and more edges now have several descriptions, which raises summarize calls from 32 to 46. With two rounds, the loop check runs after round one; MockLLM has nothing left to add and answers N, so the second continue call never happens: 24 extra loop checks, no extra continues, and an identical graph. That is the upper bound of 2g calls per chunk not being reached. The cached runs print 0 hits and 122 misses, then 122 hits and 0 misses: identical prompts produce identical keys. Token counts depend on whether tiktoken is installed, since count_tokens falls back to an estimate of 4 tokens per 3 words.

#### Exercise 26.4 Core

Choose an indexing strategy (standard GraphRAG, FastGraphRAG-style, LazyGraphRAG-style, or LightRAG-style) for each workload and justify it in terms of cost shape and question types. (a) An analyst team asks a few dozen open-ended questions a month over 20M tokens of news. (b) A support bot answers thousands of specific questions a day about 300K tokens of product docs that change weekly. (c) A due-diligence tool must show a browsable, cited graph of companies, people and deals, like the Kestrel graph, for a fixed 2M-token data room.

▸ Show answer

(a) LazyGraphRAG-style, or FastGraphRAG with global search. Standard indexing of 20M tokens is about 20 times the worked estimate, and almost all of it would summarize articles nobody asks about. Few queries a month means a higher per-query spend is fine. If you need reusable community reports for recurring themes, FastGraphRAG keeps those at the cost of a noisier graph, which matters less for sensemaking questions.

(b) LightRAG-style or standard local search with incremental updates. The corpus is small, so indexing cost is modest; the problem is query volume and churn. Global map-reduce per query is far too expensive at thousands a day. Specific questions suit entity- and keyword-anchored retrieval at one or two calls per query, and incremental merging (Chapter 27) avoids weekly full rebuilds.

(c) Standard GraphRAG, possibly with a schema. The graph itself is the product: typed relations like ACQUIRED and BOARD_MEMBER_OF, descriptions and provenance must be good enough to show to a person. The corpus is fixed, so indexing is paid once. A schema-constrained extractor in the spirit of HCG-RAG could cut calls and noise, since the entity and relation types are known in advance.

#### Exercise 26.5 Stretch

Extend the estimator with provider-side prompt caching. Assume the cached share of an input is billed at a fraction d of the normal input price, that only the extraction template is cached for the first call of each chunk, and that the template plus chunk plus all earlier transcript is cached for later calls of the same chunk. Compute the extraction cost for the 1M-token worked estimate with one gleaning round and d = 0.1, using the placeholder prices.

▸ Show answer

Per chunk with one gleaning round there are two calls.

- Call 1: 2,100 input tokens, of which the 1,500-token template is cached and 600 are not. Effective input tokens: 1,500 × 0.1 + 600 = 750.

- Call 2: 2,390 input tokens. The previous call's full input (2,100) is a cached prefix; the model output (240) and continue prompt (50) are new. Effective: 2,100 × 0.1 + 290 = 500.

Effective input per chunk: 1,250 instead of 4,490. Across 2,000 chunks: 2.5M effective input tokens. Output is unchanged at 0.72M. Extraction cost: 2.5 × 1.00 + 0.72 × 4.00 = 2.50 + 2.88 = 5.38, down from 11.86. Output tokens now dominate the stage, so the next lever is output length: terser descriptions or fewer gleaning records.

```python
def extraction_cost_with_prefix_cache(chunk_size, max_gleanings, prices, a, discount=0.1):
    first = a.output_ratio * chunk_size
    transcript = a.extraction_prompt_tokens + chunk_size
    effective = a.extraction_prompt_tokens * discount + chunk_size
    output = first
    cached_prefix = transcript          # the whole first input is now cached
    transcript += first
    for i in range(max_gleanings):
        transcript += a.continue_prompt_tokens
        effective += cached_prefix * discount + (transcript - cached_prefix)
        cached_prefix = transcript
        more = a.gleaning_output_ratio * first
        output += more
        transcript += more
        if i == max_gleanings - 1:
            break
        effective += cached_prefix * discount + (transcript - cached_prefix) + a.loop_check_prompt_tokens
        cached_prefix = transcript + a.loop_check_prompt_tokens
        output += 1
        transcript += a.loop_check_prompt_tokens + 1
    return (effective * prices.input_per_m + output * prices.output_per_m) / 1e6

# extraction_cost_with_prefix_cache(600, 1, Prices(), Assumptions()) * 2000  -> 5.38
```

## Check your understanding

Under typical settings, which indexing stage accounts for most of a standard GraphRAG index's LLM cost?

- Community report generation

- Embedding text units and descriptions

- ✓ (correct) Entity and relationship extraction, including gleaning

- Description summarization
Answer: Extraction runs over every chunk, and gleaning re-sends the transcript. The GraphRAG docs put graph extraction at roughly 75% of indexing cost, and the worked estimate gives 77%. Embeddings are under 1%.

Why does going from one to two gleaning rounds more than double the extraction input tokens?

- The second round uses a longer prompt template

- Each round re-chunks the document with more overlap

- Output tokens are counted twice

- ✓ (correct) Later calls re-send the template, chunk and all earlier outputs, and a loop-check call is added between rounds
Answer: With two rounds a chunk makes four calls whose inputs grow as the transcript grows: 2,100, 2,390, 2,550 and 2,601 tokens in the worked example, against 4,490 total for one round.

What does LazyGraphRAG do at indexing time?

- ✓ (correct) Extracts noun phrases and co-occurrences with NLP and builds a concept graph with hierarchical communities, without calling an LLM

- Extracts entities with a small LLM and defers only community reports

- Nothing: it builds the whole graph from scratch for each query

- Writes community reports but skips entity extraction
Answer: LazyGraphRAG defers all LLM use to query time. Its index uses NLP noun-phrase extraction and graph statistics, so indexing costs about what vector RAG costs.

In Microsoft GraphRAG's FastGraphRAG method, where is the LLM still used during indexing?

- Entity extraction only

- Relationship descriptions only

- ✓ (correct) Community report generation

- Nowhere; the LLM is only used at query time
Answer: FastGraphRAG uses NLP noun phrases as entities and text-unit co-occurrence as relationships, and keeps the LLM for community reports, written from the text units containing each entity. No LLM at indexing at all describes LazyGraphRAG.

You raise indexing concurrency from 32 to 128 workers and the run gets no faster, with many 429 errors. What is the most likely cause?

- The response cache is full

- Python threads cannot run LLM calls concurrently

- Gleaning makes calls depend on each other across chunks

- ✓ (correct) The provider's tokens-per-minute limit was already binding, so extra workers only trigger rate-limit errors and retries
Answer: Minimum wall-clock time is total tokens divided by TPM, whatever the concurrency. Threads are fine for I/O-bound API calls, and gleaning dependencies exist only within a chunk.

CachedLLM keys responses by a hash of model name, system prompt, prompt and JSON flag. You fix a typo in the community report prompt and re-index. What happens?

- All calls hit the cache, so the fix has no effect until you clear it

- ✓ (correct) Extraction, claims and summary calls hit the cache; report calls miss and are re-run with the new prompt

- Every call misses, because any prompt change invalidates the whole cache

- Report calls hit the cache because the community contents did not change
Answer: Only prompts whose text changed get new keys. That makes the cache both safe (no stale reports) and cheap (no repeated extraction).

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Should I use the cheapest model for every stage?

Stages have different failure costs. A weak extractor silently drops relations, and nothing downstream can recover an edge that was never extracted. A weak summarizer produces blander descriptions, which mostly hurts ranking. A weak report writer affects global answers directly. A common split is a mid-size or distilled model for extraction, a small model for summaries and relevance rating, and a stronger model for reports and final answers. Decide per stage with the stage metrics from Chapter 25.

▸ Are the placeholder prices in this chapter realistic?

They are chosen to make arithmetic easy and to reflect that output tokens usually cost several times more than input tokens. Real prices differ across providers and models and change often, so the estimator takes them as parameters. Plug in your provider's current numbers and your measured token counts from a small sample run.

▸ How do I get real token counts instead of assumptions?

Index a random 1% to 5% sample of the corpus with a counting wrapper like the one in Exercise 26.3, and read the usage fields your provider returns for each call. Fit the assumptions (output ratio, summaries and reports per thousand tokens) from the sample, then extrapolate. Summaries and reports grow a little slower than linearly as mentions of the same entities repeat, so a linear extrapolation is slightly pessimistic.

▸ Does GraphRAG scale to 100M tokens?

Indexing does, if you can pay for it and wait: cost and time grow roughly linearly and parallelize well. The harder limits are elsewhere. Static global search grows with the number of reports, so it needs dynamic selection, a coarser level or a lazy approach. Community detection on a graph with millions of nodes is fast, but the report stage above it is not. And a full rebuild becomes impractical, which is why incremental updates (Chapter 27) stop being optional.

▸ Is a lazy approach always better than building the full graph up front?

No. Deferring work is best when queries are few and touch a small part of the corpus. When many users ask overlapping questions, you pay the deferred work again and again, and precomputed summaries amortize better. Lazy indexing also gives you no graph to inspect, visualize, curate or query with Cypher. Compare total cost over the index's expected lifetime: indexing cost plus queries per day times cost per query times days.

Produce the document you would want before approving a GraphRAG build: what it will cost, how long it will take, and which settings buy what.

- minigraphrag/cost.py with estimate_index_cost and a query-cost function, prices passed as parameters, with unit tests for chunk and call counts

- A sample run on the Kestrel corpus (or 5% of your own) with a per-task counting wrapper, and the assumptions refitted from measured tokens

- A table of estimated cost and minimum indexing time (from your TPM limit) for your full corpus at max_gleanings 0, 1 and 2 and two chunk sizes

- Measured cost per query and p95 latency for basic, local, global and DRIFT search on the canonical questions

- A CachedLLM plus rate-limited, concurrent extraction run, with cache hit rate on a second run after changing a downstream setting

- One cost reduction you applied, with its effect on an answer-quality metric from Chapter 25

Done when your estimate for the sample run is within 25% of the measured cost, and you can state what the cheapest acceptable configuration costs and what quality it gives up.

## Key takeaways

- Extraction dominates indexing cost; gleaning and small chunks multiply it, and embeddings barely register.

- Write the cost model down with explicit assumptions and prices as parameters, then calibrate it on a sample run.

- Query cost ranges from one call (local, basic) to dozens (static global search); route queries and bound global search with levels, dynamic selection or deferred approaches.

- LazyGraphRAG defers all LLM use to query time; FastGraphRAG keeps the LLM only for reports; LightRAG and fast-graphrag skip reports. Each gives up something specific.

- Small or distilled extractors can be good enough, but prove it with extraction metrics and end-to-end answers, and cascade hard chunks to a stronger model.

- Cache responses by full-input hash, keep prompt prefixes stable for provider caching, and let TPM limits, not worker counts, set your concurrency.

## Incremental updates and temporal graphs

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/27-incremental-temporal.html
Summary: Upserts without full rebuilds, bi-temporal edges, invalidation, Graphiti and Zep.

# Incremental updates and temporal graphs

A GraphRAG index goes stale the day after you build it, and rebuilding it from scratch every time a document changes costs as much as the first build. In this chapter you make updates proportional to what changed, and you give edges a history, so the graph can say both who the CTO is now and who it was in August 2024.

## You will be able to

- Estimate what a full rebuild costs compared with an incremental update, and find the terms that do not shrink

- Detect changed documents and text units with content hashes, and retract or upsert graph elements by their source_ids

- Decide which descriptions, communities and reports to regenerate after an update, and when to recluster from scratch

- Model facts with valid time and transaction time, invalidate edges on contradiction, and answer as-of queries on both axes

- Explain how Graphiti and Zep, LightRAG and a Postgres-native engine handle updates and time, and map them onto your own code

## Why full rebuilds hurt

Everything you built in Part 2 assumed a fixed corpus: chunk it, extract from every chunk, resolve, summarize, cluster, write reports. Real corpora are not fixed. The Kestrel Labs assistant ingests a new podcast transcript, a board memo gets a correction, a press release is withdrawn. If each change triggers a full rebuild, three things go wrong.

- Cost scales with the corpus, not the change. Extraction is the dominant indexing cost (Chapter 26), and a rebuild pays it for every text unit, including the thousands that did not change.

- Output churns. LLM calls are not perfectly reproducible even at temperature 0, community detection can shuffle ids, and report text is rewritten. Users see answers change for no reason, and any cached answers or saved citations point at ids that no longer exist.

- History is lost. A rebuild produces a snapshot of the corpus as it is now. If the corpus says Priya Nair became CTO in March 2026, a naive rebuild either keeps both CTO edges with no way to tell which is current, or you delete the old one and can no longer answer “Who was CTO when the bleaching was detected?”

### A cost model for updates

Let U be the number of text units, g the number of gleaning rounds, S the number of nodes and edges that need an LLM summary (those with more than one description), and R the number of communities that get a report. With minigraphrag's gleaning loop, a unit costs e(g) extraction calls: 1 call when g = 0, and 2g calls otherwise (one extraction, g continue prompts, and g − 1 loop checks, because the last round skips the check). Then:

Cfull = U · e(g) + S + R      Cincremental = ΔU · e(g) + Sdirty + Rchanged

ΔU is the number of new or changed text units, Sdirty the summaries touched by them, and Rchanged the reports whose communities changed. On the Kestrel corpus, the reference chunker (300 words, 50 overlap) cuts each of the 12 documents into 2 units, 24 in all. Suppose the index was built from documents 01 to 11 (22 units) and the March 2026 interview, document 12, arrives. With g = 1:

Term | Full rebuild | Incremental

Extraction calls | 24 × 2 = 48 | 2 × 2 = 4

Description summaries | every multi-description node and edge | only nodes and edges that the 2 new units mention

Community reports | all communities | communities containing a touched node, plus their ancestors

Extraction shrinks by a factor of 12 here, and by far more at scale: a 100,000-unit corpus with 400 changed units a day does 250 times less extraction work. The other two terms are the trap. The interview mentions almost every main entity (Okafor, Vehl, Nair, Deepcast, Marlow Dynamics, Tern, Sentinel, Halden Reef, Tidewater, Brightwater, the Ocean Health Act), so it dirties most of the Kestrel graph. That is not a quirk of a tiny corpus. Hub entities such as the company itself appear in most new documents, so every update touches them, their descriptions and the reports of the communities they sit in. Incremental indexing makes extraction proportional to the change; making summaries and reports proportional too takes the extra policies in the rest of this chapter.

**Correctness target: an update equals a rebuild

The simplest definition of a correct incremental indexer is that applying an update to the index built from corpus A gives the same graph as a full build of corpus A′, up to LLM nondeterminism in summaries and reports. Nodes, edges, source_ids and weights are deterministic given the cached extractions, so you can test them for exact equality. You will write that test in the project.

## Detecting what changed

An update starts with a diff. You need to know which documents were added, changed or removed, and within a changed document, which text units actually differ.

### Document hashes and a manifest

Store a manifest from the last successful run: {doc_id: sha256(text)}. On the next run, hash the documents on disk and compare. Hash the normalized text you actually index, not file metadata; a modified timestamp changes when someone touches the file without editing it, and a hash does not.

### Content-addressed text units

Document-level diffs are too coarse: fixing a typo in the last paragraph of a long report should not re-extract its first forty chunks. So diff at the unit level too. That needs unit ids that stay the same when the text stays the same. The reference chunker names units by position, {doc_id}-{i:03d}, which is fine for full builds. For incremental builds, derive the id from the text instead. nano-graphrag does the same thing: it keys chunks by an MD5 hash of their content, so re-inserting identical text creates no duplicates.

```python  # minigraphrag/incremental.py
# Teaching module for this chapter: not part of the core indexer.
import hashlib
from dataclasses import replace

from .chunking import TextUnit, chunk_documents


def content_hash(text: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def diff_documents(manifest: dict[str, str], docs: dict[str, str]):
    """Compare {doc_id: hash} from the last run with the documents on disk now."""
    current = {doc_id: content_hash(text) for doc_id, text in docs.items()}
    added = sorted(d for d in current if d not in manifest)
    removed = sorted(d for d in manifest if d not in current)
    changed = sorted(d for d in current if d in manifest and manifest[d] != current[d])
    return added, changed, removed, current


def content_addressed(units: list[TextUnit]) -> list[TextUnit]:
    """Give each unit an id derived from its text, so unchanged text keeps its id."""
    return [replace(u, id=f"{u.doc_id}-{content_hash(u.text)[:10]}") for u in units]


def plan_unit_changes(old_units: dict[str, TextUnit], docs: dict[str, str],
                      touched_docs: set[str], size: int = 300, overlap: int = 50):
    """For added, changed and removed documents: which unit ids disappear, which units need extraction."""
    old_ids = {uid for uid, u in old_units.items() if u.doc_id in touched_docs}
    present = {d: docs[d] for d in touched_docs if d in docs}
    fresh = content_addressed(chunk_documents(present, size, overlap))
    new_ids = {u.id for u in fresh}
    removed_ids = old_ids - new_ids                       # retract these
    to_extract = [u for u in fresh if u.id not in old_ids]  # extract only these
    return removed_ids, to_extract, fresh
```

**Fixed windows shift

With fixed-size windows, inserting one sentence near the start of a document moves every later window boundary, so every later unit gets new text and a new hash. The diff is still correct; it just stops being small. Structure-aware chunking (Chapter 7) that splits on headings or paragraphs contains the damage to the section that was edited. If your documents are edited often, this is a strong argument for it.

### Cache extractions per unit

The last ingredient is to keep the raw extraction output for every unit, {unit_id: ExtractionResult}, next to the graph. You already have it in memory during a build; persist it. Two things follow. Re-indexing an unchanged unit costs nothing even when you rebuild from scratch (a CachedLLM gives you the same effect keyed by prompt hash). The larger consequence is that the graph becomes a function of the cache: every node and edge attribute can be recomputed from the extraction records that reference it. LightRAG's README describes its document deletion in the same spirit: when a document is deleted, affected entities are rebuilt from cached extraction data rather than by calling the LLM again.

## Upserts and deletes by source ids

In Chapter 9, build_graph merged extractions into nodes and edges that each carry a source_ids list: the ids of the text units that mentioned them. Read that list as a reference count. An edge mentioned by three units has three references. Retracting a unit removes one reference from everything it mentioned. An element whose count reaches zero is no longer supported by any text, and it goes.

[Diagram]

Retracting the Deepcast supply article (document 03, units 03-a and 03-b) with the reference extractions. Only elements that doc 03 mentioned are touched. The weight of a kept edge is recomputed as the sum of strengths from its remaining sources, not decremented by a guess.

### Recompute touched elements, don't patch them

It is tempting to “decrement” an edge: subtract the removed unit's strength from weight and delete its sentence from descriptions. That works until it doesn't. build_graph deduplicates descriptions, so two units that produced the same description share one entry, and removing one unit must not remove the text. Name resolution can change between runs, so the record you are subtracting may have mapped to a different node last time. The safer approach treats each touched element like a materialized view: collect the extraction records that still reference it, and recompute every attribute from scratch. Only touched elements are recomputed, so this stays cheap, and no LLM is involved.

```python  # minigraphrag/incremental.py
import networkx as nx

from .extraction import ExtractionResult
from .graph_build import add_rank_attributes


def upsert_units(G: nx.Graph, extractions: dict[str, ExtractionResult], removed_ids: set[str],
                 new_results: list[ExtractionResult], name_map: dict[str, str] | None = None):
    """Retract removed text units and add new ones, touching only affected nodes and edges.

    `extractions` is the per-unit cache {unit_id: ExtractionResult}; it is updated in place.
    Returns (dirty_nodes, dirty_edges, deleted_nodes, deleted_edges).
    """
    canon = lambda n: (name_map or {}).get(n, n)  # noqa: E731
    touched_nodes: set[str] = set()
    touched_edges: set[frozenset] = set()

    def mark(ex: ExtractionResult) -> None:
        touched_nodes.update(canon(e.name) for e in ex.entities)
        for r in ex.relationships:
            u, v = canon(r.source), canon(r.target)
            if u != v:
                touched_edges.add(frozenset((u, v)))
                touched_nodes.update((u, v))

    for uid in removed_ids:                 # 1. retract: forget the unit's records
        old = extractions.pop(uid, None)
        if old is not None:
            mark(old)
    new_ids = set()
    for ex in new_results:                  # 2. upsert: remember the new records
        extractions[ex.unit_id] = ex
        new_ids.add(ex.unit_id)
        mark(ex)

    def sources(old_ids: list[str]) -> list[ExtractionResult]:
        # Where can records for this element live? Its surviving sources plus the new units.
        ids = (set(old_ids) - removed_ids) | new_ids
        return [extractions[i] for i in sorted(ids) if i in extractions]

    deleted_nodes, deleted_edges = set(), set()
    for key in touched_edges:               # 3. recompute each touched edge
        u, v = sorted(key)
        old_ids = G.edges[u, v]["source_ids"] if G.has_edge(u, v) else []
        descs, ids, weight = [], [], 0.0
        for ex in sources(old_ids):
            for r in ex.relationships:
                if {canon(r.source), canon(r.target)} == {u, v}:
                    if r.description and r.description not in descs:
                        descs.append(r.description)
                    if r.source_id not in ids:
                        ids.append(r.source_id)
                    weight += r.strength
        if not ids:                          # reference count reached zero
            if G.has_edge(u, v):
                G.remove_edge(u, v)
                deleted_edges.add(key)
            continue
        for n in (u, v):
            if n not in G:
                G.add_node(n, descriptions=[], source_ids=[], aliases=[], type="")
        if not G.has_edge(u, v):
            G.add_edge(u, v)
        G.edges[u, v].update(descriptions=descs, source_ids=ids, weight=weight,
                             description=" ".join(descs))

    for n in touched_nodes:                 # 4. recompute each touched node
        old_ids = G.nodes[n]["source_ids"] if n in G else []
        descs, ids, aliases, votes = [], [], [], {}
        for ex in sources(old_ids):
            for e in ex.entities:
                if canon(e.name) != n:
                    continue
                if e.description and e.description not in descs:
                    descs.append(e.description)
                if e.source_id not in ids:
                    ids.append(e.source_id)
                if e.name != n and e.name not in aliases:
                    aliases.append(e.name)
                votes[e.type] = votes.get(e.type, 0) + 1
        if not ids and (n not in G or G.degree(n) == 0):
            if n in G:                       # no mentions and no edges left
                G.remove_node(n)
                deleted_nodes.add(n)
            continue
        if n not in G:
            G.add_node(n)
        G.nodes[n].update(descriptions=descs, source_ids=ids, aliases=aliases,
                          type=max(votes, key=votes.get) if votes else G.nodes[n].get("type", ""),
                          description=" ".join(descs), frequency=len(ids))

    add_rank_attributes(G)                  # degrees changed; cheap to recompute for all
    dirty_nodes = {n for n in touched_nodes if n in G}
    dirty_edges = {k for k in touched_edges if G.has_edge(*sorted(k))}
    return dirty_nodes, dirty_edges, deleted_nodes, deleted_edges
```

Run against the Kestrel corpus with MockLLM, the equivalence check holds: build from documents 01 to 11, apply document 12 with upsert_units, and the node set, edge set, source_ids and weights match a full build of all 12 documents exactly. Retracting document 03 afterwards deletes one edge whose only support was that article and leaves the rest of Deepcast's neighborhood intact, as in the diagram.

### Name resolution during an update

New mentions must resolve against names already in the graph, or “Nair” from the interview becomes a new node next to PRIYA NAIR. The simplest correct approach is to run resolve_entities over the cached raw entities of all units, old and new. It is pure string and embedding work with no LLM calls, so it is cheap. Watch for one case: if the new name map renames an existing canonical node (the update revealed that TWI and TIDEWATER INSTITUTE are the same), that is a merge of two existing nodes. Every element referencing either name is touched. Treat merges as a signal to schedule a larger rebuild of the affected neighborhood, or a full rebuild if they are frequent.

### Re-summarize only dirty elements

Dirty nodes and edges need a new description summary, and only the ones with more than one description need an LLM call. The function reuses the real prompt from prompts.py.

```python  # minigraphrag/incremental.py
import json

from . import prompts as P


def summarize_dirty(llm, G, dirty_nodes, dirty_edges, max_tokens: int = 150) -> int:
    """Like graph_build.summarize_descriptions, but only for touched elements. Returns LLM calls made."""
    calls = 0

    def summarise(name: str, descriptions: list[str]) -> str:
        nonlocal calls
        if len(descriptions) <= 1:
            return " ".join(descriptions)
        calls += 1
        return llm.complete(P.SUMMARIZE_DESCRIPTIONS_PROMPT.format(
            entity_name=name, description_list=json.dumps(sorted(descriptions)),
            max_tokens=max_tokens)).strip()

    for n in dirty_nodes:
        G.nodes[n]["description"] = summarise(n, G.nodes[n]["descriptions"])
    for key in dirty_edges:
        u, v = sorted(key)
        G.edges[u, v]["description"] = summarise(json.dumps([u, v]), G.edges[u, v]["descriptions"])
    return calls
```

For hub entities, even this is wasteful: KESTREL LABS may have hundreds of descriptions, and one new sentence triggers a summary of all of them. Two mitigations work well. Summarize incrementally: pass the previous summary plus only the new descriptions, and do a full re-summary on a schedule. Or skip re-summarizing when the new descriptions add little, for example when their embedding is very close to the existing summary.

**Human-readable ids move

add_rank_attributes assigns human_id by sorted position, so adding PORT AVALON CITY COUNCIL renumbers every entity after it. Search contexts cite those short ids ([Data: Entities (7)]). Within one query that is fine. If you store answers with citations, store the stable names or content-addressed ids instead, or citations silently point at the wrong entity after an update.

## Communities and reports under change

Descriptions are local: a new mention of Deepcast changes Deepcast. Communities are global: one new edge can move a node, and on the wrong day it can move a whole cluster. You have three strategies.

### Strategy 1: recluster, then match and reuse reports

Leiden and Louvain make no LLM calls, so rerunning them over the whole graph is cheap compared with extraction; the expensive part is the reports. So recluster with a fixed seed, then match each new community to the most similar old community at the same level using the Jaccard similarity of their member sets:

J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|

Reuse the old report only if the match is strong (say J ≥ 0.8), no member of either community is dirty or deleted, and every child community also reused its report. The last rule matters because higher-level reports in Chapter 12 are written from their children's reports; if a child changed, its parent's summary is stale.

```python  # minigraphrag/incremental.py
from .communities import Community


def jaccard(a, b) -> float:
    a, b = set(a), set(b)
    return len(a & b) / len(a | b) if a | b else 1.0


def reports_to_regenerate(old: list[Community], new: list[Community], changed_nodes: set[str],
                          min_overlap: float = 0.8) -> dict[int, int | None]:
    """Map each new community id to an old community id whose report can be reused, or None."""
    decision: dict[int, int | None] = {}
    for c in sorted(new, key=lambda c: -c.level):          # deepest level first
        same_level = [o for o in old if o.level == c.level]
        best = max(same_level, key=lambda o: jaccard(o.nodes, c.nodes), default=None)
        reusable = (best is not None
                    and jaccard(best.nodes, c.nodes) >= min_overlap
                    and not ((set(best.nodes) | set(c.nodes)) & changed_nodes)
                    and all(decision.get(ch) is not None for ch in c.children))
        decision[c.id] = best.id if reusable else None
    return decision
```

A worked example with the expected Kestrel communities. Before the interview is ingested, suppose the clusters are the five from the running example. After it, the partition is recomputed:

New community | Best old match | J | Dirty or deleted members | Decision

Kestrel Labs, Okafor, Vehl, Nair, Tern | same five | 1.0 | all five mentioned in the interview | Regenerate

Brightwater Capital, Lena Park | same two | 1.0 | Lena Park and Brightwater are mentioned | Regenerate

Ocean Health Act, City Council, Port Avalon | same three | 1.0 | Ocean Health Act and the council contract are mentioned | Regenerate

Marlow Dynamics, Deepcast | same two | 1.0 | both mentioned | Regenerate

Tidewater, Ruiz, Halden Reef, bleaching event, Sentinel | same five | 1.0 | Tidewater, Ruiz, Halden Reef and Sentinel mentioned | Regenerate

Every report regenerates, even though the partition did not move at all. On a corpus of 12 documents where the newest one is a summary interview with the leadership team, that is the right answer: the reports really are stale, because Vehl is no longer CTO. On a large corpus the same policy regenerates only the small fraction of communities a batch of documents touches. The changed test is deliberately conservative. A looser policy counts a community as changed only when the share of dirty members, weighted by degree, passes a threshold, and accepts slightly stale reports in exchange for fewer calls.

### Strategy 2: local assignment, periodic recluster

Instead of reclustering, place each new node into the neighboring community with the largest modularity gain, exactly the local move from Louvain (Chapter 11). For node i with total edge weight ki, edge weight ki,C into community C, community degree ΣC and total graph weight m:

ΔQ(i → C) = ki,C / m − γ · ΣC · ki / (2m²)

With hypothetical numbers m = 100, ki = 6, five units of weight into a community with Σ = 60 and one unit into a community with Σ = 20: ΔQ = 0.05 − 0.018 = 0.032 for the first and 0.01 − 0.006 = 0.004 for the second, so the node joins the first. Existing nodes never move, so community ids and reports are stable. The partition slowly drifts from what a fresh run would find. Track the modularity of the maintained partition and recluster from scratch when it falls noticeably below a fresh run's, or after a fixed fraction of the graph has changed.

### Strategy 3: no communities, union updates

LightRAG avoids the problem by not having community reports. The paper describes its incremental update as processing new documents with the same graph-based indexing steps and then taking the union of the new node and edge sets with the existing graph. There is nothing global to recompute, which is why updates are cheap. The trade-off is the one from Chapter 16: without community summaries, whole-corpus sensemaking questions such as “What are the main themes in this corpus?” have less to work with.

Strategy | LLM cost per update | Stability of ids and reports | Quality risk

Full rebuild | Whole corpus | Low: everything can change | None from staleness

Recluster, match, reuse reports | Changed extractions + dirty summaries + changed reports | Medium: depends on match threshold | Loose thresholds keep stale reports

Local assignment, periodic recluster | Lowest with communities | High between reclusters | Partition drifts from optimum

Union updates, no communities | Changed extractions + dirty summaries | High | Weaker global questions

Microsoft GraphRAG ships a graphrag update command (and standard-update / fast-update indexing methods) for adding documents to an existing index; see its CLI documentation for how it merges outputs. Chapter 28 covers the framework.
