## Time in a graph: valid time and transaction time

Incremental indexing keeps the graph in sync with the corpus. It does not, by itself, handle facts that change. Apply document 12 and the graph contains a JONAS VEHL – KESTREL LABS edge whose descriptions call him co-founder (the 2021 Herald article) and “chief technology officer” (the 2022 supply story), and a PRIYA NAIR – KESTREL LABS edge described as “the company's new chief technology officer”. With MockLLM the Vehl edge has eight source units and the Nair edge three; both are well supported. Local search will happily put both into the context, and the model has to guess which one is current from description wording. For canonical question 6, “Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?”, that is a coin flip you should not accept. For question 15, “Who was the CTO when the bleaching event was detected?”, deleting the old edge would make the right answer impossible.

Chapter 10 attached start and end dates to claims. Here you make time a first-class property of edges, and you separate two different clocks.

### Two timelines

- Valid time is when a fact was true in the world. Jonas Vehl held CTO_OF Kestrel Labs from 2021 until March 2026. It comes from the text.

- Transaction time (called record time in minigraphrag) is when your system learned something. The store learned about Vehl's role when it ingested the Herald article and learned that his term had ended when it ingested the interview. It comes from your ingestion clock.

A store that tracks both is bi-temporal. Each fact edge carries four timestamps: valid_from and valid_to for valid time, recorded_at for when the fact was learned, and invalidated_at for when a later fact closed its valid interval. The Zep paper uses exactly this split: a timeline T for the chronological order of events, with t_valid and t_invalid on each edge, and a timeline T′ for the order of ingestion, with t′_created and t′_expired.

Why keep transaction time at all, if valid time already says when things were true? Because your knowledge was incomplete in the past, and you will need to explain past behavior. On 1 March 2026 the assistant told a user that Vehl was CTO. That was consistent with everything it had ingested. A month later the store knows better. Transaction time lets you reproduce the old answer exactly (for debugging, audits and evaluation of past runs) without pretending the new knowledge doesn't exist.

### The Kestrel history as edges

minigraphrag.temporal.kestrel_timeline() records the dated facts of the running example in publication order, using each document's date as recorded_at. Three of its edges carry the story of this chapter. Dates are datetime.date values, intervals are half-open (start inclusive, end exclusive), and an empty end means “as far as we know, still true”.

Edge | Fact | valid_from | valid_to | recorded_at | invalidated_at | prior_valid_to

A | Jonas Vehl CTO_OF Kestrel Labs | 2021-01-01 | 2026-03-01 | 2021-10-04 (doc 01) | 2026-03-26 (doc 12) | open

B | Priya Nair CTO_OF Kestrel Labs | 2026-03-01 | open | 2026-03-26 (doc 12) | none | none

C | Deepcast SUPPLIED Kestrel Labs | 2022-08-01 | 2025-06-30 | 2022-08-09 (doc 03) | 2025-05-14 (doc 08) | open

Edge A is one edge, not two. When Nair's fact arrived, add_fact closed A's valid_to at her valid_from, stamped invalidated_at with the interview date, and saved what the store believed before in prior_valid_to (an open end). That saved value is what makes transaction-time queries possible: asked “as known on 2026-03-20”, the store ignores the invalidation that had not happened yet and uses the prior end.

Three details matter. The Herald only says Kestrel was founded “this year”, so parse_date("2021") gives 2021-01-01, a coarse lower bound; store the granularity if you can. Edge C was invalidated in May 2025 with a valid end at the end of June: the board memo announced a future end date. And because intervals are half-open, valid_to 2025-06-30 excludes the last day of June; 2025-07-01 would match “at the end of June” more precisely. Off-by-one dates like this are the most common temporal bug in practice.

In the plane of valid time against transaction time, an invalidated edge is two rectangles: before invalidated_at its valid interval runs to prior_valid_to, and after it, to valid_to. An as-of query is a point: “what was true at valid time v, according to what the store knew at transaction time t?” The answer is every rectangle containing the point.

[Interactive figure: Bi-temporal facts as rectangles — Move both sliders; the facts whose rectangle contains the point are the answer (ch27-bitemporal)]

## Invalidation, as-of queries and event sourcing

### When does a new fact contradict an old one?

Invalidation needs a rule for what counts as a contradiction. Most relations are not exclusive: Brightwater Capital INVESTED_IN Kestrel Labs twice, and Kestrel RUNS both Sentinel and Tern. A new edge of those types never closes an old one. Some relations are functional in one direction: a company has one CTO and one CEO at a time. For those, a new holder overlapping an existing holder's valid interval is a contradiction. There are three ways to detect it, from cheapest to most general.

- Schema rules. Declare CTO_OF and CEO_OF exclusive in their target, as EXCLUSIVE_RELATIONS does in minigraphrag/temporal.py. Detection is a lookup. This requires typed relations, which is one more reason to extract a relation label alongside the description (Chapter 8).

- Explicit end statements. “Deepcast will stop accepting new orders from outside customers at the end of June” ends SUPPLIED without any new supplier. Claim extraction with end_date (Chapter 10) produces this directly.

- LLM comparison. For free-text relations, retrieve existing edges between the same or semantically similar entities and ask the model whether the new edge contradicts any of them. This is how Zep describes Graphiti's approach: an LLM compares new edges against semantically related existing edges, and when it finds temporally overlapping contradictions it sets the old edge's t_invalid to the new edge's t_valid.

```python  # minigraphrag/prompts.py
# Illustrative prompt for option 3; minigraphrag's temporal module uses schema rules.
EDGE_CONTRADICTION_PROMPT = """---Role---
You maintain a knowledge graph whose facts change over time.

---New fact---
{new_fact} (valid from {new_valid_from})

---Existing facts about the same entities---
{existing_facts}

---Goal---
List the ids of existing facts that can no longer be true from {new_valid_from} onward
because of the new fact. A fact that can be true at the same time as the new fact
is NOT contradicted. Return JSON: {{"contradicted": [<id>, ...], "reason": "<one sentence>"}}
"""
```

### Implementing add_fact, as_of and holders

minigraphrag/temporal.py stores facts as edges in a networkx.MultiDiGraph, because the same pair of entities can hold many facts over time. New facts never delete old ones. For exclusive relations, a new holder closes the valid interval of the current holder and remembers the previous end. Here is the module, lightly trimmed.

```python  # minigraphrag/temporal.py
from datetime import date

import networkx as nx

# Relations where a target can have only one source at a time (one CTO per company).
EXCLUSIVE_RELATIONS: set[str] = {"CTO_OF", "CEO_OF"}


def parse_date(value: str | date | None) -> date | None:
    """Accept date objects or ISO-ish strings: '2026', '2026-03', '2026-03-26'."""
    if value is None or isinstance(value, date):
        return value
    parts = [int(p) for p in str(value).split("-")]
    return date(parts[0], parts[1] if len(parts) > 1 else 1, parts[2] if len(parts) > 2 else 1)


def new_temporal_graph() -> nx.MultiDiGraph:
    """Directed multigraph: the same pair can hold many facts over time."""
    return nx.MultiDiGraph()


def add_fact(G, source, relation, target, valid_from, valid_to=None, recorded_at=None,
             description="", exclusive=None) -> int:
    """Add a fact edge, invalidating contradicting facts. Returns the new edge key."""
    vf, vt = parse_date(valid_from), parse_date(valid_to)
    rec = parse_date(recorded_at) or vf
    exclusive = relation in EXCLUSIVE_RELATIONS if exclusive is None else exclusive

    if exclusive and target in G:
        for old_source, _, key, d in list(G.in_edges(target, keys=True, data=True)):
            if d["relation"] != relation or old_source == source or d["invalidated_at"] is not None:
                continue
            if d["valid_to"] is None or d["valid_to"] > vf:
                # Close the old interval where the new one begins; remember what we believed before.
                d["prior_valid_to"] = d["valid_to"]
                d["valid_to"] = vf
                d["invalidated_at"] = rec

    return G.add_edge(source, target, relation=relation, description=description,
                      valid_from=vf, valid_to=vt, recorded_at=rec,
                      invalidated_at=None, prior_valid_to=None)


def is_valid(d: dict, at: date, known_at: date | None = None) -> bool:
    """Was this fact true at `at`, according to what was recorded by `known_at` (default: now)?"""
    valid_to = d["valid_to"]
    if known_at is not None:
        if d["recorded_at"] > known_at:
            return False                      # we hadn't learned this fact yet
        if d["invalidated_at"] is not None and d["invalidated_at"] > known_at:
            valid_to = d["prior_valid_to"]    # the invalidation hadn't happened yet
    return d["valid_from"] <= at and (valid_to is None or at < valid_to)


def as_of(G, at, known_at=None) -> nx.MultiDiGraph:
    """Snapshot of the facts valid at `at` (optionally as believed at `known_at`)."""
    at_d, known_d = parse_date(at), parse_date(known_at)
    snap = nx.MultiDiGraph()
    snap.add_nodes_from(G.nodes(data=True))
    for u, v, k, d in G.edges(keys=True, data=True):
        if is_valid(d, at_d, known_d):
            snap.add_edge(u, v, key=k, **d)
    return snap


def holders(G, relation, target, at, known_at=None) -> list[str]:
    """Sources holding `relation` to `target` at a date, e.g. holders(G, 'CTO_OF', 'Kestrel Labs', '2024-08')."""
    snap = as_of(G, at, known_at)
    if target not in snap:
        return []
    return sorted({u for u, _, d in snap.in_edges(target, data=True) if d["relation"] == relation})
```

Three design choices deserve a comment. Storing one prior_valid_to instead of versioned rows keeps the graph small and queries simple, at the price of remembering only one previous belief per edge; the SQL design later in this chapter versions rows instead and keeps unlimited history. as_of returns a snapshot graph, so every retrieval method from Part 3 can run on it unchanged. And add_fact assumes facts arrive in the order they became true: it closes any open holder whose interval reaches the new fact's valid_from, without asking which of the two started first. kestrel_timeline ingests in publication order, so that assumption holds here; Exercise 27.5 shows what happens when it does not, and how to fix it. Replaying the running example:

```python  # examples/temporal_kestrel.py
from minigraphrag.temporal import holders, kestrel_timeline

G = kestrel_timeline()   # dated Kestrel facts, recorded in publication order

print(holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-09-16"))                        # ['Priya Nair']  question 6
print(holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2024-08"))                           # ['Jonas Vehl']  question 15
print(holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-06", known_at="2026-02"))       # ['Jonas Vehl']  what we believed in February
print(holders(G, "SUPPLIED", "Kestrel Labs", "2024-06"))                         # ['Deepcast']    question 7
print(holders(G, "SUPPLIED", "Kestrel Labs", "2025-09", known_at="2025-03"))     # ['Deepcast']    before the board memo
print(holders(G, "SUPPLIED", "Kestrel Labs", "2025-09"))                         # []
```

Explicit end statements do not need a contradicting fact. kestrel_timeline closes the Deepcast edge directly when the board memo is recorded, setting the same three fields add_fact sets:

```python  # minigraphrag/temporal.py
    # The supply ended when the board memo recorded it: close that edge explicitly.
    for u, v, d in G.edges(data=True):
        if d["relation"] == "SUPPLIED":
            d["prior_valid_to"], d["valid_to"], d["invalidated_at"] = None, date(2025, 6, 30), date(2025, 5, 14)
```

**Resolve relative dates at ingestion

The interview says “as of March 2026” but also “big news this month” and “bought Deepcast last year”. Pass the document's own date (its publication or recording date) into the extraction prompt so the model can turn relative expressions into absolute ones. Graphiti's add_episode takes a reference_time for the same reason. Without it, “last year” resolves relative to whenever the extractor happens to run.

### Using time at query time

Temporal edges plug into the retrieval methods you already have. Before building a local search context (Chapter 14), take the snapshot as_of(G, question_time) and retrieve over it, where the question time defaults to today and is overridden when the question names a date (“in 2024”, “when the bleaching event was detected”). For questions about change (“How has Kestrel Labs' leadership evolved?”) do the opposite: include the whole history, ordered by valid_from, with the intervals printed. In both cases, put the dates and today's date into the context. The post-graph-rag paper reports that grounding the prompt in temporal information at synthesis time measurably helps temporal reasoning, which matches what you would expect: a model cannot reason about an interval it cannot see.

```python  # examples/temporal_context.txt
Today is 2026-09-16.
-----Relationships (with valid time)-----
id|source|relation|target|valid_from|valid_to
0|Jonas Vehl|CTO_OF|Kestrel Labs|2021-01-01|2026-03-01
1|Priya Nair|CTO_OF|Kestrel Labs|2026-03-01|present
2|Deepcast|SUPPLIED|Kestrel Labs|2022-08-01|2025-06-30
```

### Event sourcing

You can go one step further and store the log rather than the current edges: every ingestion appends events such as assert(fact, at), close(fact, valid_to, at) and retract(source_id, at). The fact graph is a fold over the log. This is event sourcing, and it pairs naturally with both halves of this chapter. The state as known at transaction time t is the fold over events with at ≤ t. A bug in contradiction detection can be fixed and the log replayed to rebuild a corrected graph. It also removes the one-level limit of prior_valid_to: every past belief is in the log. And the text-unit retractions from the incremental indexer become events in the same log, so “why did this edge disappear?” has an answer with a timestamp and a source.

Two kinds of “removal” are easy to confuse. Retracting a document means the store no longer has evidence for the facts it asserted: record the retraction in transaction time. A fact ending in the world, like Vehl's CTO term, is a change of valid time, and the closed edge is still believed. Mixing the two is the most common temporal modeling bug.

## Graphiti, Zep and a Postgres-native design

### Zep and Graphiti

Zep is a memory service for agents, and Graphiti is the open-source temporal knowledge graph engine at its core. The Zep paper organizes the graph in three tiers, each built from the one below.

[Diagram]

The episode tier keeps the raw inputs, so every fact can be traced to what was said and when. When the interview episode produces PRIYA NAIR CTO_OF KESTREL LABS, the contradiction check invalidates Vehl's edge rather than deleting it. Communities summarize the entity tier.

- Episode subgraph. Episodes hold raw input data: messages, text or JSON. They are the provenance layer, playing the role that text units play in GraphRAG.

- Semantic entity subgraph. Entities extracted from episodes and resolved against existing graph entities. The paper describes resolution as a combination of embedding similarity search, a full-text search over existing names and summaries for extra candidates, and an LLM deduplication prompt. Edges between entities are facts carrying the four bi-temporal timestamps.

- Community subgraph. Clusters of strongly connected entities with high-level summaries, the same idea as GraphRAG community reports.

Retrieval is hybrid. The paper lists three search functions (cosine similarity, Okapi BM25 full-text search and breadth-first search over the graph) and rerankers that include reciprocal rank fusion and maximal marginal relevance (Chapter 21), an episode-mentions reranker, a node-distance reranker and cross-encoders. The paper reports that Zep edges out MemGPT on the Deep Memory Retrieval benchmark (94.8% against 93.4%) and, on LongMemEval, improves accuracy by up to 18.5% while cutting response latency by 90% against baseline implementations. Those are the authors' own measurements; the design is what transfers.

Here is the Kestrel leadership change through Graphiti's Python API. Graphiti needs a graph database (Neo4j or FalkorDB, among others) and an LLM API key.

```python  # examples/graphiti_kestrel.py
import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.nodes import EpisodeType

CORPUS = Path("data/corpus")
EPISODES = [  # (file, reference time = when the text was published or recorded)
    ("01_herald_kestrel_founding.md", datetime(2021, 10, 4, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
    ("12_interview_leadership_change_2026.md", datetime(2026, 3, 26, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
]


async def main():
    graphiti = Graphiti("bolt://localhost:7687", "neo4j", "password")
    try:
        await graphiti.build_indices_and_constraints()
        for name, when in EPISODES:           # ingest in publication order
            await graphiti.add_episode(
                name=name,
                episode_body=(CORPUS / name).read_text(),
                source=EpisodeType.text,
                source_description="Kestrel Labs corpus document",
                reference_time=when,
            )
        for edge in await graphiti.search("Who is the CTO of Kestrel Labs?"):
            print(edge.fact, "| valid:", edge.valid_at, "| invalid:", edge.invalid_at)
    finally:
        await graphiti.close()


asyncio.run(main())
```

After the second episode you should see a fact about Vehl as CTO with an invalid_at around March 2026 and a fact about Nair with no invalid_at. Exact fact wording depends on the LLM. Compare the concepts with what you built: episodes are text units, reference_time is the document date you pass to extraction, valid_at/invalid_at are valid_from/valid_to, and Graphiti's created_at/expired_at on each edge play the role of recorded_at/invalidated_at.

**Rasmussen et al., Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory (2025)

Zep's design choice worth copying is that invalidation never deletes. Old edges get an invalid time, so the graph can answer both “what is true now” and “what was true then”, and every fact still points back to the episode that asserted it. The choice to run an LLM contradiction check on new edges buys generality over free-text relations at the price of extra LLM work on every ingested episode.

### A Postgres-native bi-temporal design

You don't need a graph database to do this. The post-graph-rag paper describes an open-source engine that keeps chunks with embeddings, a canonical entity graph and community summaries in a single PostgreSQL database. It validates extraction output at write time, rejecting vague predicates and unresolved entities, and adds a bi-temporal layer that records both when a relation held and when the system learned it, which lets it supersede incompatible earlier assertions. Its evaluation also highlights putting temporal grounding into the synthesis prompt.

Postgres has the pieces built in. Range types represent intervals, and an exclusion constraint can enforce the functional rule for CTO_OF inside the database. The schema below is an illustration of the technique, not post-graph-rag's actual schema.

```python  # sql/bitemporal_edges.sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

CREATE TABLE fact (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  subject     text      NOT NULL,
  relation    text      NOT NULL,
  object      text      NOT NULL,
  valid       daterange NOT NULL,                        -- valid time, [from, to)
  tx          tstzrange NOT NULL DEFAULT tstzrange(now(), NULL),  -- transaction time
  source_id   text      NOT NULL,
  -- Among rows we currently believe, a company cannot have two CTOs at overlapping times.
  EXCLUDE USING gist (object WITH =, relation WITH =, valid WITH &&)
    WHERE (relation = 'CTO_OF' AND upper_inf(tx))
);

-- Question 15 as the store knows it today: who was CTO on 15 August 2024?
SELECT subject FROM fact
WHERE relation = 'CTO_OF' AND object = 'KESTREL LABS'
  AND valid @> DATE '2024-08-15'
  AND tx    @> now();

-- What did we believe on 1 March 2026 about who would be CTO in May 2026?
SELECT subject FROM fact
WHERE relation = 'CTO_OF' AND object = 'KESTREL LABS'
  AND valid @> DATE '2026-05-01'
  AND tx    @> TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-01';
```

The exclusion constraint turns a forgotten invalidation into an insert error instead of a silently inconsistent graph. Unlike minigraphrag's single edge with prior_valid_to, this design versions rows: invalidating Vehl's term closes the tx range of his current row and inserts a corrected row with a closed valid range. The price is ordering: that close and insert must happen in the same database transaction as Nair's insert, before it.

### Trade-offs

Approach | Answers “now” | Answers “then” | Explains past answers | Cost

Overwrite edges on change | Yes | No | No | Lowest

Valid time only (Chapter 10 claims) | Yes | Yes | No: corrections overwrite history | Low

Bi-temporal edges or rows | Yes | Yes | Yes | More rows, two-axis filters in every query

Event-sourced log + folded table | Yes | Yes | Yes, and replayable after bug fixes | Log storage, replay tooling

#### Exercise 27.1 Warm-up

A small graph has these elements (unit ids abbreviated, strengths in parentheses):

- Edge MARLOW DYNAMICS – DEEPCAST: 07-a (9), 08-a (7), 12-a (6)

- Edge PRIYA NAIR – MARLOW DYNAMICS: 05-a (8), 12-a (5)

- Edge MARLOW DYNAMICS – KESTREL LABS: 12-b (6)

- Node MARLOW DYNAMICS mentioned by 05-a, 07-a, 08-a, 12-a, 12-b

Document 12 is retracted (units 12-a and 12-b). By hand, give each element's new source_ids, weight and fate, and list the dirty and deleted sets.

▸ Show answer

- MARLOW DYNAMICS – DEEPCAST: sources 07-a, 08-a; weight 9 + 7 = 16 (was 22); kept, dirty.

- PRIYA NAIR – MARLOW DYNAMICS: sources 05-a; weight 8 (was 13); kept, dirty.

- MARLOW DYNAMICS – KESTREL LABS: no sources left; reference count 0; deleted.

- MARLOW DYNAMICS: sources 05-a, 07-a, 08-a; frequency 3; kept, dirty. DEEPCAST, PRIYA NAIR and KESTREL LABS are touched as endpoints, so they are dirty too (their degree changed and, if 12-a or 12-b described them, so did their descriptions).

Dirty edges: {MARLOW–DEEPCAST, NAIR–MARLOW}. Deleted edges: {MARLOW–KESTREL LABS}. Dirty nodes: {MARLOW DYNAMICS, DEEPCAST, PRIYA NAIR, KESTREL LABS}. Deleted nodes: none, because every endpoint still has mentions. Weights are recomputed from the surviving records (9 + 7), not decremented (22 − 6), which gives the same number here but stays correct when records were deduplicated or name mapping changed.

#### Exercise 27.2 Core

Using edges A, B and C from the table and the semantics of is_valid, work out by hand what holders(G, relation, target, at, known_at) returns for each call, and which branch of is_valid decides it.

- holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-04-15", known_at="2026-03-20")

- holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-04-15", known_at="2026-04-01")

- holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2021-06-01", known_at="2021-06-01")

- holders(G, "SUPPLIED", "Kestrel Labs", "2025-08-01", known_at="2025-05-14")

- holders(G, "SUPPLIED", "Kestrel Labs", "2025-06-30")

▸ Hint

Check recorded_at > known_at first, then whether the invalidation had happened by known_at (if not, use prior_valid_to), then the half-open valid interval.

▸ Show answer

- ['Jonas Vehl']. Edge A was recorded 2021-10-04 ≤ 2026-03-20, and its invalidation (2026-03-26) is after known_at, so valid_to falls back to prior_valid_to = open. 2021-01-01 ≤ 2026-04-15, valid. Edge B was recorded 2026-03-26 > 2026-03-20: not yet learned.

- ['Priya Nair']. By 2026-04-01 the invalidation has happened, so A uses valid_to = 2026-03-01 and 2026-04-15 is outside. B is recorded and valid from 2026-03-01.

- []. A's valid interval covers 2021-06-01, but A was recorded on 2021-10-04, after known_at. The store had not heard of Kestrel Labs yet. With valid time alone, a replay of June 2021 would wrongly answer Vehl.

- []. C's invalidation date 2025-05-14 is not after known_at (they are equal), so the closed valid_to 2025-06-30 applies and 2025-08-01 is outside it. From the day the memo was recorded, the store knows Deepcast will not be supplying in August.

- [], which is arguably wrong. valid_to is exclusive, so 2025-06-30 is outside the interval even though the memo says supply stops “at the end of June”. holders(..., "2025-06-29") returns ['Deepcast']. The fix is in the data, not the code: an end “at the end of June” should be recorded as valid_to=date(2025, 7, 1).

You can confirm all five with kestrel_timeline(); they are the values the reference implementation returns.

#### Exercise 27.3 Core

Write a pytest test that proves incremental indexing is equivalent to a full build on the Kestrel corpus: build from documents 01–11, apply document 12 with plan_unit_changes and upsert_units, and compare with a full build of all 12 documents. Use MockLLM and skip description summaries. What must be identical, and what can legitimately differ?

▸ Show answer

```python
from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents, chunk_documents
from minigraphrag.extraction import extract_from_unit
from minigraphrag.graph_build import build_graph
from minigraphrag.llm import MockLLM
from minigraphrag.resolution import resolve_entities
from minigraphrag.incremental import (content_addressed, content_hash, diff_documents,
                                      plan_unit_changes, upsert_units)

def extract_all(llm, units):
    return {u.id: extract_from_unit(llm, u, None, 1) for u in units}

def name_map_for(extractions):
    return resolve_entities([e for ex in extractions.values() for e in ex.entities])

def test_incremental_equals_full_build():
    llm = MockLLM()
    docs = load_documents("data/corpus")
    old_docs = {d: t for d, t in docs.items() if not d.startswith("12_")}

    # Old index
    old_units = content_addressed(chunk_documents(old_docs, 300, 50))
    cache = extract_all(llm, old_units)
    G = build_graph(list(cache.values()), llm=None, name_map=name_map_for(cache))

    # Incremental update
    manifest = {d: content_hash(t) for d, t in old_docs.items()}
    added, changed, removed, _ = diff_documents(manifest, docs)
    assert added == ["12_interview_leadership_change_2026"] and not changed and not removed
    removed_ids, to_extract, _ = plan_unit_changes({u.id: u for u in old_units}, docs,
                                                   set(added + changed + removed))
    calls_before = llm.calls
    new_results = [extract_from_unit(llm, u, None, 1) for u in to_extract]
    assert llm.calls - calls_before == 2 * len(to_extract)      # e(1) = 2 calls per unit
    new_cache = {**cache, **{ex.unit_id: ex for ex in new_results}}
    upsert_units(G, cache, removed_ids, new_results, name_map_for(new_cache))

    # Full build of everything
    full_cache = extract_all(MockLLM(), content_addressed(chunk_documents(docs, 300, 50)))
    F = build_graph(list(full_cache.values()), llm=None, name_map=name_map_for(full_cache))

    assert set(G.nodes) == set(F.nodes)
    assert {frozenset(e) for e in G.edges} == {frozenset(e) for e in F.edges}
    for u, v in F.edges:
        assert sorted(G.edges[u, v]["source_ids"]) == sorted(F.edges[u, v]["source_ids"])
        assert G.edges[u, v]["weight"] == F.edges[u, v]["weight"]
    for n in F.nodes:
        assert sorted(G.nodes[n]["source_ids"]) == sorted(F.nodes[n]["source_ids"])
        assert G.nodes[n]["type"] == F.nodes[n]["type"]
```

Identical: node and edge sets, source_ids, weights, types and the per-unit extraction records (MockLLM is deterministic). Allowed to differ: the order of descriptions and source_ids lists (hence the sorts), and with a real LLM, the text of summaries and reports. The test also pins the extraction call count to 2 × ΔU, which catches a regression where the updater silently re-extracts old units. If you enable summaries, compare the sets of descriptions rather than the summary text.

#### Exercise 27.4 Core

You maintain a corpus of 40,000 text units. Each day 1% of units change. Extraction uses g = 1. Summaries: a full build makes 9,000 summary calls; each changed unit dirties on average 6 elements that need a summary, and dirty sets of different units overlap by 50%. Reports: 1,200 communities; an update regenerates 15% of them. (a) Compute daily LLM calls for a nightly full rebuild and for an incremental update. (b) Which term dominates the incremental cost, and what would you do about it?

▸ Show answer

(a) Full rebuild: extraction 40,000 × 2 = 80,000; summaries 9,000; reports 1,200. Total 90,200 calls per day.

Incremental: ΔU = 400 units. Extraction 400 × 2 = 800. Summaries: 400 × 6 = 2,400 raw, halved by overlap = 1,200. Reports: 0.15 × 1,200 = 180. Total 2,180 calls, about 41 times fewer.

(b) Summaries now dominate (1,200 of 2,180, 55%), not extraction. That is the hub effect: many changed units mention the same popular entities, and each summary for a hub re-reads its whole description list, so the token cost is even more skewed than the call count. Fixes, in order of effort: batch updates (once a day already helps because overlaps collapse); summarize hubs incrementally from their previous summary plus new descriptions; skip re-summarizing when new descriptions are near-duplicates of the existing summary; refresh hub summaries fully on a slower schedule. For reports, raise the regeneration threshold so a community with one dirty low-degree member keeps its report until the next weekly refresh.

#### Exercise 27.5 Stretch

Ingestion is not always in publication order. (a) On a fresh new_temporal_graph(), call add_fact for Priya Nair's CTO fact first (valid from 2026-03, recorded 2026-03-26) and Jonas Vehl's second (valid from 2021, recorded 2026-04-02). Trace what the reference add_fact does and what holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-09-16") returns. (b) Fix it, and state one limitation of the prior_valid_to design that your fix does not address.

▸ Hint

Look at the condition that decides whether an existing holder gets closed. Does it compare the two valid_from dates?

▸ Show answer

(a) The first call adds Nair: valid [2026-03-01, open), recorded 2026-03-26. The second call finds Nair's edge: same relation and target, different source, not invalidated, and valid_to is None, so it closes it at the new valid_from: Nair's valid_to becomes 2021-01-01, which is before her valid_from, and invalidated_at becomes 2026-04-02. Vehl's edge is added with an open end. holders(..., "2026-09-16") returns ['Jonas Vehl']: the store now believes Vehl is CTO today. The code assumes new facts are about later holders; an older fact arriving late silently erases the newer one.

(b) Compare start dates. If the existing holder started at or after the new fact, the new fact is about an earlier period: cut the new fact short and leave the existing edge alone.

```python
    if exclusive and target in G:
        for old_source, _, key, d in list(G.in_edges(target, keys=True, data=True)):
            if d["relation"] != relation or old_source == source or d["invalidated_at"] is not None:
                continue
            if d["valid_from"] >= vf:
                # Out-of-order arrival: the new fact is about an earlier holder.
                vt = d["valid_from"] if vt is None else min(vt, d["valid_from"])
            elif d["valid_to"] is None or d["valid_to"] > vf:
                d["prior_valid_to"] = d["valid_to"]
                d["valid_to"] = vf
                d["invalidated_at"] = rec
```

With the fix, the same two calls give Vehl [2021-01-01, 2026-03-01) and Nair [2026-03-01, open), nothing invalidated. holders returns Nair for today and Vehl for 2024-08, the same as in-order ingestion. Asked with known_at="2026-03-30" about 2024-08 it returns [], which is correct: Vehl's fact had not been recorded yet. A regression test that ingests the Kestrel facts in shuffled order and compares holders answers with the in-order graph catches this whole class of bug.

Limitations the fix leaves: an edge remembers only one previous belief, and the invalidated_at is not None guard means an already-closed edge is never corrected again. If you later learn of an interim CTO inside Vehl's closed term, his edge cannot be split. Versioned rows (the SQL design) or an event log handle both, at the cost of more rows.

## Check your understanding

Why should text unit ids be derived from content for incremental indexing?

- Hashes are shorter than positional ids

- Positional ids cannot be stored in JSON

- ✓ (correct) Unchanged text keeps its id, so its cached extraction is reused and only changed text is re-extracted

- Content hashes make fixed-size windows stop shifting when text is inserted
Answer: With content-addressed ids, the diff between old and new unit ids is exactly the set of units whose text changed. They do not stop window boundaries from shifting; that needs structure-aware chunking.

An edge has source_ids [03-a, 03-b, 12-a]. Document 03 is retracted. What should happen?

- Delete the edge, because most of its sources are gone

- ✓ (correct) Keep it with source 12-a, recomputing weight and descriptions from 12-a's records

- Keep it unchanged until the next full rebuild

- Subtract one third of the weight
Answer: The source list is a reference count. One reference survives, so the edge stays, and its attributes are recomputed from the surviving extraction records rather than patched.

On 2026-03-20 the assistant told a user that Jonas Vehl is CTO. Today you want to reproduce exactly what it would have said. Which call?

- holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-09-16")

- holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-03-20")

- holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-09-16", known_at="2026-03-20")

- ✓ (correct) holders(G, "CTO_OF", "Kestrel Labs", "2026-03-20", known_at="2026-03-20")
Answer: Both axes must be at the time of the original question: it asked about the present at that moment, using what the store knew then. Option 2 uses today's knowledge: Vehl's edge now ends on 2026-03-01, so it returns Priya Nair, which is not what the assistant said on that day.

The interview says Priya Nair became CTO in March 2026. Why not simply delete Vehl's CTO_OF edge?

- Graph databases cannot delete edges

- Deleting edges changes community ids

- ✓ (correct) Questions about the past, such as who was CTO when the bleaching was detected, would lose their answer

- The LLM might re-extract the edge later
Answer: The old fact is still true for its interval. Invalidation closes its valid interval and remembers the previous end in prior_valid_to, so both “now” and “then” questions remain answerable.

After reclustering, a level-1 community has exactly the same members as before (Jaccard 1.0), but one member is dirty. Under reports_to_regenerate, what happens to its report and to its level-0 parent's report?

- Neither is regenerated, because membership did not change

- Only the child's report is regenerated; the parent's membership is also unchanged

- Only the parent's report is regenerated

- ✓ (correct) Both are regenerated: the child has a dirty member, and a parent is never reused when a child was regenerated
Answer: A dirty member makes the child stale regardless of membership. Parents summarize their children's reports (and contain the dirty node too), so staleness propagates upward.

Kestrel Labs appears in almost every new document. What is the main cost consequence for incremental updates?

- Extraction calls for Kestrel documents double

- ✓ (correct) The hub's description summary and its communities' reports are touched by nearly every update, so those terms stop shrinking with the change size

- Content hashes collide more often

- Reference counts for Kestrel Labs overflow
Answer: Extraction stays proportional to changed units. Summaries and reports are keyed on touched elements, and hubs are always touched. Incremental summaries and slower refresh schedules for hubs address this.

A press release in the corpus is withdrawn because it was wrong. How should the temporal store record this?

- Set valid_to on its facts to the withdrawal date

- ✓ (correct) Stamp a retraction in transaction time on facts supported only by that source, leaving their valid intervals alone

- Delete the edges physically

- Add new edges with the opposite relation
Answer: A retraction is about evidence, which is transaction time. Setting valid_to would claim the facts were true until the withdrawal date, which is exactly what the withdrawal denies. (Physical deletion is sometimes legally required; that is a separate purge process.)

## Questions learners often ask

▸ My corpus is small. Can I just rebuild nightly?

Yes, and with a CachedLLM in front of extraction, a rebuild only pays for LLM calls whose prompts changed, which is most of the benefit of incremental extraction for free. The remaining costs of rebuilds are churn (report text and ids change daily) and lost history. If neither matters to your users, rebuild. Add temporal edges whenever answers depend on when something was true; that is independent of how you index.

▸ When should I do a full rebuild anyway?

When something global changes: the extraction prompt or model, entity types, chunking parameters, the embedding model, or the resolution thresholds. Cached extractions from the old prompt are not comparable with new ones, and embeddings from two models do not share a space. Also rebuild on a slow schedule (weekly or monthly) to reset drift in locally assigned communities and to catch bugs in the incremental path. Run the rebuild in the background and compare it with the incrementally maintained index; the diff is a free test.

▸ Where do valid times come from? The text rarely gives exact dates.

From three places, in order of preference: dates stated in the text (“in April 2025”), relative expressions resolved against the document date (“last year” in a 2026 interview), and, as a fallback, the document date itself as the earliest time the fact is known to hold. Keep the granularity (year, month, day) so you do not claim precision you lack, and store the source id so a reader can check. Chapter 10's claim extraction produces start and end dates in exactly this shape.

▸ How reliable is an LLM at deciding that two facts contradict?

Reasonably good on clear cases and noticeably worse on subtle ones: roles that can be shared (co-leads of Project Tern), titles that sound exclusive but are not (“a chief scientist”), and facts about different time periods written in the present tense. Use schema rules for the relations that matter most, send only the candidate edges between the same or closely related entities to the LLM, always log invalidations with their reason and source, and build a small test set of contradiction and non-contradiction pairs from your corpus to evaluate the prompt (Chapter 25).

▸ Append-only history conflicts with a deletion request under privacy law. What now?

Bi-temporal invalidation is not deletion: the text is still stored. For a legal erasure you need a separate purge path that physically removes the source text units, their extraction cache entries, the facts and descriptions derived only from them, embeddings, and any report text that quotes them, followed by regenerating affected summaries and reports. The source_ids reference counts from this chapter are what make that purge possible; without provenance you cannot find everything a document contributed.

▸ Does incremental indexing change retrieval quality?

It should not, if the update is equivalent to a rebuild. In practice two things drift: locally assigned communities diverge from what a fresh clustering would find, and relaxed report regeneration thresholds leave some reports stale. Evaluate the incrementally maintained index against a fresh build on your golden question set periodically, especially the global and temporal questions, which are the most sensitive to both.

### Project: a living Kestrel index

Replay the Kestrel corpus as if it arrived over five years, and keep an index and a temporal store current as each document lands.

- An update command that diffs documents against a manifest, extracts only new or changed content-addressed units, and applies upsert_units using a persisted per-unit extraction cache

- An equivalence test: ingesting the 12 documents one at a time in publication order yields the same nodes, edges, source_ids and weights as a full build

- Selective summaries and reports: only dirty elements are re-summarized and only changed communities (and ancestors) get new reports; log the calls saved per update

- A temporal graph fed by claim extraction with document dates as recorded_at, built with add_fact, an explicit close for end statements, the out-of-order fix from Exercise 27.5, and a retraction path for withdrawn documents

- Local search that filters relationships with as_of and prints valid intervals and today's date into the context; correct answers to questions 6, 7, 14 and 15 from data/questions.jsonl

- A short report: LLM calls for incremental ingestion of all 12 documents versus 12 full rebuilds, and which cost term dominated

Done when the equivalence test passes, question 15 is answered “Jonas Vehl” and question 6 “Priya Nair” from the same store, and you can replay what the assistant would have answered to question 6 on 2026-03-20.

## Key takeaways

- Full rebuilds cost as much as the corpus, churn ids and reports, and lose history. Incremental updates make extraction proportional to the change.

- Content-addressed text units plus a per-unit extraction cache turn the graph into a function of its sources. source_ids act as reference counts: recompute touched elements, delete at zero.

- Summaries and reports do not shrink automatically, because hub entities are touched by almost every update. Regenerate only dirty elements and changed communities with their ancestors, and handle hubs with incremental summaries or slower schedules.

- Separate valid time (when it was true) from transaction time (when you believed it). Invalidate on contradiction by closing intervals and remembering the previous belief, never by deleting.

- As-of queries take a point on both axes. Put valid intervals and today's date into the prompt so the model can reason about time.

- Zep and Graphiti build this around episodes, bi-temporal edges, LLM contradiction checks and hybrid search; a relational database with range types and exclusion constraints can do the same.
