### From graph to answer

The graph gives you the set; the LLM turns it into an explanation (“generate_report calls data.get(...) on the result and has no try around the parse, so a raise there aborts report generation and, with it, build_index”). Context construction follows Chapter 22: a compact table of callers ranked by distance, then source excerpts for the closest ones, then the question. It uses the same LLM.complete(prompt, system=None, json=False) interface as the rest of minigraphrag.

```python  # code_qa.py
from pathlib import Path

from code_graph import build_code_graph, impact_of

REPO = Path("code")   # the directory that contains the package

CODE_QA_PROMPT = """You answer questions about a Python repository.
Use only the symbols and source excerpts below. Cite symbols by their qualified name.
If the context does not contain the answer, say what is missing.

---Target---
{target}

---Callers (distance: symbol, file:line)---
{callers}

---Source excerpts---
{excerpts}

---Question---
{question}"""


def source_of(G, qname: str, max_lines: int = 25) -> str:
    d = G.nodes[qname]
    lines = (REPO / d["file"]).read_text().splitlines()[d["lineno"] - 1 : d["end_lineno"]]
    body = "\n".join(lines[:max_lines]) + ("\n    ..." if len(lines) > max_lines else "")
    return f"# {qname} ({d['file']}:{d['lineno']})\n{body}"


def answer_impact_question(llm, G, target: str, question: str, max_excerpts: int = 4) -> str:
    impact = impact_of(G, target)
    callers = "\n".join(f"{k}: {n}, {G.nodes[n]['file']}:{G.nodes[n]['lineno']}" for n, k in impact.items())
    direct = [n for n, k in impact.items() if k == 1][:max_excerpts]   # closest callers first
    excerpts = "\n\n".join(source_of(G, n) for n in [target, *direct])
    prompt = CODE_QA_PROMPT.format(target=target, callers=callers or "(none found)",
                                   excerpts=excerpts, question=question)
    return llm.complete(prompt)
```

Budget matters here as much as anywhere: source excerpts are expensive. Ranking by distance and truncating each function to its first 25 lines keeps a 15-caller answer under a few thousand tokens. If you need more, rank distance-1 callers by how the return value is used (assigned and indexed vs. ignored) before including their full bodies.

### Where static call graphs lie

Our resolver returns None rather than guessing, which makes the gap measurable. On the same run the collector saw 1,507 call expressions and resolved 279 of them to package symbols. Most of the other 1,228 are harmless: len alone accounts for 88, then sorted, set, dict.get, str.join and NetworkX methods. But 17 of them were .complete(...) on an llm value. That parameter is typed as the LLM protocol, and the graph has no idea whether it will be MockLLM, CachedLLM or AnthropicLLM at run time. Ask the graph “what calls CachedLLM.complete?” and it answers “nothing”, which is exactly wrong.

Blind spot | Example | Mitigation

Dynamic dispatch through protocols or base classes | llm.complete(prompt) | Use type annotations: link calls on a parameter typed LLM to every class implementing complete, marked as a weaker MAY_CALL edge

Re-exports | from .search import local_search in __init__.py | Follow import chains until you reach a definition

Decorators, registries, callbacks | Functions registered in a dict and called by key | Add edges from registration sites; or fall back to runtime traces from the test suite

String-based and dynamic imports | importlib.import_module(name) | Flag as unresolved; do not pretend completeness

Staleness | The graph was built three commits ago | Store a content hash per file; re-parse only changed files on each commit (Chapter 27)

Language servers and type checkers such as pyright resolve much more than a hundred-line visitor, and tools like tree-sitter give you one parser interface across languages. The graph design stays the same; only pass two gets smarter.

**Report what you could not resolve

An impact answer that silently omits dynamic callers is worse than no answer, because it sounds complete. Keep the unresolved call texts on each node and have the answer say, for example, “3 call sites through the LLM protocol could not be resolved statically.”

### What the research systems add

Four papers show how far the idea goes, each at a different granularity.

**Ouyang et al., RepoGraph (2024)

RepoGraph is a plug-in module that manages a repository-level structure for AI software-engineering systems and serves them as repository-wide navigation. Plugged into four existing methods on SWE-bench, it improved all four and, by the abstract's account, produced a new state of the art among open-source frameworks; the authors also test it on CrossCodeEval. The design lesson: the graph plugs into an agent that already exists.

**Liu et al., CodexGraph (2024)

CodexGraph extracts a code graph into a graph database with a unified schema and lets an LLM agent write and run graph queries against it, instead of relying on similarity retrieval or task-specific tools. It is evaluated on CrossCodeEval, SWE-bench and EvoCodeBench. This is Text2Cypher applied to code, with all the validation lessons of that chapter.

**Liu et al., GraphCoder (2024) and Du et al., CodeGRAG (2024)

Both go below the function level. GraphCoder builds a code context graph of control flow and data and control dependence between statements, and uses coarse-to-fine retrieval to find context-similar snippets for repository-level code completion. CodeGRAG builds graphical views of code blocks from control and data flow, and injects them either as a structured prompt for tuning-free models or as soft prompts from a GNN expert. Statement-level graphs help generation; symbol-level graphs, like ours, help navigation and impact questions.

A CodexGraph-style query for impact analysis over the same schema, if you load it into Neo4j with qname as a property:

```python  # queries/impact.cypher
MATCH p = (caller:Function)-[:CALLS*1..3]->(f:Function {qname: $target})
RETURN caller.qname AS caller, caller.file AS file, min(length(p)) AS distance
ORDER BY distance, caller
LIMIT 50
```

### Evaluating a code graph assistant

Code gives you something no other domain does: a free, objective oracle. Pick commits from history that changed one function and broke tests. Predict the impact set before looking, then compare with the tests that actually failed. Precision and recall of the predicted affected tests are honest metrics. For question answering (“where is the chunk size configured?”), ground truth can come from the graph itself, and you can grade the LLM's explanation separately with a pairwise judge (Chapter 25). Capstone 2 builds this harness end to end.

## Medicine: trusted sources and safety

Clinical questions combine three kinds of knowledge that live in different places: facts about a specific patient (notes, labs, medication lists), general medical knowledge (guidelines, drug labels, papers) and definitions (controlled vocabularies such as SNOMED CT, RxNorm, ICD-10 and MeSH, which give every concept a stable code and an IS_A hierarchy). A medical GraphRAG system is mostly the work of linking these three layers so that an answer about a patient can be traced to an authoritative source.

### What the graph is

- Concept nodes keyed by vocabulary codes, not by surface strings. “Warfarin”, “Coumadin” and a misspelling in a note all resolve to one code. This is entity resolution done by a curated authority rather than by fuzzy matching.

- Hierarchy edges (IS_A) from the vocabulary: warfarin IS_A vitamin K antagonist IS_A anticoagulant. Retrieval uses these to find a guideline written about the class when the question names the drug.

- Knowledge edges (TREATS, CONTRAINDICATED_WITH, INTERACTS_WITH), each linked to the source passage that asserts it.

- Patient event nodes (a prescription on a date, a lab value, a diagnosis), linked to concepts and to the exact note span or record row they came from.

[Diagram]

The triple-linked structure described by Medical Graph RAG: entities from user documents are linked to credible sources, which are linked to controlled vocabulary definitions. The right-hand notes paraphrase the paper's U-Retrieval idea at a high level.

**Wu et al., Medical Graph RAG (2024)

MedGraphRAG proposes Triple Graph Construction, which connects user documents to credible medical sources and controlled vocabularies, and U-Retrieval, which combines top-down precise retrieval with bottom-up response refinement. The stated goal is safety: evidence-based answers that include source documentation and definitions. It is evaluated on nine medical QA benchmarks, two health fact-checking benchmarks and one dataset the authors collected themselves.

### Retrieval patterns

Two patterns matter more in medicine than elsewhere.

Expand up, not down. If the question is about warfarin, a guideline about anticoagulants applies, so walk IS_A edges upward from the question's concepts, with a small hop limit and a preference for closer ancestors. Walking downward is dangerous: a finding about warfarin does not apply to every anticoagulant. This is a metapath constraint (Chapter 21) with a safety reason behind it.

Seek evidence on both sides, then decide narrowly. A retrieved note that says “no evidence of bleeding” mentions bleeding; a lab value from last year is about the right patient but the wrong time; a forum post is on topic but not authoritative. Relevance is not admissibility. A 2026 system for longitudinal clinical records makes this explicit.

**Lin et al., Evidence-Admissible GraphRAG for clinical event verification (2026)

MedEventGraph-RAG represents event occurrences in a patient-specific graph linked to source evidence (structured rows, note spans, timestamps, numerical trajectories). It retrieves candidate event chains with evidence from both supporting and contradicting sides, filters that evidence through a query-specific contract (patient identity, scope, occurrence binding, source traceability), and has a separate assessor output supported, conflicting, refuted or insufficient. The authors argue that separating broad discovery from narrow assessment reduces unsupported conclusions.

Here is a teaching version of that contract. It is deliberately boring code: the safety comes from refusing to let the LLM see, or reason from, evidence that fails a deterministic check.

```python  # examples/medical_gate.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

@dataclass
class Evidence:
    text: str
    source_type: str              # "note", "lab", "guideline", "drug_label", "paper"
    source_uri: str | None        # where a clinician can read it
    patient_id: str | None = None # None for literature, labels and guidelines
    observed: date | None = None
    stance: str = "supports"      # "supports" or "contradicts" the claim being checked
    negated: bool = False         # "no evidence of bleeding" mentions bleeding but negates it

TRUSTED_GENERAL = {"guideline", "drug_label", "paper"}

def admissible(ev: Evidence, patient_id: str, window: tuple[date, date]) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    if not ev.source_uri:
        return False, "untraceable"
    if ev.patient_id is not None and ev.patient_id != patient_id:
        return False, "different patient"
    if ev.patient_id is None and ev.source_type not in TRUSTED_GENERAL:
        return False, "untrusted general source"
    if ev.patient_id is not None and ev.observed and not (window[0] <= ev.observed <= window[1]):
        return False, "outside time window"
    return True, "ok"

def decide(evidence: list[Evidence], patient_id: str, window: tuple[date, date]):
    admitted = [e for e in evidence if admissible(e, patient_id, window)[0]]
    support = [e for e in admitted if e.stance == "supports" and not e.negated]
    against = [e for e in admitted if e.stance == "contradicts" or e.negated]
    if not admitted:
        return "insufficient", []
    if support and against:
        return "conflicting", admitted
    return ("supported" if support else "refuted"), admitted
```

The LLM still does the hard parts: deciding stance, detecting negation and hedging (“possible”, “ruled out”), and writing the explanation. But the verdict categories and the admissibility rules are code you can test and audit.

[Interactive figure: A safety-gated clinical answer (flow)]

### Evaluation and pitfalls

Benchmarks such as medical multiple-choice QA test knowledge, not safety. For a deployed system, measure: citation validity (does every cited span exist and say what the answer claims?), abstention quality (on questions with deliberately missing evidence, does it say “insufficient”?), and clinician agreement on a sample, with disagreements triaged by cause. The pitfalls are sharp:

- Negation and uncertainty turn mentions into their opposites. Extraction must carry a polarity attribute, and retrieval must treat negated mentions as contradicting evidence.

- Stale knowledge. Guidelines are revised. Treat guideline versions as temporal facts (Chapter 27) and prefer the current version explicitly.

- The model's own knowledge. A strong LLM will “helpfully” fill gaps from pretraining. The prompt should require every claim to cite a context item, and a post-check should flag uncited sentences.

- Privacy. Patient graphs are protected health information. Per-patient partitioning and access control on nodes, edges and summaries are requirements, not options; Chapter 29 covers how summaries leak across access boundaries.

## Finance: filings, tables and time

Financial questions are entity-heavy, table-heavy and time-bound. “How did segment revenue change between fiscal 2023 and 2024, and what did management say caused it?” needs the right company, the right two periods, a number from a table in each filing, a calculation, and a passage from the narrative section. Chunking a 10-K into 300-token windows destroys most of what makes that answerable: tables split across chunks, section headings lost, fiscal years detached from numbers.

### What the graph is

Two graphs, joined by entity nodes:

- An evidence graph of the documents. Filing → section → text unit or table unit, with metadata nodes for company and fiscal year. This is a lexical graph (Chapter 6) that preserves the structure financial documents already have.

- A domain graph of entities and facts. Companies, subsidiaries, officers and directors, investors, and metric facts. A metric fact is not an edge but a node with attributes: value, unit, scale, period start and end, whether it is restated, and the table cell it came from.

[Diagram]

Retrieval follows document, section, unit paths instead of free-floating chunks, and every number carries its unit, scale, period and cell. The company here is a placeholder; Kestrel Labs is private and does not file annual reports.

**Chen et al., HC-RAG (2026)

HC-RAG organizes filings into a typed financial evidence graph with document, section, text unit, table unit and metadata nodes. It retrieves through document-section-unit paths, aligns text and table evidence in a shared retrieval space, and routes evidence by query intent: calculation, trend, fact or comparison. The authors also release Multi-Doc-2025, 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs over 179 SEC 10-K filings from 87 S&P 500 companies across fiscal years 2022 to 2024, labelled with intent, difficulty and structural evidence attributes. They report better answer quality and evidence localization, with the largest gains in long-document, table-related and cross-document settings.

**Sarmah et al., HybridRAG (2024)

HybridRAG combines knowledge-graph retrieval with vector retrieval for question answering over financial earnings call transcripts, motivated by domain terminology and complex document formats that trouble vector-only RAG. Evaluated on transcripts that already come as question-and-answer pairs, it reports that the combination beats either retriever alone at both the retrieval and the generation stage. It is an early, concrete example of the hybrid pattern from Chapter 21 in a financial setting.

### Temporal facts and the double-counting trap

The Kestrel corpus has a tiny financial subgraph that already shows the main modeling trap. Brightwater Capital led a $12M Series A in March 2022 and a $40M Series B in September 2025, and the Series A also had two angel groups participating. If you store the amount on each investor's INVESTED_IN edge, adding the angels means summing edges counts $12M three times. Make the round a node that holds the amount and date; investors connect to the round, and the round connects to the company. This is the n-ary fact problem of Chapter 31 showing up with money attached.

```python  # examples/funding_facts.py
import networkx as nx
from datetime import date

G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
G.add_node("KESTREL LABS", type="ORGANIZATION")
G.add_node("BRIGHTWATER CAPITAL", type="ORGANIZATION")
rounds = [
    ("round:kestrel-series-a", "Series A", 12_000_000, date(2022, 3, 15), "02_brightwater_series_a"),
    ("round:kestrel-series-b", "Series B", 40_000_000, date(2025, 9, 23), "10_brightwater_series_b"),
]
for rid, name, amount, when, doc in rounds:
    # One node per round: the amount lives on the round, not on each investor edge.
    G.add_node(rid, type="FUNDING_ROUND", name=name, amount_usd=amount, date=when, source_doc=doc)
    G.add_edge(rid, "KESTREL LABS", key="RAISED_BY")
    G.add_edge("BRIGHTWATER CAPITAL", rid, key="LED")

def total_raised(G, company: str, as_of: date) -> int:
    return sum(G.nodes[r]["amount_usd"] for r, _, k in G.in_edges(company, keys=True)
               if k == "RAISED_BY" and G.nodes[r]["date"] <= as_of)

print(total_raised(G, "KESTREL LABS", date(2023, 1, 1)))    # 12000000
print(total_raised(G, "KESTREL LABS", date(2025, 12, 31)))  # 52000000
```

The as-of query returns $52M at the end of 2025, which matches the Series B press release's own statement of total funding raised. That agreement is a useful consistency check: when a document states an aggregate, compare it with the aggregate your graph computes, and flag disagreements for review.

### Retrieval, evaluation and pitfalls

Route by intent, as HC-RAG does. A fact question (“who chairs the audit committee?”) is a local lookup. A calculation (“what was the operating margin?”) should retrieve the two table cells and hand the arithmetic to code, not the LLM. A trend question needs the same metric across periods, which is an as-of query repeated. A comparison needs balanced retrieval across companies, so that one company's detailed filing does not crowd out the other in the token budget.

Evaluate numbers with exact match after normalizing unit and scale, with a small relative tolerance for rounding, and score evidence localization separately: did the system cite the right table and period? A right number from the wrong year is a lucky failure.

- Units and scale. Tables state “in thousands” once in a header. Carry scale into every fact at extraction time.

- Fiscal vs. calendar periods. A fiscal 2024 that ends in June is not calendar 2024. Store period start and end dates, not labels.

- Restatements. A later filing may revise an earlier number. Both are true facts about different reports; the bi-temporal model of Chapter 27 (valid time vs. reported time) handles this directly.

- Entity identity. Subsidiaries, former names and tickers. Resolve to registry identifiers where available rather than names.

## Law: citation graphs and precedent

Legal research is graph traversal that lawyers have done by hand for centuries. Statutes are interpreted by cases; cases cite earlier cases; and each citation has a treatment. A later court may follow a precedent, distinguish it (agree with the rule but find the facts different), criticize it, or, if it has the authority, overrule it. Citators exist precisely to answer “is this case still good law?” A legal GraphRAG system that retrieves by similarity alone will happily quote a well-written opinion that was overruled last year.

### What the graph is

- Nodes: cases (with court, jurisdiction and decision date), statutes and their sections, regulations, and optionally holdings extracted from opinions.

- Edges: CITES with a treatment attribute (FOLLOWS, DISTINGUISHES, OVERRULES, REVERSES), INTERPRETS from a case to a statute section, APPEAL_OF between decisions in the same matter, and a court hierarchy that decides who can overrule whom.

- Sources: citation strings are highly regular and can be parsed deterministically; court and date come from metadata. The treatment of a citation is the part that needs an LLM (or a human editor), because it lives in the prose around the citation.

The example below is invented for this chapter and is not part of the Kestrel corpus. It asks a question the Port Avalon City Council, which contracted Kestrel Labs for Ocean Health Act compliance monitoring, might plausibly ask its lawyers.

[Interactive figure: Following a citation chain, and checking it is still good law — Fictional cases interpreting the Ocean Health Act (graph-steps)]

### Ranking by authority

Ranking legal sources mixes three signals that similarity search does not see:

- Validity: a hard filter. Overruled or reversed decisions are never presented as supporting authority. They may still be retrieved, labeled, to explain history.

- Binding force: decisions from higher courts in the same jurisdiction bind lower ones; other jurisdictions are only persuasive. This is a path constraint over the court hierarchy.

- Influence and recency: how often and how recently a case is followed. PageRank over the citation graph (Chapter 17) is a reasonable influence prior, but raw citation counts favor old cases, and negative citations also count as citations. Weight edges by treatment before running it.

In Cypher, the good-law filter is a negative pattern over incoming edges:

```python  # queries/good_law.cypher
MATCH (c:Case)-[:INTERPRETS]->(:Section {id: $section})
WHERE NOT EXISTS {
  MATCH (later:Case)-[t:CITES]->(c)
  WHERE t.treatment IN ['OVERRULES', 'REVERSES']
    AND later.court_level >= c.court_level
    AND later.decided >= c.decided
}
RETURN c.name, c.court, c.decided
ORDER BY c.court_level DESC, c.decided DESC
```

### Evaluation and pitfalls

The first metric is citation existence: every cited authority must exist and be quoted accurately, which you can check deterministically against the graph. The second is citation validity: no bad law presented as support. The third, holding accuracy, needs expert review on a sample. Pitfalls:

- Holding vs. dicta. An opinion says many things; only the holding binds. Extraction prompts should separate them and cite paragraph numbers.

- Jurisdiction mixing. A persuasive out-of-jurisdiction case ranked above a binding local one is a wrong answer even if every sentence is true.

- Treatment extraction errors. Misreading “declined to follow” as “followed” flips validity. Treat LLM-extracted treatments as claims with confidence, and prefer editorial citator data where you have it.

- Time. “Good law” is as of a date. Store decision dates and answer as of the question's date, rather than assuming today.

## Other domains: threat intelligence, science and support

### Cyber threat intelligence

Threat reports describe attackers, malware, techniques, infrastructure and indicators such as IP addresses and file hashes. A natural schema maps these to a standard vocabulary: MITRE ATT&CK for tactics and techniques, CVE identifiers for vulnerabilities. The interesting design question is which facts to retrieve. Indicators are trivial to extract but easy for attackers to rotate; behaviors and techniques are harder to extract but durable. Security teams call this ordering the Pyramid of Pain.

**Kabra et al., Operationalizing Cyber Threat Intelligence with GraphRAG (2026)

The authors fed threat reports into Microsoft GraphRAG and into a vector-only RAG with the same model and instructions, and asked both to write detection plans. In a detailed case study of one APT28 report, the GraphRAG plan kept firing on all of its detections after every IP address, domain and file hash was rotated, while the vector RAG plan kept 29%. Across nine reports from four vendors, GraphRAG plans consistently reached higher, harder-to-evade levels of the pyramid, even when the two systems ended up close on total score. They also found that the wording of the generation prompt mattered almost as much as the retrieval back end.

### Scientific literature

Papers form a citation graph, and research questions often need to combine a claim in one paper with the method in a paper it cites. The lexical-plus-domain design of this course applies directly, with one twist: citations carry context (the sentence around a citation says why it is cited), which is a free edge description.

**Hu et al., CG-RAG (2025)

CG-RAG proposes a contextual graph representation of citation graphs that captures explicit and implicit connections within and across documents, and Lexical-Semantic Graph Retrieval (LeSeGR), which integrates sparse and dense retrieval signals with graph encoding. It targets research question answering and reports gains over RAG combined with a range of retrieval methods.

### Customer support

Support tickets have internal structure (summary, steps to reproduce, resolution) and relations between tickets (duplicates, clones, “caused by”). Xu et al. build a knowledge graph from historical issues that keeps both the intra-issue structure and the inter-issue relations, then retrieve sub-graphs for new customer queries. Their abstract reports a 77.6% improvement in MRR over the baseline and, after about six months in production at LinkedIn's customer service team, a 28.6% drop in median per-issue resolution time. It is a reminder that “structure-aware chunking” (Chapter 7) and a domain graph are often the same design decision.

## What transfers from Kestrel, and a checklist for a new domain

Almost every technique in this course survives the move to a specialized domain. What changes is which technique does the heavy lifting.

Kestrel technique | Code | Medicine | Finance | Law

LLM extraction (Ch. 8) | Mostly replaced by the parser; used for docs and issues | Notes and papers, with polarity | Narrative sections and calls | Treatments and holdings

Entity resolution (Ch. 9) | Symbol resolution | Vocabulary codes | Registry identifiers, tickers | Citation normalization

Claims and time (Ch. 10, 27) | Commit history | Event dates, guideline versions | Periods, restatements | Decision dates, good law as of

Communities and reports (Ch. 11, 12) | Package and subsystem summaries | Topic summaries per condition | Sector or segment summaries | Doctrine area summaries

Local search (Ch. 14) | Symbol neighborhood | Patient timeline around a concept | Company profile | Case with its citing cases

Paths and PPR (Ch. 17, 18) | Reverse reachability for impact | Upward IS_A expansion | Ownership chains | Citation chains, influence

Text2Cypher (Ch. 20) | CodexGraph-style agents | Cohort queries over coded data | Metric lookups | Good-law filters

**Checklist before you build a domain graph

1. List twenty real questions users ask, and mark which need multi-hop, global, temporal or numeric reasoning. 2. For each node and edge type the questions need, write down its cheapest trustworthy source: parser, curated identifier, metadata, or LLM. 3. Decide the identifier for “the same thing” before extracting anything. 4. Decide what the system does when evidence is missing or conflicting. 5. Find the domain's free oracle (tests, citators, stated totals, clinician review) and build evaluation on it first.

## Exercises

#### Exercise 32.1 Warm-up

A small repository has these CALLS edges (caller → callee): cli.main → index.run, index.run → extract.parse, index.run → chunk.split, index.run → report.build, report.build → context.fit, query.local → context.fit, query.global → report.load, test_parse → extract.parse. By hand, compute the impact set of changing context.fit, with distances. Which tests would you run, and what does the result tell you about the test suite?

▸ Show answer

Reverse the edges and run BFS from context.fit:

- Distance 1: report.build, query.local (both call context.fit directly).

- Distance 2: index.run (calls report.build). Nothing calls query.local.

- Distance 3: cli.main (calls index.run).

Impact set: {report.build: 1, query.local: 1, index.run: 2, cli.main: 3}. Not affected: extract.parse, chunk.split, query.global, report.load. extract.parse and chunk.split are called by an affected function, which is the wrong direction: a change to context.fit cannot break code that index.run calls.

The only test, test_parse, reaches extract.parse, which is not in the impact set, so no existing test exercises the change. The graph has just told you something valuable: context.fit is untested along every path. Write a test for query.local or report.build before refactoring.

#### Exercise 32.2 Core

Extend the code graph to select tests. Parse the package and its tests/ directory into one graph, and write tests_to_run(G, target) that returns the test functions whose code transitively reaches target. Make sure a test that reaches the target through a helper function is included.

▸ Hint

build_code_graph already accepts several directories and resolves calls across all of them in pass two. A test that calls a helper that calls the target is just another node in the reverse BFS.

▸ Show answer

```python
from code_graph import build_code_graph, impact_of

def tests_to_run(G, target: str) -> list[str]:
    if target not in G:
        raise KeyError(f"unknown symbol: {target}")
    affected = set(impact_of(G, target)) | {target}
    return sorted(n for n in affected
                  if G.nodes[n]["kind"] == "function" and G.nodes[n]["name"].startswith("test_"))

G = build_code_graph("code/minigraphrag", "code/tests")
print(tests_to_run(G, "minigraphrag.llm.parse_json_response"))
```

Run against the course repository while this chapter was written, it selected six tests, including tests.test_llm.test_parse_json_response_handles_fences, tests.test_reports.test_generate_report_structure and the end-to-end CLI test in tests.test_search_e2e. We also checked a small synthetic test module containing test_parse_fenced (calls parse_json_response directly), test_report (calls a helper that calls generate_report, which calls the target) and test_unrelated. For that module the result was ['tests.test_llm.test_parse_fenced', 'tests.test_llm.test_report']: the helper path is found because reverse BFS does not care whether an intermediate node is a test. Two caveats to state in your tool's output: pytest fixtures are called by the framework, not by the test body, so a target reached only through a fixture is missed; and calls through llm.complete are unresolved, so tests that exercise a specific LLM class through the protocol are missed. Running the full suite nightly covers both gaps.

#### Exercise 32.3 Core

Using the funding model from the finance section, answer by hand and then in code: (a) the total raised by Kestrel Labs as of 1 January 2023 and as of 31 December 2025; (b) what the total as of 31 December 2025 would be if you had instead stored amount_usd on INVESTED_IN edges and recorded Brightwater plus the two angel groups as Series A investors; (c) a validation rule that would have caught (b).

▸ Show answer

(a) As of 2023-01-01 only the Series A (15 March 2022) counts: $12M. As of 2025-12-31 both rounds count: $12M + $40M = $52M, which matches the Series B press release's statement that total funding reached $52 million. The code in the chapter prints 12000000 and 52000000.

(b) Series A would appear on three edges with $12M each, $36M, plus Series B on Brightwater's edge, $40M: $76M. It overstates by $24M, and adding more participants makes it worse. (If Series B also had edges for the two new infrastructure funds the corpus mentions, it would be $156M.)

(c) Two rules. Structural: amounts belong to round nodes, and investor edges carry only role (led, participated). Numeric: whenever a document states an aggregate (“brings total funding raised to $52 million”), extract it as a claim and compare it with the computed aggregate; flag any difference beyond rounding.

```python
def check_stated_total(G, company, stated_usd, as_of, tolerance=0.01):
    computed = total_raised(G, company, as_of)
    ok = abs(computed - stated_usd) <= tolerance * stated_usd
    return ok, computed
```

#### Exercise 32.4 Core

Write citator_status(G, case) for the fictional citation graph in the legal visualization. It should return “bad law” if a decision from the same or a higher court, decided in the same year or later, overrules or reverses the case; “caution” if the case follows a case that is bad law; otherwise “good law”, plus a list of reasons such as distinguishing cases. Run it on all five cases.

▸ Show answer

```python
import networkx as nx

LEVEL = {"trial": 1, "appeal": 2, "supreme": 3}
NEGATIVE = {"OVERRULES": "overruled", "REVERSES": "reversed"}

def citator_status(G: nx.MultiDiGraph, case: str) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    d = G.nodes[case]
    reasons = []
    for citing, _, e in G.in_edges(case, data=True):
        c = G.nodes[citing]
        if (e["treatment"] in NEGATIVE and LEVEL[c["court"]] >= LEVEL[d["court"]]
                and c["year"] >= d["year"]):
            return "bad law", [f"{NEGATIVE[e['treatment']]} by {citing} ({c['year']})"]
        if e["treatment"] == "DISTINGUISHES":
            reasons.append(f"distinguished by {citing}")
    for _, cited, e in G.out_edges(case, data=True):
        if e["treatment"] == "FOLLOWS" and citator_status(G, cited)[0] == "bad law":
            reasons.append(f"relies on {cited}, which is bad law")
    return ("caution" if any("relies on" in r for r in reasons) else "good law"), reasons

G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
for name, court, year in [("Avalon Anglers v. City", "trial", 2025),
                          ("Coastal Trust v. Harbor Board", "trial", 2025),
                          ("Reef Guardians v. City", "appeal", 2026),
                          ("Seaway Marina v. City", "trial", 2026),
                          ("Harbor Pilots v. City", "trial", 2026)]:
    G.add_node(name, kind="case", court=court, year=year)
G.add_node("Ocean Health Act s.4", kind="statute")
for src, dst, t in [("Avalon Anglers v. City", "Ocean Health Act s.4", "INTERPRETS"),
                    ("Reef Guardians v. City", "Ocean Health Act s.4", "INTERPRETS"),
                    ("Coastal Trust v. Harbor Board", "Avalon Anglers v. City", "FOLLOWS"),
                    ("Reef Guardians v. City", "Avalon Anglers v. City", "OVERRULES"),
                    ("Seaway Marina v. City", "Reef Guardians v. City", "FOLLOWS"),
                    ("Harbor Pilots v. City", "Reef Guardians v. City", "DISTINGUISHES")]:
    G.add_edge(src, dst, key=t, treatment=t)

for n, d in G.nodes(data=True):
    if d["kind"] == "case":
        print(n, citator_status(G, n))
```

Output:

```python
Avalon Anglers v. City ('bad law', ['overruled by Reef Guardians v. City (2026)'])
Coastal Trust v. Harbor Board ('caution', ['relies on Avalon Anglers v. City, which is bad law'])
Reef Guardians v. City ('good law', ['distinguished by Harbor Pilots v. City'])
Seaway Marina v. City ('good law', [])
Harbor Pilots v. City ('good law', [])
```

Two design notes. The court-level check matters: a trial court cannot overrule an appellate decision, so an extracted “OVERRULES” edge from a lower court is an extraction error to flag, not a validity signal. And the recursion in the caution rule can loop on cyclic citation data (rare but possible with same-day decisions); add a visited set in production.

#### Exercise 32.5 Stretch

Implement upward concept expansion for medical retrieval. Given a vocabulary graph with IS_A edges (warfarin → vitamin K antagonist → anticoagulant; apixaban → factor Xa inhibitor → anticoagulant) and guidelines indexed by concept (g1: anticoagulant, g2: apixaban, g3: vitamin K antagonist), return the guidelines applicable to a question about warfarin, most specific first. Then explain, with an example, why the same function must never expand downward.

▸ Show answer

```python
import networkx as nx

V = nx.DiGraph()   # edge child -> parent means child IS_A parent
V.add_edges_from([("warfarin", "vitamin K antagonist"), ("vitamin K antagonist", "anticoagulant"),
                  ("apixaban", "factor Xa inhibitor"), ("factor Xa inhibitor", "anticoagulant")])
guidelines = {"g1": {"anticoagulant"}, "g2": {"apixaban"}, "g3": {"vitamin K antagonist"}}

def expand_up(V, concept: str, max_hops: int = 3) -> dict[str, int]:
    if concept not in V:
        return {concept: 0}
    return nx.single_source_shortest_path_length(V, concept, cutoff=max_hops)

def guidelines_for(V, concept: str) -> list[str]:
    up = expand_up(V, concept)          # {'warfarin': 0, 'vitamin K antagonist': 1, 'anticoagulant': 2}
    hits = [(min(up[c] for c in cs if c in up), g) for g, cs in guidelines.items() if cs & up.keys()]
    return [g for _, g in sorted(hits)]

print(guidelines_for(V, "warfarin"))    # ['g3', 'g1']
```

Warfarin reaches “vitamin K antagonist” at distance 1 and “anticoagulant” at distance 2, so g3 (more specific) ranks before g1, and g2 is correctly excluded. Following edges out of the child is what makes the walk upward.

Why never downward: expanding “anticoagulant” down would retrieve g2, a guideline written about apixaban specifically, for a question about anticoagulants in general or, via a sibling path, about warfarin. Drug-specific guidance (dosing, reversal agents, monitoring such as INR for warfarin) does not transfer to siblings. Upward expansion applies general rules to specific cases, which is sound; downward or sideways expansion applies specific rules to other cases, which is exactly the kind of plausible, dangerous error a medical system must not make. Record the expansion distance in the context so the answer can say “this guidance is for the drug class.”

## Check your understanding

Why can a code graph's CALLS edges be built without an LLM, while Kestrel's ACQUIRED edges cannot?

- Code is shorter than news articles

- LLMs cannot read code

- ✓ (correct) Calls are explicit in the syntax tree and can be recovered by a parser; acquisitions exist only as statements in prose

- Graph databases only support code schemas
Answer: The compiler's grammar already structures code, so a parser extracts relationships exactly. Natural-language facts have no such grammar, which is why Chapter 8 needed extraction prompts.

In the impact visualization, drift_search calls both parse_json_response and local_search. Is local_search in the impact set of a change to parse_json_response?

- ✓ (correct) No: it is called by an affected function but does not itself reach the target

- Yes: it is two hops away in the undirected graph

- Yes: every neighbor of an affected function is affected

- Only if it is in the same module
Answer: Impact follows CALLS edges backwards from the target. Undirected neighborhood expansion, which is fine for Kestrel's local search, gives wrong answers here.

A clinical note says “no evidence of GI bleeding.” How should a medical GraphRAG system treat it when checking whether the patient had a bleed?

- As supporting evidence, since it mentions GI bleeding

- Ignore it, since negated sentences carry no information

- As supporting evidence with low confidence

- ✓ (correct) As admissible contradicting evidence, carried with a negation flag and its source span
Answer: A negated mention is evidence against the claim. Similarity search ranks it highly because the words match; polarity must be extracted and used when deciding.

Your finance graph reports total Series A funding of $36M for a $12M round. What is the most likely modeling error?

- The embedding model confused Series A and Series B

- ✓ (correct) The round amount was stored on each investor edge and summed across three participants

- The fiscal year was wrong

- The LLM hallucinated two extra rounds
Answer: An n-ary fact (round, company, investors, amount, date) was flattened into binary edges. Model the round as a node that holds the amount.

Two trial court decisions agree on an interpretation of a statute, and both are highly similar to the question. What must a legal GraphRAG system check before citing them?

- That their embeddings are above a similarity threshold

- That they have the highest PageRank in the citation graph

- ✓ (correct) Incoming citations with negative treatment from courts with authority to overrule them

- That they were decided in the same year
Answer: Validity is decided by later treatment, found on incoming CITES edges, and constrained by the court hierarchy. Similarity and influence are ranking signals, not validity checks.

In the cyber threat intelligence study by Kabra et al., what distinguished GraphRAG's detection plans from vector RAG's?

- They contained more IP addresses and file hashes

- They were produced by a larger language model

- They required no prompt at all

- ✓ (correct) They relied more on durable, higher-level behaviors, so they kept firing after indicators were rotated
Answer: Both systems used the same model and instructions. GraphRAG plans reached higher levels of the Pyramid of Pain, and the authors report that prompt wording mattered a great deal.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Should I still embed code chunks if I have a call graph?

Yes. The graph answers structural questions (who calls, what inherits, what imports), and embeddings answer conceptual ones (“where do we handle rate limits?”) where the user does not know a symbol name. The usual pattern is hybrid: embed function bodies and docstrings, use vector or BM25 search to find seed symbols, then expand over the graph. That is local search (Chapter 14) with symbols as entities.

▸ Do I need a medical vocabulary license to build this?

Some vocabularies are freely available and others require a license or an agreement depending on your country and use. Check the terms before you ship. For prototyping, a small hand-built IS_A hierarchy for the drugs and conditions in your test questions is enough to validate the retrieval logic, as in Exercise 32.5.

▸ Can an LLM do the arithmetic in financial answers if I give it the right table cells?

It often gets simple arithmetic right, but “often” is the wrong standard for numbers someone will act on. Have the LLM produce the formula and the cell references, compute the result in code, and put both the formula and the result in the answer. This also makes answers auditable.

▸ Should domain graphs use community reports and global search at all?

Sometimes. Package-level summaries of a large repository, sector summaries across many filings, and doctrine-area summaries in law are useful for orientation questions. But domain users ask more precise questions than “what are the themes?”, and summaries lose the exact provenance these domains require. Build local, path and query-based retrieval first; add community reports when you see orientation questions in your logs.

▸ How do I keep a code graph current as the repository changes?

Hash each file's contents. On each commit, re-parse only changed files, delete their old definition nodes and outgoing edges, re-add them, and then re-run pass two for calls into the changed files from unchanged ones, since a renamed function breaks resolution elsewhere. This is the incremental update pattern of Chapter 27 with a parser instead of an LLM, so it is cheap enough to run in CI.

### Project: an impact bot for your own repository

Turn the code graph into a tool that comments on a change before it is merged. This is the foundation you will extend in Capstone 2.

- codegraph build <dirs> writes the graph as JSON (nodes with file and line ranges, edges with relation and call line)

- codegraph impact <qualified name> prints callers by distance and lists unresolved call sites that might hide more callers

- A git diff mode: map changed line ranges to the functions that contain them, then union their impact sets and select tests

- An LLM explanation step using LLM.complete with the caller table and the closest callers' source, citing file and line

- An evaluation over 10 historical commits that broke tests: precision and recall of predicted affected tests against the tests that actually failed

Done when the bot's test selection catches the failing tests in most of your historical commits, and you can explain each miss by a specific blind spot from the table in this chapter.

## Key takeaways

- The GraphRAG skeleton transfers unchanged; what changes is where edges come from, what counts as the same entity, and what a wrong answer costs.

- Parse what is parseable and link to curated identifiers; spend LLM extraction only on relations that live in prose.

- Code graphs answer impact questions with reverse reachability, but static resolution misses dynamic dispatch, so report what you could not resolve.

- Medicine needs trusted-source linking, upward-only concept expansion, evidence on both sides and a deterministic admissibility gate that can abstain.

- Finance needs typed document structure, n-ary fact nodes with units and periods, and arithmetic done in code.

- Law needs treatment-labeled citation edges and a good-law check before anything is cited; relevance is not authority.

## The research map

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/33-research-map.html
Summary: A taxonomy of the field, key papers by stage, benchmarks, and open problems in 2026.

# The research map

Hundreds of GraphRAG papers have appeared since 2023, and more arrive every week. This chapter gives you a map to place each one on, a timeline of the milestones, the directions the 2026 papers are pushing, and a checklist for deciding whether a result is worth building on.

## You will be able to

- Place any GraphRAG paper in a three-stage taxonomy: knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval and knowledge integration

- Trace the field's milestones from Think-on-Graph and From Local to Global to the 2026 work on cost, time, provenance and modality

- Summarize what the 2026 papers claim, using only what their abstracts actually say

- Read a GraphRAG paper critically with a checklist covering baselines, cost, leakage, judges and statistics

- Set up a weekly routine to keep up with the literature without drowning in it

## Why you need a map

By now you have built every major piece of GraphRAG yourself: extraction and resolution (Chapters 8 and 9), communities and reports (11 and 12), local, global, PPR and path retrieval (14 to 19), evaluation (25) and agents with memory (30). The research literature is the same set of ideas recombined, pushed further, and occasionally renamed.

Without a map, every new paper looks like a new system you have to learn from scratch. With one, most papers reduce to a sentence: “a new way to build the index,” “a new policy for walking the graph,” or “a new way to feed the retrieved subgraph to the model.” That sentence tells you which chapter's code it would change, which baseline it should beat, and whether it matters for your use case.

### Three surveys, three framings

Three surveys from late 2024 and early 2025 are the standard entry points. They slice the same field differently, and it helps to know all three because papers borrow their vocabulary.

Survey | How it divides the pipeline | Most useful for

Peng et al., Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey (2408.08921) | Graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval, graph-enhanced generation; also downstream tasks, evaluation and industrial use | A first formal description of the workflow and the training methods at each stage

Han et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Graphs (GraphRAG) (2501.00309) | Components: query processor, retriever, organizer, generator, data source; then techniques per domain | Seeing how GraphRAG designs differ by domain; its abstract argues that graphs in different domains have distinct relational patterns and need dedicated designs

Zhang et al., A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized LLMs (2501.13958) | Knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, knowledge integration | Its companion list, DEEP-PolyU/Awesome-GraphRAG, which uses the same headings

This chapter uses the third framing because the curated list that follows it gives you a live, categorized feed. The mapping to the course is direct: Part 2 is knowledge organization, Part 3 is knowledge retrieval, Part 4 is knowledge integration.

**One paper, several boxes

Many papers span categories. The curated list files Think-on-Graph under “GraphRAG with existing KGs,” “logical reasoning-based retriever,” “LLM-based retriever” and “graph-enhanced chain of thought,” because it does all four. When you need a single place for a paper, use its main contribution: the component its ablation shows matters.

## Knowledge organization: what the graph is for

The first question to ask about any system is what role the graph plays. The distinction is subtle and it predicts almost everything else about the design.

[Diagram]

The same Kestrel corpus can be organized three ways. In the index role, the edge between Marlow Dynamics and Deepcast only helps you find the passage about the acquisition. In the carrier role, the edge itself is evidence. Hybrids keep both.

### Graphs for knowledge indexing

Here the graph is a navigation structure over the original text. RAPTOR builds a tree of recursive summaries over chunks; HippoRAG 2 links phrase nodes to passage nodes so a PageRank walk ends on passages; LinearRAG argues that relation extraction is the unstable, expensive step and builds its graph without it, for large corpora. The retrieved unit is still a passage, so answers inherit the passages' fidelity and citations come for free. The weakness is that the graph can only be as good as the co-occurrence or similarity signals used to link nodes.

### Graphs as knowledge carriers

Here the graph is the knowledge. The list splits this in two. Graphs built from a corpus is Microsoft's From Local to Global (entity graph, communities, reports), GraphReader, Medical Graph RAG, PathRAG and Youtu-GraphRAG; this is what you built in Part 2. GraphRAG with existing knowledge graphs is the older KGQA tradition: Think-on-Graph, Think-on-Graph 2.0 and Reasoning on Graphs walk Freebase or Wikidata. The strength is compact, composable evidence. The weakness is extraction error: a wrong edge is a wrong fact, and nothing in the retrieved context reveals it.

A newer strand questions whether you should build the graph ahead of time at all. You Don't Need Pre-built Graphs for RAG (2508.06105, the method is called LogicRAG) argues that corpus-to-graph conversion costs tokens and update latency, and that a fixed graph may not match the reasoning structure a particular query needs. Instead it decomposes each query into sub-problems, builds a directed acyclic graph of their dependencies at inference time, and retrieves for them in topological order. AutoGraph-R1 (2510.15339) goes the other way: it keeps the pre-built graph but trains the constructor with reinforcement learning, rewarding graphs by how well they serve a downstream RAG pipeline, with separate rewards for the carrier and index roles.

### Hybrid GraphRAG

Hybrids treat the graph and the text as complementary. KG²RAG retrieves seed chunks semantically, then expands and organizes them using the knowledge graph. HybGRAG answers questions that need both textual and relational knowledge bases. CodexGraph puts a code repository into a graph database and lets the model query it. Capstones 2 and 4 are hybrids in exactly this sense.

## Knowledge retrieval: how the graph is searched

Given a graph, the second question is how a query becomes a subgraph, a path set or a list of passages. The curated list uses seven retriever families. The explorer below shows every family with representative papers, placed where the list files them except where a note says otherwise, plus pointers to the chapter where you implemented the idea.

[Interactive figure: GraphRAG taxonomy explorer — Click a category to see its papers; use the buttons to filter by stage (ch33-taxonomy)]

### What the seven families trade off

Family | Query-time LLM calls | Main strength | Main risk | Where you built it

Similarity-based | 0 to 1 | Fast, cheap, easy to cache | Misses bridge entities that do not resemble the query | Ch 14, 19

Logical reasoning | Few | Interpretable paths, precise on KGs with typed relations | Brittle when relations are free text or the schema is incomplete | Ch 18, 20

LLM-based | One per step, batch or community | Handles vague and global questions | Cost and latency grow with graph size; the LLM's judgment is a black box | Ch 15, 16

GNN-based | 0 for retrieval | Learns multi-hop relevance, fast at inference | Needs training data; may not transfer across graphs | Ch 19

Multi-round | Several rounds | Recovers from a bad first retrieval | Loops, drift and unbounded cost without a stopping rule | Ch 30

Post-retrieval | 1 or more | Faithfulness: removes unsupported evidence before generation | Adds a stage that can drop the one fact you needed | Ch 23

Hybrid | Varies | Covers more question types | More moving parts to tune and evaluate | Ch 21

Map the canonical Kestrel questions onto these families and the trade-offs become concrete. “What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?” is a path question: logical or PPR retrieval finds PRIYA NAIR → MARLOW DYNAMICS → DEEPCAST with zero or one LLM call. “What are the main themes in this corpus?” has no path to find; only an LLM-based map-reduce over community reports answers it, at one call per batch of reports. “Why did Kestrel Labs start Project Tern?” sits in between and is where multi-round and hybrid retrievers earn their cost.

## Knowledge integration: how evidence reaches the model

The third stage is how retrieved graph knowledge changes what the model generates. There are two broad routes.

### Fine-tuning

Fine-tuning methods change the model's weights so it can consume graph structure directly. The list groups them by granularity. Node-level methods such as GraphGPT tune the model on instructions about individual nodes and their attributes. Path-level methods train on sequences: Reasoning on Graphs tunes the model to generate relation paths that are then instantiated in the KG, and MuseGraph turns graphs into compact descriptions for instruction tuning. Subgraph-level methods such as LLaGA encode whole neighborhoods into the model's input space. Since 2025 a related line trains the retrieval policy rather than the reader with reinforcement learning: Graph-R1 frames retrieval as a multi-turn agent-environment interaction with an end-to-end reward, and AutoGraph-R1 trains the graph constructor. Chapter 24 covers these.

### In-context learning

Most production systems never fine-tune. They linearize graph evidence into the prompt (Chapter 22) and structure the reasoning. Graph-enhanced chain of thought interleaves reasoning steps with graph lookups (Think-on-Graph, Graph Chain-of-Thought). Collaborative KG refinement lets the model detect and repair problems in the retrieved graph or its own plan, as Plan-on-Graph does with self-correction. Everything you built in minigraphrag is in-context integration: the [Data: Entities (3)] citation format is a lightweight form of grounding that keeps the model tied to specific records.

**A three-question classifier

For any paper, answer: (1) What does a graph node stand for, text or fact? (2) Who decides what to retrieve: similarity, rules, an LLM, a GNN or a trained policy? (3) Are model weights changed? Those three answers place most papers in the explorer above. The rest are benchmarks, surveys, systems papers or critiques, which you should tag as such.

## A timeline of milestones, 2023 to 2026

The field did not start in 2024. Knowledge-graph question answering and graph neural networks have long histories. What changed in 2023 is that LLMs became good enough to both build graphs from text and walk them with language. The timeline below lists the papers and releases that each changed what practitioners built. Dates are the month of first arXiv submission.

[Diagram]

Milestones by month of first arXiv submission. The open-source release and maintenance-mode entries are project events, not papers; the microsoft/graphrag README dates its first release to July 2024 but gives no date for maintenance mode, so that entry is placed by year only. Dot colors: teal for knowledge organization and systems, amber for retrieval, purple for training, surveys, evaluation and critiques.

Read the timeline as three waves. In 2023 the work came from the knowledge-graph QA community: the graph already existed and the question was how an LLM should walk it. In 2024 From Local to Global and its open-source release shifted attention to graphs built from your own documents, and a burst of retrieval ideas followed (PPR, keywords, paths, subgraphs). In 2025 the field turned on itself: unified comparisons such as DIGIMON and GraphRAG-Bench asked when graphs help, while RL-trained constructors and agents tried to make every stage learnable. The 2026 papers, next, mostly attack the costs and blind spots that those comparisons exposed.

## What 2026 is pushing on

This section summarizes a sample of 2026 arXiv papers. Every description below restates what the paper's own abstract says, including the numbers, which are the authors' self-reported results. None of them has been independently reproduced in this course. Treat them as claims to test, which is exactly what the checklist later in the chapter is for.

### Cost-efficient GraphRAG

LiteRAG (2609.10239) targets query-time cost. Its abstract describes replacing expensive retrieval-time LLM control with query-conditioned algorithmic exploration and reasoning-chain context construction. On DistComp, a multi-hop benchmark over distributed-systems papers, it reports the highest overall quality among the evaluated methods (0.798) while cutting per-query latency by over 100× and cost by over 99% relative to GraphRAG Global and DRIFT; on UltraDomain it reports matching LinearRAG's quality with about 14× fewer tokens. The ablation credits query-adaptive thresholding and community-aware hub penalization. If you have run global search from Chapter 15, the direction makes sense: map-reduce calls the LLM once per batch of reports on every query.

The Commercial Tax (2608.16096) is a critique of how benchmarks report multi-hop retrieval. It audits four leading MuSiQue systems (HippoRAG-2, PropRAG, SAG, KET-RAG) and reports that three depend on NV-Embed-v2, which is licensed cc-by-nc-4.0, for their best numbers without saying so. It measures thirteen embedders on one MuSiQue harness with bootstrap confidence intervals, and reports that a commercially licensed gap to that anchor existed until mid-2026 and was closed by a model released in July 2026. On cost, it reports that three of five audited systems, including Microsoft's GraphRAG, do not disclose indexing cost, and that the only published GraphRAG dollar figures it found span 11× inside a single third-party paper. Its cost model separates one-time embedding from graph construction and recurring answering. The lesson for you: a leaderboard number without a license and a cost is not yet a decision.

### Query-adaptive exploration

MOSAIC (2609.11065) starts from an observation you may have made in Chapter 21: direct facts need compact neighborhoods, comparisons need balanced coverage of several targets, and mediated questions need deeper paths. It is training-free: an LLM analyzer turns each query's evidence requirements into a bounded policy over seed selection, traversal, stopping and evidence selection, while the graph, indexes, scoring, grounding and generator stay shared. On GraphRAG-Bench it reports query-weighted answer correctness of 76.97 (Medical) and 64.33 (Novel), and in controlled comparisons on the same graph and generator it reports that no fixed narrow, medium or wide policy was consistently best, with MOSAIC 9.96 points above the strongest fixed policy while evaluating 81.9% fewer paths than the wide one. That controlled comparison, same graph and same generator, is the kind of experiment the checklist below asks for.

### Provenance and lineage

LineageRAG (2608.16004) argues that existing GraphRAG methods leave the link between finding evidence and grounding it in source text implicit. It derives “evidence demands” from the query, builds one evidence lineage per demand through demand-conditioned retrieval over the corpus graph, keeps the demand attached to every candidate, and completes a lineage with a verbatim source span when the evidence supports the demand. On HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue it reports average gains of 3.51 R@5, 5.96 EM and 5.22 F1 over leading GraphRAG baselines. For Kestrel, a lineage for “Why did Kestrel start Project Tern?” would carry two demands (why the supply ended, what Kestrel did about it), each ending in a quoted sentence.

### Time: bi-temporal and spatio-temporal graphs

post-graph-rag (2608.24921) is an open-source engine that puts chunks with embeddings, a canonical entity graph and community summaries in one PostgreSQL database (pgvector plus edge tables). It validates extraction output before writing, rejecting vague predicates, pronominal names and bare quantities, and it adds a bi-temporal layer that records when a relation held and when the system believed it, superseding incompatible earlier assertions. The abstract reports 94.0% on LongMemEval and attributes the largest single gain to carrying each relation's validity period into the synthesis prompt, which moved temporal reasoning from 0.496 to 0.881 in its ablation. It also reports 0.807 on ECT-QA, an earnings-call benchmark in which every metric is restated each quarter, against published figures of 0.599, 0.406 and 0.405 for TG-RAG, LightRAG and GraphRAG. That is the design you built in Chapter 27 and will extend in Capstone 3. Notice one detail when you read it: the abstract names gemini-3.6-flash for its own 94.0% and gpt-4o for Zep's 71.2, and does not name a generator for the full-context 60.2.

NS-ST-GraphRAG (2609.05139) applies temporal and spatial graphs to long literary narratives, where relations evolve over narrative time. It combines ontology-guided extraction, deterministic constraint checking, dual temporal coordinates, spatial scene attributes and dynamic subgraph retrieval that selects the graph state valid for a query's scope, and introduces Red-Chamber-QA for classical Chinese literature. Its abstract is unusually candid: on a 120-question held-out split it reports 0.733 against 0.675 for the baseline with McNemar exact p = 0.092, described as “directionally favorable but not significant,” notes a closed-book model scores 0.083, and says a pre-specified condition of one of its hypotheses was not supported. Reward that kind of reporting when you see it.

### Hypergraphs

HyCE-RAG (2607.22597) notes that pairwise edges cannot represent associations among several entities and contexts at once. It organizes entities, relations and contextual evidence into hyperedges, builds a query-aware evidence hypergraph, propagates confidence over entity-hyperedge incidences, and assembles ranked evidence chains before generation, scoring semantic relevance, connectivity, coverage, relation reliability, extraction confidence and propagated confidence. It reports consistent gains over standard and graph-based RAG on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue and two GraphRAG-Bench subsets in accuracy, context relevance and faithfulness, and frames hypergraphs as a direction for post-retrieval reasoning. Chapter 31 covers the representation.

### Multimodal documents

HVM-GraphRAG (2607.24861) addresses question answering over complex documents where evidence spans regions and modalities. It identifies two problems in existing multimodal GraphRAG, unreliable cross-modal evidence indexing and expensive traversal, and responds with a holistic view that guides graph construction, a compact concept-level graph indexed to supporting multimodal chunks (so retrieval avoids walking a dense entity graph), and modality-specific grouping of retrieved chunks. It reports the best answer performance in most evaluated settings on three datasets with better online retrieval efficiency.

ColGraphRAG (2607.16208) is a narrow, well-controlled study: in a graph-grounded multimodal QA pipeline it replaces only the ranking operator for graph-linked image nodes, swapping single-vector similarity for late-interaction MaxSim scoring in the ColBERT/ColPali lineage, and keeps everything else unchanged. On MultimodalQA it reports improved retrieval-stage estimates and downstream QA gains where visual evidence matters most, mixed trends on text-dominant questions, and explicitly calls for broader validation. Single-operator swaps like this are the easiest papers to reproduce and trust.

### Agentic GraphRAG

Two 2025 papers anchor the agentic direction that 2026 work builds on. GraphSearch (2509.22009) names two limitations, shallow retrieval that misses important evidence and inefficient use of the pre-built graph, and proposes a six-module agentic workflow with dual-channel retrieval: semantic queries over chunks and relational queries over the graph, reporting consistent gains on six multi-hop benchmarks. Youtu-GraphRAG (2508.19855) unifies construction and retrieval around one schema: a seed schema bounds an extraction agent and expands to new domains, “dually-perceived” community detection fuses topology with subgraph semantics into a hierarchical knowledge tree, and an agentic retriever uses the same schema to split queries into parallel sub-queries with reflection. It also introduces an anonymized dataset and an “Anonymity Reversion” task to reduce knowledge leakage from pre-training. Its arXiv abstract reports up to 90.71% token-cost savings and 16.62% higher accuracy over the strongest baselines it compares against; the later ICLR listing reports 33.60% lower token cost with the same accuracy gain, so cite the version you evaluate.

Trend | Representative papers | What it changes in your minigraphrag

Cost-efficient retrieval | LiteRAG, The Commercial Tax | Replace per-query LLM calls with algorithmic exploration; always report indexing and query cost

Query-adaptive exploration | MOSAIC | A per-query policy for seeds, hops and stopping instead of fixed top_k and depth

Provenance | LineageRAG | Carry evidence demands through retrieval; end each chain in a verbatim span

Time | post-graph-rag, NS-ST-GraphRAG | Validity intervals on edges, and put them in the prompt

Higher-order facts | HyCE-RAG | Hyperedges for n-ary evidence; confidence propagation

Multimodal | HVM-GraphRAG, ColGraphRAG | Concept graphs indexing images and tables; better image scoring

Agentic | GraphSearch, Youtu-GraphRAG | Multi-turn tool use over graph and text channels

## Open problems

The same problems recur across surveys, critiques and your own experiments in this course. Each is a good place to contribute.

- When do graphs actually help? GraphRAG-Bench was motivated by reports that GraphRAG often underperforms vanilla RAG on real tasks. Your own Kestrel results probably showed the same shape: graphs win on multi-hop and global questions and can lose on single-hop lookups. A reliable way to predict, per query or per corpus, whether to use the graph is still open. Routers in Capstone 1 are a practical but crude answer.

- Cost that scales with the corpus. LLM extraction and per-community summarization dominate indexing (Chapter 26). Relation-free graphs (LinearRAG), lazy indexing and trained small extractors all help, but systems still rarely publish cost next to quality, as The Commercial Tax documents.

- Graph quality you cannot see. A wrong edge looks exactly like a right one in the prompt. Validating extraction before writing (post-graph-rag), training constructors against downstream utility (AutoGraph-R1) and verbatim grounding (LineageRAG) are three different answers to the same problem.

- Change over time. Most benchmarks are static snapshots. Real corpora supersede facts, as the Kestrel CTO change shows. Evaluations of incremental updates and temporal correctness are still thin.

- Evaluation validity. LLM judges have position and length bias (Chapter 25), public benchmarks leak into pre-training (the motivation for Youtu-GraphRAG's anonymized dataset), and comparisons often change the generator or embedder along with the method.

- Security and access control. Community summaries mix text from documents with different permissions, and injected instructions can ride along with retrieved evidence (Chapter 29). There is little published work on ACL-correct GraphRAG; Capstone 4 makes you confront it.

- Beyond binary text graphs. Hyperedges, images, tables, code and time all strain the entity-relation-entity model, and each extension currently comes with its own pipeline.

## Reading a GraphRAG paper critically

A paper's abstract is an advertisement for its best result. Your job is to find out whether that result will survive on your data, with your models, at your budget. Use this checklist on every paper you are considering building on. Most items can be checked in ten minutes with the paper's tables and repository.

# | Question | Why it matters | Red flag

1 | Which part of the taxonomy does the contribution change? | Tells you which baseline is the fair one | A “retrieval” paper that also changes extraction, chunking and the generator

2 | Do all systems use the same generator, embedder and graph? | Otherwise the comparison measures models, not methods | Baseline numbers copied from other papers that used different models

3 | Is vanilla RAG a baseline, tuned fairly? | Many GraphRAG gains shrink against a well-tuned vector or hybrid baseline | Top-k = 1 or tiny chunks for the baseline only

4 | What does indexing cost, and what does a query cost? | A method 2 points better at 20× the tokens may be worse for you | No token, dollar or latency numbers at all

5 | Which question types are in the benchmark? | Graphs help multi-hop and global questions; single-hop may regress | One aggregate score, no per-type breakdown

6 | Could the answers be in the model's pre-training data? | Wikipedia-based multi-hop sets can be answered closed-book | No closed-book baseline, no anonymized or new data

7 | If an LLM judges, how was bias controlled? | Position, length and self-preference bias can decide pairwise wins | Single ordering, judge is the same model as the system

8 | Are differences significant? | Benchmarks with a few hundred questions have wide intervals | Sub-point gains with no confidence intervals or tests

9 | Does an ablation show which component matters? | Lets you adopt the one idea that carries the gain | Every component added at once, nothing removed

10 | Can you run it: code, prompts, licenses? | Reproducibility and whether you may deploy it commercially | Non-commercial model weights behind the best number, undisclosed

**The checklist applied to one abstract

Take post-graph-rag's LongMemEval claim: 94.0% for its engine versus 71.2% for Zep and 60.2% for full context. Item 2 flags it immediately: the abstract names gemini-3.6-flash for its own run and gpt-4o for the Zep number, so part of the gap may come from the generator. Item 9 is answered well: the abstract reports a paired ablation on the same graph for its largest single contribution (temporal grounding in the prompt, 0.496 to 0.881 on temporal reasoning). Item 10 is answered well too: code links are given. A fair next step is to rerun the Zep comparison with the same generator before concluding the architecture is the cause.

Read beyond the abstract in this order: the experimental setup table (models, datasets, sizes), the main results table with per-type breakdowns, the ablation table, the cost or efficiency section, the limitations section, and only then the method section. You will skip the method section of most papers, and that is the point.

**Curated lists have errors too

Lists are edited by hand and papers change after they are listed. arXiv 2412.12612, for example, first appeared as SynthCypher and is now titled Auto-Cypher, so a list entry and the paper can disagree. Before you cite or classify a paper, open its arXiv page and check the current title and authors.

## How to keep up

### A query that finds the new papers

arXiv's export API is free, needs no key, and supports field queries and sorting by submission date. The script below fetches the latest matches, proposes taxonomy tags from keyword rules, and flags two checklist signals visible in the abstract alone: whether cost is reported and whether code is linked. It uses only the standard library. Be gentle with the API; one request per run with a few dozen results is plenty.

```python  # research/radar.py
"""Weekly GraphRAG radar: fetch new arXiv papers, tag them with the taxonomy, write a triage list."""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import sys
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

API = "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query"
QUERY = ('abs:GraphRAG OR ti:GraphRAG OR abs:"graph retrieval-augmented generation" '
         'OR (abs:"knowledge graph" AND abs:"retrieval-augmented")')
ATOM = {"a": "http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"}

# Keyword rules that propose a place in the taxonomy. A human confirms it after reading the abstract.
TAGS = {
    "organization/indexing": r"\bindex(ing)?\b|tree|hierarch|passage graph",
    "organization/kg-construction": r"construct|extraction|schema|ontolog",
    "retrieval/llm-agent": r"agent|agentic|iterative|multi-turn|reflection",
    "retrieval/gnn": r"\bGNN\b|graph neural",
    "retrieval/ppr-paths": r"pagerank|path|random walk|traversal",
    "integration/fine-tuning": r"fine-tun|reinforcement|\bRL\b|instruction tun",
    "cross-cutting/cost": r"cost|latency|token|efficien",
    "cross-cutting/temporal": r"temporal|time-aware|bi-temporal",
    "cross-cutting/multimodal": r"multimodal|image|visual|table",
    "cross-cutting/hypergraph": r"hypergraph|hyperedge|n-ary",
    "cross-cutting/evaluation": r"benchmark|evaluat",
    "cross-cutting/provenance": r"provenance|lineage|grounding|citation",
}


def fetch(max_results: int = 50) -> list[dict]:
    params = urllib.parse.urlencode({"search_query": QUERY, "sortBy": "submittedDate",
                                     "sortOrder": "descending", "max_results": max_results})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f"{API}?{params}", timeout=30) as resp:
        root = ET.fromstring(resp.read())
    papers = []
    for e in root.findall("a:entry", ATOM):
        abstract = " ".join(e.find("a:summary", ATOM).text.split())
        papers.append({
            "id": e.find("a:id", ATOM).text.rsplit("/", 1)[-1],
            "date": e.find("a:published", ATOM).text[:10],
            "title": " ".join(e.find("a:title", ATOM).text.split()),
            "abstract": abstract,
            "tags": [t for t, pat in TAGS.items() if re.search(pat, abstract, re.I)],
            # Checklist signals visible in the abstract alone.
            "reports_cost": bool(re.search(r"cost|token|latency|\$|USD", abstract)),
            "has_code": bool(re.search(r"github\.com|code (is )?available|open-source", abstract, re.I)),
        })
    return papers


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for p in fetch(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 25):
        flags = ("cost " if p["reports_cost"] else "") + ("code" if p["has_code"] else "")
        print(f"{p['date']}  {p['id']:<14} {p['title'][:80]}\n    tags: {', '.join(p['tags']) or '-'}  {flags}")
```

Run it once a week (python research/radar.py 50). The tags are suggestions, not truth: in a sample run, MOSAIC was tagged “ppr-paths” because its abstract mentions paths, while a human would file it under query-adaptive LLM-based retrieval. That gap is why the triage step below exists.
