## Exercises

#### Exercise 33.1 Warm-up

Classify each paper into the taxonomy using only the one-line summary of its abstract. Give the main category and, where it applies, a secondary one. (a) HyperGraphRAG (2503.21322): represents n-ary facts as hyperedges, with hypergraph construction, retrieval and generation. (b) Graph-R1 (2507.21892): lightweight hypergraph construction, retrieval as multi-turn agent-environment interaction, optimized with end-to-end RL. (c) DIGIMON (2503.04338): a unified framework and systematic comparison of graph-based RAG methods. (d) MOSAIC (2609.11065): an LLM analyzer sets a per-query exploration policy on a shared graph. (e) LiteRAG (2609.10239): algorithmic, query-conditioned exploration replaces retrieval-time LLM control. (f) HyCE-RAG (2607.22597): confidence propagation over a query-aware evidence hypergraph, then evidence-chain assembly.

▸ Hint

Ask the three questions: what does a node stand for, who decides what to retrieve, and are weights trained? One of the six is not a method at all.

▸ Show answer

Paper | Main | Secondary | Reasoning

(a) HyperGraphRAG | Organization: KG built from corpus (as a hypergraph) | Retrieval over hyperedges | The contribution is the representation; retrieval and generation follow from it

(b) Graph-R1 | Integration: fine-tuning (RL-trained retrieval policy) | Retrieval: multi-round | Weights change, and what they learn is when and what to retrieve over several turns

(c) DIGIMON | Not a method: benchmark and analysis | n/a | Tag it as evaluation; use it to find fair baselines rather than to place a technique

(d) MOSAIC | Retrieval: LLM-based (query-adaptive control) | Retrieval: hybrid of traversal policies | No training, graph fixed; an LLM decides seeds, depth and stopping per query

(e) LiteRAG | Retrieval: similarity and algorithmic exploration | Cross-cutting: cost | The point is to remove the LLM from the retrieval loop; graph and generator are not the contribution

(f) HyCE-RAG | Retrieval: post-retrieval | Organization: hypergraph | Its own abstract frames the hypergraph as a direction for post-retrieval reasoning over assembled evidence chains

Reasonable people will place (a) and (f) differently. What matters is that your placement names the component a fair baseline should hold fixed: for (e), the same graph and generator with LLM-controlled retrieval; for (b), the same retriever tools without RL training.

#### Exercise 33.2 Core

Critique the LiteRAG abstract with the ten-item checklist. For each item, write “answered by the abstract,” “needs the paper,” or “red flag,” with one sentence of justification. Then write the two questions you would most want the full paper to answer before adopting the method for Kestrel-style global questions.

▸ Show answer

- Taxonomy. Answered: retrieval-time control and context construction change; the graph is presumably reused.

- Same generator, embedder, graph. Needs the paper: the abstract compares to GraphRAG Global, DRIFT and LinearRAG but does not say whether all used the same models and graph.

- Vanilla RAG baseline. Needs the paper: not mentioned in the abstract.

- Cost. Answered, strongly: latency over 100× lower and cost over 99% lower than GraphRAG Global and DRIFT, 14× fewer tokens than LinearRAG. Check whether indexing cost is also reported, since the abstract talks about query time.

- Question types. Needs the paper: DistComp is multi-hop; UltraDomain is closer to sensemaking. Look for a per-type breakdown.

- Leakage. Partly reassuring: a benchmark over distributed-systems papers is less likely to be memorized as QA pairs than Wikipedia, but the papers themselves may be in pre-training.

- Judge bias. Needs the paper: “overall quality 0.798” suggests a judged or composite score; check how it was produced.

- Significance. Needs the paper: no intervals in the abstract. “Matches LinearRAG” in particular needs an interval to mean anything.

- Ablation. Answered: query-adaptive thresholding and community-aware hub penalization drive the token efficiency.

- Reproducibility. Needs the paper: no code link in the abstract.

Two questions for Kestrel: (1) Global questions such as “What are the main themes?” have no seed entities. How does query-conditioned exploration choose where to start, and how does quality on UltraDomain's broad questions compare with map-reduce global search per question type? (2) Is the 99% cost reduction measured against global search at a fixed community level or with dynamic community selection, which already cuts map calls substantially?

#### Exercise 33.3 Core

Design an experiment, runnable with minigraphrag on the Kestrel corpus, that tests MOSAIC's central claim at small scale: that no single fixed exploration policy is best for every question type. Specify the policies, the fixed components, the question sets, the metrics, how you control for cost, and what result would falsify the claim on this corpus.

▸ Show answer

Fixed components. One index built once with build_index; one embedder; one generator model for every answer; the same response type and a fixed context budget (say 4,000 tokens) so a wider policy cannot win by reading more.

Policies. Three fixed policies over hipporag_search, differing in how many passages reach the context: narrow (3), medium (5) and wide (10, truncated to the budget). Seed selection stays fixed at the five seeds link_query_to_nodes returns, because hipporag_search does not expose that parameter; varying seeds as well means calling link_query_to_nodes and personalized_pagerank yourself. Add an oracle-routed policy that picks, per question, the best fixed policy in hindsight (an upper bound), and a simple rule-based router that picks narrow for single-hop, wide for multi-hop.

Questions. The 23 questions in data/questions.jsonl sliced by type (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, global), plus 20 new ones you write so the router is not tuned on its test set.

Metrics. Context recall against supporting_docs (retrieval quality, no judge needed), token F1 against the gold answers, and LLM calls and context tokens per question.

```python
from minigraphrag.evaluation import context_recall, load_questions
from minigraphrag.indexer import load_index
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
from minigraphrag.search.ppr import hipporag_search

POLICIES = {"narrow": 3, "medium": 5, "wide": 10}
index, llm = load_index(".index"), get_llm("openai", cache_dir=".cache/llm")
rows = []
for q in load_questions("data/questions.jsonl"):
    for name, k in POLICIES.items():
        r = hipporag_search(index, q["question"], llm, top_k_passages=k, max_context_tokens=4000)
        rows.append((q["type"], name, context_recall(r.sources, q["supporting_docs"])))
for qtype in sorted({t for t, _, _ in rows}):
    print(qtype, {p: round(sum(s for t, n, s in rows if t == qtype and n == p) /
                           sum(1 for t, n, _ in rows if t == qtype and n == p), 2) for p in POLICIES})
```

Analysis. Compute per-type means with bootstrap intervals over questions. The claim is supported on Kestrel if the best fixed policy differs between types with non-overlapping (or paired-significant) intervals, and if the oracle-routed policy beats the best single fixed policy overall. It is falsified here if one fixed policy is within the interval of the best on every type. With about 5 to 8 questions per type, expect wide intervals; say so, and treat the result as a pilot that motivates a larger question set rather than a verdict.

#### Exercise 33.4 Core

Extend radar.py so that it (a) remembers which arXiv IDs it has already shown, (b) writes new papers to a triage.md file with empty fields for your three-question classification and checklist items 2, 4, 5 and 8, and (c) never shows a paper twice across versions (2609.11065v1 and v2 are the same paper).

▸ Show answer

```python
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

from radar import fetch

SEEN = Path("research/seen.json")


def base_id(arxiv_id: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"v\d+$", "", arxiv_id)          # 2609.11065v2 -> 2609.11065


def triage(max_results: int = 50) -> int:
    SEEN.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    seen = set(json.loads(SEEN.read_text())) if SEEN.exists() else set()
    new = [p for p in fetch(max_results) if base_id(p["id"]) not in seen]
    lines = []
    for p in new:
        lines += [f"## {p['title']} ({base_id(p['id'])}, {p['date']})",
                  f"https://arxiv.org/abs/{base_id(p['id'])}",
                  f"- Suggested tags: {', '.join(p['tags']) or 'none'}",
                  "- Node meaning (text or fact):",
                  "- Who decides retrieval:",
                  "- Weights trained (yes/no):",
                  f"- [2] same models/graph as baselines: ",
                  f"- [4] cost reported: {'abstract mentions cost' if p['reports_cost'] else 'check paper'}",
                  "- [5] per-type results: ",
                  "- [8] intervals or tests: ",
                  "- Decision (skip / read / reproduce):", ""]
        seen.add(base_id(p["id"]))
    if lines:
        with Path("research/triage.md").open("a") as f:
            f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    SEEN.write_text(json.dumps(sorted(seen)))
    return len(new)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"{triage()} new papers added to research/triage.md")
```

Storing base IDs handles version bumps. Appending rather than overwriting keeps your notes. If you run this in a scheduled job, commit seen.json and triage.md so your notes have history.

#### Exercise 33.5 Stretch

GraphRAG-Bench asks when graphs help. Answer that question for the Kestrel corpus with minigraphrag: run basic, local, global, ppr and hybrid on all 23 questions with a real LLM, and produce a table of context recall and token F1 by question type with bootstrap intervals and LLM calls per question. Then write a one-paragraph “when to use graphs on this corpus” recommendation that a reader could act on.

▸ Show answer

```python
import random
from collections import defaultdict

from minigraphrag.cli import make_search
from minigraphrag.evaluation import load_questions, run_eval
from minigraphrag.indexer import load_index
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm

index, llm = load_index(".index"), get_llm("openai", cache_dir=".cache/llm")
methods = ["basic", "local", "global", "ppr", "hybrid"]
questions = load_questions("data/questions.jsonl")
result = run_eval(questions, {m: make_search(m, index, llm) for m in methods})


def ci(xs, n=2000, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    means = sorted(sum(rng.choice(xs) for _ in xs) / len(xs) for _ in range(n))
    return means[int(0.025 * n)], means[int(0.975 * n) - 1]


groups = defaultdict(list)
for row in result["rows"]:
    groups[(row["type"], row["system"])].append(row)
print("| type | method | recall [95% CI] | F1 [95% CI] |")
for (qtype, method), rs in sorted(groups.items()):
    rec, f1 = [r["context_recall"] for r in rs], [r["token_f1"] for r in rs]
    (rl, rh), (fl, fh) = ci(rec), ci(f1)
    print(f"| {qtype} | {method} | {sum(rec)/len(rec):.2f} [{rl:.2f}, {rh:.2f}] | {sum(f1)/len(f1):.2f} [{fl:.2f}, {fh:.2f}] |")
```

Pair it with the LLM call counts from each SearchResult. What a defensible write-up looks like: on single-hop questions, basic search is usually as good as any graph method at one call, so use it. On multi-hop questions, PPR or hybrid retrieval should bring more supporting documents into context; recommend them if their recall interval sits above basic's. On global questions, only map-reduce global search sees the whole corpus, at a higher call count that grows with the number of community reports; token F1 is a poor metric here, so add the pairwise judge from Chapter 25 before recommending it. State the sample size per type (5 to 8 questions) and say the recommendation is provisional until a larger question set confirms it.

## Check your understanding

In HippoRAG 2, PageRank mass ends on passage nodes, and the LLM reads those passages. Where does it belong in the organization taxonomy?

- Graph as knowledge carrier, because it has entity nodes

- ✓ (correct) Graphs for knowledge indexing, because the graph navigates to text that the LLM reads

- Hybrid GraphRAG, because it uses embeddings

- Knowledge integration, because it changes the prompt
Answer: The deciding question is what the LLM consumes as evidence. HippoRAG 2 uses the graph to rank passages; the passages are the evidence. The curated list files it under graphs for indexing.

A paper reports that its GraphRAG method beats a baseline by 6 points. The baseline numbers were copied from an earlier paper that used a different generator. Which checklist item fails?

- Leakage

- Reproducibility

- Ablation

- ✓ (correct) Same generator, embedder and graph for all systems
Answer: With different generators, part or all of the 6 points may come from the model rather than the method. Copied baseline numbers are one of the most common ways this happens.

According to its abstract, what is post-graph-rag's largest single contribution in its ablation?

- Storing everything in PostgreSQL with pgvector

- Rejecting vague predicates during extraction

- ✓ (correct) Carrying each relation's validity period into the synthesis prompt

- Community summaries
Answer: The abstract attributes the largest single contribution to temporal grounding at synthesis, which moved temporal reasoning from 0.496 to 0.881 in a paired ablation on one graph per instance.

Which question is The Commercial Tax (2608.16096) mainly asking of multi-hop retrieval benchmarks?

- Whether GraphRAG beats vector RAG on MuSiQue

- ✓ (correct) Whether published numbers can be deployed commercially and what they cost to build

- Whether LLM judges are biased

- Whether hypergraphs outperform graphs
Answer: It audits licensing of the embedding backbone behind leading systems' numbers and the missing indexing-cost disclosures, and models one-time versus recurring costs.

MOSAIC reports that in controlled comparisons no fixed narrow, medium or wide policy was consistently best. What does “controlled” most importantly mean here?

- The experiments were run several times

- The questions were written by the authors

- ✓ (correct) The graph and the generator were identical across policies, so only the exploration policy varied

- Temperature was set to zero
Answer: Holding the graph and generator fixed isolates the variable under study, which is what makes the finding about policies rather than about models or indexes.

GraphRAG-Bench (2506.05690) was motivated by what observation?

- Knowledge graphs are too expensive to store

- LLMs cannot read graphs

- Community detection is unstable

- ✓ (correct) GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks, so it is unclear when graphs help
Answer: Its abstract frames the benchmark around the question of whether and in which scenarios graph structures provide measurable benefits.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Should I read the surveys cover to cover?

No. Read the framework section of one survey (the knowledge organization, retrieval and integration sections of 2501.13958 map directly to this course), then use the surveys as indexes: when a paper cites an idea you don't recognize, look it up in the survey's table of methods. Surveys date quickly; use the curated lists for anything after early 2025.

▸ How do I know whether a 2026 result is worth building on when nobody has reproduced it?

Look for three things: a controlled comparison (same graph and generator), an ablation that isolates one component, and released code. If all three are present, reimplement just that component inside minigraphrag and test it on Kestrel and on your own data. ColGraphRAG-style single-operator papers are the easiest to verify this way. If none are present, wait.

▸ Is GraphRAG research converging, or fragmenting?

Both. The pipeline stages have converged: nearly every paper fits the organization, retrieval, integration frame, and the same baselines (GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG) recur. The extensions are fragmenting into time, modality, hypergraphs, code and agents, each with its own benchmarks. For practitioners the convergence matters more: a small set of patterns, which you have now built, covers most systems.

▸ Microsoft GraphRAG is in maintenance mode. Does that mean the approach is dead?

No. It means one reference implementation is no longer being actively extended. The ideas it popularized (entity graphs from text, community reports, local and global search) are in LightRAG, neo4j-graphrag, LlamaIndex and many 2026 papers, and several of those papers still use GraphRAG Global and DRIFT as baselines. Chapter 28 discusses what to use instead.

▸ Where can I contribute as an engineer rather than a researcher?

Reproductions with honest cost numbers, evaluations on new domains with per-type breakdowns, and security work (ACL-correct summaries, injection through documents) are all underserved and valued. A well-documented reproduction that shows a published gain shrinking under a fair baseline is a real contribution.

### Project: your own research radar

Build a personal, versioned map of the literature that you will actually maintain, and use it once to change your system.

- A research/ folder with the radar and triage scripts from Exercise 33.4, run weekly for four weeks

- A taxonomy file with at least 25 papers, each with its three-question classification and a one-line claim restated from the abstract

- Full checklist write-ups for three papers, including one that you decided not to adopt and why

- One reproduced component inside minigraphrag, evaluated on Kestrel with per-type results and cost

- A half-page “state of the field for my use case” note that names the open problem most likely to hurt you

Done when you can take any new GraphRAG abstract, place it on your map in two minutes, and say which experiment would convince you to use it.

## Key takeaways

- Place papers with three questions: what a node stands for, who decides what to retrieve, and whether weights are trained.

- Knowledge organization distinguishes graphs that index text from graphs that carry facts; hybrids keep both.

- Retrieval families trade query-time LLM calls against flexibility; integration is either fine-tuning at node, path or subgraph level or in-context prompting.

- The 2026 papers push on cost, query-adaptive exploration, provenance, time, hyperedges, modality and agents; their numbers are self-reported claims until reproduced.

- Read results critically: same models across systems, fair vanilla baselines, cost, per-type results, leakage, judge bias, significance, ablations and licenses.

- Keep up with a small weekly routine and reproduce one component a month rather than reading everything.

# Part: Capstone projects

## Capstone 1: ship MiniGraphRAG end to end

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/c1-minigraphrag.html
Summary: Index a corpus, serve local, global and PPR search behind an API, and prove it beats vector RAG.

# Capstone 1: ship MiniGraphRAG end to end

You have built every stage of GraphRAG in isolation. In this capstone you ship them as one service: index a corpus, answer questions through a router over five retrieval methods behind a streaming API with citations, and write the evaluation and cost report that shows where the graph earns its keep and where it does not.

## You will be able to

- Run the full minigraphrag indexing pipeline on Kestrel and on a corpus you choose, and inspect every artifact it writes

- Serve basic, local, global, PPR and hybrid search behind one FastAPI service with server-sent events and resolvable citations

- Build and measure a query router that sends each question to the cheapest method likely to answer it

- Produce an evaluation report with context recall, token F1 and order-swapped pairwise judging, sliced by question type with intervals

- Produce a cost report that attributes every token to an indexing stage or query method

## Overview and architecture

A GraphRAG demo answers one question well. A GraphRAG service answers every question it is asked, says where its answer came from, costs a known amount, and comes with evidence that it is better than the simpler thing it replaces. That last part is what most projects skip, and it is what this capstone is graded on.

The architecture has two halves. Offline, build_index from Chapter 13 turns Markdown documents into plain artifacts in an out/ folder. Online, a small application package, mgr_app, loads those artifacts once and exposes them over HTTP. Everything that talks to a model goes through a metering wrapper, so the cost report and the evaluation read from the same ledger the service writes to.

[Diagram]

The service layer is deliberately thin: every retrieval method is minigraphrag's own function. The new code is the router, the citation resolver, the HTTP layer, the measurement tools and two small scripts: about 450 lines across the eight reference modules in mgr_app.

### Repository layout

```python  # capstone1/
capstone1/
  data -> ../code/data          # symlink: corpus/ and questions.jsonl
  mgr_app/
    build.py                    # M1: index and inspect
    citations.py                # M2: resolve [Data: ...] markers
    service.py                  # M3: one entry point for five methods
    router.py                   # M4: pick a method per question
    api.py                      # M5: FastAPI + server-sent events
    evaluate.py                 # M6: evaluation report
    metering.py, cost_report.py # M7: cost report
    prepare_corpus.py           # M8: your own corpus
  tests/
  out/                          # index artifacts (gitignored)
```

[Interactive figure: Eight milestones — Each ends with a checkpoint you can verify offline with MockLLM (flow)]

## Requirements

### Functional

- Index the Kestrel corpus (code/data/corpus) and one corpus of your choice of at least 50 documents or 50,000 words.

- POST /query accepts {"question", "method"} where method is auto, basic, local, global, ppr or hybrid, and returns the answer, the method used, the router's reason, citations and source documents.

- POST /query/stream returns the same information as server-sent events: route, sources, a sequence of token events, citations, done.

- Every citation resolves to a document id and a character span in that document; markers that resolve to nothing are dropped and counted.

- GET /health reports entity, relationship, community and text unit counts.

### Evidence

- An evaluation report comparing all methods and auto against basic vector RAG, by question type, with context recall, token F1 and pairwise judge win rates with 95% intervals, following Chapter 25: swapped order, inconsistent verdicts counted as ties, answer length reported.

- A claim you can defend: graph methods beat basic RAG on multi-hop and global questions (or an honest report that they do not on your corpus, with the reason).

- A cost report: indexing tokens and dollars by stage, and per-query dollars and latency by method.

### Constraints

- Everything runs offline with MockLLM and HashingEmbedder, so tests pass in CI with no keys. Real providers are a configuration change (MGR_LLM=openai).

- Use minigraphrag's functions for indexing and retrieval; do not fork them. New behavior goes in mgr_app.

- The judge model must not be the model that generated the answers when you run the real evaluation.
**MockLLM numbers prove plumbing, not quality

MockLLM answers by copying sentences that overlap the question, and its judge scores answers with simple counts. Use it to check that every milestone runs end to end and that numbers are computed correctly. Every claim about which method is better must come from a run with real models.

▸ Show reference solution

The metering wrapper (built fully in M7) goes inside the cache, so the ledger only counts calls that actually reach the provider.

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/build.py
"""Milestone 1: index a folder of Markdown documents and print what each stage produced."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

from minigraphrag.embeddings import get_embedder
from minigraphrag.indexer import IndexConfig, build_index
from minigraphrag.llm import CachedLLM, get_llm

from .metering import MeteredLLM


def main(docs_dir: str = "data/corpus", out_dir: str = "out", llm_name: str = "mock", embedder: str = "hashing"):
    metered = MeteredLLM(get_llm(llm_name))             # counts only calls that reach the provider
    llm = CachedLLM(metered, ".cache/llm")              # re-runs after a crash or code change are free
    index = build_index(docs_dir, out_dir, llm, get_embedder(embedder), IndexConfig(), log=print)
    G = index.graph
    print("entity types:", Counter(d.get("type", "") for _, d in G.nodes(data=True)).most_common())
    print("top entities by degree:", sorted(G.degree, key=lambda x: -x[1])[:5])
    for c in index.communities:
        report = index.report(c.id)
        print(f"community {c.id} (level {c.level}, {len(c.nodes)} nodes): {report.title if report else '-'}")
    print(f"cache hits {llm.hits}, provider calls {llm.misses}")
    Path(out_dir, "build_ledger.json").write_text(json.dumps(metered.snapshot(), indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:])
```

#### Milestone C1.2 Answers with resolvable citations

Answers from local_search cite records such as [Data: Entities (11); Sources (09_kestrel_eng_blog_project_tern-000)]. A UI needs documents and spans, not table row ids. Write the resolver.

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/citations.py
"""Turn [Data: Sources (a, b); Entities (3)] markers into citations a UI can link."""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

MARKER = re.compile(r"\[Data:([^\]]+)\]")
PART = re.compile(r"(Sources|Entities|Relationships|Reports)\s*\(([^)]*)\)")


def extract_citations(index, answer: str) -> list[dict]:
    G = index.graph
    by_human_node = {d["human_id"]: n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True)}
    by_human_edge = {d["human_id"]: (u, v) for u, v, d in G.edges(data=True)}
    out, seen = [], set()
    for marker in MARKER.finditer(answer):
        for table, ids in PART.findall(marker.group(1)):
            for raw in [i.strip() for i in ids.split(",") if i.strip() and i.strip() != "+more"]:
                key = (table, raw)
                if key in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(key)
                units = []
                if table == "Sources":
                    units = [raw]
                elif table == "Entities" and raw.isdigit() and int(raw) in by_human_node:
                    units = G.nodes[by_human_node[int(raw)]].get("source_ids", [])
                elif table == "Relationships" and raw.isdigit() and int(raw) in by_human_edge:
                    units = G.edges[by_human_edge[int(raw)]].get("source_ids", [])
                elif table == "Reports" and raw.isdigit():
                    comm = next((c for c in index.communities if c.id == int(raw)), None)
                    units = [u for n in (comm.nodes if comm else []) for u in G.nodes[n].get("source_ids", [])]
                docs = list(dict.fromkeys(index.text_units[u].doc_id for u in units if u in index.text_units))
                if not docs:
                    continue  # a marker that points at nothing is dropped, and counted by the eval
                first = index.text_units.get(units[0]) if units else None
                out.append({"table": table, "id": raw, "doc_ids": docs[:5],
                            "snippet": first.text[:200] if first else "",
                            "span": [first.start, first.end] if first else None})
    return out
```

A test that pins the span property, which is what a front end relies on to highlight text:

#### Milestone C1.3 Five methods, one entry point

The API, the evaluator and the cost report must all call retrieval the same way, or their numbers will not agree. Wrap minigraphrag's five search functions in one answer() that returns a plain dict.

- Map method names to basic_search, local_search, global_search, hipporag_search and hybrid_search.

- Tag each call with the method name when the LLM supports it, so the ledger splits cost by method.

- Return method, router reason, answer, citations, source documents, LLM calls and latency.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/service.py
"""One entry point for every method, used by the API, the evaluator and the cost report."""
from __future__ import annotations

import time
from contextlib import nullcontext

from minigraphrag.search.basic import basic_search
from minigraphrag.search.global_ import global_search
from minigraphrag.search.hybrid import hybrid_search
from minigraphrag.search.local import local_search
from minigraphrag.search.ppr import hipporag_search

from .citations import extract_citations
from .router import route

METHODS = {
    "basic": lambda index, q, llm: basic_search(index, q, llm),
    "local": lambda index, q, llm: local_search(index, q, llm),
    "global": lambda index, q, llm: global_search(index, q, llm, dynamic=False),
    "ppr": lambda index, q, llm: hipporag_search(index, q, llm),
    "hybrid": lambda index, q, llm: hybrid_search(index, q, llm),
}


def run_method(index, llm, question: str, method: str):
    tag = llm.tagged(f"query:{method}") if hasattr(llm, "tagged") else nullcontext()
    with tag:
        return METHODS[method](index, question, llm)


def answer(index, llm, question: str, method: str = "auto") -> dict:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    decision = route(index, question, llm) if method == "auto" else None
    chosen = decision.method if decision else method
    result = run_method(index, llm, question, chosen)
    return {"question": question, "method": chosen,
            "route_reason": decision.reason if decision else "forced",
            "answer": result.answer, "citations": extract_citations(index, result.answer),
            "sources": result.sources, "llm_calls": result.llm_calls,
            "latency_ms": round(1000 * (time.perf_counter() - t0), 1)}
```

Two design decisions to notice. The router runs inside answer() so that auto is evaluated exactly as it is served. And global search is called with dynamic=False because the Kestrel hierarchy has one level; on a larger corpus, try dynamic=True (dynamic community selection from Chapter 15) and record the call counts in M7.

#### Milestone C1.4 The query router

Global search costs a map call per batch of reports and is poor at “Who directs Tidewater Institute?”. Basic search is cheap and poor at “What are the main themes?”. A router picks per question. Build the cheapest one that works and measure it.

- Find named entities in the question with map_query_to_entities and keep only those whose name actually appears.

- Rules: sensemaking cues with at most one named entity go to global; multi-hop cues or three or more entities go to ppr; one or two named entities go to local.

- If no rule fires, ask the LLM for a JSON route; if that fails, use hybrid.

- Measure routing accuracy against the type labels in questions.jsonl, then write 15 new questions and measure again.

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/router.py (starter)

    # TODO: named entities, cue regexes, LLM fallback, default
```

Checkpoints

- Routing accuracy on the 23 labelled questions, where global questions must go to global, multi-hop to ppr or hybrid, single-hop to local or basic, temporal to local or hybrid.

- Accuracy on your own held-out questions, reported separately.

- Every route carries a human-readable reason that the API returns.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/router.py
"""Pick a retrieval method per question: cheap rules first, an LLM only when the rules are unsure."""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass

from minigraphrag.llm import parse_json_response
from minigraphrag.search.local import map_query_to_entities

GLOBAL_CUES = re.compile(r"\b(main themes?|overall|summari[sz]e|trends?|risks?|landscape|evolved|big picture|role does)\b", re.I)
MULTIHOP_CUES = re.compile(r"\b(why|connect(s|ed|ion)?|relat(e|ed)|whose|path|link(ed)?|previously|used by|"
                           r"the company that|both|and how)\b", re.I)
TEMPORAL_CUES = re.compile(r"\b(19|20)\d\d\b|\b(as of|when|currently|now|before|after|since)\b", re.I)

ROUTER_PROMPT = """Classify the question for a GraphRAG system. Routes:
- "global": asks about themes, trends or a summary across the whole corpus
- "ppr": needs a chain of facts across several entities (multi-hop)
- "local": about one or two named entities and their direct facts
- "basic": a narrow factual lookup likely answered by one passage
Return JSON {{"route": "...", "reason": "..."}}.
Question: {question}"""


@dataclass
class Route:
    method: str
    reason: str
    entities: list[str]


def route(index, question: str, llm=None) -> Route:
    named = [e for e in map_query_to_entities(index, question, top_k=5, include_name_matches=True)
             if re.search(re.escape(e.split()[-1]), question.upper())]
    if GLOBAL_CUES.search(question) and (len(named) <= 1 or question.lower().startswith("summari")):
        return Route("global", "sensemaking cue with at most one named entity", named)
    if MULTIHOP_CUES.search(question) or len(named) >= 3:
        return Route("ppr", f"multi-hop cue or {len(named)} named entities", named)
    if named:
        why = "temporal lookup on a named entity" if TEMPORAL_CUES.search(question) else "named-entity lookup"
        return Route("local", why, named)
    if llm is not None:
        choice = parse_json_response(llm.complete(ROUTER_PROMPT.format(question=question), json=True))
        if choice.get("route") in {"global", "ppr", "local", "basic"}:
            return Route(choice["route"], "llm: " + str(choice.get("reason", "")), named)
    return Route("hybrid", "no confident signal; fuse everything", named)
```

```python  # capstone1/tests/test_router.py

    hit = r.method in EXPECTED[q["type"]]

print(f"routing accuracy {ok}/{len(qs)}")
```

Be suspicious of that 22/23. Cues such as “previously”, “used by” and “role does” are in the lists because someone read the misses on these same 23 questions and added words until they routed correctly. That is tuning on the test set. The number that belongs in your report is accuracy on questions written after the rules were frozen. #### Milestone C1.5 A streaming API

Global search can take many seconds with a real model. Users tolerate waiting when they see progress, so stream it. Server-sent events (SSE) are plain HTTP: the response is text/event-stream and each event is an event: line, a data: line and a blank line.

- Load the index and the metered LLM once at startup from environment variables.

- Implement GET /health, POST /query and POST /query/stream with a Pydantic request model that restricts method to known values.

- Emit events in order: route (as soon as the router decides), sources, token chunks, citations, done with call count and cost.

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/api.py (starter)
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI(title="MiniGraphRAG")


class Query(BaseModel):
    question: str
    method: str = "auto"      # TODO: restrict to known methods


@app.post("/query/stream")
def query_stream(q: Query):
    def events():
        yield "event: route\ndata: {}\n\n"   # TODO
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

Checkpoints

- curl -N -X POST localhost:8000/query/stream -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"question":"What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?"}' prints a route event before any token event.

- An unknown method returns HTTP 422, not a stack trace.

- The concatenated token texts equal the answer field from POST /query for the same question.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/api.py
"""FastAPI service: POST /query for JSON, POST /query/stream for server-sent events."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
from typing import Literal

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel

from minigraphrag.indexer import load_index
from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm

from .metering import MeteredLLM
from .service import answer, run_method
from .router import route
from .citations import extract_citations

INDEX_DIR = os.getenv("MGR_INDEX", "out")
index = load_index(INDEX_DIR)
# No response cache here: identical questions should still reach the model, and the meter must see real spend.
llm = MeteredLLM(get_llm(os.getenv("MGR_LLM", "mock")), price_key=os.getenv("MGR_PRICE", "mock"))
app = FastAPI(title="MiniGraphRAG")


class Query(BaseModel):
    question: str
    method: Literal["auto", "basic", "local", "global", "ppr", "hybrid"] = "auto"


@app.get("/health")
def health():
    G = index.graph
    return {"entities": G.number_of_nodes(), "relationships": G.number_of_edges(),
            "communities": len(index.communities), "text_units": len(index.text_units)}


@app.post("/query")
def query(q: Query):
    return answer(index, llm, q.question, q.method)


def _sse(event: str, data) -> str:
    return f"event: {event}\ndata: {json.dumps(data)}\n\n"


def _stream_text(text: str, size: int = 24):
    # minigraphrag's LLM interface returns whole strings. If your client supports token
    # streaming, yield its deltas here instead; the event protocol stays the same.
    for i in range(0, len(text), size):
        yield text[i:i + size]


@app.post("/query/stream")
def query_stream(q: Query):
    def events():
        decision = route(index, q.question, llm) if q.method == "auto" else None
        method = decision.method if decision else q.method
        yield _sse("route", {"method": method, "reason": decision.reason if decision else "forced"})
        result = run_method(index, llm, q.question, method)
        yield _sse("sources", {"doc_ids": result.sources})
        for delta in _stream_text(result.answer):
            yield _sse("token", {"text": delta})
        yield _sse("citations", extract_citations(index, result.answer))
        yield _sse("done", {"llm_calls": result.llm_calls, "cost_usd": round(llm.cost(), 6)})
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

Run it with MGR_INDEX=out uvicorn mgr_app.api:app --reload. The stream for the Priya Nair question begins like this with MockLLM:

```python  # capstone1/tests/test_api.py
import json
import os

os.environ.setdefault("MGR_INDEX", "out")
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from mgr_app.api import app

client = TestClient(app)


def parse_sse(body: str) -> list[tuple[str, dict]]:
    events = []
    for block in body.strip().split("\n\n"):
        lines = dict(line.split(": ", 1) for line in block.splitlines())
        events.append((lines["event"], json.loads(lines["data"])))
    return events


def test_stream_matches_json_answer():
    q = {"question": "What connects Priya Nair to Deepcast?", "method": "ppr"}
    with client.stream("POST", "/query/stream", json=q) as r:
        events = parse_sse("".join(r.iter_text()))
    names = [e for e, _ in events]
    assert names[0] == "route" and names[-1] == "done" and "citations" in names
    streamed = "".join(d["text"] for e, d in events if e == "token")
    assert streamed == client.post("/query", json=q).json()["answer"]


def test_unknown_method_is_rejected():
    assert client.post("/query", json={"question": "x", "method": "magic"}).status_code == 422
```

The reference streams the finished answer in chunks because minigraphrag's LLM.complete returns a whole string. The events that matter most for perceived latency, route and sources, already arrive before generation starts. To stream real tokens, add a stream(prompt, system) generator to your provider client and yield its deltas in _stream_text; the event protocol does not change.

#### Milestone C1.6 The evaluation report

This is the milestone that turns a demo into an argument. Follow the methodology from Chapter 25.

- For each of the 23 questions, run basic, local, global, ppr, hybrid and auto.

- Compute context recall against supporting_docs and token F1 against the gold answer with minigraphrag's context_recall and token_f1.

- For every non-basic answer, run llm_judge_pairwise against the basic answer on the four criteria. It asks twice with the order swapped and keeps a winner only when both orders agree. Score a win 1, a tie or inconsistent pair 0.5, a loss 0.

- Report the mean win rate per method and question type with a 95% bootstrap interval over questions, next to recall, F1 and calls.

- With real models: use a different, stronger judge than the generator, cache judge calls, and report mean answer length per method, since comprehensiveness and diversity reward longer answers.

Checkpoints

- The report has one row per question type and method, 24 rows in all, and basic is marked as the baseline.

- Win rates lie in [0, 1]; a method judged against itself scores exactly 0.5.

- With real models, your report states whether the lower bound of the interval for global on global questions and for ppr or hybrid on multi-hop questions is above 0.5.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/evaluate.py
"""Evaluation report: context recall and token F1 per method, pairwise judge win rates against basic RAG."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import random
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

from minigraphrag.evaluation import context_recall, llm_judge_pairwise, load_questions, token_f1

from .service import answer

CRITERIA = ("comprehensiveness", "diversity", "empowerment", "directness")
POINTS = {"A": 1.0, "TIE": 0.5, "B": 0.0}


def bootstrap_ci(values: list[float], n: int = 2000, seed: int = 0) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """95% percentile bootstrap interval of the mean (resampling questions)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    means = sorted(sum(rng.choice(values) for _ in values) / len(values) for _ in range(n))
    return means[int(0.025 * n)], means[int(0.975 * n) - 1]


def run(index, llm, judge, questions, methods=("basic", "local", "global", "ppr", "hybrid", "auto")) -> list[dict]:
    rows = []
    for q in questions:
        results = {m: answer(index, llm, q["question"], m) for m in methods}
        baseline = results["basic"]["answer"]
        for m, r in results.items():
            row = {"id": q["id"], "type": q["type"], "method": m, "routed_to": r["method"],
                   "recall": context_recall(r["sources"], q.get("supporting_docs", [])),
                   "f1": token_f1(r["answer"], q["answer"]),
                   "citations": len(r["citations"]), "llm_calls": r["llm_calls"]}
            if m != "basic":
                # The candidate is always answer A; llm_judge_pairwise asks again with the order
                # swapped and only keeps a winner both orders agree on.
                verdicts = llm_judge_pairwise(judge, q["question"], r["answer"], baseline, CRITERIA)
                row.update({c: POINTS[verdicts[c]["winner"]] for c in CRITERIA})
            rows.append(row)
    return rows


def report(rows: list[dict]) -> str:
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for r in rows:
        groups[(r["type"], r["method"])].append(r)
    out = ["| question type | method | n | context recall | token F1 | win rate vs basic [95% CI] |",
           "|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for (qtype, method), rs in sorted(groups.items()):
        recall = sum(r["recall"] for r in rs) / len(rs)
        f1 = sum(r["f1"] for r in rs) / len(rs)
        if method == "basic":
            win = "(baseline)"
        else:
            per_q = [sum(r[c] for c in CRITERIA) / len(CRITERIA) for r in rs]
            lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(per_q)
            win = f"{sum(per_q) / len(per_q):.2f} [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]"
        out.append(f"| {qtype} | {method} | {len(rs)} | {recall:.2f} | {f1:.2f} | {win} |")
    return "\n".join(out)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from minigraphrag.indexer import load_index
    from minigraphrag.llm import get_llm
    index_dir, llm_name, judge_name = (sys.argv[1:] + ["out", "mock", "mock"][len(sys.argv) - 1:])[:3]
    index = load_index(index_dir)
    llm = get_llm(llm_name, cache_dir=".cache/llm")          # cached: re-running the report is free; cost lives in M7
    judge = get_llm(judge_name, cache_dir=".cache/judge")   # use a different, stronger model than llm
    rows = run(index, llm, judge, load_questions("data/questions.jsonl"))
    Path("eval_rows.jsonl").write_text("\n".join(json.dumps(r) for r in rows))
    Path("eval_report.md").write_text(report(rows))
    print(report(rows))
```

A MockLLM run prints a table like this (excerpt). Read it only as proof that the harness works:

```python
| question type | method | n | context recall | token F1 | win rate vs basic [95% CI] |
| global | basic | 5 | 0.37 | 0.16 | (baseline) |
| global | global | 5 | 1.00 | 0.20 | 0.55 [0.50, 0.65] |
| multi-hop | basic | 8 | 0.60 | 0.19 | (baseline) |
| multi-hop | hybrid | 8 | 0.73 | 0.18 | 0.50 [0.50, 0.50] |
| multi-hop | ppr | 8 | 0.50 | 0.16 | 0.58 [0.52, 0.66] |
```

Three things in it will still be true when you swap in real models, so write them down now:

- Global recall of 1.00 is flattering. Global search's sources are the documents behind every community it used, so it “retrieves” nearly the whole corpus. Context recall cannot distinguish reading everything from reading the right thing; this is why global questions are judged pairwise instead.

- Token F1 is nearly useless for long answers. Gold answers are one or two sentences; a multi-paragraph answer containing them scores low. Use F1 for single-hop and temporal questions only.

- Five to eight questions per type give wide intervals. With real models, a 0.70 win rate on five global questions can still have a lower bound near 0.5. Add questions until the intervals answer your question, 30 per type is a reasonable target, and say how many you have.

A report template that passes the rubric: one paragraph of setup (models, embedder, judge, question counts), the table, one paragraph per question type stating the claim and its interval, a paragraph on cost from M7, and a limitations paragraph (judge bias controls used, questions written by you, small n).

#### Milestone C1.7 The cost report

“GraphRAG is expensive” is not a number. Attribute every token to an indexing stage or a query method, then price it.

- Write MeteredLLM: same complete() signature, counts calls, input and output tokens with count_tokens, and seconds, keyed by stage.

- Name indexing stages automatically from each prompt's marker in prompts.MARKERS (extraction, continue, claims, summarize, report), and query stages from a tagged() context manager.

- Put the meter inside CachedLLM so cache hits cost nothing.

- Report indexing cost per stage and per million corpus tokens, and mean dollars, p50 and p95 latency and calls per query for each method.

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/metering.py (starter)
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

PRICES = {"mock": (0.0, 0.0)}   # USD per million (input, output) tokens


class MeteredLLM:
    def __init__(self, llm, price_key="mock"):
        self.llm, self.price_key, self.ledger = llm, price_key, {}

    def complete(self, prompt, system=None, json=False):
        out = self.llm.complete(prompt, system=system, json=json)
        # TODO: stage name, calls, tokens in/out, seconds
        return out
```

Checkpoints

- The indexing ledger has rows for extraction, continue (gleaning), claims, summarize and report, and its call total equals the provider calls printed by M1.

- Run the cost report twice. With a fresh cache directory the indexing ledger matches the first run; with the warm cache it records zero indexing calls and zero indexing cost.

- Per-query cost is reported for every method including auto.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/metering.py
"""Count every LLM call, its tokens and its cost, tagged with the pipeline stage."""
from __future__ import annotations

import time
from collections import defaultdict
from contextlib import contextmanager

from minigraphrag import prompts as P
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

# USD per million tokens. Placeholders: copy your provider's current price sheet.
PRICES = {"mock": (0.0, 0.0), "gpt-4o-mini": (0.15, 0.60), "local": (0.0, 0.0)}


class MeteredLLM:
    """Wraps any minigraphrag LLM. Same complete() signature, plus a ledger."""

    def __init__(self, llm, price_key: str = "mock"):
        self.llm, self.price_key = llm, price_key
        self.name = getattr(llm, "name", type(llm).__name__)
        self.stage = "unlabelled"
        self.ledger = defaultdict(lambda: {"calls": 0, "in": 0, "out": 0, "seconds": 0.0})

    @contextmanager
    def tagged(self, stage: str):
        previous, self.stage = self.stage, stage
        try:
            yield self
        finally:
            self.stage = previous

    def complete(self, prompt: str, system: str | None = None, json: bool = False) -> str:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        out = self.llm.complete(prompt, system=system, json=json)
        stage = self.stage
        if stage == "unlabelled" or stage.startswith("query:"):
            # Name the job from the prompt's marker (same trick MockLLM uses): extraction, report, map...
            task = next((t for t, m in P.MARKERS.items() if m in f"{system or ''}\n{prompt}"), "other")
            stage = task if stage == "unlabelled" else f"{stage}/{task}"
        row = self.ledger[stage]
        row["calls"] += 1
        row["in"] += count_tokens(prompt) + count_tokens(system or "")
        row["out"] += count_tokens(out)
        row["seconds"] += time.perf_counter() - t0
        return out

    def cost(self, stage: str | None = None) -> float:
        p_in, p_out = PRICES[self.price_key]
        rows = [self.ledger[stage]] if stage else self.ledger.values()
        return sum(r["in"] * p_in + r["out"] * p_out for r in rows) / 1e6

    def snapshot(self) -> dict:
        return {k: dict(v) for k, v in self.ledger.items()}
```

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/cost_report.py
"""Index a corpus through a metered LLM, run the question set, and write cost_report.md."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import statistics
import sys
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

from minigraphrag.chunking import load_documents
from minigraphrag.indexer import IndexConfig, build_index
from minigraphrag.llm import CachedLLM, get_llm
from minigraphrag.tokens import count_tokens

from minigraphrag.evaluation import load_questions
from .metering import MeteredLLM
from .service import answer


def pct(values, q):
    values = sorted(values)
    return values[min(len(values) - 1, int(q * len(values)))]


def main(docs_dir: str, out_dir: str, llm_name: str = "mock", price_key: str = "mock"):
    # Meter *inside* the cache: cache hits cost nothing, so the ledger shows real provider spend.
    llm = MeteredLLM(get_llm(llm_name), price_key)
    corpus_tokens = sum(count_tokens(t) for t in load_documents(docs_dir).values())
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    index = build_index(docs_dir, out_dir, CachedLLM(llm, ".cache/llm"), config=IndexConfig())
    index_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
    index_ledger = llm.snapshot()
    index_cost = llm.cost()

    per_method = defaultdict(list)
    for q in load_questions("data/questions.jsonl"):
        for method in ("basic", "local", "global", "ppr", "hybrid", "auto"):
            before = llm.cost()
            r = answer(index, llm, q["question"], method)
            per_method[method].append((llm.cost() - before, r["latency_ms"], r["llm_calls"]))

    lines = [f"# Cost report ({llm.name}, prices: {price_key})", "",
             f"Corpus: {corpus_tokens:,} tokens, {len(index.text_units)} text units. "
             f"Indexing took {index_seconds:.1f}s and cost ${index_cost:.4f} "
             f"(${1e6 * index_cost / max(corpus_tokens, 1):.2f} per million corpus tokens).", "",
             "| indexing stage | calls | input tokens | output tokens |", "|---|---|---|---|"]
    for stage, row in sorted(index_ledger.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]["in"]):
        lines.append(f"| {stage} | {row['calls']} | {row['in']:,} | {row['out']:,} |")
    lines += ["", "| query method | mean $/query | p50 ms | p95 ms | LLM calls/query |", "|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for method, xs in per_method.items():
        costs, lat, calls = zip(*xs)
        lines.append(f"| {method} | {statistics.mean(costs):.5f} | {pct(lat, .5):.0f} | {pct(lat, .95):.0f} | "
                     f"{statistics.mean(calls):.1f} |")
    Path("cost_report.md").write_text("\n".join(lines))
    Path("cost_ledger.json").write_text(json.dumps(llm.snapshot(), indent=1))
    print("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:])
```

Running it with MockLLM's outputs priced at the placeholder rates in PRICES["gpt-4o-mini"]:

```python
$ python -m mgr_app.cost_report data/corpus out2 mock gpt-4o-mini
Corpus: 7,241 tokens, 24 text units. Indexing took 0.2s and cost $0.0241 ($3.33 per million corpus tokens).
| indexing stage | calls | input tokens | output tokens |
| continue | 24 | 26,503 | 2,738 |

| extraction | 24 | 16,007 | 9,541 |
```

The token counts are real counts of the prompts minigraphrag sends; only the outputs are fake. Even so, the shape is informative. Gleaning (continue) is the largest input consumer because each round resends the extraction prompt plus the first answer, the effect Chapter 8 warned about. Claims extraction is a third pass over every chunk; if no question in your set is temporal, IndexConfig(extract_claims=False) is the cheapest saving available. Check these conclusions against a real-model run before acting on them: real extraction outputs are longer and summaries run on more merged entities.

Projecting to a larger corpus: extraction, gleaning and claims scale linearly with the number of chunks; summarization scales with the number of entities and relationships that appear in more than one chunk; reports scale with communities. Estimate each from a 5% sample of your corpus rather than multiplying the Kestrel numbers.

#### Milestone C1.8 Your own corpus

Kestrel was written to reward graphs. Your corpus was not. Repeat M1 to M7 on documents you choose: product docs, meeting notes, a public-domain book, a set of RFCs, or a wiki export.

- Convert sources to Markdown with stable, readable file names; those names become doc ids in every citation.

- Choose entity types that match your questions and pass them in IndexConfig(entity_types=[...]).

- Write at least 40 questions with gold answers and supporting_docs: 10 single-hop, 10 multi-hop, 10 global and 10 of a type that matters for your domain.

- Index with a real LLM on a 10% sample first, read 20 random extracted relationships and fix the prompt before indexing everything.

- Run the evaluation and cost report and write the final report.

Checkpoints

- A spot-check of 20 relationships with a precision estimate (how many are supported by their source text).

- The evaluation table for your corpus, with the router frozen before you wrote the questions.

- A cost projection for ten times the corpus size.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # capstone1/mgr_app/prepare_corpus.py
"""Milestone 8: turn .txt, .html and .md files into the Markdown folder build_index expects."""
from __future__ import annotations

import html
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def html_to_text(raw: str) -> str:
    raw = re.sub(r"(?is)<(script|style|nav|footer|header)\b.*?</\1>", " ", raw)
    raw = re.sub(r"(?i)<h([1-3])[^>]*>", lambda m: "\n\n" + "#" * int(m.group(1)) + " ", raw)
    raw = re.sub(r"(?i)</(p|div|li|h[1-6]|tr)>|<br\s*/?>", "\n", raw)
    text = html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", raw))
    return re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", re.sub(r"\n\s*\n+", "\n\n", text)).strip()


def prepare(src: str, dst: str, min_words: int = 50) -> None:
    out = Path(dst)
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    kept = skipped = 0
    for path in sorted(Path(src).rglob("*")):
        if path.suffix.lower() not in {".md", ".txt", ".html", ".htm"}:
            continue
        raw = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        text = html_to_text(raw) if path.suffix.lower() in {".html", ".htm"} else raw
        if len(text.split()) < min_words:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        # The file stem becomes the doc_id used in every citation, so make it stable and readable.
        stem = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "_", str(path.relative_to(src).with_suffix("")).lower()).strip("_")
        (out / f"{stem}.md").write_text(f"# {path.stem}\n\n{text}\n", encoding="utf-8")
        kept += 1
    print(f"wrote {kept} documents to {out} (skipped {skipped} shorter than {min_words} words)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    prepare(*sys.argv[1:3])
```

The evaluator reads data/questions.jsonl; point it at your file (copy it there or add a path argument). For entity types, start from your 40 questions: underline every noun phrase a question asks about, group them, and keep five to eight types. A corpus of meeting notes might use PERSON, TEAM, PROJECT, DECISION, RISK, SYSTEM.

What to expect, and to report honestly: on corpora without many cross-document relationships, local and PPR search often tie with basic search on multi-hop questions, while global search still tends to win on themes and summaries. If that is what you find, the useful conclusion is a routing policy (basic by default, global for sensemaking), and the cost report tells you whether the index is worth building for global questions alone. A result where the graph does not help, measured carefully, passes this capstone.

## Evaluation rubric

Area | Weight | Meets expectations | Exceeds expectations

Indexing | 10% | Kestrel and own corpus indexed through a cache; artifacts inspected | Relationship precision spot-check with prompt changes justified by it

Retrieval service | 15% | Five methods and auto behind POST /query; health endpoint | Dynamic global search and DRIFT added and evaluated

Streaming and citations | 15% | SSE events in order; citations resolve to doc spans; tests pass | Real token streaming; unresolved-marker rate reported per method

Router | 10% | Rules plus LLM fallback; accuracy on labelled questions | Accuracy on a held-out set written after freezing; cost-aware routing

Evaluation | 25% | Recall, F1 and order-swapped win rates by type with intervals; separate judge model | 30+ questions per type; answer length reported; judge calibrated against 20 human labels

Cost report | 15% | Indexing by stage and per-query cost and latency by method | Projection to 10× corpus with a sample-based estimate; one cost reduction implemented and measured

Written report | 10% | Claims match the numbers; limitations stated | A clear routing recommendation with its evidence and cost

## Stretch goals

- Real token streaming. Add a stream() method to an OpenAI-compatible client and stream the reduce step of global search.

- Cost-aware routing. Give the router a budget per request and fall back from global to hybrid when the estimated map calls exceed it; measure the quality lost.

- DRIFT and dynamic selection. Add drift_search and global_search(dynamic=True) as methods, and report how many map calls dynamic selection saves on your corpus.

- Incremental indexing. Add a document, rebuild through the cache, and report how many provider calls the rebuild needed compared with a cold build (the update pattern from Chapter 27, applied to your own index).

- A small UI. A single HTML page that consumes the event stream and highlights cited spans in the source document.

- Judge calibration. Label 20 pairs yourself, measure agreement with the LLM judge, and report it next to the win rates.

## Check your understanding

Why does the reference put MeteredLLM inside CachedLLM rather than outside it?

- The cache needs token counts to build its keys

- ✓ (correct) So the ledger counts only calls that reach the provider, which is what you pay for

- So that cached responses are re-metered on every run for accuracy

- MeteredLLM cannot wrap objects that have a hits attribute
Answer: Wrapped outside the cache, the meter would count cache hits as spend, and a re-run would appear to cost as much as the first run.

Global search shows context recall 1.00 on global questions while basic search shows 0.37. What is the right conclusion?

- Global search is proven better on global questions

- Basic search has a bug

- ✓ (correct) Recall is inflated for global search because its sources include documents behind every community used, so judge the answers pairwise instead

- Context recall should be replaced by exact match
Answer: Retrieving nearly everything guarantees recall. For sensemaking questions, compare answers with order-swapped pairwise judging and report the interval.

The router scores 22/23 on the labelled questions after its cue lists were extended based on its misses. Which number belongs in the report?

- 22/23, because it is the latest measurement

- The score from before the cue lists were extended

- The average of the two

- ✓ (correct) Accuracy on new questions written after the rules were frozen, alongside 22/23 labelled as a training score
Answer: Rules tuned on the evaluation questions overfit them. Held-out accuracy estimates how the router will behave on real traffic.

In the stream, why does the route event come before generation even though the reference streams the finished answer in chunks?

- SSE requires the first event to be metadata

- ✓ (correct) The router decides in milliseconds, so the client can show progress and the chosen method while slow retrieval and generation run

- FastAPI sends events in alphabetical order

- The route determines the HTTP status code
Answer: Perceived latency depends on the time to first useful feedback. Route and sources arrive early; token events follow.

## Questions learners often ask

▸ Why FastAPI with SSE instead of WebSockets?

A question produces one stream of events in one direction, which is exactly what SSE is for. It is plain HTTP, works through most proxies, is trivial to test with curl -N, and browsers reconnect automatically with EventSource. Use WebSockets when the client needs to send messages mid-stream, for example to cancel or refine a query, as a chat agent might in Capstone 3.

▸ The judge prefers global search on almost everything, including single-hop questions. Is the judge broken?

Probably biased rather than broken. Comprehensiveness and diversity reward longer answers, and map-reduce produces longer answers. Check three things: that the order swap is on (inconsistent verdicts become ties), that both systems use the same response_type, and the mean answer length per method. If global still wins on single-hop questions on directness, look at the answers yourself; if it does not deserve to, calibrate the judge on 20 pairs you label by hand and report the agreement.

▸ Should the router use an LLM for every question?

Not by default. A routing call adds latency and cost to every request, while rules decide most questions correctly for free. Use the LLM only when rules do not fire, and log how often that happens. If the fallback rate is high on real traffic, collect those questions and either add rules or train a small classifier on logged, labelled routes.

▸ How do I serve an index that is rebuilt while the service is running?

Build into a new directory, then switch atomically: point a symlink such as out_current at the new folder and have the service reload on a signal or when a version file changes. Never rebuild in place under a running service; load_index reads several files and a half-written folder produces inconsistent ids between entities and embeddings.

▸ My corpus is private. Can I still use a hosted model for the judge?

The judge sees questions and answers, which contain your corpus's content, so the same data policy applies as for generation. If hosted models are not allowed, use a local model through get_llm("ollama") for both, pick the strongest local model you can run as the judge, and calibrate it against your own labels, since smaller judges are noisier.

## Key takeaways

- Keep the service thin: minigraphrag's search functions do retrieval; your code routes, cites, streams and measures.

- One answer() function used by the API, the evaluator and the cost report guarantees their numbers agree.

- Citations must resolve to documents and spans, and unresolved markers are a measurable hallucination signal.

- Evaluate by question type with order-swapped pairwise judging, intervals and a separate judge; context recall flatters global search.

- Meter inside the cache and attribute tokens to stages; gleaning and claims are often the largest avoidable indexing costs.

- An honest report that the graph does not help on your corpus, with numbers, is a successful capstone.

## Capstone 2: a codebase assistant on a code graph

URL: https://graphrag.xinbetween.com/chapters/c2-code-graph.html
Summary: Parse a repository into a symbol graph and answer questions about call chains and impact.

# Capstone 2: a codebase assistant on a code graph

Code is the one corpus where the graph comes for free: imports, calls and class hierarchies are already there, precisely, in the syntax tree. In this capstone you parse a real Python repository into a symbol graph and build an assistant that answers “what calls this?”, “what breaks if I change it?” and “how is this package organized?” with evidence it can cite by file and line.

## You will be able to

- Parse a Python package with ast into modules, classes, functions, methods and CALLS, IMPORTS, CONTAINS and INHERITS edges, with docstrings as text

- Answer structural questions with symbol lookup, call-chain paths and reverse-BFS impact analysis

- Summarize architecture with community detection and minigraphrag's report generator

- Load the graph into Neo4j and answer counting and listing questions with validated Text2Cypher

- Combine BM25 over identifiers, embeddings over docstrings and call-graph expansion with reciprocal rank fusion

- Evaluate the assistant on a golden set for a real repository and explain where static analysis misses edges

## Overview and architecture

Ask a vector RAG system over a repository “what breaks if I change fit_to_budget?” and it returns chunks that mention budgets. The answer you need is a set of functions reachable backwards through the call graph, most of which never mention budgets at all. That is a graph traversal, and Chapter 32 showed the two-pass parser that recovers the graph. This capstone turns it into an assistant with the same shape as the GraphRAG systems in the rest of the course: an index (the symbol graph plus text units), several retrievers, a router, cited answers and an evaluation harness.

[Diagram]

The symbol graph is the index. Each question type gets a deterministic tool; the LLM only writes the final answer from the facts and code snippets those tools return, and Text2Cypher is the one place the model writes a query.

### Which repository?

Use two. Develop against minigraphrag itself (code/minigraphrag): you know it well, so you can write gold answers quickly and notice wrong ones. Then evaluate on a small, well-known open-source package you did not write. requests is a good choice: about 18 modules, real class hierarchies, and a famous indirection (a session picks a transport adapter at run time) that exposes the limits of static call graphs. click, attrs or httpx work too. Pin the version you parse; call graphs change between releases.

[Interactive figure: Impact analysis is reverse BFS over CALLS — What breaks if context.fit_to_budget changes? All callers live in reports.py (graph-steps)]

## Requirements

### Functional

- Parse any pure-Python package directory into a networkx.MultiDiGraph with node kinds module, class, function and method, and edge keys CONTAINS, CALLS, IMPORTS and INHERITS. Each node keeps its path, line range, signature, docstring and source.

- Tools: lookup(name), call_chains(src, dst, k), impact(symbol, max_depth), architecture reports, Text2Cypher over Neo4j with validation, and hybrid search.

- An assistant that classifies each question, runs the right tool, falls back to hybrid search when a tool returns nothing, and answers with file:line citations.

### Evidence

- A golden set of at least 30 questions about your chosen repository, covering callers, impact, chains, locate-by-description and structural counts, with hand-checked gold symbol sets.

- Per-type precision and recall of retrieved symbols, validity of returned call chains, and routing accuracy.

- A written list of the false negatives with their cause (dynamic dispatch, local variables, callbacks, decorators).

### Constraints

- Parsing and every structural tool run without an LLM. The LLM writes Cypher and final answers only.

- Generated Cypher is validated with minigraphrag's validate_cypher before it reaches the database, and runs in a read transaction.

- Never execute the code you analyze.

## Milestones

#### Milestone C2.1 Parse the repository into a symbol graph

Build the index. Resolution is the hard part: count_tokens(text) in chunking.py must become an edge to minigraphrag.tokens.count_tokens, which requires knowing that chunking.py did from .tokens import count_tokens.

- Pass one: walk every .py file, compute its dotted module name, declare modules, classes, functions and methods (qualified ids such as minigraphrag.indexer.Index.report), and record each module's import table, resolving relative imports.

- Pass two: add IMPORTS edges between modules, INHERITS edges for base classes, and CALLS edges by resolving each call's dotted name through: self.method within a class, the import table, then the current module.

- Calling a class is a call to its constructor: resolve to the class node (or __init__).

- Keep the source text of every symbol; docstrings plus signatures are the text units for search.

```python  # codegraph/parse.py (starter)
import ast
from pathlib import Path

import networkx as nx


def parse_repo(package_dir) -> nx.MultiDiGraph:
    root = Path(package_dir).resolve()
    G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*.py")):
        tree = ast.parse(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        # TODO pass 1: module name, declarations, import table (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom with level)
    # TODO pass 2: IMPORTS, INHERITS, CALLS via name resolution
    return G
```

Checkpoints

- On minigraphrag, the callers of minigraphrag.tokens.count_tokens match what grep -rn "count_tokens(" --include='*.py' finds, attributed to their enclosing functions (13 at the time of writing).

- build_index has CALLS edges to chunk_documents, extract_from_unit, resolve_entities, build_graph, hierarchical_communities and generate_all_reports.

- On requests, class HTTPAdapter has an INHERITS edge to BaseAdapter.

▸ Show reference solution

```python  # codegraph/parse.py
"""Parse a Python repository into a symbol graph with Python's own ast module."""
from __future__ import annotations

import ast
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import networkx as nx


@dataclass
class Symbol:
    id: str              # qualified name, e.g. minigraphrag.chunking.chunk_fixed
    kind: str            # module | class | function | method
    path: str
    lineno: int
    end_lineno: int
    signature: str = ""
    docstring: str = ""
    source: str = ""


@dataclass
class ModuleInfo:
    name: str
    tree: ast.Module
    imports: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)   # local alias -> qualified target


def module_name(root: Path, path: Path) -> str:
    rel = path.relative_to(root.parent).with_suffix("")
    parts = list(rel.parts)
    return ".".join(parts[:-1] if parts[-1] == "__init__" else parts)


def _resolve_relative(current: str, is_package: bool, level: int, target: str | None) -> str:
    base = current.split(".")
    base = base if is_package else base[:-1]
    if level > 1:
        base = base[: len(base) - (level - 1)]
    return ".".join(base + ([target] if target else []))


def _signature(node: ast.FunctionDef | ast.AsyncFunctionDef) -> str:
    return f"def {node.name}({ast.unparse(node.args)})" + (f" -> {ast.unparse(node.returns)}" if node.returns else "")


def parse_repo(package_dir: str | Path) -> nx.MultiDiGraph:
    root = Path(package_dir).resolve()
    G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
    modules: dict[str, ModuleInfo] = {}

    # Pass 1: declare every module, class, function and method, and record imports.
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*.py")):
        name = module_name(root, path)
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        tree = ast.parse(text, filename=str(path))
        info = modules[name] = ModuleInfo(name, tree)
        G.add_node(name, **vars(Symbol(name, "module", str(path), 1, len(text.splitlines()),
                                       docstring=ast.get_docstring(tree) or "")))
        for node in ast.walk(tree):
            if isinstance(node, ast.Import):
                for a in node.names:
                    info.imports[a.asname or a.name.split(".")[0]] = a.name if a.asname else a.name.split(".")[0]
            elif isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom):
                src = _resolve_relative(name, path.name == "__init__.py", node.level, node.module) if node.level else node.module
                for a in node.names:
                    info.imports[a.asname or a.name] = f"{src}.{a.name}"
        for node in tree.body:
            _declare(G, node, name, "module", str(path), text)

    # Pass 2: IMPORTS edges, then CALLS and INHERITS edges resolved through each module's names.
    for name, info in modules.items():
        for target in set(info.imports.values()):
            mod = target if target in modules else target.rsplit(".", 1)[0]
            if mod in modules and mod != name:
                G.add_edge(name, mod, key="IMPORTS", type="IMPORTS")
        for node in ast.walk(info.tree):
            if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
                cls = f"{name}.{node.name}"
                for base in node.bases:
                    target = _resolve(G, info, ast.unparse(base), None)
                    if target:
                        G.add_edge(cls, target, key="INHERITS", type="INHERITS")
                for item in node.body:
                    if isinstance(item, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
                        _add_calls(G, info, f"{cls}.{item.name}", item, cls)
            elif isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)) and f"{name}.{node.name}" in G:
                if G.nodes[f"{name}.{node.name}"]["kind"] == "function":
                    _add_calls(G, info, f"{name}.{node.name}", node, None)
    return G


def _declare(G, node, parent: str, parent_kind: str, path: str, text: str) -> None:
    lines = text.splitlines()
    if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
        qid, kind, sig = f"{parent}.{node.name}", "class", f"class {node.name}"
    elif isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
        qid, kind, sig = f"{parent}.{node.name}", "method" if parent_kind == "class" else "function", _signature(node)
    else:
        return
    source = "\n".join(lines[node.lineno - 1: node.end_lineno])
    G.add_node(qid, **vars(Symbol(qid, kind, path, node.lineno, node.end_lineno, sig,
                                  ast.get_docstring(node) or "", source)))
    G.add_edge(parent, qid, key="CONTAINS", type="CONTAINS")
    if kind == "class":
        for item in node.body:
            _declare(G, item, qid, "class", path, text)


def _resolve(G, info: ModuleInfo, dotted: str, cls: str | None) -> str | None:
    """Map a name used in module `info` to a declared symbol id, or None if it is external."""
    head, _, rest = dotted.partition(".")
    candidates = []
    if head == "self" and cls and rest:
        candidates.append(f"{cls}.{rest}")
    if head in info.imports:
        candidates.append(info.imports[head] + (f".{rest}" if rest else ""))
    candidates.append(f"{info.name}.{dotted}")
    for c in candidates:
        if c in G:
            return c
        if c.endswith("__init__") is False and f"{c}.__init__" in G:
            return f"{c}.__init__"   # calling a class runs its constructor
    return None


def _add_calls(G, info: ModuleInfo, caller: str, fn, cls: str | None) -> None:
    for node in ast.walk(fn):
        if isinstance(node, ast.Call):
            try:
                dotted = ast.unparse(node.func)
            except Exception:
                continue
            target = _resolve(G, info, dotted, cls)
            if target and target != caller:
                G.add_edge(caller, target, key="CALLS", type="CALLS", lineno=node.lineno)
```

Counts at the time of writing: minigraphrag parses to about 220 nodes and 510 edges; requests 2.32.3 to 292 nodes (18 modules, 44 classes, 72 functions, 158 methods) and 568 edges (274 CONTAINS, 207 CALLS, 55 IMPORTS, 32 INHERITS). Your numbers will differ with versions.

Two simplifications to know about. Nested functions are not declared, so calls inside them are attributed to the enclosing function (which is what you want for impact analysis). And ast.walk over a method includes calls in nested lambdas and comprehensions, also attributed to the method.

#### Milestone C2.2 Lookup, call chains and impact

Three deterministic tools cover most developer questions about structure.

- lookup(name): exact qualified id, then suffix match (report matches Index.report), then fuzzy match on short names for typos.

- edge_view(G, *types): a simple DiGraph with only the requested edge types, so traversals do not wander through CONTAINS or IMPORTS.

- call_chains(src, dst, k): the k shortest simple paths over CALLS with nx.shortest_simple_paths.

- impact(symbol, max_depth): BFS over reversed CALLS and INHERITS edges, grouped by distance.
